intro.heading: A new course with no revision industry behind it yet
paragraphs: Digital Society is the newest subject in this group and the only one where the usual revision machinery does not exist. It replaced Information Technology in a Global Society, was first taught from September 2024, and was first examined in May 2026. That means a Dubai student sitting it in the next two sessions has almost no past papers to work from, few published mark schemes with worked examples, a small bank of exemplar inquiry projects, and commercial revision material that is either absent or quietly adapted from the retired ITGS course it replaced.

Every one of those gaps changes how the subject should be taught. Revision by past paper is the default method across the Diploma, and here it is largely unavailable. Students cannot calibrate their own answers against published exemplars because there are barely any. A revision guide written for ITGS teaches a different course with different content and a different internal assessment, and a student working from one will revise material this course does not examine. The honest version of tutoring in this subject starts by saying so.

What replaces the missing material is the assessment criteria themselves, read properly and used as the specification they are. A student who knows exactly what each component credits can calibrate their own work without an exemplar, because the criteria describe the standard directly. That is slower and less comfortable than working through a decade of past papers, and it is also the only method available. It has a side benefit: students who learn to read criteria carry that skill into every other subject they take.

The second thing a Dubai family should do is confirm the specifics with the school. Weightings, durations, the exact word limit on the inquiry project, and the arrangements for the Higher Level extension material are all set out in the current subject guide, and a new course is exactly the situation where third-hand figures go stale. Your IB coordinator can confirm all of it in one message, and any tutor worth paying will ask you for that message before planning anything. It takes five minutes and it prevents a revision plan built on a figure somebody read on a forum in 2024.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, scheduled around Dubai school hours in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to any UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India. In a subject this new that matters more than usual: tutors who have taught the current guide through a full cohort are rare everywhere, not just in this emirate, and restricting the search to people willing to drive to your community narrows a small pool to almost nothing. The first lesson is free and no package has to be bought first.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Digital Society exists only at Diploma level, and the useful question for younger students is which habits prepare them for it. IB Gram teaches the Diploma course, the Middle Years groundwork that makes it manageable, and the Career-related version where it sits alongside a career-related study.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Digital Society
programmes.description: An inquiry-led course built on interlinked concepts, content topics and real-world contexts, assessed through written papers and an internally assessed inquiry project, with Higher Level adding an extension on challenges and interventions. The inquiry project is the largest single component at Standard Level, which makes it the first thing a tutoring plan should address rather than the last.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai is an unusually good place to study this course and an awkward place to find a tutor for it. The emirate runs large-scale digital government, smart-city and AI initiatives that give students genuine local material for an inquiry, but the subject is new and few Dubai schools have taken a full cohort through it. KHDA recorded 387,441 private-school students across 227 schools in 2024-25, with the IB at 7 per cent of enrolment, and Digital Society sits at the newest edge of that.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Design and Individuals and Societies
programmes.description: No Middle Years course is called Digital Society, and the preparation that matters is the ability to write about a technology's social effects without either praising or condemning it. Design projects build the technical vocabulary; Individuals and Societies builds the analytical frame. Students who have both arrive in DP1 able to do the one thing this course asks for.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students reach DP1 with strong digital fluency and almost no practice at analysing digital systems as social systems. They can explain how a recommendation engine works and struggle to write about who gains and who loses from it. A first session tends to show exactly that split, which is useful because it is the whole skill the subject examines.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme with Diploma Digital Society
programmes.description: Career-related students take Diploma courses alongside a career-related study, a reflective project and service learning. Digital Society pairs naturally with business, media and technology pathways, and the inquiry project can be planned so that it draws on the same sector as the career-related study without either piece of work overlapping into the other.
programmes.countryNote: A Career-related Digital Society candidate in Dubai may be the only one in the school, in a subject where there is no established body of exemplars to learn from either. That combination is the strongest argument for one-to-one teaching in this subject: there is no class, no bank of past submissions, and no commercial revision guide that fits.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Digital Society is organised around three interlinked dimensions rather than a list of units, which is why it confuses students who expect topics. These are the parts of the course IB Gram's tutors teach. Check your school's course outline, because this is a new guide and schools are still settling their sequence.

subjects.name: Content: data
subjects.description: How data is collected, structured, stored, shared and governed, and what happens when it is wrong, incomplete or taken without consent. The foundational topic for most of the rest of the course, and the one where students confuse a technical description with an analysis of consequences.

subjects.name: Content: algorithms
subjects.description: How algorithmic systems make decisions and recommendations, how bias enters them, and who is accountable for an output. Students explain the mechanism competently and stop short of the question the examination asks, which is about effects on people and institutions.

subjects.name: Content: computers
subjects.description: Computing systems, processing, storage and the physical infrastructure behind digital life. The least intuitive topic for students who have only used devices, and the one where a small amount of accurate technical grounding prevents vague answers elsewhere.

subjects.name: Content: networks and the internet
subjects.description: Connectivity, access, infrastructure, governance of the internet and the inequalities that follow from how networks are built and regulated. Access and the digital divide recur throughout the course and are examined in context rather than in the abstract.

subjects.name: Content: media
subjects.description: Digital media production, distribution, amplification and trust, including misinformation and the economics of attention. Rich material and a strong temptation to write opinion columns, which earn nothing without the course's concepts doing analytical work.

subjects.name: Content: artificial intelligence
subjects.description: Machine learning systems, their capabilities, limits and governance, and the social questions they raise about work, decision-making and accountability. Fast-moving, which makes dated examples a real risk and current, specific, sourced examples a real advantage.

subjects.name: Content: robots and autonomous technologies
subjects.description: Automation, autonomous systems and their effects on labour, safety, cities and responsibility. Dubai offers unusually concrete local examples here, from autonomous transport trials to logistics and service automation, which beat generic ones in any answer.

subjects.name: The seven concepts
subjects.description: Change, expression, identity, power, space, systems and values. These are the analytical tools of the course, not vocabulary to recite. An answer that names a concept and then does nothing with it has made the commonest mistake in the subject.

subjects.name: The real-world contexts
subjects.description: Cultural, economic, environmental, health, human knowledge, political and social. Every question lands in a context, and the same content topic produces a different answer in a health context than in a political one. Reading the context in the question is a markable skill.

subjects.name: The inquiry project
subjects.description: An internally assessed investigation into a real-world example involving digital society, written up within the word limit set in the current guide. The largest single component at Standard Level. Topic choice sets the ceiling, and a topic with no recent, sourceable material cannot be rescued by effort.

subjects.name: Higher Level extension: challenges and interventions
subjects.description: Higher Level students study global challenges in digital society and the interventions proposed to address them, examined in an additional paper. Confirm with your coordinator how the material for that paper is released for your cohort, because the arrangements matter for timing revision.

sections.heading: What exists for a two-year-old course, and what to use instead
paragraphs: The single most useful thing a parent can understand about Digital Society is that the normal study aids are not there yet. The course was first taught from September 2024 and first examined in May 2026, which means the archive every other Diploma subject is revised from has not had time to accumulate. A student who sits down in February to work through ten years of past papers will find almost nothing to work through, and will usually conclude that they are looking in the wrong place rather than that the papers do not exist.

The risk is not the absence itself but what fills it. Material adapted from the retired ITGS course circulates widely, sometimes relabelled, and it teaches different content against different criteria. A student revising from an ITGS-era guide will spend weeks on material this course does not examine and will arrive at the paper having practised the wrong task. Checking the provenance of any resource before using it is therefore a real part of studying this subject, which is not true of History or Geography.

What works instead is criteria-led preparation. The published assessment criteria describe the standard directly, so a student who reads them properly can calibrate their own work without an exemplar to compare against. Questions can be written from the criteria. Drafts can be scored against them. Mock answers can be marked against them. It is slower than past-paper drilling and it produces a student who understands what is being asked rather than one who has memorised a pattern.

The table below sets out the gap resource by resource, with what to substitute. Take it to your tutor in the first conversation and ask which substitutes they actually use. A tutor who claims a large bank of Digital Society past papers is describing something that does not exist, and that answer tells you more about them than any credential.

sections.heading: Concepts, content and contexts: how the course is actually built
paragraphs: Students who expect a list of units find this course disorienting, because it is organised as three interlinked dimensions rather than as topics to be covered in order. The concepts are the analytical tools: change, expression, identity, power, space, systems and values. The content topics are the subject matter: data, algorithms, computers, networks and the internet, media, artificial intelligence, and robots and autonomous technologies. The contexts are where questions land: cultural, economic, environmental, health, human knowledge, political and social.

Any examination question combines all three, and that combination is what students miss. A question about algorithms in a health context is not the same question as one about algorithms in a political context, even though the technical content is identical. The content supplies the facts, the concept supplies the analytical move, and the context decides which effects matter and to whom. A student who reads only the content topic in a question will write an answer that is accurate and misdirected.

The repair is a reading routine, practised until it is automatic. Identify the content topic. Identify the context. Identify which concept the question is really about. Then plan an answer that uses the concept to analyse the content inside that context. Thirty seconds of that discipline changes the shape of an answer more than any amount of extra content knowledge, which is the same lesson every subject in this group teaches and is especially stark here.

Confirm the exact lists with your school, because this is a new guide and schools are still settling how they sequence it. The table below is the working map a student should have on their wall, and the final row is the one to take to your coordinator.

sections.heading: The inquiry project: the biggest component and the earliest decision
paragraphs: The inquiry project is an internally assessed investigation into a real-world example involving digital society, written up within the word limit the current guide sets, which schools generally run as a maximum of 3,000 words. Confirm that figure with your coordinator. It is the largest single component at Standard Level, which should make it the first thing a tutoring plan addresses. In practice it is usually the last, because it has no exam date attached and therefore no urgency until it suddenly has too much.

Topic choice sets the ceiling and cannot be fixed later. Three things make a topic work: a real-world example specific enough to investigate rather than a theme, recent and citable material that genuinely exists and can be reached, and a question that the course's concepts can actually analyse. A project on artificial intelligence in general fails the first test. A project on a technology with no published material fails the second. A project on how something technically works fails the third, because there is nothing for a concept to do.

The word budget is the second decision, and it is made at the planning stage or not at all. Description of the example earns the least and expands the fastest. The marks sit in the investigation, the analysis through the concepts, and the evaluation. Students write a thousand words of background on a company or a system, then compress the analysis into the final pages and run out of room for evaluation entirely. Planning the split before drafting prevents a problem that cannot be solved by editing.

Dubai gives students a genuine advantage here that most do not use. The emirate publishes a great deal about digital government, smart-city programmes, autonomous transport trials and artificial intelligence strategy, which means a locally grounded inquiry can be built on primary and recent material rather than on a global case study every examiner has read. A tutor can help test a topic, teach the method and read one draft against the criteria. The project itself has to be the student's own work from first word to last.

sections.heading: The Higher Level extension: writing about interventions properly
paragraphs: Higher Level students study global challenges in digital society and the interventions proposed to address them, examined in an additional paper. Confirm with your IB coordinator how the material for that paper is released for your cohort, because the arrangements affect when revision should happen and a new course is exactly where second-hand information goes out of date.

What makes the extension distinctive is that it asks for evaluation of an intervention, which is a different skill from analysing a technology. An intervention has an intention, a design, an implementation and an effect, and those four things routinely diverge. A student who can separate what a measure was meant to do from what it actually did, identify who gained and who bore the cost, and then state the criteria by which they are judging it, has performed the task. A student who writes that an intervention was a good idea has not.

That makes a repeatable structure the most valuable thing a Higher Level student can own here. What was the challenge, stated precisely and with evidence of its scale. What intervention was proposed, by whom, and with what stated aim. What happened in implementation, including what resisted it. Who was affected and unevenly how. And on what criteria it should be judged, named explicitly rather than assumed. Five moves, applied to any intervention, produce a competent answer under time pressure.

Timing matters more than usual because this content comes last in most schemes of work and the paper rehearses a skill nothing else rehearses. Timed practice from early in DP2, using challenges already covered, is worth more than detailed knowledge acquired in the final weeks. It is the same conclusion every component of this course points at: in the absence of a past-paper archive, deliberate practice against the criteria is the method.
bullets: Separate what an intervention intended from what it actually achieved
Name the criteria you are judging it by rather than implying them

sections.heading: Why technically confident students underperform in this subject
paragraphs: The most common profile in a Dubai Digital Society group is a student who is genuinely good with technology and scores in the middle. They can explain how a recommendation system is trained, what a data pipeline does, and why a network behaves as it does. The examination does not reward that beyond accuracy. It rewards using a concept to analyse the social consequences of the technology inside a named context, and the technical explanation is the groundwork rather than the answer.

The mirror-image failure is just as common. A student with strong opinions about technology writes a confident piece of commentary with no accurate content underneath it and no concept doing analytical work. Both profiles land in the same mark band for opposite reasons, and both are visible in a single marked answer. The subject sits precisely between the two, which is why it suits neither a pure Computer Science student nor a pure essayist without adjustment.

A third pattern is specific to this course's subject matter: examples go stale fast. Artificial intelligence and media move quickly, and an answer built on an example from four years ago reads as dated to an examiner who has watched the field change. Students need a small bank of current, specific, sourced examples refreshed through the two years, rather than a long list learned once in DP1. Three or four live examples per content topic, with dates and sources, is the working standard.

Sessions work on all three by marking the student's own writing and naming which of the three patterns it shows. The repair for each is different: more precise content for one, concept discipline for another, and example maintenance for the third. Treating them as one general weakness called 'needs to improve analysis' is what report cards do, and it is not actionable.

sections.heading: Evidence of progress when there is no past-paper archive
paragraphs: Parents paying for tutoring in a new subject are in an awkward position: there is no familiar benchmark, and the usual proof of progress is a rising past-paper score. That proof is unavailable, so the evidence has to be built deliberately instead. Everything in the pack below can be produced inside a tutoring relationship without a single past paper, and all of it is readable by a parent who does not know the subject.

The distinctive item is the criterion-scored answer. A question written from the assessment criteria, answered under time, and then scored against those criteria with the reasoning shown, gives a comparable mark week after week. The absolute number matters less than the trend and the reasons attached to it. Over six weeks a flat trend with the same reason repeating means the feedback is not being acted on, and that is a conversation worth having early.

The example bank is the second item and the easiest for a parent to check. Ask to see it. Three or four current, dated, sourced examples per content topic is the working standard, and a bank that has not grown in a month is a sign that sessions are producing discussion rather than preparation. The inquiry project score by criterion is the third, and it is the most consequential, because that component carries more weight at Standard Level than anything else.

None of this requires a parent to understand algorithms or data governance. It requires a tutor who writes things down and shows them to you. In a subject where nobody can point to a past-paper percentile, written records are the only honest answer to the question of whether the money is doing anything.

sections.heading: Digital Society is not Computer Science, and the name misleads
paragraphs: A Dubai Year 11 student choosing options needs this stated plainly, because the title attracts the wrong students and repels the right ones. Digital Society is not a programming course. There is no requirement to write code, build software or solve computational problems, and a student who wants those should be looking at Computer Science. Equally, it is not a soft option for students who dislike technical material: accurate content about data, algorithms, computing systems and networks underpins every answer, and vague answers about technology score badly.

The course sits between the technical and the social, and it suits a particular kind of student: one who is comfortable with how systems work and interested in what they do to people and institutions. That student is well served and often overlooked, because the Diploma's subject groups historically forced a choice between the two. Digital Society is also a reasonable route for a student who wants a technology-facing subject without the mathematical load that Computer Science carries at Higher Level.

The comparison with Business Management is worth making too, since both touch digital transformation. Business Management examines organisations and decisions through business tools. Digital Society examines digital systems through concepts like power, identity and values across named contexts. A student interested in the effects of technology on society should take the latter; a student interested in how firms operate should take the former. Taking both is possible and the overlap is smaller than it looks.

The practical advice for a Dubai family at option-choice stage is to ask the school three questions: who is teaching it and what have they taught before, how many cohorts the school has put through the course, and whether there are submitted inquiry projects a student could look at. The answers decide how much external support a student is likely to want, and asking them in Year 11 is considerably cheaper than discovering them in DP2.

sections.heading: Honesty with AI tools in a course about AI, plus the permit question
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject now has an academic-honesty conversation about generative tools. In this one it is the subject matter, which gives it an edge other courses lack: a student who has studied how these systems work, where their outputs come from and who is accountable for them cannot plausibly claim not to have understood the rules. The line is the same as everywhere else. A student may use these tools to find reading, to check their own grammar, or as an object of study. A student may not use them to produce sentences that go into an assessed piece.

For the inquiry project this needs handling explicitly, because the project may legitimately involve examining an artificial intelligence system as its real-world example. Studying a tool is not using it to write. Keeping a short log of where material came from, including any use of such tools in the research process, makes the authorship of the work straightforward to evidence rather than something to be anxious about. Dubai schools are increasingly asking for exactly that.

The tutoring boundary is unchanged by any of it. A tutor may teach the content and the concepts, write practice questions from the criteria, explain what each criterion credits, discuss a topic the student has chosen, and read one draft and give written feedback. A tutor may not supply paragraphs, provide analysis or hand over anything for submission. Published IB material and specimen papers are cited and linked at source rather than reproduced, which is both a copyright matter and, for unreleased material, a malpractice exposure.

One regulatory point every Dubai parent should know and almost none are told: private tutoring in the UAE requires the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and granted free of charge for two years, with MoHRE's own service page listing no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Dubai's private schools are overseen by KHDA; Abu Dhabi and Al Ain by ADEK; Sharjah by SPEA; Ras Al Khaimah by its Department of Knowledge; and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah by the federal Ministry of Education. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or endorsement from any of those bodies, nor from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and occupies no office in the UAE.

sections.heading: What a Digital Society tutor costs in the Dubai market
paragraphs: Rates read from Dubai providers' own published pages in October 2026 put shared online sessions between about AED 33 and AED 150 an hour, qualified subject tutors at AED 150 to AED 300, in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to AED 500, and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with one named premium tutor advertising AED 650. Monthly packages appear at AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. None of those are IB Gram prices; IB Gram quotes per match in AED per 60 minutes after a free trial lesson.

Digital Society has a supply problem rather than a prestige premium. The course is two years old, so nobody anywhere has taught many cohorts of it, and a tutor claiming long experience of it is describing something that is not yet possible. The useful question is narrower: have you taught the current guide, how many inquiry projects have you supported through to submission, and which parts of the course have you not taught. A tutor who answers the third question honestly is worth more than one who answers the first two expansively.

The in-home premium is harder to justify in this subject than in most. Teaching here involves screen-shared sources, data sets, the student's own draft and the criteria side by side, which works better over a shared screen than across a table. Paying AED 180 to AED 500 for a visit when the better medium costs less is a choice worth making deliberately rather than by default, and the travel component of that rate buys nothing a Digital Society session needs.

Three questions separate a useful quote from a vague one, and they are the same three that apply across this market: is the rate per 60 minutes or per session, is marking between sessions included or billed on top, and what happens if the match does not work. Three of the six most visible pages in this search publish no price at all and two quote in US dollars, so a provider willing to answer all three in AED before the first lesson is already behaving better than the field.

process.title: Get the specifics from your coordinator first
process.description: On a course this new, ask the school in writing for the component weightings, durations, the inquiry project word limit and how the Higher Level extension material is released. One message covers it. Any tutor planning revision without those figures is working from something they read rather than something your child sits.

process.title: Send one marked answer and the course outline
process.description: The outline shows the school's sequence, which is still settling across Dubai. A marked answer shows which of the three failure patterns your child has: technical description without analysis, opinion without content, or dated examples. The trial lesson then starts on that rather than on diagnosis.

process.title: Ask the tutor what they have not taught
process.description: Nobody has many cohorts of a two-year-old course. A tutor who says which components they have taken through to a submission and which they have not is giving you information you can act on. One who claims a large past-paper bank for Digital Society is describing a resource that does not exist.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: One full session at no cost, no card, no package. Watch for whether the tutor works from the published criteria and marks your child's own writing against them. In a subject with no exemplar archive, criteria-led teaching is not a style preference, it is the only method available.

process.title: Review the evidence pack every six weeks
process.description: Criterion-scored timed answers, the concept-use check, the current example bank, and the inquiry project score by criterion. If the same reason keeps appearing in the feedback after six weeks, the plan or the tutor changes, and that conversation is scheduled rather than left to you to raise.

whyPoints.title: The new-course problem named, not hidden
whyPoints.description: Digital Society was first examined in May 2026, so past papers, mark schemes and exemplars are scarce and some circulating material is adapted from the retired ITGS course. Sessions start from the published criteria and say plainly which resources do not exist, because a student revising from an ITGS guide practises the wrong task.

whyPoints.title: Criteria-led rather than pattern-led
whyPoints.description: With no archive to drill, the assessment criteria are the specification. Questions are written from them, answers scored against them, and the standard explained rather than assumed. Students who learn to read criteria carry that skill into every other Diploma subject they take.

whyPoints.title: The inquiry project treated as the big component
whyPoints.description: It is the largest single component at Standard Level and is usually left last because it has no exam date. Topic choice sets its ceiling, so three candidates are tested for recent, citable, reachable material before any writing, and Dubai's published digital-government and smart-city material gives local inquiries an advantage.

whyPoints.title: Examples kept current
whyPoints.description: Artificial intelligence and media move faster than any syllabus, and an answer built on a four-year-old example reads as dated. The example bank carries three or four live, dated, sourced items per content topic and is refreshed through DP2 rather than learned once in DP1.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what a tutor has taught
whyPoints.description: Nobody has long experience of a two-year-old course, and claims to the contrary are a warning rather than a credential. IB Gram tutors state which components they have taken through to a submission and which they have not, before you book anything.

whyPoints.title: Online, which suits this subject best anyway
whyPoints.description: Sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with sources, data sets, the student's draft and the criteria shared on screen. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; that service exists only in India, and the travel premium would buy nothing this subject needs.

faqs.question: Is IB Digital Society a brand-new subject, and does that affect my child?
faqs.answer: It replaced Information Technology in a Global Society, was first taught from September 2024 and first examined in May 2026. The practical effect is that the archive every other Diploma subject is revised from has not accumulated yet: few past papers, thin mark schemes with worked examples, a small bank of exemplar inquiry projects, and commercial revision material that is sometimes adapted from the retired ITGS course. A student revising from an ITGS-era guide practises the wrong task against the wrong criteria. Checking the provenance of any resource is a genuine part of studying this subject.

faqs.question: How can my child revise Digital Society without past papers?
faqs.answer: Through the published assessment criteria, used as the specification they are. The criteria describe the standard directly, so a student can write questions from them, answer under time, and score their own work against them without needing an exemplar to compare with. Specimen material supplied through the school and school-written mocks fill some of the gap. It is slower than past-paper drilling and it produces a student who understands the task rather than one who has memorised a pattern. Ask any tutor which substitutes they actually use.

faqs.question: What are the seven concepts in Digital Society?
faqs.answer: Change, expression, identity, power, space, systems and values. They are the analytical tools of the course rather than vocabulary to recite, and the commonest mistake in the subject is naming one in the introduction and then never using it. Every examination question combines a concept with a content topic and a real-world context, so an answer that identifies the content and ignores the concept will be accurate and misdirected. Confirm the exact list against your school's course outline, since this is a new guide and schools are still settling their sequence.

faqs.question: Why does the context in a Digital Society question matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because the same content topic produces a different answer depending on where the question lands. Algorithms in a health context raise different questions about who is affected, and how, than algorithms in a political or economic context. The contexts in the course are cultural, economic, environmental, health, human knowledge, political and social. Reading the context is a markable skill, and the reading routine is quick: identify the content topic, identify the context, identify which concept the question is really about, then plan an answer that uses the concept inside that context.

faqs.question: How long is the Digital Society inquiry project and what is it worth?
faqs.answer: It is an internally assessed investigation into a real-world example involving digital society, written up within the word limit the current guide sets, which schools generally run as a maximum of 3,000 words. Confirm the figure and the weighting with your IB coordinator, because this is a new course. It is the largest single component at Standard Level, which should make it the first thing a study plan addresses. In practice it is usually last, because it has no exam date and therefore no urgency until it has far too much.

faqs.question: What makes a good inquiry project topic for a student in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Three things. A real-world example specific enough to investigate rather than a broad theme. Recent, citable material that genuinely exists and can be reached. And a question the course's concepts can actually analyse, which rules out projects that only explain how something works. Dubai is unusually well supplied here: the emirate publishes extensively on digital government, smart-city programmes, autonomous transport trials and artificial intelligence strategy, so a locally grounded inquiry can rest on recent primary material rather than a global case study every examiner has already read.

faqs.question: My child is technically confident but keeps scoring in the middle. Why?
faqs.answer: Because technical explanation is the groundwork rather than the answer. The examination rewards using a concept to analyse the social consequences of a technology inside a named context, and a student who explains how a recommendation system is trained has supplied the facts without performing the analysis. The mirror-image failure is a confident opinion piece with no accurate content and no concept doing work. Both land in the same band for opposite reasons, and both are visible in a single marked answer, which is why diagnosis comes before any content coverage.

faqs.question: Do Digital Society examples go out of date?
faqs.answer: Faster than in any other Diploma subject. Artificial intelligence and digital media move quickly, and an answer built on an example from four years ago reads as dated to an examiner who has watched the field change. The working standard is three or four current, specific, sourced examples per content topic, refreshed through DP2 rather than learned once in DP1 and left alone. Students who maintain that bank write with more precision and less hedging, because they have something concrete to point at rather than a general impression of a trend.

faqs.question: What is the Higher Level extension in Digital Society?
faqs.answer: Higher Level students study global challenges in digital society and the interventions proposed to address them, examined in an additional paper. Ask your IB coordinator how that paper's material is released for your child's cohort, since the arrangements affect revision timing and second-hand information on a new course goes stale. The skill it tests is evaluation of an intervention, which differs from analysing a technology: an intervention has an intention, a design, an implementation and an effect, and those four routinely diverge.

faqs.question: How should a Higher Level answer about an intervention be structured?
faqs.answer: Five moves, applied to anything. State the challenge precisely, with evidence of its scale. Identify the intervention, who proposed it and what it was meant to achieve. Describe what happened in implementation, including what resisted it. Identify who gained, who bore the cost, and how unevenly. Then name the criteria by which you are judging it rather than implying them. A student who can produce that structure cold, to time, on an unfamiliar intervention is prepared for the paper, and that is practised from early in DP2 rather than in the final term.

faqs.question: Is Digital Society the same as Computer Science?
faqs.answer: No, and the name misleads in both directions. There is no requirement to write code, build software or solve computational problems; a student who wants those should take Computer Science. Equally it is not a soft option, because accurate content about data, algorithms, computing systems and networks underpins every answer and vague writing about technology scores badly. The course suits a student who is comfortable with how systems work and interested in what they do to people and institutions, which is a combination the Diploma's subject groups historically forced students to choose between.

faqs.question: Should my child take Digital Society or Business Management?
faqs.answer: They overlap less than they appear to. Business Management examines organisations and decisions using business tools and frameworks. Digital Society examines digital systems through concepts such as power, identity and values across named real-world contexts. A student interested in the effects of technology on society should take the latter; one interested in how firms operate and compete should take the former. Taking both is entirely possible. At option-choice stage, ask the school who teaches each subject, how many cohorts it has run, and whether submitted coursework is available to look at.

faqs.question: Can my child use AI tools while studying a course about AI?
faqs.answer: Studying such a system is legitimate and may be exactly what an inquiry project examines. Using one to produce sentences that go into an assessed piece is not. A student may use these tools to find reading or to check their own grammar, and may analyse them as an object of study. Keeping a short log of where material came from, including any use of such tools in research, makes authorship straightforward to evidence rather than something to worry about. Dubai schools increasingly ask for that record, and it takes a couple of minutes a week.

faqs.question: How do I judge a Digital Society tutor when the course is this new?
faqs.answer: Ask three narrow questions. Have you taught the current guide. How many inquiry projects have you supported through to submission. And which parts of the course have you not taught. The third answer is the most informative, because nobody anywhere has many cohorts of a two-year-old course and a tutor claiming long experience of it is describing something that is not yet possible. A tutor who also claims a large bank of Digital Society past papers is describing a resource that does not exist, which tells you more than any credential.

faqs.question: What does Digital Society tutoring cost in Dubai, and is online cheaper?
faqs.answer: Figures read from Dubai providers' own pages in October 2026: shared online sessions from about AED 33 to AED 150 an hour, qualified subject tutors AED 150 to AED 300, in-home visits AED 180 to AED 500, IB specialists AED 200 to AED 450 and above. Online is both cheaper and better suited here, because teaching involves screen-shared sources, data sets, the student's draft and the criteria side by side. The travel component of an in-home rate buys nothing this subject needs. IB Gram quotes per match in AED per 60 minutes after a free trial.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-home-tutor.closingHeading: Ask your coordinator two questions, then send us the answers
dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-home-tutor.closingBody: Message your IB coordinator for the component weightings, durations and the inquiry project word limit for your child's cohort, and for how the Higher Level extension material is released if they are at Higher Level. Send those answers with the school's course outline, one marked piece of writing, and the hours that work in Gulf Standard Time. What comes back is a proposed tutor who will tell you which components they have taken through to a submission, a rate in AED per 60 minutes with marking stated as included, and a free trial lesson with no card and no package attached.

intro.heading: A young course, taught thinly, with almost no reliable revision material
paragraphs: Digital Society is the newest subject in Group 3 and it behaves like one. It replaced Information Technology in a Global Society, which means that a large share of what a Dubai parent finds when they search is ITGS material: old papers, old mark schemes, revision sites written for a course with different components and a different internal assessment. A student revising from that is not revising badly, they are revising for a different examination, and the first job of any competent support is to clear it out.

The second difficulty is staffing. Most schools teaching this course assigned it to someone whose background is Computer Science, Business Management, Geography or ITGS, because almost nobody trained in it. Those teachers are frequently excellent and are also learning the guide at the same pace as their students. The consequence is not weak teaching; it is thin individual feedback, especially on the inquiry project, where a department running one teacher across two year groups simply cannot read every draft twice.

The third thing families underestimate is how little of the grade is recall. Digital Society is built from three interacting parts: concepts that frame any question, content about digital systems and data, and contexts in which those systems operate. The papers hand students source material and ask them to analyse it using that framework, supported by real-world examples they have researched themselves. A student who has memorised definitions and has no examples will write fluent, empty answers.

An IB DP digital society online tutor in Dubai therefore spends most sessions on two things: building an examples file that is current, sourced and tied to named concepts, and supervising the inquiry project so that it asks a question the student can actually investigate. Neither is glamorous and both are measurable. A student with twelve dated, sourced examples across the contexts is a different candidate from one with four vague ones, and the difference shows in a single marked answer. Both jobs also accumulate, which is why the hours are worth far more in DP1 than in the term before the papers.

Delivery for families in the Emirates is live, one-to-one and over video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. Home visits are not something IB Gram sells anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. For this subject the online model is not a compromise but the only realistic route to a match, because the number of people who have taught the current Digital Society guide to examination is small, and the chance that one of them lives twenty minutes from your district is smaller still. Restricting the search by driving distance in a subject this new is how a family ends up with a competent Geography teacher aiming at the wrong assessment.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Dubai students reach Digital Society from unusually varied places: MYP Design, MYP Individuals and Societies, IGCSE Computer Science, IGCSE Business, or nothing related at all. That variety is one reason classes in this subject are hard to teach as a group and respond well to one-to-one work. Here is what each IB stage contributes.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Digital Society sits in Group 3, Individuals and Societies, alongside History, Economics, Geography and Psychology. Candidates study a framework of concepts, digital content and real-world contexts, sit source-based written papers, and complete an internally assessed inquiry project. Higher Level candidates take an additional extension on challenges and interventions, with its own assessment.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the subject is often timetabled against Computer Science or Business Management, which means a student may have to choose between the two rather than take both. Ask the school early whether Digital Society will run at Higher Level, because several Dubai schools offer it at Standard Level only, and that constrains anyone hoping to use it as a Higher Level social science.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Two MYP subjects feed this course. Design teaches the inquiry cycle, which is the nearest thing in the IB to the Digital Society inquiry process. Individuals and Societies teaches the critical-thinking criterion that the written papers depend on. Students who have done both arrive better prepared than those who have taken Computer Science alone.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's MYP schools vary in how much Design is taught in Years 10 and 11, with some reducing it to make room for IGCSE options. Where a student has had little Design, the inquiry process has to be taught from scratch in DP1, and that is one of the clearest, most predictable uses of paid hours in this subject.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP contributes research habits rather than content: forming a question, finding sources, recording where information came from. The exhibition in the final PYP year is a student's first supervised, documented investigation, and the skills it builds are the ones the Digital Society inquiry project assumes are already in place.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a large PYP sector, and students who move through PYP and MYP in the same school usually arrive at the inquiry project able to design an investigation. Those arriving from exam-led systems often cannot, because nothing in their prior schooling asked them to choose a question. That gap is worth diagnosing in the first term of DP1 rather than in DP2.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Career-related Programme students combine Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project and a personal and professional skills course. Digital Society fits well where the career-related study is in technology, media or business, because the contexts in the course map onto the workplace material the student is already covering.
programmes.countryNote: Very few Dubai schools run the Career-related Programme, so a CP student taking Digital Society is often the only candidate. The practical risk is overlap between the reflective project and the inquiry project: they must be separate pieces of work on separate questions, and a supervisor checking that in the first term prevents an uncomfortable conversation with the coordinator later.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Digital Society is not organised as a list of topics to be revised in sequence. It is a framework in which content is examined through concepts and situated in contexts, with the student's own researched examples as the evidence. Below is what a tutor works across, and what each part is actually assessed on.

subjects.name: Concepts: change, identity, power and values
subjects.description: The lenses every question is answered through. A paragraph that describes a technology without naming the concept at stake reads as commentary. Students who learn to open an answer by identifying which concept the source is really about score consistently higher than those who lead with the technology.

subjects.name: Concepts: space, systems and expression
subjects.description: The structural half of the conceptual framework, covering how digital systems reorganise distance, interaction and voice. Useful for source analysis because most stimulus material is about a system behaving in a way its designers did not plan for.

subjects.name: Content: data, databases and data governance
subjects.description: How data is collected, stored, structured, shared and protected. Students need enough technical accuracy to describe a process correctly without turning the answer into Computer Science. Data protection is also where UAE-specific material is available and almost nobody uses it.

subjects.name: Content: algorithms and automated decision-making
subjects.description: What algorithms do, where bias enters, and how automated decisions are justified and contested. The commonest failure is asserting that an algorithm is biased without explaining the mechanism by which the bias was introduced.

subjects.name: Content: artificial intelligence and machine learning
subjects.description: Training data, model behaviour, explainability and the social consequences of deployment. The fastest-moving part of the course, which means examples go stale within a year and a student's examples file needs reviewing every term rather than once.

subjects.name: Content: networks, the internet and connectivity
subjects.description: Infrastructure, access, platform architecture and the geography of connectivity. Good material for a student in the Gulf, where connectivity policy and infrastructure investment are visible and documented, and where comparisons across the region are easy to source.

subjects.name: Content: media, platforms and information
subjects.description: How content is produced, distributed, moderated and monetised, and what that does to information quality. Students bring strong instincts here and weak sourcing; the work is converting opinion into evidenced analysis.

subjects.name: Content: robots, autonomous technologies and computers
subjects.description: Physical computing, autonomy, sensing and the labour and safety questions that follow. Underused by students, which makes it a reliable place to find a distinctive example when everyone else writes about social media.

subjects.name: Contexts: cultural, social and political
subjects.description: Where a digital system meets people, institutions and governance. Answers are credited for situating an example in a named place with named actors, which is exactly where generic examples fall down.

subjects.name: Contexts: economic, environmental and health
subjects.description: Labour markets, energy and materials, and clinical or public-health applications. The environmental context is the most neglected by students and the most rewarding, because the physical footprint of computation is well documented and rarely written about.

subjects.name: The Inquiry Project
subjects.description: A student-designed investigation of a real digital-society question, documented and reported. The component with the widest gap between what students produce and what the criteria reward, and the one that receives the least class time in a school running a single teacher across two cohorts.

subjects.name: HL Extension: challenges and interventions
subjects.description: Contemporary challenges arising from digital systems and the interventions proposed to address them, assessed through its own component. It rewards students who can evaluate whether an intervention actually addresses the mechanism causing the problem, rather than listing proposals.

subjects.name: The real-world examples file
subjects.description: A maintained set of dated, sourced examples spanning the content strands and contexts, each tagged with the concepts it illustrates. Not a syllabus item, but the single thing that most reliably separates a top-band candidate from a fluent one, and the easiest asset to build with supervision.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-online-tutor.regionsIntro: For this subject the district a family lives in matters less for content than for two practical things: when a session can start, and what local material a student can realistically use in their inquiry project. Dubai is unusually rich in the second. These are the areas the enquiries come from.

regions.name: Dubai Internet City and Dubai Media City
regions.note: Where a high proportion of parents in technology and media actually work, which makes interviews and workplace observation genuinely available for an inquiry project. Students here often have the best access to primary material in the whole emirate and the least idea that it counts as evidence.

regions.name: Dubai International Financial Centre and Zabeel
regions.note: A dense professional-services population with short commutes and early session availability. Inquiry projects from this band frequently look at automated decision-making in finance, which works well provided the student keeps the analysis conceptual rather than technical.

regions.name: Discovery Gardens and The Gardens
regions.note: High-density, mixed-income apartment communities where questions about connectivity, access and the cost of being online are not abstract. A strong setting for an inquiry on digital access, and one that avoids the overused social-media topic entirely.

regions.name: International City and Warsan
regions.note: One of the most internationally mixed residential areas in Dubai, with substantial use of remittance and messaging platforms. Rich territory for an inquiry on platform dependence, provided the student handles consent and data collection through the school.

regions.name: Dubai Investments Park and Green Community
regions.note: Industrial and logistics employment alongside residential, which makes automation in warehousing and transport observable rather than theoretical. Sessions here start later because the run back from the older Diploma schools is long.

regions.name: Damac Hills and Dubailand
regions.note: Newer villa communities a long way out, where the daily school commute already takes an hour each way. The argument for online delivery is strongest in this band simply because the alternative consumes the time the work needs.

regions.name: Al Mizhar and Al Twar
regions.note: Established eastern suburbs with families who have often been in Dubai a long time and students who attend schools on the Deira side. Cohorts in this band tend to be smaller, which means less class discussion and more need for one-to-one argument practice.

regions.name: Expo City Dubai and Dubai South
regions.note: Planned districts built around a documented infrastructure programme, which gives a student an unusually well-evidenced local case to analyse. Few candidates use it, which is precisely why it works as a distinctive example in an answer.

schoolClusters.city: Schools most likely to run Digital Society at both levels
schoolClusters.note: Larger Diploma cohorts make a newer subject viable at Higher Level as well as Standard. Ask the department two specific questions before choosing: whether the Higher Level extension will run, and whether the teacher has taken a cohort through to examination on the current guide yet.

schoolClusters.city: Schools where the subject may be Standard Level only
schoolClusters.note: At many Dubai schools a new Group 3 option is introduced at Standard Level first and extended later if numbers hold. That matters for anyone who needs a Higher Level social science, and it is a question worth asking in Year 11 rather than discovering at DP1 registration.

schoolClusters.city: Newer Diploma schools building their Group 3 offer
schoolClusters.note: Recently opened schools often shape their options around available staff, so a subject can appear and disappear between cohorts. Families planning two years should ask whether the teacher is contracted through DP2, because a change of teacher in a young subject costs more than it does in an established one.

dubai/ib-dp-digital-society-online-tutor.modesIntro: Support in this subject splits into three jobs that need different session shapes: building the examples file, supervising the inquiry project, and training source analysis under time. The first is cheap and cumulative, the second is project work, the third is drilling.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one with an examples file as the running output
modes.description: A single weekly session in which every topic taught ends with two or three new examples added to a maintained file, each with a source, a date, a named place and the concepts it illustrates. By the end of DP1 the student owns an asset nobody can revise from a textbook, and by DP2 it is the thing they revise.
bullets: Two or three sourced examples added every session, never retrospectively
Each example tagged to concepts and to at least one context

Session recordings shared so the file can be rebuilt if it is lost

modes.title: Inquiry project supervision block
modes.description: Four to six sessions placed across months: testing whether the question can actually be investigated, choosing methods and sources, checking the documentation as it accumulates, then reading the student's own draft once against the criteria. This is project supervision rather than teaching and it is scheduled, not improvised.
bullets: Question narrowed until it is answerable with reachable evidence

modes.title: Source-analysis drilling before the papers
modes.description: Six to eight sessions in the final two terms on the written components, worked entirely from source material under time. Students learn to identify the concept at issue in the first minute, quote the source precisely, bring their own examples in deliberately, and finish the long answers rather than stopping when time runs out.

modes.description: Three to five sessions on challenges and interventions, built around the discipline of asking whether a proposed intervention addresses the mechanism causing the problem. Students arrive able to list interventions and leave able to evaluate them, which is the difference the descriptors are looking for.

sections.heading: What a Digital Society tutor in Dubai is hired for, and why there are so few
paragraphs: Three requests dominate. The first is a student revising from the wrong material, because searching the subject returns a decade of ITGS content with different components and a different internal assessment. The second is an inquiry project that has no investigable question, usually discovered in the second term of DP2. The third is a candidate who writes fluently about technology and scores mid-band, because the answers carry no sourced examples and never name the concept at issue.

The scarcity is structural rather than accidental. This course is young, so almost no practising teacher trained in it, and the people teaching it came from Computer Science, Business Management, ITGS or Geography. That is not a criticism of the teaching; it is a statement about how many people have taken a cohort through to examination on the current guide. In the UAE that number is small, and it is the single best question to put to a prospective tutor before discussing anything else.

What that means practically is that matching matters more here than in any other Group 3 subject, and that online delivery is what makes a match possible at all. A Geography specialist who has read the Digital Society guide is not an equivalent, and neither is a Computer Science teacher who will quietly turn the course into programming. Ask whether the tutor has supervised an inquiry project to submission, and ask what they would do about an examples file. The answers separate people quickly.

sections.heading: The course in three interacting parts, and how the papers use them
paragraphs: Digital Society is organised as concepts, content and contexts, and the examination assumes all three are in play at once. Concepts are the analytical lenses: change, identity, power, values, space, systems, expression. Content is the digital substance: data, algorithms, artificial intelligence, networks, media, robots and autonomous technologies, and the computing systems underneath them. Contexts are the human settings in which those operate: cultural, social, political, economic, environmental and health.

The written papers hand candidates source material and ask them to analyse it within that framework, supported by examples they researched themselves. That is why memorising definitions produces fluent, empty answers: the marks are for applying a concept to a situation and evidencing it, not for defining the concept. A student who opens an answer by naming the concept the source is really about has already done the hardest thing the question asks.

Component formats, weightings and durations are set out in the current subject guide, and because this course is young there is more out-of-date information circulating about it than about any other Diploma subject. Get the assessment outline from your child's coordinator in writing, including whether the Higher Level component uses pre-released material, and treat anything found online that predates the current guide as describing ITGS until proven otherwise. The same outline names the command terms and assessment objectives, and it is the document a tutor should plan from rather than any commercially published revision guide for this subject.

One further consequence of the three-part design is worth stating for parents who find the framework abstract. Because any content strand can be examined through any concept in any context, there is no finite list of questions to prepare for. What a candidate prepares instead is a method and an evidence base: a routine for identifying the concept at issue, and a file of examples strong enough to support an argument about it. That is why this subject rewards steady accumulation across two years and punishes a revision sprint more sharply than History or Economics do.

sections.heading: The inquiry project, counted backwards from the school's deadline
paragraphs: The internally assessed inquiry project asks a student to design and carry out their own investigation of a real digital-society question and report it. It is the component that most determines whether a candidate ends up in the top bands, and it is also the one that gets the least class time, because supervising twenty individual investigations is beyond any single teacher covering two year groups.

The failure is nearly always the question. Students choose something enormous, such as whether artificial intelligence is good for education, and then cannot investigate it, so the project becomes a literature summary with a conclusion attached. A workable question is narrow, located, and answerable with evidence a seventeen-year-old in Dubai can actually obtain: a specific system, a specific group of people, a specific claim to test. Narrowing it is an hour of work that saves a term.

Word limits, permitted formats and the number of supporting items are specified in the current guide and have moved since the course launched, so confirm them with the coordinator rather than from any search result, including this page. What does not change is the chain: question tested, evidence planned, documentation kept as it happens, one feedback round on a student-written draft, final submission inside the school's own internal deadline, which is always earlier than the external one. Ask for the department's dates in writing at the start of DP1, because a Dubai school that wants inquiries in before the winter break has moved the whole chain forward by two months.

sections.heading: From ITGS to Digital Society: what changed, and what to ask the school
paragraphs: This matters more than it sounds, because it determines whether your child's revision is useful. Information Technology in a Global Society was organised around social and ethical significance, application areas and IT systems, assessed with a written project and papers built on those divisions. Digital Society reorganises the same territory into concepts, content and contexts, and replaces the old project with an inquiry process the student designs.

The practical consequences are everywhere. ITGS past papers do not practise the current components. ITGS revision guides teach a structure the descriptors no longer use. Tutors whose experience is ITGS will teach a related subject competently and aim at the wrong assessment. And because the transition happened recently, some Dubai departments are still carrying material from the old course into lessons, which is normal and worth asking about politely.

The table below sets out the shift and the question each row generates for the school. None of them is confrontational; they are the questions a coordinator expects from a family who has read the guide. The most important is the last one: whether the teacher has taken a cohort through to examination under the current guide, because that single fact predicts how much outside supervision the inquiry project will need. None of this reflects badly on a department that has handled a syllabus change competently; it simply tells a family where the scarce resource is, and the scarce resource is individual feedback rather than teaching.

sections.heading: Where the marks go: examples that are not actually examples
paragraphs: The commonest reason a confident Digital Society candidate sits in the middle bands is that their examples do not function as evidence. An answer that refers to social media companies collecting data, or to facial recognition being used in some countries, has named a category rather than a case. The descriptors reward a located, dated, sourced instance with identifiable actors, because that is what allows an analytical claim to be tested rather than asserted.

The fix is an examples file built from DP1 and maintained. The target is roughly a dozen cases spread across the content strands and contexts, each with the system involved, the place, the year, one or two specifics, the source it came from, and a tag for the concepts it illustrates. Students resist this because it feels like admin. It is the single highest-return piece of work in the subject, and it is also the only revision asset in it that cannot be bought in a book.

Two Dubai-specific points are worth making. First, students here default to the same handful of American platform examples as everyone else in the world, which makes their answers interchangeable; regional and local material is better evidenced than they assume and almost nobody uses it. Second, this is the fastest-moving subject in Group 3, so examples go stale inside a year. Reviewing the file each term, replacing what has dated, is part of the work rather than an optional tidy-up.

sections.heading: The Higher Level extension: challenges, and whether interventions actually work
paragraphs: Higher Level candidates take an extension on contemporary challenges arising from digital systems and the interventions proposed to address them. It is assessed in its own component, and students consistently prepare it as a research task when it is assessed as an evaluative one. Arriving with a list of eight proposed interventions earns much less than arriving with three, each traced to the mechanism causing the problem and assessed against it.

The discipline that lifts this component is mechanical and teachable. For any challenge, identify the mechanism that produces it: an incentive, a design decision, an absence of accountability, a data asymmetry. Then ask of each proposed intervention whether it touches that mechanism or only its symptoms, who bears the cost, and what it might cause instead. Students who run that routine on five challenges can run it on an unseen sixth, which is what the component tests.

Where the guide uses pre-released material for this component, working through it early is the obvious move, and it is the one thing a department under pressure is most likely to leave until late. Confirm the format with the coordinator rather than assuming, since this course is young and its arrangements have been revised. Three to five focused sessions is usually the whole intervention, which makes it one of the better marginal purchases for a Higher Level candidate. It is also the component where a student's examples file pays off twice, because a challenge analysed with a located case behind it reads as evidence rather than as a position.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a subject that is partly about generative AI
paragraphs: This subject puts a student in an awkward position: they are studying artificial intelligence while being assessed under rules about using it. The rules themselves are not ambiguous. Work submitted must be the student's own, and any use of a tool that contributes to the work has to be acknowledged in the way the student's school requires. Ask the coordinator for the school's written policy on acknowledgement, because schools in Dubai apply the same IB requirement with different local procedures.

For the inquiry project the boundary is the familiar one. A tutor may comment once on a student-written draft, name a criterion that is not met, point out that a claim is unevidenced, or ask why a source was trusted. A tutor may not supply sentences, reorganise the report on the student's behalf, or return a version that only needs accepting. Treat any provider who describes their service as editing a draft to completion as a risk to your child rather than a convenience.

The same reasoning applies to the student's own use of tools. Using a model to find candidate sources and then reading, verifying and citing those sources is research. Pasting generated text into a report is not, and in this subject a marker is unusually likely to notice, because the generated account of a digital phenomenon tends to be exactly the undated, unlocated generality the descriptors penalise. The honest route is also the higher-scoring one, which is a convenient alignment worth pointing out to a tempted seventeen-year-old.

sections.heading: What KHDA requires alongside the Diploma in Dubai
paragraphs: Families choosing Diploma options in Dubai sometimes discover late that the timetable carries compulsory subjects on top of the six Diploma courses. Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's published requirements state they must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The arrangements are specific. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with the licensed curriculum's language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies.

Two details matter for anyone planning tutoring hours. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least twenty-five minutes. And for these subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, which is a real constraint on how any Arabic or Islamic Education support may be described. Schools must also ensure teachers of these subjects hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach them.

sections.heading: Availability, matching and what happens when nobody is free
paragraphs: This is the point on which a page about a scarce subject should be blunt. There are not many people anywhere who have taught the current Digital Society guide through to examination, and there are fewer in the UAE time zone. A family asking for Higher Level extension coaching plus inquiry project supervision at seven in the evening Dubai time may find that nobody matching that description is free, and the honest answer is to say so rather than to supply a near miss.

The realistic alternatives are worth setting out, because competitors in this market conceal them. A tutor in a time zone whose working day overlaps a Dubai evening can cover the slot, which works because sessions are recorded and the subject needs no laboratory. A different weekly slot, often earlier or at the weekend, widens the pool substantially. A short wait for a specific tutor is sometimes the best option, particularly for inquiry supervision, which is more valuable done well in DP1 than done immediately.

Lessons are delivered live over video, one-to-one, and nothing is sent to an address in the Emirates; home visits are an India-only service. Scheduling in Dubai normally runs between half past four and seven, later for the outer communities, and Ramadan usually shifts sessions to after iftar or into a compressed block afterwards, which works better when planned in advance. The first lesson is free, limited to one per student, needs no card details, and is spent diagnosing rather than selling.
