sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level Economics, quantified
paragraphs: Families choosing between the two levels usually ask which is harder, and the more useful question is which is different. Higher Level adds a third examination paper, additional content within the same three units, and a shift in the balance of what is tested. Standard Level candidates sit two papers and are examined on extended response and data response. Higher Level candidates sit those two plus a third paper built around calculation, data handling and policy reasoning, which is a genuinely different competence.

The internal assessment is the same in form at both levels: a portfolio of three commentaries on published news articles, each capped at 800 words. Its weighting differs, and because Higher Level has more external assessment to distribute, the portfolio is proportionally less of the final grade at Higher Level than at Standard Level. That matters for planning: a Standard Level student who neglects the portfolio is risking more of the grade than a Higher Level student doing the same thing, while the Higher Level student is risking more by neglecting the quantitative paper.

Content depth is the third difference. Higher Level goes further inside microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy rather than adding a fourth unit, which means a student finding a topic difficult at Standard Level will find the Higher Level treatment of it difficult in the same direction. That makes the choice a reliable one to take on evidence: two Standard Level answers and one Higher Level answer, all marked against the descriptors, usually settle it inside a fortnight.

University requirements are the one part of the decision a tutor cannot soften. Some economics degrees specify mathematics at Higher Level and treat economics as recommended rather than required, which surprises families who assumed the opposite. Others accept any combination with a strong overall score. Three named programme pages for the current admissions cycle will answer it; a general statement about the IB will not.

sections.heading: The quantitative half: calculation marks both mathematics routes lose
paragraphs: Higher Level Economics asks for arithmetic, and the students who lose marks on it fall into two groups with opposite causes. The first group finds the calculation itself hard: percentage change, index numbers, real against nominal values, elasticity coefficients, tax incidence, and reading proportions out of a table. For them the fix is drill, and it is quick, because the arithmetic is simple once the convention is clear. The second group calculates accurately and loses the interpretation mark, because a figure with no units and no sentence explaining what it means is an incomplete answer.

That second failure is the more common one in Dubai classrooms, and it catches strong mathematics students in particular. An elasticity coefficient of 0.4 is not an answer; it is an answer when accompanied by a statement that demand is price inelastic over this range, so a price rise would increase total revenue. The mark scheme awards those separately, and a student who has produced the number and moved on has done the harder half and collected the smaller part of the credit.

The conventions are where marks quietly disappear. Sign conventions on elasticity, whether a coefficient is reported as an absolute value, the base year in an index calculation, converting nominal to real using the correct deflator, and the direction of a percentage change when the base moves. Each is a single decision applied consistently, and each costs marks every time it is applied inconsistently. Writing out the convention on a reference card and using it for a fortnight is usually enough.

The third paper rewards something beyond calculation, which is policy reasoning expressed through the numbers. A question may give data and ask what a government should do, and the answer has to use the figures rather than discussing the policy in the abstract. That is a combination of the fourth assessment objective and the third, and practising it requires questions with data attached rather than essay titles.

sections.heading: Reading your own answer like a marker: a four-pass routine
paragraphs: The highest-value habit a Higher Level economics student can build is marking their own work, and the reason it usually fails is that students reread rather than mark. Rereading produces the judgement that an answer seems fine, because the student who wrote it understands what it meant. Marking requires looking for specific things in a specific order, and the order is what makes it work.

The first pass is definitions. Every economic term introduced in the answer either carries a precise definition or does not, and the student circles each term and checks it against their own definition list. The second pass is the diagram: is there one, is it labelled, and does the prose refer to it by naming the axes, the shift and the new equilibrium? If the diagram is never mentioned, the answer has a drawing rather than a skills mark.

The third pass is the chain. For each effect claimed, is there a path from cause to consequence, or does the answer jump? Students write that a subsidy increases output, which is a claim with the mechanism omitted; marking for the chain forces the intermediate steps onto the page. The fourth pass is judgement: is a position stated, does it follow from what precedes it, and is there a condition under which it would change? An answer that fails the fourth pass is a middle-band answer regardless of how good the first three were.

Four passes take about eight minutes on a fifteen-mark answer and they convert practice into information. A student who does this before a tutorial arrives with a specific question rather than a general one, which changes what the session is for. We teach the routine in the first fortnight and then expect it, because a student who can mark their own work no longer needs a tutor for the things it finds.

sections.heading: Choosing the three articles: the decision that settles most portfolio marks
paragraphs: The portfolio is three commentaries, each based on a published news article, each capped at 800 words, and worth 45 marks in total. Most of the marks are decided before a word is written, at the point the articles are chosen. An article that is really an opinion piece with no economic event in it gives a student nothing to apply a model to. An article that is too broad forces a shallow commentary. An article already saturated with economic analysis leaves the student restating someone else's reasoning, which scores badly on application and analysis.

The requirements themselves constrain the choice, and reading them before searching saves weeks. The three commentaries must between them cover different units of the course, use different key concepts, and draw on articles from different sources published within a defined recent window. A student who writes two strong commentaries on macroeconomic articles and then discovers the third must cover a different unit has lost choices, and often has to write the hardest commentary on the least interesting article.

What makes a good article is specific: a single identifiable economic event or policy, a market or economy named, some data or a quantity mentioned, and enough detail to support a diagram. Articles about a tax change, a subsidy, a price control, an exchange-rate movement or a trade measure are reliable. Articles about sentiment, forecasts or general conditions are not, because there is no event to model. In the Gulf, policy coverage of fuel pricing, utility tariffs, free-zone rules, tourism demand and trade agreements routinely meets the test.

On the boundary, the rule is the same as everywhere else in the Diploma. A tutor may explain the requirements, say whether a chosen article will support a diagram, comment on a draft the student has produced, and note that a key concept is asserted rather than used. A tutor may not select the article, supply the analysis, restructure the commentary or provide text. The portfolio is submitted as the student's own work and the school certifies it; we keep a dated record of drafts received and comments returned.

sections.heading: How part (a) and part (b) of one essay interact
paragraphs: An extended-response economics question typically comes in two parts: a shorter part asking for explanation and a longer part asking for evaluation, both on the same topic. Students treat them as two questions and lose marks in a specific way, because the two halves are connected. The explanation in the first part is the foundation the second part is supposed to evaluate, and a thin first part leaves the second with nothing to weigh.

The commonest error is spending the available time unevenly in the wrong direction. A student who writes generously on the shorter part, because explanation is comfortable, arrives at the longer part with less time for the harder task that carries more marks. The reverse error also appears: a student who rushes the explanation and then evaluates a model they have not properly set out, which produces judgement with no support underneath it.

There is a structural trick that helps. Draw the diagram in the shorter part, label it fully, and use it there. In the longer part, refer back to it rather than redrawing, and use the remaining time for conditionality and prioritisation. This treats the two halves as one argument, which is how the marking reads them, and it buys several minutes that would otherwise go into a duplicate diagram.

Time allocation should follow the marks rather than comfort. A student practising this with a timer, allocating minutes in proportion to the marks and stopping when the time is up, will leave a short part slightly thinner than they would like and a long part substantially stronger. The net effect on the total is reliably positive, and a student has to feel it once on a marked script to believe it.

sections.heading: Economics HL, degree routes and what support costs in Dubai
paragraphs: Most Dubai families buying Higher Level economics support are doing it with a destination in mind, and the requirements are frequently misunderstood. Economics degrees at selective universities often specify mathematics at Higher Level and list economics as recommended rather than required, which means a student optimising the economics grade while carrying Standard Level mathematics may be solving the wrong problem. Business, management, finance, policy and international relations programmes vary widely. Three named programme pages for the current admissions cycle will settle it; a summary on a tutoring site will not.

The UAE Ministry of Education's certificate equivalency process is separate from admission and has its own documented requirements. For the British track, five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 are needed, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five, plus one A-Level at no less than E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. For the American track, mathematics requires at least 450 in SAT Math, and English is evidenced by IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section. No IB points threshold should be quoted unless read on the Ministry's own site, and no tutoring is needed for the process.

On cost, published Dubai rates read in October 2026 run from roughly AED 33 to AED 65 an hour for budget online providers, AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 180 to AED 500 for an in-home visit including travel, and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an IB specialist, with monthly packages of about AED 799 for eight online sessions advertised in the same market. Those are market figures rather than a price list of ours. In economics specifically, the thing worth paying for is marking against the descriptors, because the fault this page describes is invisible without it.

Two closing practicalities. Anyone paid to tutor privately in the UAE needs a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued free of charge for two years through MoHRE's own service; no schedule of penalties for working without one is published, so any amount quoted to you is unverified. And where no Higher Level economics specialist is free in the slot a family needs, we say so and charge nothing rather than allocating someone who has not taught the course.

process.title: Send one of your child's own written answers
process.description: Not a report and not a topic list. One answer, ideally a longer evaluation question, with whatever mark the school gave it. That single document tells us more about where the marks are going than a term of grade data.

process.title: Free first session spent marking it
process.description: The session is spent scoring that answer against the four assessment objectives separately, with the descriptors visible. The written note afterwards says which objective is missing and what the next answer should do differently.

process.title: Teach the four-pass self-marking routine
process.description: Definitions, diagram use, causal chain, stated judgement. Eight minutes per answer. A student who can mark their own work arrives at a tutorial with a specific question, which changes what the hour is worth.

process.title: Fix the portfolio choices early
process.description: Article selection decides most portfolio marks, and the requirements constrain the set of three. We check eligibility and diagram potential before the student starts writing, rather than rescuing a commentary built on an unusable article.

process.title: Review at six weeks against the objective record
process.description: Four marked answers with the objectives scored separately show whether the weakest one is moving. The review states continue, change focus, or stop. We do not predict a grade and we do not claim credit for a mock.

whyPoints.title: The four objectives are scored separately
whyPoints.description: An aggregate mark hides the fault in economics. Recording knowledge, application, evaluation and skills separately in every session note shows a parent which competence is capping the answers, usually evaluation or diagram use rather than content.

whyPoints.title: Definitions are treated as examinable content
whyPoints.description: Around eighty terms need stating precisely rather than described accurately, and the mark goes to the specific elements. Twenty written out, tested cold and rewritten is the highest return per hour available in this subject, and almost nobody does it.

whyPoints.title: The student learns to mark their own work
whyPoints.description: A four-pass routine takes eight minutes and converts practice into information. The aim is a student who no longer needs a tutor for the faults the routine catches, which shortens the arrangement rather than extending it.

whyPoints.title: Portfolio help starts at article selection
whyPoints.description: Most commentary marks are decided by the choice of article, and the published requirements constrain the set of three. Checking eligibility and diagram potential first prevents the commonest and least recoverable portfolio problem.

whyPoints.title: Claims are limited to what can be evidenced
whyPoints.description: No grade prediction, no attribution of a mock result to our sessions. AED figures are published Dubai market rates from October 2026, regulator statements come from KHDA, MoHRE and u.ae, and IB session dates are absent because they could not be verified.

faqs.question: What are the four assessment objectives in IB Economics?
faqs.answer: Knowledge and understanding, which covers defining, listing, outlining and stating. Application and analysis, which covers explaining, applying a model to a given context and analysing a chain of effects. Synthesis and evaluation, which covers discussing, evaluating, justifying and reaching a position. And the use of appropriate skills, which covers diagrams, calculation and handling data. Fluent writing satisfies the first two comfortably and frequently leaves the third and fourth untouched, which is why an articulate student can score in the middle bands. Recording the four separately on marked answers makes the gap visible in a way an aggregate grade cannot.

faqs.question: How does a 15-mark Economics answer differ from a 10-mark one?
faqs.answer: In kind, not in length. The shorter question wants explanation: a model applied to the context with a chain of effects and a diagram the prose uses. The longer one wants that plus judgement, and the judgement carries the top band. A longer version of the shorter answer reaches the middle band and stops, which is the commonest pattern on Dubai scripts. Evaluation itself has levels: acknowledging drawbacks, estimating magnitude, naming the conditions under which the conclusion changes, prioritising what matters most here, and stating a position that follows from the reasoning. A margin plan written before the essay produces the last three reliably.

faqs.question: Why do definitions matter in an Economics HL answer?
faqs.answer: Because the mark is awarded for specific elements rather than for meaning the right thing. A student who writes that price elasticity of demand measures how much demand changes when price changes has described it and usually will not score fully; the definition wants responsiveness of quantity demanded to a proportionate change in price. Across the three units there are perhaps eighty terms worth stating precisely, and the work is twenty written out, tested cold and rewritten where wrong. It feels like memorisation and delivers more marks per hour than any other revision in the subject, and it also helps keep a commentary inside 800 words.

faqs.question: What extra work does Economics Higher Level add over Standard Level?
faqs.answer: A third examination paper, built around calculation, data handling and policy reasoning, plus additional depth inside the same three units rather than a fourth unit. The portfolio is identical in form at both levels: three commentaries on published articles, each capped at 800 words, 45 marks in total. Because Higher Level distributes more of the grade across external assessment, the portfolio is proportionally a smaller share at Higher Level, so a Standard Level student neglecting it risks more. The decision between levels is best taken on marked evidence: two Standard Level answers and one Higher Level answer usually settle it in a fortnight.

faqs.question: Where should a Dubai student find real-world economics examples?
faqs.answer: From policy coverage with a date and a named market, not from general commentary. The test is whether there is a single identifiable event to which a model can be applied: a tax change, a subsidy, a price control, an exchange-rate movement, a trade measure. In the Gulf, coverage of fuel pricing, utility tariffs, free-zone rules, tourism demand and trade agreements routinely qualifies, and the UAE's own position gives a student unusually concrete material: an oil-linked economy diversifying deliberately, a currency pegged to the dollar, and intervention visible enough to discuss with dates attached. Record each example with its date and source, since an undated example is weak evidence.

faqs.question: How are the three IA commentaries marked?
faqs.answer: Each commentary is based on a published news article, capped at 800 words, and marked on diagrams, terminology, application and analysis, the key concept used, and evaluation, with the portfolio carrying 45 marks in total including marks for meeting the portfolio requirements themselves. The three must between them cover different units of the course, use different key concepts, and draw on articles from different sources published within the defined recent window. Most of those marks are decided at the point the articles are chosen, which is why reading the requirements before searching for articles saves weeks of unproductive drafting later.

faqs.question: What may an Economics tutor do with a commentary draft?
faqs.answer: Explain the portfolio requirements, say whether a chosen article will support a diagram, comment on a draft the student has produced, note where a key concept is asserted rather than used, and point out that an evaluation has no stated position. What a tutor may not do is select the article, supply the analysis, restructure the commentary or provide text. The portfolio is submitted as the student's own work and the school certifies it on that basis. We keep a dated record of drafts received and comments returned, which is the only authorship evidence anyone can produce if a school raises the question.

faqs.question: What does a marked Economics answer show that a term grade does not?
faqs.answer: Which of the four assessment objectives was missing. A term grade of 5 tells a family that something is capping the work; a marked answer shows that definitions scored two out of four, the diagram was drawn and never referred to, the causal chain jumped a step, and no position was stated. Those are four different tasks with four different fixes, and three of them have nothing to do with revising content. The record worth keeping is therefore marks available against marks gained per objective, across four or five answers, which makes movement visible in weeks rather than at the next report.

faqs.question: Is Economics HL needed for an economics degree?
faqs.answer: Often recommended, less often required, and frequently not the binding condition. Selective economics programmes commonly specify mathematics at Higher Level and list economics as useful rather than necessary, which catches families who have optimised the economics grade while carrying Standard Level mathematics. Other institutions accept any subject combination with a strong overall score. Business, finance, policy and international relations programmes vary widely, and some UAE universities set placement tests after admission rather than subject prerequisites. Read three named programme pages for the current admissions cycle, then confirm with each admissions office, before the DP1 change window closes.

faqs.question: Does the Economics grade matter for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is a certificate-recognition process run by the Ministry of Education and its published requirements are expressed per curriculum rather than per subject grade, so no single economics grade determines it. For the British track, five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 are required, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five, plus one A-Level at no less than E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. For the American track, mathematics requires at least 450 in SAT Math, with English evidenced by IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in SAT reading and writing. Verify through the official channel; no tutoring is required.

faqs.question: How much does an Economics HL tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates read in October 2026 run from roughly AED 33 to AED 65 an hour for budget online providers, AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 180 to AED 500 for an in-home visit including the tutor's travel, and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an IB specialist, with premium named tutors advertised up to AED 650. Monthly packages of about AED 799 for eight online sessions appear in the same market. Those are market figures, not our price list. In economics the variable worth paying for is marking against the published descriptors, since the fault that caps most answers is invisible without it.

faqs.question: How many Economics HL sessions does a DP2 student usually need?
faqs.answer: Four to six weekly sessions is often enough to shift the specific thing that is capping the answers, because the faults in this subject are structural rather than content gaps. The pattern is one of the student's own answers marked before each session, with the four objectives scored separately, and the session spent on the weakest. Students who also need the quantitative paper usually add a short block of three or four sessions on calculation and interpretation. Longer arrangements make sense where a portfolio is being drafted in parallel. Beyond that, a student who has learned the four-pass routine often does not need the hours.

faqs.question: Can Economics HL lessons fit around a Dubai school week?
faqs.answer: Yes, with one caveat worth planning for. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit under KHDA guidance, so the week has less slack than six subjects suggests. We ask for the timetable at booking and fix one protected slot. Communities differ: central areas such as Al Satwa and Deira can usually manage a 4.30pm or 6.30pm start, while outer communities like Mira and Al Barari rarely settle before 5.30pm, and written work is better set for weekends there.

faqs.question: How does Paper 3 differ from Paper 1 and Paper 2 in Economics HL?
faqs.answer: It is the quantitative paper and only Higher Level candidates sit it. Where the first paper asks for extended response and the second for data response, the third is built around calculation, manipulation of given data and policy reasoning expressed through the numbers. Essay-confident students practise it least and lose marks in two ways: the arithmetic itself, which is simple once the conventions are clear, and the interpretation, where a correct figure with no units and no sentence of meaning collects only part of the credit. Preparing for it requires questions with data attached rather than essay titles.

faqs.question: What happens if no Economics Higher Level tutor is free?
faqs.answer: We say so before anything is booked and nothing is charged. Higher Level Economics is widely taught across the UAE, so a complete absence of availability is uncommon; the usual constraint is a specific recurring slot in term time that cannot be filled by a UAE-based tutor. The alternatives offered are the nearest workable time, a weekend block, or a specialist in another time zone whose working hours overlap Gulf Standard Time. What we will not do is accept the booking and allocate someone who has not taught this course at this level, because in economics the marking is the product and a generalist cannot supply it.

Lessons run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around the school timetable and mandatory subject periods.

intro.heading: Standard Level Economics is a different subject from Higher Level, and the plan should reflect that
paragraphs: Most advice written about IB Economics is written about Higher Level. It talks about Paper 3, about the Keynesian multiplier, about terms of trade and the Marshall-Lerner condition. A Standard Level student in a Dubai DP2 class does not sit Paper 3 and is not examined on any of that extension content. Half of what they read online is about somebody else's course.

What Standard Level actually consists of is two external papers and one internal portfolio. Paper 1 is an extended-response paper of 1 hour 15 minutes carrying 30%. Paper 2 is a data-response paper of 1 hour 45 minutes carrying 40%, which makes it the largest single component of the Standard Level grade by a clear margin. The portfolio of three commentaries carries the remaining 30%. Confirm current weightings and timings against the published subject guide on ibo.org or with your school's DP coordinator before building a schedule on them.

Those three numbers produce a different plan from the Higher Level one. At SL the portfolio is worth half as much again as it is at HL, and it is finished months before the examination session. That makes it the only part of the grade a student can bank early with certainty. A Standard Level student who leaves the commentaries until DP2 term two has thrown away the easiest 30% available to them, and no amount of Paper 2 practice in April gets it back.

The second consequence is that Paper 2 deserves more attention than it usually gets. It is the heaviest component at SL, it is marked out of 40, and it is structured as a series of short parts that build to a 15-mark evaluation drawing on a provided text. Students lose marks in it predictably: definitional answers that paraphrase instead of defining, a calculation attempted without units, diagrams drawn but never referred to, and a final answer argued from theory while the supplied figures sit unused on the page.

There is a third consequence, and it is the one parents raise first. Because Standard Level has no Paper 3 and no extension content, a weak Economics grade at SL is rarely a knowledge problem. It is usually a writing problem, a timing problem, or a portfolio that was left too late. Those three causes look identical on a school report and need entirely different work, which is why the first conversation here asks for a marked paper rather than a description of how revision is going at home.

On delivery: tutoring for Dubai families is delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or elsewhere in the UAE — a tutor arriving at a residence is something we offer only in India. For Economics SL the practical effect is that the tutor is chosen for knowing the Standard Level course precisely, including what it excludes, rather than for living near your community. A tutor who teaches HL by default will spend your child's hours on content that is not on their paper.

dubai/ib-dp-economics-sl-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Where a Standard Level Economics student came from changes the first month of work more than their current grade does. These four entries describe the handovers we see in Dubai, and what each one leaves missing.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Economics is a group 3 choice at Standard or Higher Level. The Standard Level course covers four units — introduction to economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy — taught around nine key concepts. Assessment is Paper 1, Paper 2 and a portfolio of three commentaries. Standard Level students sit neither Paper 3 nor the HL extension topics, which is a smaller course than it is usually described as.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma cohorts frequently teach SL and HL together in one timetabled class, with HL extension content delivered separately. For an SL student that arrangement is mostly beneficial, but it produces a specific risk: sitting through HL material and revising it. Knowing what is not on the Standard Level paper is worth an hour of a tutor's time in the first week.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Individuals and Societies provides the first contact with markets, incentives and government intervention. MYP assessment uses four criteria scored 1-8 against task-specific descriptors, which trains investigation and extended writing but not short, timed, precisely worded answers. Students coming from MYP into Economics SL are usually comfortable with the commentaries and uncomfortable with the opening parts of Paper 2.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Dubai school runs MYP to the end of Year 11 with no external examinations, a DP1 Economics SL student may sit their first formal timed paper in October of Year 12. The marks on that paper tend to understate what the student knows, which is worth explaining to a parent before it causes a decision about dropping to a different subject.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: CP students take DP courses alongside a career-related study and four compulsory components, including a reflective project. Economics SL inside CP is assessed identically to Economics SL inside the full Diploma. The difference is deadline shape: the reflective project and the three commentaries commonly fall in the same term, and the commentaries are the ones with a fixed external weighting.
programmes.countryNote: A handful of Dubai schools run CP, and the Economics group inside it can be very small. Where CP and DP students share one Economics class, internal commentary deadlines are set once for the whole group, so a CP student carrying a reflective project gets no extra time on the portfolio.

programmes.name: IGCSE and Year 11 into Economics SL
programmes.description: The common route in Dubai. A student finishing Cambridge IGCSE Economics 0455 or Business Studies 0450 in June starts Economics SL in late August with real advantages: the demand and supply apparatus, elasticity and the basic macroeconomic indicators are familiar. The gap is in command terms. IGCSE 'explain' and Diploma 'evaluate' want different paragraphs, and the first mock usually proves it.
programmes.countryNote: Because British-curriculum schools dominate Dubai enrolment at 37% of private-school students in 2024-25, the IGCSE handover is the standard case here. A student who scored a grade 8 or 9 at 0455 and then gets 10 out of 25 on an SL Paper 1 has not forgotten economics; they have written an IGCSE answer to a Diploma question.

dubai/ib-dp-economics-sl-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Economics at Standard Level is the subject of this page. The rest of the list is what Dubai Standard Level students most often take alongside it, described by the assessment load each adds rather than by its syllabus.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.levels: SL (the subject of this page) and HL
subjects.description: Four units taught around nine key concepts. At Standard Level the assessment is Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and a portfolio of three 800-word commentaries at 30%. Standard Level does not include Paper 3 or the HL extension topics, so market power, asymmetric information, the Keynesian multiplier and terms of trade are not examined content for an SL candidate.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The most frequent group 3 alternative, and the subject SL Economics students most often also take. Its Paper 1 uses a pre-released case study, which changes revision shape entirely. Students taking both tend to carry Business tools into Economics answers, where an Ansoff matrix earns nothing and a correctly labelled diagram earns marks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The usual mathematics pairing for Economics SL at Dubai schools. Regression, correlation, percentage change and confident calculator use all support the quantitative parts of Paper 2. Standard Level Economics requires no calculus, so an AI SL student is not at a disadvantage against an AA student in this subject.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Chosen mainly for university prerequisites rather than for Economics support. Differentiation touches marginal reasoning, but Standard Level Economics never requires it. A student choosing AA because they expect it to help with Economics SL is choosing it for the wrong reason; check the target degree's stated requirement instead.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Overlaps the global economy unit through trade, development and resource topics. Its internal assessment is a fieldwork report, so a student taking Geography and Economics faces a field report and three commentaries in one year. Both sets of internal deadlines should go on one calendar in DP1 term two, before either school sets them.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Strong preparation for the 15-mark parts of Economics papers because it trains sustained argument and the weighing of evidence. The transfer runs one way: History students write at length, and the second part of an Economics Paper 1 question allows roughly 45 minutes. Length is not what the Economics band descriptors reward.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Its experimental internal assessment teaches a discipline of method and evidence that transfers directly to commentary writing, where weak drafts assert a link without showing a mechanism. Behavioural material in the Economics course gives the two subjects a genuine conceptual overlap around rationality assumptions.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Covers the same international territory as the global economy unit from a political angle. The engagement activity requires sourcing and defending evidence on a self-chosen issue, which is close to what commentary criterion C wants. Students often find the politics material easier to evaluate than the economics, and the habit transfers if it is pointed out.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Shares the market-failure ground — common pool resources, externalities, sustainability — from an ecological direction. One body of reading can inform both subjects, but the written work must be independently produced for each; reusing a passage across two subjects is an academic-honesty question rather than efficient study.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The close-reading skill it trains is the one weak commentaries lack. Criterion C marks are lost more often to loose paraphrase of the chosen article than to shaky theory, and a student who can quote the precise clause that supports a claim writes better commentaries without learning any more economics.

subjects.name: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies
subjects.description: Dubai private schools must deliver Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of the licensed international curriculum, under KHDA requirements. These sit outside the Diploma's points but inside the student's week, and they are a real part of the timetable pressure a Standard Level Economics plan has to fit around.

sections.heading: What Standard Level Economics actually contains, and what it leaves out
paragraphs: An IB DP Economics SL home tutor in Dubai is, in market terms, a specialist who works one-to-one with a Standard Level Diploma Economics student. In this city that phrase has historically described a tutor who drives to a residence and charges a rate that absorbs the journey. IB Gram teaches the same course the other way: one-to-one over live video, on Gulf Standard Time. Home visits in the UAE are not a service we sell at any price; they exist in our India operation only.

The course itself is smaller than the internet suggests. Standard Level Economics covers four units: introduction to economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy, taught around nine key concepts — scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention. Assessment is two papers and a portfolio. There is no Paper 3 at Standard Level and no HL extension content, which means several topics that dominate online revision material are simply not on an SL candidate's paper.

This matters practically because so much Economics support is written for Higher Level by default. A student spending February evenings on the Keynesian multiplier or terms of trade because a revision channel covered them is spending time on content that cannot appear on their examination. The first thing a Standard Level student should get from a tutor is an accurate map of their own syllabus, with the extension material crossed out.

What remains is demanding in a different way. Standard Level rewards precision rather than range. A definition must be the definition, not a paraphrase. A diagram must be labelled and referred to. A 15-mark answer must evaluate rather than explain twice. And 30% of the grade sits in three pieces of coursework that the student writes themselves and that are finished long before the examination session. The order of priorities follows directly from that, and the next sections set it out.

sections.heading: Standard Level against Higher Level, line by line
paragraphs: Parents choosing between the two levels, and students considering a switch, deserve the comparison set out rather than summarised. The differences are structural and they change the number of hours a student needs, which is the only reason the comparison belongs on a tutoring page at all.

The content difference is the extension topics. Higher Level adds micro material on market power, asymmetric information and the market's inability to achieve equity, macro material including the multiplier, and global economy content covering terms of trade and the Marshall-Lerner condition with the J-curve effect. The assessment difference is Paper 3, a Higher Level-only policy paper carrying 30% that combines calculation with a justified policy recommendation.

The weighting difference runs the other way and favours Standard Level students who plan early. The portfolio is the same three commentaries at both levels, but it carries 30% at SL against 20% at HL. In other words a Standard Level student has a larger share of their grade in work with no time limit, no examination hall and published criteria they can see in advance. Treating that as the easy part is the single most common Standard Level planning error we see in Dubai.

The tutoring-hours consequence is straightforward. An HL student usually needs a dedicated calculation block for Paper 3 and a longer run of content teaching. An SL student usually needs fewer content hours and more hours on Paper 2 technique and on commentary drafting. Always confirm current weightings and content against the live subject guide on ibo.org before planning, since syllabus detail is revised between cohorts.

sections.heading: Paper 2 at Standard Level: the 40% nobody prepares properly
paragraphs: Paper 2 is the largest single component of a Standard Level Economics grade and the one students revise for least deliberately. It lasts 1 hour 45 minutes, offers a choice of questions, and is marked out of 40. The question is built around a provided extract — text, and usually figures — and the parts run from short definitional answers up to a final 15-mark evaluation that must be grounded in the material supplied.

The losses are specific and repeatable. The early parts ask for definitions and students paraphrase instead. Two marks for 'define opportunity cost' go to the student who gives the definition, not to the one who gestures at the idea. The diagram parts carry marks for axes, labels, the correct shift and an indicated outcome, and further marks for the prose referring to the diagram; a correct unreferenced diagram is decorative. The calculation parts are lost to missing units, wrong bases for a percentage change, and working that cannot be followed.

The final part is where the biggest single block of marks sits and where the most time is wasted. It asks for evaluation using the extract. An answer that could have been written without reading the extract caps itself in the middle band however good the economics is. The habit that fixes it is mechanical: quote or cite a figure or phrase from the text in every analytical paragraph, then weigh one effect against another and state a reasoned preference in the closing lines.

The table below sets out the shape of a typical Standard Level data-response question with the mark pattern and the behaviour each part rewards. Part structures vary between sessions, so treat it as the anatomy of the paper rather than as a fixed template, and check a recent past paper through your school to see the current arrangement.

sections.heading: The portfolio is 30% of the grade and the only part with no clock on it
paragraphs: Three commentaries. Each responds to a published article the student chooses, each addresses a different unit of the syllabus, each is capped at 800 words, each is marked out of 15 across five criteria. Forty-five raw marks, scaled to 30% of a Standard Level grade. The criteria are published in advance, there is no time limit, and the work happens at a desk at home with the subject guide open. There is no other component in the Diploma with that profile.

Which is why the Standard Level plan should start here. A student who completes three well-scored commentaries by the end of DP1 has secured the largest tranche of their grade and faces the examination session needing a pass-level performance on two papers rather than a rescue. A student who begins the first commentary in DP2 term one is doing the hardest available version of the same task, under deadline, while the syllabus is still being taught.

The criteria divide cleanly into cheap marks and earned marks. Criterion A on diagrams and criterion B on terminology are close to free once a student knows that an unlabelled axis costs a mark and that a term must be used where it belongs. Criterion C, application and analysis, is where competent students sit mid-band because they explain theory well and connect it loosely to the article. Criterion D requires the chosen key concept to run through the commentary rather than appear once. Criterion E, evaluation, is usually absent from a first draft altogether.

The boundary on tutoring help is firm and it is in the student's interest, not ours. A tutor may teach the theory, explain the criteria, check that an article is inside the permitted window and suits the unit, read a draft and score it, and ask what a weak paragraph is missing. A tutor may not write, rewrite or complete any part of the commentary. Under IB rules that is malpractice and the sanction falls on the candidate. Services selling finished Internal Assessments exist in this market; one was found during research advertising them openly. Verify current rubric wording, word limits and article rules in the live subject guide before submission.

sections.heading: Where Standard Level students lose marks, unit by unit
paragraphs: Generic study advice does not help here, because the losses are specific to content. In the introduction unit, marks go to loose handling of opportunity cost and to production possibility diagrams drawn without stating what the axes represent. The fix is a single session on the vocabulary of the unit, because every later question reuses it.

Microeconomics produces the largest share of lost marks at Standard Level. Elasticity is the first offender: students know the formulae and misread the signs, or compute a value and then say nothing about what it means for the firm or the government. Market failure is the second: externality diagrams drawn with the welfare loss unshaded, or shaded in the wrong triangle. Indirect taxes and subsidies are the third, where the incidence split between consumer and producer is asserted rather than shown on the diagram.

Macroeconomics loses marks to vagueness. A question on demand-side policy wants a mechanism — interest rate to borrowing cost to investment to aggregate demand to output and price level — and students frequently jump from the first term to the last. The aggregate demand and supply diagram is often drawn correctly and then not used to support the written claim. Unemployment and inflation questions reward distinguishing types; answers that treat unemployment as one thing lose the marks for identifying which kind the data shows.

The global economy unit loses marks to assertion. Trade protection questions want the effect on named groups — domestic producers, consumers, the government, foreign exporters — rather than a general statement that protection is harmful. Exchange-rate questions want a direction and a mechanism. Development questions want a measure named before a judgement is offered. Each of these is a writing habit rather than a knowledge gap, which is why they respond quickly to marked practice.

sections.heading: What a Standard Level Economics plan costs in Dubai
paragraphs: Dubai's tutoring market publishes very little about price. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project quote no figure at all, and the two that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. The bands below are market figures in AED, attributed to whoever published them, and they are not IB Gram's price list; our arrangement begins with a free trial lesson and a consultation, and the rate for a specific subject and session length is quoted after that.

The more useful question for a Standard Level family is not the hourly rate but the total cost of a plan, because Standard Level plans are shorter than Higher Level ones. A portfolio-first block in DP1 is a defined piece of work with a defined end: three commentaries, three or four passes each, perhaps ten to twelve sessions in total. A Paper 2 technique block before the examination session is another defined piece, typically eight sessions. Those are numbers a household budget can be set against, in a way an open-ended hourly rate is not.

Standard Level also tends to cost less than Higher Level for the same provider, because the HL extension content and Paper 3 narrow the pool of people who can teach the course and the market prices that scarcity. A tutor comfortable with Standard Level Economics is easier to find than one who can drill terms-of-trade calculations, and the rate reflects it.

One piece of context from the emirate itself: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private-school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package. That does not reduce tutoring costs, but it does mean a family budget set last year is not being compressed from the school-fee side at the same time.

sections.heading: Online or an in-home tutor: deciding it properly for a Standard Level student
paragraphs: This is a real decision with real trade-offs, and the parent asking it deserves the trade-offs rather than a pitch. An in-home tutor in Dubai offers things that are genuinely hard to replicate: a person in the room reading a student's body language, a pen picked up mid-sentence, no device between the two of them. For a student who disengages the moment a screen is involved, those advantages decide the matter.

IB Gram does not sell that format in the UAE. A tutor travelling to a residence is part of our India service and nothing on this site offers it here, so a family that concludes they want somebody in the room should hire locally and should expect the in-home market band, which absorbs a journey across a city where a 17:00 crossing can take fifty minutes.

What online delivery adds for a Standard Level Economics student is narrower and concrete. The tutor is chosen for knowing this course, including its exclusions, rather than for living nearby. Screen-sharing suits diagram work, because a curve can be shifted, undone and redrawn and the final version saved to a file. Commentary drafts move as documents, scored and returned, with every version kept. Sessions can be recorded with consent, which is the feature families use most in the fortnight before the session. And the full hour is teaching.

sections.heading: Switching between Standard and Higher Level: when, and what it costs
paragraphs: Standard Level Economics students in Dubai raise the switch question in two directions, and both have deadlines that belong to the school rather than to the student. A student thriving at SL may want to move up for a university prerequisite; a student struggling at HL may want to drop down to protect the rest of their Diploma. The IB permits level changes within windows that schools administer, and the practical constraint is almost always the school's own internal cut-off rather than any external rule. Ask the DP coordinator for the date in writing.

Moving up from Standard to Higher Level means acquiring the extension content and preparing for Paper 3, which is a quantitative paper carrying 30% that the student has never sat. A switch made in DP1 is a manageable piece of catch-up work, usually a dedicated block on the extension topics plus a calculation strand. A switch attempted in DP2 is a different proposition, and the honest advice is often that the university condition should be met another way.

Moving down from Higher to Standard Level changes the weightings in the student's favour but also raises the stake on work already done. The portfolio moves from 20% to 30% of the grade, so commentaries written and scored under an HL plan suddenly carry more weight, and any compliance weakness in them matters more. The first session after a downward switch should be a re-score of the existing drafts against the criteria, not a celebration of the lighter content load.

A third situation is more common in Dubai than either switch: a student who transferred from A Level Economics into the Diploma mid-Year 12. A Level Economics is a strong foundation for content and no preparation at all for the commentaries, because the coursework instrument does not exist in that qualification. These students need the portfolio brief explained from the beginning and a realistic count of how many weeks remain before the school's first internal deadline.

sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects sitting alongside the Diploma
paragraphs: Something no competitor page in this market addresses, and a real constraint on a Dubai student's week. Private schools in Dubai must deliver Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of which international curriculum they are licensed to teach. KHDA's own guidance states that its requirements must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 applying to schools whose year begins in April. Federally, private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations.

The rules are specific enough to matter for timetabling. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes.

Language of instruction is also prescribed: Standard Arabic as the main language for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. KHDA further requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, and for these subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is strictly prohibited.

Why this belongs on an Economics page: a Standard Level student's available study hours are what remain after the Diploma and these mandatory subjects. A DP2 student carrying Arabic alongside six Diploma subjects has a materially different week from one who does not, and a tutoring plan built without knowing that will be abandoned by October. It is also the reason we schedule Economics sessions by Dubai area rather than offering one standard slot.

sections.heading: Permits, regulators and what a Dubai parent can actually verify
paragraphs: Private schools in Dubai are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Across the UAE the map is complete and worth knowing: ADEK in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, the Sharjah Private Education Authority in Sharjah, the Department of Knowledge in Ras Al Khaimah, and the Ministry of Education supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities also approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods.

Private tutoring is separately regulated. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. MoHRE's own service page is titled 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

A tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram operates no premises in the UAE, holds no such permit, and is not approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Any page claiming regulator-approved tutors for this market should be read sceptically, including on that specific point.

There is one more rule worth knowing for Abu Dhabi families reading this page: ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, with the MoHRE permit's code of conduct carrying a similar bar. Treat that as press-reported and verify against the current ADEK policy document. The practical takeaway everywhere in the UAE is the same: never arrange for your child's own class teacher to tutor them privately.

process.title: Tell us the level and the deadline
process.description: The first message needs three things: that the course is Standard Level, the school and DP year, and the next internal commentary deadline if one exists. Standard Level plans are built around the portfolio clock, so that date changes the order of work more than any grade does.

process.title: Free trial lesson with a Standard Level specialist
process.description: A full one-to-one session over live video, free and with no card details taken. The tutor works a real Paper 2 part or reads a commentary draft, then returns a short written note: what is secure, what is not, and which of the three components should be worked on first.

process.title: A plan in component order
process.description: A short written plan naming the component, the session count and the sequence. For most Standard Level students in DP1 the order is portfolio, then Paper 2 technique, then Paper 1 evaluation. For a DP2 student in February it is usually Paper 2 alone, because it carries 40%.

process.title: Sessions that end with marked work
process.description: A fixed slot on Gulf Standard Time with a timed question marked between lessons. Commentary drafts come back scored against criteria A to E with written reasons and questions. The revision is always done by the student, and the keyboard stays with them.

process.title: Checkpoint at the portfolio milestone
process.description: When each commentary is submitted internally, the plan is reviewed: what score did the school's marking suggest, and does the remaining time go to Paper 2 or Paper 1. This checkpoint replaces the vaguer monthly progress call, because it attaches to a real event.

whyPoints.title: Taught as Standard Level, not as diluted HL
whyPoints.description: A Standard Level student's first hour with us includes marking the extension topics off their syllabus. No time is spent on Paper 3 content, market power or the Marshall-Lerner condition, because none of it can appear on their examination. That alone recovers several evenings of misdirected revision.

whyPoints.title: The portfolio is treated as the priority
whyPoints.description: Thirty per cent of the grade, published criteria, no time limit and finished before the examination session. We work on it first and in DP1 where possible, because it is the only component a student can bank with near-certainty, and the hardest to rescue late.

whyPoints.title: Paper 2 taught by its parts
whyPoints.description: The heaviest Standard Level component is practised part type by part type — definition, explanation, diagram, calculation, 15-mark evaluation — against a written mark allocation, until the student can predict what the marker wants before writing the first line.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives the Dubai week
whyPoints.description: Slots are set by area and by what else is in the timetable, including the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies lessons Dubai schools must deliver. During Ramadan sessions move to post-Iftar timing rather than pausing, because a paused DP2 spring does not get its weeks back.

whyPoints.title: Sources named, unsourced numbers omitted
whyPoints.description: AED bands on this page are attributed to the provider or rate table that published them and marked as market rates. Regulatory statements cite u.ae, KHDA or MoHRE. Where nothing could be sourced — IB session dates, an IB equivalency threshold — the page says so rather than guessing.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Commentary support is scoring and questioning the student's own drafts. We do not write, rewrite, edit to completion or supply text for assessed work, and we state it here rather than in terms and conditions. Malpractice sanctions fall on the candidate, which settles the matter.

faqs.question: What is the difference in assessment between IB Economics SL and HL?
faqs.answer: Standard Level sits two papers and a portfolio: Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and three commentaries at 30%. Higher Level sits three papers and the same portfolio, weighted differently — Paper 1 at 20%, Paper 2 at 30%, the Higher Level-only Paper 3 at 30% and the portfolio at 20%. Higher Level also adds extension content including market power, asymmetric information, the Keynesian multiplier and terms of trade. The practical consequence is that the portfolio matters more at Standard Level and the quantitative load is much lighter. Confirm current weightings on ibo.org.

faqs.question: Does my Standard Level child sit Paper 3?
faqs.answer: No. Paper 3 is a Higher Level-only policy paper, and a Standard Level candidate sits Paper 1 and Paper 2 only. This matters more than it sounds, because a great deal of freely available IB Economics revision material is written for Higher Level and covers Paper 3 content such as the multiplier, terms of trade and the Marshall-Lerner condition. A Standard Level student revising that material is spending evenings on topics that cannot appear on their examination. The first thing we do is mark the extension content off their syllabus map.

faqs.question: Why does the Economics portfolio matter more at Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Because it carries 30% of a Standard Level grade against 20% at Higher Level, while being exactly the same piece of work: three commentaries, each on a different unit, each capped at 800 words, each marked out of 15 across five published criteria. It has no time limit and no examination hall. A Standard Level student who finishes three well-scored commentaries by the end of DP1 has secured almost a third of their grade before the session is a concern. One who starts in DP2 is doing the same task under the worst possible conditions.

faqs.question: How should a Standard Level student prepare for Paper 2 specifically?
faqs.answer: By part type rather than by topic. Paper 2 is marked out of 40 and built around a provided extract, running from short definitions through explanation and diagram parts to a 15-mark evaluation. Each part type rewards a different behaviour: a definition wants the definition, a diagram part wants labels and a prose reference to the diagram, a calculation wants units and visible working, and the final part wants the extract used. Practising each type separately against a written mark allocation works better than sitting full papers early, because it isolates the behaviour being fixed.

faqs.question: My child writes good explanations but still scores mid-band. What is missing?
faqs.answer: Almost always evaluation. The 15-mark parts of both Standard Level papers use command terms such as discuss, evaluate and examine, and those ask for a judgement that weighs one effect against another, considers a time horizon or magnitude, or questions an assumption. A clear, accurate explanation followed by a restatement of that explanation sits in the middle band by design. The fix is a closing paragraph that prioritises one effect over another and says why, and it is a writing habit rather than new content, so it responds quickly to marked practice.

faqs.question: Which Economics topics cause Standard Level students the most trouble?
faqs.answer: Microeconomics produces the largest share of lost marks. Elasticity is misread rather than miscalculated — students get the value and say nothing about what it means for a firm or a government. Externality diagrams are drawn with the welfare loss unshaded or shaded in the wrong triangle. Indirect tax and subsidy incidence is asserted in words instead of shown on the diagram. In macroeconomics the recurring loss is a missing transmission mechanism: a leap from an interest rate change straight to an output change, with nothing in between.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting Economics SL support in DP1 rather than waiting for mock results?
faqs.answer: Yes, for one structural reason: in DP1 the portfolio is still open, and it is 30% of the grade. Starting early means articles can be checked before writing, drafts scored against the criteria with time to revise, and the three commentaries spread across two terms instead of compressed into one. Waiting for DP2 mock results means arriving after the largest recoverable component has closed. The second reason is cheaper: the same number of sessions buys more when they are not competing with a deadline.

faqs.question: Can the tutor choose my child's commentary article for them?
faqs.answer: No, and a tutor who offers to is a problem rather than a service. A tutor may explain what makes an article usable — enough economics for the chosen unit, a date inside the permitted window, a source different from the other two commentaries — and may tell a student that a candidate article will not support the analysis they are planning. The selection itself is the student's, as is every word of the commentary. We give feedback as scores and questions, and the keyboard stays with the student throughout.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our home in Dubai for Economics SL lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; a tutor travelling to a residence is part of our India service only. Standard Level Economics for Dubai families is taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with screen-sharing for diagram work and marked scripts returned as files. The search phrase in this page's address is the one parents use, and the honest answer to it is that the teaching is the same and the delivery is online. Families wanting somebody in the room should hire locally.

faqs.question: How much should we budget for a Standard Level Economics plan in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Think in plans rather than in hours. A portfolio-first block is roughly ten to twelve sessions across two terms; a Paper 2 technique block is about eight. Market rates for qualified subject tutors in Dubai start around AED 150 per hour according to Unitors' published figures, with IB specialist bands at AED 200-450 in Bestimate's 2026 rate table and monthly online packages seen at AED 799 for eight sessions. Those are market figures, not ours. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson and a consultation, for the specific level and session length.

faqs.question: Can my child move from Standard Level to Higher Level Economics partway through?
faqs.answer: Level changes are possible within windows that schools administer, and the binding constraint is almost always the school's own internal cut-off date rather than an external rule — ask the DP coordinator for it in writing. Moving up means learning the extension content and preparing for Paper 3, a quantitative paper worth 30% that the student has never sat. In DP1 that is manageable with a dedicated block. In DP2 it rarely is, and if the reason is a university condition, it is usually worth asking the university whether another route satisfies it.

faqs.question: How do the mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education lessons affect a tutoring schedule?
faqs.answer: They occupy real timetable space. Dubai private schools must deliver Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies whatever international curriculum they are licensed for, and KHDA counts the instructional time in 40-minute lesson units with a 25-minute advised minimum per lesson. A DP2 student carrying Arabic alongside six Diploma subjects has a materially shorter week than one who is not. We ask what else is in the timetable before proposing a slot, which is why session times differ by school and by area across Dubai.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Dubai need a permit, and can we check?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible categories include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Anyone tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no figure should be quoted at you. You can simply ask a tutor whether they hold one.

faqs.question: What if our Standard Level tutor turns out to be the wrong match?
faqs.answer: Say so and a different tutor is proposed. The free trial lesson exists for precisely this: a full one-to-one session with no cost and no card details, after which the match is either right or it is not. Subject fit matters more at Standard Level than people expect, because the main risk is a tutor who teaches Higher Level by habit and spends hours on content that is not on your child's paper. If the written note after the trial reads like a Higher Level plan, that is the signal to change.

faqs.question: Are Economics SL lessons available during Dubai school holidays and Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the pattern changes rather than stops. During Ramadan the UAE school day shortens and sessions usually move to post-Iftar timing, which works better than pausing — a DP2 spring does not return the weeks it loses. Over the winter and spring breaks, families who are travelling often keep sessions running at a shifted hour because live video follows the student, while those staying in Dubai frequently use the break for the longer uninterrupted blocks that commentary drafting actually needs.

dubai/ib-dp-economics-sl-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Economics at Diploma level and nothing adjacent. Each one has marked student scripts against the current Economics guide, knows what a 15-mark part (b) needs that a 10-mark part (a) does not, and can read a commentary draft in criterion order rather than as an essay.

intro.heading: Judge an Economics tutor on what they hand back, not on what they promise
paragraphs: Most families looking for Economics help in Dubai start from a report card comment: works hard, needs to develop evaluation. That comment is accurate and useless. Evaluation in IB Economics is a specific, markable behaviour with a mark band attached, and a student who has never seen their own script marked against that band has no way of knowing which sentence lost the mark. The point of one-to-one tuition is to close that gap with paper, not with encouragement.

So this page is organised around evidence. Not a philosophy of learning, not a promise about grades, but the actual artefacts a Dubai family should expect to accumulate: scripts with mark allocations written beside each paragraph, commentary drafts where criterion C comments sit separately from criterion E comments, a running note of which syllabus unit has been covered and which has not, and a session log showing what was attempted and what was still wrong at the end. If a tutor cannot produce that file after six weeks, there is nothing to judge them on.

Economics SL is a three-component course and each component fails differently. Paper 1 is an extended-response paper where students answer one question from a choice, in two parts, and the commonest loss is a part (a) that describes instead of explaining and a part (b) that asserts instead of evaluating. Paper 2 is data response, where the marks sit in the data: a student who answers from memory and ignores the figures in the extract will cap out in the middle bands however well they write. The portfolio is three commentaries of 800 words each, assessed against five criteria, and most of the lost marks there are procedural rather than intellectual.

The online format earns its place in Dubai for a reason that has nothing to do with convenience. A student at a school in Mirdif or Al Barsha who needs an Economics HL-trained specialist for an SL course is choosing from whoever happens to be free within a thirty-minute drive. Over live video that constraint disappears, and the relevant question becomes whether the tutor can mark a data-response script properly. Screen sharing also suits this subject: a diagram drawn badly is the single most common deduction in Economics, and watching a student draw it live, axis labels and all, catches the habit in a way that marking a photographed page does not.

What follows is the full picture: how the three components are weighted, what each portfolio criterion rewards and the deduction we see most against it, where Paper 1 and Paper 2 marks actually go missing, what Dubai's market charges per hour and who charges it, what a tutor may and may not touch on an assessed piece under IB academic-honesty rules, and how a Dubai Year 12 timetable with mandatory KHDA subjects in it absorbs a weekly Economics session. Read the cost table before you ring anyone. Three of the six pages currently ranking for this search publish no price at all.
