sections.heading: Economics, mathematics and the route out of Dubai
paragraphs: Most families buying Economics tuition are buying a university application as much as a grade, so it is worth being clear about what actually gates that application. For economics degrees, the binding requirement is usually mathematics rather than Economics itself: competitive programmes commonly ask for Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and some will accept Applications and Interpretation. Economics at Standard Level is rarely the obstacle. A student taking Standard Level Economics and Standard Level mathematics who is aiming at a quantitative economics degree has a mathematics problem, not an Economics one.

For universities inside the UAE, there is a second process. The Ministry of Education operates certificate equivalency, and the requirements differ by curriculum. On the British track, students must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. On the American track, English proficiency can be shown with IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61, or 450 in SAT reading and writing, with at least 450 in SAT Mathematics.

For the IB specifically, do not accept a points threshold from a tutoring website, including this one. No IB equivalency figure in this project has been read on a Ministry of Education page, so the honest answer is to check moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation channel directly. Equivalency is a process the family and the university complete; it is not something IB Gram performs, guarantees or accelerates, and tutoring is not a requirement for it. Anyone implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency around a regulatory procedure.

process.title: Tell us the level and the deadline, not just the subject
process.description: The first message that helps names the level, the school's next internal deadline, and which units are already shaky. Standard Level Economics support is only as good as that information, because a tutor who has spent three years on Higher Level quantitative work is the wrong match for a family whose real problem is three commentaries due in five weeks.

process.title: A free diagnostic hour that produces a marked script
process.description: The first lesson is free, one per student, with no card details taken, and it ends with something you can read: a timed question marked against the band descriptors, with the diagram marked separately. That tells you whether you are buying content, technique, structure or timing, which is the only way to know what the following months should cost.

process.title: A written plan with hours and a number you can check
process.description: After the diagnostic you get a plan: which component first, how many sessions, how long each one runs, and what the total comes to, with marking either included or itemised. Compare that figure against the published market bands on this page. A plan you cannot price is a plan you cannot evaluate.

process.title: Review monthly against the plan, with the option to stop
process.description: Each month you receive the marked work and a short note on what moved and what did not. If the marks are flat after six weeks of consistent attendance, the diagnosis was wrong and the plan changes or stops. Stopping is a normal outcome and costs nothing beyond the sessions already taught.

whyPoints.title: A Standard Level specialist, not a Higher Level tutor working downwards
whyPoints.description: Standard Level Economics has its own shape: two papers, a portfolio carrying more proportional weight, and no quantitative paper. We match on that rather than on general subject knowledge, because the commonest waste in a Dubai tutoring budget is a term spent on content your child will never be examined on.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted against what the market publishes
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page is attributed to the provider that published it, with the band stated. Three of the six pages competing for this search publish no price at all, and two quote in US dollars. You cannot judge whether a quote is reasonable without knowing what the market charges.

whyPoints.title: Marking included or itemised, never implied
whyPoints.description: Reading and marking a timed data-response paper properly takes a tutor between twenty-five and forty minutes. Whether that sits inside the hourly rate or on top of it is the largest hidden variable in a Dubai tutoring invoice, so we state it before you pay rather than after the first month.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery, which is why the match is to the component
whyPoints.description: There are no home visits in the UAE, and that is a deliberate design choice rather than a limitation. It means a family in Arabian Ranches is choosing among everyone who teaches Standard Level Economics at six in the evening, instead of among the specialists willing to drive inland at that hour.

whyPoints.title: What a tutor will not do, written down before you pay
whyPoints.description: A commentary is the student's own work. We teach the unit, read drafts against the criteria and ask the questions an examiner would ask. We do not supply text, select articles or rework a draft to completion, and we say so in writing, because the pages selling the alternative in this search are selling your child a malpractice finding.

faqs.question: What should we expect to pay for Economics Standard Level tuition in Dubai per 60 minutes?
faqs.answer: Published rates in the emirate run from roughly AED 45 an hour at the budget end, where EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, through AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor, to AED 200 to 450 and above for a Diploma specialist on Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table. BartyED publishes AED 650 for premium named tutoring. Most families hiring for a Standard Level Economics component land between AED 200 and AED 450 per sixty minutes. Convert any quote to a sixty-minute equivalent first, because 45, 60, 90 and 120-minute sessions are all sold as a session fee here.

faqs.question: Is a 45-minute Economics session ever good value?
faqs.answer: For one specific job, yes. Forty-five minutes is enough to teach a single concept, drill two diagrams, or work through one section of a commentary against its criterion. It is not enough for anything involving a marked paper, because reading back a data-response script mark by mark takes longer than that on its own. The mistake families make is buying 45-minute sessions for exam preparation and wondering why the technique never changes. Price it per sixty minutes before deciding: a quote of AED 180 for 45 minutes is AED 240 an hour, which sits in the specialist band rather than the budget one.

faqs.question: Which Economics component gives the most marks back per hour paid?
faqs.answer: The portfolio, in almost every case. It is internally assessed, it has no clock on it, the criteria are published, and a draft can be rewritten before the school deadline. Six to nine hours of criterion-by-criterion work across DP1 and early DP2 moves it more reliably than the same hours spent on either written paper. Paper 2 is next, but roughly half the work there is marking rather than teaching, and it takes eight to twelve hours spread across a term. Exam-room timing is the cheapest intervention of all and the one Dubai families usually buy last, often in the final fortnight.

faqs.question: Does a Standard Level student need a tutor who has taught Higher Level Economics?
faqs.answer: No, and it can work against you. A tutor used to Higher Level depth will often teach the Higher Level version of a topic by default, including quantitative material that never appears on a Standard Level paper. The hours are billed either way. What you want is someone who can say, in one sentence, what they would cut from a Higher Level scheme of work to build a Standard Level one, and who has supervised Standard Level portfolios through to submission. Ask how many Standard Level candidates they have taken to a May session. A specific number is a better signal than a list of qualifications.

faqs.question: Why does starting Economics support in the final term cost more overall?
faqs.answer: Because the quantity of hours changes, not the hourly rate. In DP1 a tutor closes one gap at a time as it appears, at the single-topic price of two to four hours. In the final term the same gaps are being closed simultaneously, under a clock, usually at two sessions a week rather than one, and alongside five other subjects doing the same thing. Families who start in March typically buy twice the hours for a smaller movement, because exam technique takes repetition and repetition takes weeks. Nobody in the Dubai market raises their headline rate before the May session; the invoice grows because the plan has to.

faqs.question: Should we buy a monthly package or pay by the session?
faqs.answer: It depends on which component you are buying. Weekly consolidation through DP1 suits a monthly arrangement, because the work is continuous and a standing slot is useful. Portfolio work does not: commentary deadlines arrive in clusters, so three sessions in one fortnight and none for a month is the efficient shape, and a monthly package pays for the quiet weeks. Monthly online blocks advertised in the emirate sit around AED 799 for eight sessions, which looks competitive until you ask how long each session runs. Ask for the session length in minutes and the cancellation terms before committing to any block.

faqs.question: Is marking of a timed paper normally included in a Dubai tutor's rate?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is rarely stated. Marking a Standard Level data-response paper properly takes between twenty-five and forty minutes of a tutor's unpaid-looking time, so some providers include it, some bill it as a separate line, and some simply discuss the paper during the next session instead of marking it. That last version is the cheapest and the least useful, because the hour goes on reading rather than on correcting. Ask the question directly before you pay: is a timed paper marked between sessions, is the feedback written, and is any of that inside the quoted rate?

faqs.question: Can my child use UAE examples in an Economics answer?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they usually should. Examiners reward examples that are named, located, reasonably recent and genuinely used in the argument, and a Dubai student has strong material close at hand: the 5% VAT regime for tax incidence, the dirham's fixed exchange-rate arrangement for policy constraints, KHDA's decision that private school fees would not rise for 2026-27 as an intervention case, free zones for inward investment. The discipline is verification. Check the Federal Tax Authority, the Central Bank or KHDA's own newsroom before citing, and keep the answer on economic mechanisms and trade-offs rather than on political commentary.

faqs.question: How many diagrams does a Standard Level candidate actually need to draw accurately?
faqs.answer: Around ten cover almost everything that can be asked. Demand and supply with a determinant change, an indirect tax with incidence and welfare loss, a subsidy, a price ceiling and a price floor, a negative production externality, AD-AS with an output gap, and a tariff on an imported good are the recurring ones at this level. Each has a fixed checklist: labelled axes, a title, correctly directed shifts, the new equilibrium marked, and annotation tying the figure to the argument. Five minutes of drilling at the start of each session clears more marks than an hour of explanation, because these are habits rather than gaps in understanding.

faqs.question: Who sets the deadline for the Economics portfolio, the IB or the school?
faqs.answer: The school, within the IB's own submission requirements, and this surprises families every year. Dubai schools set internal deadlines for the portfolio that can differ by several weeks between two schools in the same district, and the coordinator's deadline is the one that governs your child's life. Most want the three commentaries finished during the first term of DP2. Ask the department for its dates in writing at the start of DP1 and plan the portfolio hours around them, rather than around the examination session. The commonest avoidable crisis in DP2 is internal assessment that arrives late in several subjects at once.

faqs.question: What may a tutor legally and ethically do with a commentary draft?
faqs.answer: Teach the unit, explain what each criterion rewards, ask whether the diagram supports the claim, point out where a paragraph fails to answer its own opening sentence, and ask the questions an examiner would ask. What a tutor may not do is supply sentences, choose the article, or rework a draft to completion. The commentary has to be the student's own work, and the consequence of crossing that line falls on the candidate, not on the tutor. Any provider offering a finished commentary is selling an academic-honesty finding. We state the boundary in writing before the first session rather than after a problem.

faqs.question: Are AI article summaries allowed in portfolio research?
faqs.answer: The source has to be read, and a summary is not the source. A student who writes a commentary from a model-generated précis usually produces something recognisable: a discussion of the economy in general terms with no figures from the article and no quotation that could only have come from it. The worse risk is fabrication, because an invented detail published under the candidate's own name is a serious problem. Several Dubai schools now ask for the article to be submitted alongside the commentary. The safe practice is simple: read the piece, annotate it by hand, and keep the original file with the draft.

faqs.question: How do the mandatory UAE subjects change how much tutoring time is available?
faqs.answer: Substantially, and families underestimate it. Every private school in Dubai teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies alongside its licensed curriculum, with KHDA requiring those arrangements from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. KHDA calculates the time on a 40-minute lesson unit and advises that no mandatory lesson run shorter than 25 minutes, and separate classes are required for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies. Add that to six Diploma subjects and the core, and most Year 12 weeks have one usable weekday evening plus part of a weekend.

faqs.question: Does my child need Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches to study economics at university?
faqs.answer: For many competitive economics degrees, the mathematics course is the binding requirement rather than the Economics one. Quantitative programmes commonly ask for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and a number will accept Applications and Interpretation, so the answer depends entirely on the universities on your child's list. Standard Level Economics is accepted widely. A student taking Standard Level mathematics and aiming at a quantitative economics degree has a mathematics problem, not an Economics one, and the fix is a conversation with the school's counsellor rather than more Economics tuition. Read the published entry requirements for the actual courses before changing anything.

faqs.question: How do we check that a tutor charging AED 400 an hour is worth it?
faqs.answer: Use the free first lesson as a test rather than an introduction. Ask for a timed fifteen-mark question requiring a diagram, sat before the session and marked before it starts. Then read what comes back. A specialist marks the diagram separately, names the missing label, states which band the answer sits in and why, and says what the next three sessions would do. A generalist writes encouraging comments on the prose and suggests a package. The rate is not the signal; the marked script is. Ask as well how many Standard Level candidates they have taken to a May session, and whether they hold a MoHRE private tuition work permit.

faqs.question: What happens if no Standard Level Economics specialist is free in our slot?
faqs.answer: We tell you, rather than filling the slot with whoever is available. Economics is one of the more commonly taught Group 3 subjects in Dubai Diploma schools, so coverage at this level is usually good, but a 5pm Gulf Standard Time request in the week before mock examinations can be genuinely full. The options are an alternative time with the specialist you want, a different tutor with a clear statement of what they have and have not taught, or a wait with a date attached. No competitor page in this search discloses a coverage limit at all, which does not mean they never hit one.

dubai/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.closingHeading: Fix what you are buying, then compare the price
dubai/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.closingBody: If your child sits Standard Level Economics at a Dubai school, the cheapest useful next step is a diagnostic rather than a package: one timed data-response question and one extended-response question, marked against the band descriptors with the diagrams marked separately, so you know whether you are buying content, technique, structure or timing. Tell us the level, the school's next internal deadline, and which units are shaky. The first lesson is free, one per student, with no card details taken. Lessons run live and one-to-one over video on Gulf Standard Time; there are no home visits in the UAE, and that service runs only in India.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach English A: Language and Literature as four distinct assessments rather than as one subject. Each card shows the components covered, levels taught, availability in Gulf Standard Time and whether they are currently taking Paper 1 drill work.

intro.heading: The paper that decides this subject contains nothing the student has studied
paragraphs: English A: Language and Literature is the most commonly chosen Group 1 course in Dubai's IB schools, and it is the one where students most often arrive at the mock papers with a nasty surprise. They have read the set works carefully. They can discuss the novel. Then Paper 1 puts an unseen text in front of them — a charity appeal, a political speech, a cartoon, a corporate apology, an infographic about water use — and asks for a guided analysis in timed conditions. Nothing on the paper has been studied, by design, and Paper 1 carries 35% of the grade at both levels.

That design is the whole character of the course, and it explains why tutoring here looks different from tutoring in Literature. The skill being examined is not knowledge of texts. It is the ability to read an unfamiliar text quickly, identify what it is trying to do to a reader, and build an argument about how its language, structure and visual choices achieve that. It is a trainable skill. It is trained by analysing many unseen texts under a clock, with someone marking the output against the criteria, and it is almost never trained adequately by a school teaching a cohort of twenty.

The other three components fail in their own characteristic ways. Paper 2 asks for a comparative essay on two studied works with no texts in the room, so students who memorised quotations but never built a comparative argument write two separate essays joined by a conjunction. The individual oral asks for a fifteen-minute analysis of a global issue through one literary work and one non-literary body of work, and students routinely choose a global issue so broad that neither extract can evidence it. The HL essay asks for 1,200 to 1,500 words on one body of work, and students treat it as an opportunity to write everything they know.

In Dubai there is a further layer worth naming. A large share of the students taking this course are working in English as an additional language at a high level, in a city where KHDA records 227 private schools teaching 17 different curricula to 387,441 students. Those students frequently have stronger analytical instincts than their written English suggests, which means criterion D — language — is costing them marks that criterion B would have given them. Separating those two problems is one of the first things a decent tutor does.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai. Home visiting is a service we offer only in India, which is stated on every page in our UAE set. Dubai students work with us one to one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with the paper or draft on a shared screen and the criterion wording beside it. For a subject assessed on timed writing and close reading, that is not a compromise — it is the format in which a tutor can mark a paragraph the moment it is written.

Paper 2 is a comparative essay sat without the studied works in the room
The individual oral is marked out of 40, ten marks on each of criteria A to D

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.programmesIntro: Students reach this course from several different places in Dubai's school system, and the entry route predicts which component gives trouble. These are the stages we support.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme English A: Language and Literature
programmes.description: Two years studying literary works alongside non-literary bodies of work, assessed through Paper 1 (guided analysis of unseen non-literary texts), Paper 2 (comparative essay on studied literary works), the individual oral on a global issue, and at Higher Level an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words. A learner portfolio runs underneath the whole course without being marked directly.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai this is the default Group 1 choice at most IB schools, with Literature offered as the smaller alternative. Class sizes mean individual timed-paper marking is scarce, and that scarcity is almost always what families are buying when they look for outside help.

programmes.name: MYP Language and Literature
programmes.description: Assessed on analysing, organising, producing text and using language, each on an eight-point scale. MYP 4 and 5 introduce non-literary text analysis in a form close to what Paper 1 demands, which gives students from a full MYP route a genuine advantage in DP1 that students arriving at 16 do not have.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools running MYP straight into DP, among them Dubai International Academy and GEMS World Academy, give five years of this. Students joining a Dubai IB sixth form from an IGCSE or CBSE background start Paper 1 work effectively from scratch.

programmes.name: IGCSE English Language and English Literature
programmes.description: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE English Language both examine reading of unseen non-fiction, which transfers usefully. What does not transfer is the analytical register: IGCSE rewards identifying a technique and stating its effect, while DP Paper 1 rewards an argument about how the whole text positions a reader. Rebuilding that register is a specific, short piece of work.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for 37% of Dubai private-school enrolment (KHDA, 2024-25), so the IGCSE-to-DP crossover is the most common route into this course in the emirate, and the technique-spotting habit is the most common thing we have to unpick.

programmes.name: English B, for students deciding between courses
programmes.description: The language acquisition course, assessed on productive writing, reading and listening comprehension and an individual oral. Some Dubai students are placed in English A when English B would serve them better, or the reverse, and the decision has consequences for the bilingual diploma and for university applications.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's cohorts are unusually multilingual, so this placement question comes up constantly here. It is a decision for the school's DP coordinator with the family, and we will give an honest view of the written evidence rather than a recommendation dressed as one.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.subjectsIntro: This course is rarely the only one a Dubai Diploma student needs help with in the same term. These are the subjects we most often run alongside it.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 guided analysis of unseen non-literary texts, Paper 2 comparative essay, individual oral on a global issue, and at HL a 1,200 to 1,500 word essay. Marks are lost to unseen-text panic and to criterion D language control.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: The same assessment architecture applied entirely to literary works, with Paper 1 offering unseen literary extracts rather than non-literary texts. Students sometimes move between the two courses in DP1 and need the difference mapped properly.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word prescribed-title essay plus an exhibition of three objects with commentaries. Language and Literature students usually write well here because the course already trains them to ask how a text makes a claim credible.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source papers requiring evaluation of origin, purpose, value and limitations, plus a historical investigation. The closest analytical neighbour: both subjects reward reading a document for what it was built to do.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches with an experimental study report. Command-term discipline decides marks here, and students who write loosely in English A tend to write loosely in Psychology too.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics, the global economy and a portfolio of commentaries on published articles. The commentaries demand exactly the close reading of a non-literary source that Paper 1 trains.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Organisational structure, marketing, operations and finance with a research project. Students frequently take it alongside this course and find the written register the harder half.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics-led mathematics with a graphical-calculator paper and a mathematical exploration. The usual maths pairing for humanities-weighted Dubai timetables, and the exploration lands in the same term as the HL essay.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Comparative study, process portfolio and exhibition. The comparative study rewards the same analytical move as a Paper 1 response: reading a made object for the choices behind it.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay. Studies in Language and Literature is a popular EE category in Dubai, and the commonest problem is a question that invites summary rather than analysis.

sections.heading: Language and Literature or Literature: which course is your child actually in?
paragraphs: Parents searching for an IB DP english A language and literature home tutor in Dubai are sometimes searching for the wrong course, because the two English A options share an assessment architecture and differ in their material. Both have a Paper 1 guided analysis, a Paper 2 comparative essay, an individual oral on a global issue and an HL essay. The difference is what Paper 1 contains and what the course studies: Language and Literature puts non-literary texts in Paper 1 and studies non-literary bodies of work alongside literary ones, while Literature stays within literary texts throughout.

The consequence for tutoring is substantial. A student in Language and Literature needs practice reading advertisements, speeches, columns, cartoons, photographs and infographics as constructed arguments. A student in Literature needs practice reading unseen poetry and prose extracts. Hiring a tutor who drills the wrong one is a common and expensive error, and it happens because school documentation often says only English A and parents reasonably assume one course exists.

The quickest way to check is the individual oral. In Language and Literature the oral pairs one literary work with one non-literary body of work — a set of advertising campaigns, a photographer's output, a politician's speeches. In Literature both extracts come from literary works, one of them originally written in another language. If your child's oral involves a corpus of advertisements or a news photographer, they are in Language and Literature, and the table below sets out what follows from that.

sections.heading: Paper 1: analysing a text nobody has prepared for
paragraphs: Paper 1 presents unseen non-literary texts, each with a guiding question, and asks for an analysis in timed conditions. Standard Level candidates respond to one text in 75 minutes; Higher Level candidates respond to both in 135 minutes. The paper carries 35% of the grade at both levels, which makes it the single heaviest component in the course and the one where a few weeks of properly marked practice changes an outcome most reliably.

The mark distribution tells you where the work is. The response is marked out of 20, five marks each on criterion A understanding and interpretation, criterion B analysis and evaluation, criterion C focus and organisation, and criterion D language. Those are equal weights, which students almost never behave as though they believe. The typical weak response spends its energy on A — explaining what the text says — and treats B as a list of techniques, C as whatever order things came out in, and D as a matter of luck. Four criteria at five marks each means structure and language control are worth exactly as much as insight.

The guiding question is also routinely ignored. It is there to focus the response, and a response that answers a different question has capped its criterion C mark before it starts. In a session we read the text cold, spend four minutes on what it is built to do to a reader, write an opening paragraph to the clock, and then mark that paragraph aloud against all four criteria with the marks stated. Doing that ten or twelve times, with the text type changing each time, is what Paper 1 preparation actually consists of. No tutor can promise a grade from it, and no honest one will.

sections.heading: Paper 2: one comparative argument, not two essays side by side
paragraphs: Paper 2 asks for a comparative essay on two of the literary works studied, chosen in response to one of four general questions, sat without the texts in the room. It is worth 35% at Standard Level and 25% at Higher Level. The marks are out of 30: ten for criterion A knowledge, understanding and interpretation, ten for criterion B analysis and evaluation, five for criterion C focus and organisation, and five for criterion D language.

The characteristic failure is structural rather than textual. A student writes four paragraphs on the first work, four on the second, and a closing paragraph observing that both are concerned with power. That is two essays with a conjunction between them, and it caps criterion B regardless of how good the individual readings are, because comparison is the thing being analysed. A response built around points of comparison — where the two works do the same thing differently, and what that difference reveals — can score well on both A and B with fewer quotations.

The second failure is preparation shaped by the wrong assumption. Students revise by memorising quotations, which helps criterion A a little and nothing else, when the productive revision is building three or four flexible comparative frames across the studied works that can be bent to whichever of the four questions appears. In sessions we build those frames with the student and then test them against past general questions, which is uncomfortable because the frames usually fail the first two questions they meet. That failure is the useful part.
bullets: 30 marks: A 10, B 10, C 5, D 5 — analysis and knowledge carry two-thirds between them

sections.heading: The individual oral: a global issue narrow enough to be evidenced
paragraphs: The individual oral asks the student to examine, through one literary work and one non-literary body of work, the ways in which a global issue of their choice is presented. It runs fifteen minutes — ten minutes of student presentation and five minutes of teacher questions — and is marked out of 40, with ten marks on each of criteria A to D. At Standard Level it is worth 30% of the grade; at Higher Level, 20%.

Almost every weak oral has the same root cause: the global issue is too large. A student chooses the representation of gender, or climate change, or migration, and then has ten minutes to show how two extracts present something that could fill a library. The response becomes general, criterion A loses marks for thin interpretation of the extracts themselves, and criterion B has nothing specific to analyse. A narrow issue — how a particular kind of institutional language transfers blame away from an institution, say — gives two extracts something to do and gives the student something arguable to say.

The second common problem is the pairing. The literary work and the non-literary body of work have to illuminate the same issue, and students frequently choose a non-literary corpus because it is available rather than because it connects. In a session we test the pairing by asking the student to state, in one sentence, what the non-literary body of work shows about the issue that the literary work does not. If they cannot, the pairing is decorative. Beyond that, the work is timed rehearsal with marks given, and the student's own extract annotations — which they take into the oral — audited for whether they are prompts or a script.
bullets: Fifteen minutes: ten of presentation, five of questions. 40 marks, ten per criterion
Narrow the global issue until two extracts can genuinely evidence it
Test the pairing: what does the non-literary work show that the literary one does not?
Annotations are prompts, not a script — reading aloud from a script costs criterion C and D

sections.heading: The four criteria, by letter and by mark, across every component
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes the criterion marks, and it is the single most useful thing a parent can see. The same four criteria run across every component of the course — A knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B analysis and evaluation; C focus and organisation; D language — but the marks attached to each change from component to component, and so does where a student can afford to be weak.

The practical reading of the table below is that organisation and language are not the soft half of the mark scheme. On Paper 1 they are half the marks. On the individual oral they are twenty marks out of forty. A student who writes brilliantly unstructured analysis is losing a quarter to a half of the available credit on every component, and because teachers tend to comment on content first, that student often has no idea it is happening.

This matters particularly for Dubai's multilingual cohorts. A student writing in English as an additional language at a high level may hold criterion A and B marks that are genuinely strong while criterion D holds them two grades below what their thinking deserves. The teaching response to that is not more content and not more reading; it is targeted work on sentence control, register and the precision of analytical verbs. Diagnosing which of the four criteria is actually costing the grade takes one marked paper and about twenty minutes, and it changes what the next ten sessions should contain.

sections.heading: The HL essay and the learner portfolio: the two things students underrate
paragraphs: The HL essay is 1,200 to 1,500 words on one literary work or one non-literary body of work studied during the course, developed from a line of inquiry the student chooses. It carries 20% of the Higher Level grade and is marked out of 20, five marks on each criterion. Its difficulty is entirely in the question. A line of inquiry that can be answered by describing the work will produce an essay that describes the work, and no amount of good writing afterwards will recover criterion B.

The test we use is simple and students dislike it: state the line of inquiry, then ask whether a well-read person could answer it in two sentences from a summary of the work. If they could, it is not a line of inquiry. The usable version is narrow enough to require evidence from specific moments in the text and open enough that the answer is not obvious before the research starts. Getting there usually takes two sessions of discarding questions, which feels like no progress and is the most valuable part of the process.

The learner portfolio is the other underrated element. It is not directly assessed, which students read as meaning it does not matter. In practice it is where the material for the individual oral and the HL essay accumulates, and a student with two years of recorded responses to texts has a bank of possible global issues and lines of inquiry. A student with an empty portfolio in DP2 is inventing both from memory under deadline pressure. We ask to see the portfolio in a first session for exactly this reason: it predicts how much groundwork the next components will need.
bullets: HL essay: 1,200 to 1,500 words, 20 marks, five per criterion
A line of inquiry answerable from a summary is not a line of inquiry

sections.heading: Language subjects in Dubai: what KHDA requires alongside the IB course
paragraphs: Dubai families looking at English A support frequently have a second language question running in parallel, because Dubai private schools carry mandatory UAE subjects regardless of the international curriculum they are licensed to teach. KHDA's published guidelines make Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies compulsory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with the requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The operational detail in those guidelines is specific and worth knowing, because it affects timetables and therefore when a DP student is actually free. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, KHDA requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, stating that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of differing curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

Two further points come up often. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. And for these subjects the guidelines state that using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited — which is a real constraint on how any tutoring in those subjects can be described, including ours. Teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic are required to hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach them.

sections.heading: Honesty, drafts and the question a tutor will not answer
paragraphs: This course has three places where honesty gets complicated, and all three come up in Dubai sessions regularly. The HL essay is submitted work, so the boundary around drafting matters. The individual oral is delivered live from the student's own annotations, which is a safeguard but also a place where over-prepared scripts cause problems. And the availability of generative text tools has made it trivially easy for a student to submit prose that is not theirs, in a subject where language control is a quarter of the marks.

Our boundary is the one we state on every page. A tutor teaches, explains the criteria, questions a draft and gives feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor does not produce assessed work — not the HL essay, not the oral script, not a Paper 2 answer for memorisation. Providers in this market do sell completed Internal Assessments, one of them openly, and a student who submits bought work faces an IB malpractice finding that no refund addresses. We also reference and link official IB subject documents rather than reproducing or supplying them.

The practical version in a session: when a student asks what to write, the answer is a question about what they think the text is doing. Feedback names the criterion and the sentence; the rewriting is the student's. On the oral, we will tell a student when their annotations have become a script, because a read-aloud oral loses marks on criteria C and D and reads to an examiner exactly as it sounds. And where a draft's register shifts abruptly mid-paragraph, we will ask about it, which is occasionally an awkward conversation and is better had with us than with a coordinator.

If the diagnosis says the individual oral or criterion D language control is where the marks are, we will say so even when that means fewer sessions than you expected to book.

process.description: The trial session runs on the student's own paper or draft, with the criterion wording on screen. By the end the student should be able to say which criterion each of their own paragraphs is serving, and you should have enough to decide whether to continue.

process.description: Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice is written to the clock and returned with a mark against each criterion rather than a general comment. Those marks are tracked across cycles so progress is a pattern you can see, not a claim we make.

process.description: One session before the school's deadline spent only on word count against the 1,200 to 1,500 band, whether every paragraph answers the line of inquiry, and whether the evidence comes from the work itself rather than from secondary criticism.

whyPoints.title: Paper 1 practice that is timed and marked
whyPoints.description: Unseen non-literary analysis is a trainable skill and it is trained by writing to a clock and having the output marked against criteria. Untimed practice builds confidence and not much else, which is why school-set homework often fails to move a Paper 1 mark.

whyPoints.description: A multilingual student with strong criterion A and B marks and weak criterion D has a specific, fixable problem that looks like weak comprehension and is not. Separating the two at the diagnosis stage changes what the next ten sessions contain.

faqs.question: What is actually on Paper 1 in English A: Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: Unseen non-literary texts, each with a guiding question, and nothing the student has studied. Standard Level candidates analyse one text in 75 minutes; Higher Level candidates analyse both in 135 minutes. The text could be a charity appeal, a political speech transcript, an opinion column, an infographic, an advertisement, a cartoon or a memoir extract. The response is marked out of 20, five marks each on understanding, analysis, organisation and language. It carries 35% of the grade at both levels, which makes it the heaviest single component.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether my child is in Language and Literature or Literature?
faqs.answer: Look at the individual oral. In Language and Literature the oral pairs one literary work with one non-literary body of work — a set of advertising campaigns, a photographer's output, a politician's speeches. In Literature both extracts come from literary works, one of them originally written in another language. The other giveaway is Paper 1: unseen non-literary texts in Language and Literature, unseen literary extracts in Literature. School documents often say only English A, which is why families regularly book the wrong drill material.

faqs.question: Why is my child scoring well on analysis but not on the overall mark?
faqs.answer: Almost always criteria C and D. Across the components, focus and organisation plus language control carry between a quarter and half of the available marks: on Paper 1 they are ten of the twenty, and on the individual oral twenty of the forty. Because teachers comment on content first, a student with strong insight and loose structure can go a long time without being told what is costing them. One marked paper, read against the criterion marks, usually identifies it in twenty minutes.

faqs.question: My child writes excellent ideas in slightly imperfect English. Is that fixable?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a different problem from weak comprehension, which is the main thing to establish. A student working in English as an additional language at a high level often holds genuinely strong marks on understanding and analysis while language control holds the overall grade down. The response is not more reading and not more content; it is targeted work on sentence control, register and the precision of analytical verbs. That is narrow, teachable and measurable across a handful of marked responses.

faqs.question: How many Paper 1 practice responses does a student actually need?
faqs.answer: For most Dubai students, ten to twelve written to the clock and marked criterion by criterion, with the text type rotating each time so no genre becomes a comfort zone. Fewer than that and the student has met too narrow a range of texts; many more and the returns flatten unless the marking is changing their behaviour. Untimed practice is close to worthless here, because the skill being examined includes deciding what to analyse in the first four minutes.

faqs.question: What makes a good global issue for the individual oral?
faqs.answer: Narrowness. A student who chooses the representation of gender, or climate change, has ten minutes to show how two extracts present something that could fill a library, and the response goes general. A narrow issue — how a particular kind of institutional language shifts blame away from an institution, for instance — gives both extracts something specific to do and gives the student something arguable to say. The test is whether the student can state in one sentence what each extract contributes to the issue that the other does not.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help choose the extracts for the individual oral?
faqs.answer: A tutor can pressure-test a pairing and explain what the criteria reward, but the choice is the student's and the school's teacher supervises it. What we do is ask the one question that exposes a decorative pairing: what does the non-literary body of work show about this global issue that the literary work does not? If the student cannot answer, the second extract is there because it was available rather than because it connects, and the oral will lose marks on interpretation and analysis.

faqs.question: Why does my child's Paper 2 essay score lower than their individual essays?
faqs.answer: Usually structure. A response that gives four paragraphs to the first work, four to the second and a closing observation that both concern power is two essays joined by a conjunction, and it caps the analysis criterion however good the individual readings are. Paper 2 marks comparison itself. An essay built around points of comparison — where the two works do the same thing differently, and what the difference reveals — scores better with fewer quotations. It is a planning fix rather than a content one.

faqs.question: How should a student revise for Paper 2 when they cannot take the texts in?
faqs.answer: By building three or four flexible comparative frames across the studied works rather than memorising quotations. Quotation accuracy helps the knowledge criterion slightly and nothing else. A frame is a comparative angle robust enough to be bent to whichever of the four general questions appears: how each work handles time, or authority, or an unreliable narrating voice. The productive work is stress-testing those frames against past questions, where they usually fail the first two they meet.

faqs.question: What length should the HL essay be and how narrow should the question be?
faqs.answer: Between 1,200 and 1,500 words, on one literary work or one non-literary body of work studied during the course, marked out of 20 with five marks on each criterion. The question matters more than the length. Our test: state the line of inquiry, then ask whether a well-read person could answer it in two sentences from a summary. If they could, it will produce an essay that describes rather than analyses. Narrowing usually takes two sessions of discarding questions.

faqs.question: Does the learner portfolio matter if it is not marked?
faqs.answer: It is not directly assessed and it still decides how hard DP2 is. The portfolio is where two years of responses to texts accumulate, and a student with a full one arrives at the individual oral and the HL essay with a bank of possible global issues and lines of inquiry already half-formed. A student with an empty portfolio invents both from memory under deadline pressure. We ask to see it in a first session because it predicts how much groundwork the remaining components will need.

faqs.question: Do you visit students at home in Dubai for English sessions?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not operate home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visiting is a service we run only in India. Dubai students work with us one to one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, with the paper or draft on a shared screen beside the criterion wording. For a subject assessed on timed writing, that is genuinely the better format — a paragraph can be marked the moment it is written, and a mark can be attached to each criterion while the student still remembers what they were trying to do.

faqs.question: Does my child still have to take Arabic alongside the IB Diploma in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Dubai private schools carry mandatory UAE subjects regardless of the international curriculum they are licensed to teach. KHDA's published guidelines make Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies compulsory in all Dubai private schools, with separate classes required for Arabs and non-Arabs — combined classes are stated to be strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. Your school's own timetable is the place to confirm how it applies to your child.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark my child's HL essay draft?
faqs.answer: A tutor can read a draft, name which criterion each paragraph is serving, point out where evidence comes from secondary criticism rather than from the work, and say where the line of inquiry has stopped being answered. A tutor cannot rewrite it, and should not type a replacement sentence. Producing part of an assessed component is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student. Families sometimes find that limit frustrating in the final fortnight; it is still the only safe version of the work.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if the exams are a few months away?
faqs.answer: For Paper 1, no — it is the most responsive component to late, properly marked practice, because the skill is procedural rather than cumulative. For Paper 2, partly: comparative frames can be built in a few weeks if the works have genuinely been read. For the HL essay and the individual oral, a late start means working with whatever groundwork exists rather than choosing freely, because both depend on material gathered earlier. Nobody can promise a specific grade from a short run, and anyone who does is selling something else.

faqs.question: What does English A tutoring cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates as of October 2026 put budget online tuition at roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, qualified subject specialists online at AED 150 to 300, and IB specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above — TutorChase publishes AED 270, Unitors lists IB from AED 200, and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table gives 200 to 450-plus. In-home one-to-one runs AED 180 to 500 once travel is priced in. Those are other providers' published figures, cited so you can check them; ask any provider whether a quoted rate includes VAT.

intro.heading: What a marked script shows that a report card cannot
paragraphs: A Dubai parent usually discovers an English A problem through a number. A predicted grade arrives, or a mock comes back, and it says 4 where the family expected 6. What the number does not say is which of four criteria produced it, and that is the whole question. A script that loses marks on criterion B, analysis and evaluation, needs a different term of work from one that loses marks on criterion D, language. The first needs a method for reading effect; the second needs sentence-level editing. Treating them as the same problem wastes a term.

This page is built around that distinction, because the evidence is available and almost nobody uses it. Your child's school holds marked Paper 1 scripts, Paper 2 essays, recordings of practice orals and drafts of the HL essay. Each one carries a criterion-by-criterion breakdown. Read four of them together and a pattern appears within twenty minutes: the same criterion is capping the grade across every component, and it is usually the same one in a given student from Year 12 onwards.

The second thing a marked script shows is whether the problem is knowledge or transfer. A student who can talk fluently about a poem in class and then produces a thin Paper 1 is not short of understanding. They are short of a procedure for turning understanding into a marked answer in seventy-five minutes under exam conditions, including the decision about what to leave out. That is a trainable thing, and it is trained by doing timed work and having it marked, not by discussing the texts again. The distinction is worth holding on to, because it decides whether the next six weeks are spent rereading the set works or building a planning routine that survives a seventy-five minute paper.

Language and Literature has a particular version of this problem. Half the course is non-literary: advertisements, speeches, opinion columns, photographs, infographics, cartoons, political campaign material. Students tend to be taught the literary half with more rigour, because that is what English teaching has traditionally been, and then meet an unseen non-literary text in Paper 1 with no stable method for handling it. In Dubai, where many students arrive from a British Year 11 that taught literature almost exclusively, this gap is the single commonest diagnosis we make.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We hold no accreditation from the IB, KHDA or any other authority, we have no centre in Dubai, and we do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India. What we do is match your child to a named English A specialist, run one-to-one lessons over live video on Gulf Standard Time, mark the work in writing, and keep a record you can read. The first lesson is free.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.programmesIntro: English A: Language and Literature sits in Group 1 of the Diploma, and Dubai students reach it from three main directions: up through the MYP in the same school, across from a British Year 11 doing IGCSE English Language and Literature, or in from another system entirely. Each arrival needs a different first six weeks, so the programme notes below are about the handover rather than about the course in general.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Available at Standard and Higher Level. Both levels sit Paper 1, a guided textual analysis of unseen non-literary material, and Paper 2, a comparative essay on literary works, and both submit the individual oral. Higher Level adds the HL essay and requires six literary works against four at Standard Level, alongside a wider set of non-literary bodies of work. The learner portfolio runs underneath the whole course and is compulsory even though it is not directly assessed.
programmes.countryNote: Most Dubai IB schools stream Group 1 by prior attainment rather than by preference, so families often find the course was chosen for them. Language and Literature is the commoner of the two English A options in the emirate's full-continuum schools, including Dubai International Academy Emirates Hills, Uptown International School and Raffles World Academy. KHDA mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education sit on top of the six Diploma subjects, which is why evening drafting time is tighter here than families expect.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language and Literature is assessed on four criteria - analysing, organising, producing text, and using language - and on-screen eAssessment is available in Year 11. Students who worked seriously with those criteria recognise the Diploma's A to D structure immediately. Students who were marked holistically find criterion B the hardest adjustment, because the Diploma wants evaluation of effect rather than identification of technique.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the MYP-to-DP transition usually happens inside one school, so the same department teaches both. The practical consequence is that a student carries their MYP habits straight into Year 12 without anyone naming them. An outside reader looking at four marked MYP pieces alongside the first Diploma script is often the first person to point out that the student has been listing devices for three years.

programmes.name: IGCSE to Diploma handover
programmes.description: A large share of Dubai students arrive from Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE English rather than from the MYP. IGCSE rewards accurate identification and well-organised response; the Diploma rewards argument about effect and context. The gap is not vocabulary or reading speed, it is the move from what the writer does to why it works on this reader, and it takes roughly a term of marked work to close.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools dominate Dubai private enrolment, so the IGCSE route into the Diploma is common across the emirate. Students coming from an IGCSE literature-heavy diet are the ones most exposed by Paper 1's non-literary material, and a tutor's first job is usually to build a repeatable procedure for an unseen advertisement or opinion column rather than to revise the set texts.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.subjectsIntro: On a Language and Literature page the useful list is the list of things actually marked, plus the courses Dubai students most often carry next to it. Each entry names the format, where the marks sit and the commonest reason a script scores below its potential.

subjects.name: Paper 1: guided textual analysis
subjects.description: One unseen non-literary text with a guiding question at Standard Level in 1 hour 15 minutes; two texts, one analysis each, in 2 hours 15 minutes at Higher Level. Worth 35% at both levels. Scripts lose marks when a student identifies features without arguing their effect on a specified reader.

subjects.name: Paper 2: comparative essay
subjects.description: 1 hour 45 minutes, four general questions, one chosen, two studied literary works compared. Worth 35% at Standard Level and 25% at Higher Level. No text is available in the room, so the limiting factor is usually recall of precise detail rather than analytical ability.

subjects.name: Individual oral
subjects.description: A 10-minute prepared presentation followed by 5 minutes of teacher questions, examining how a global issue is presented in one literary work and one non-literary body of work. Worth 30% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher Level. Weak orals describe the global issue instead of analysing its construction.

subjects.name: HL essay
subjects.description: A 1,200-1,500 word essay on a literary work or non-literary body of work studied in the course, developed from the learner portfolio and worth 20% of the Higher Level grade. The line of inquiry has to be narrow enough to sustain, which is where most drafts go wrong.

subjects.name: Non-literary bodies of work
subjects.description: Advertising, speeches, opinion journalism, photography, infographics, cartoons and campaign material studied as a coherent body rather than as isolated examples. Under-taught in many schools, and the direct cause of weak Paper 1 performance for students arriving from a literature-heavy IGCSE.

subjects.name: The learner portfolio
subjects.description: Compulsory and not directly assessed, which is why students neglect it. It is the source material for both the individual oral and the HL essay, so a thin portfolio in Year 12 becomes a scramble for a line of inquiry in Year 13.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: The other Group 1 English option, built entirely from literary works - nine at Standard Level and thirteen at Higher Level - with no non-literary material. Dubai schools usually decide which course a student sits, but understanding the difference explains what Paper 1 will contain.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The language acquisition course for students who are not working at first-language level. Placement between English A and English B is made by the school and occasionally challenged by families; the honest test is whether the student can sustain analysis of an unseen text, not how fluently they speak.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Shares the Diploma's analytical vocabulary and competes for the same drafting weeks as the HL essay. Students who can argue in English A usually find the TOK exhibition straightforward; the traffic runs in that direction rather than the reverse.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in English
subjects.description: A 4,000-word essay supervised by a school teacher. A tutor may discuss a research question, method and the shape of an argument, and may give written feedback on the student's own drafts, but the essay is the student's work throughout and the school supervisor stays the examining relationship.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.regionsTitle: Scheduling an English A session around a Dubai week
dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.regionsIntro: What matters for this subject is not distance but when a student can realistically sit down with a marked script and concentrate for an hour. The notes below record what each community's school run and evening commitments do to that window, because a session booked at the wrong hour gets cancelled twice and then abandoned.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Lake Towers
regions.note: Apartment living, short school runs and a lot of households where both parents work late. A 17:00 or 18:00 slot sticks better here than 16:00, and the student is usually working at a desk in a shared room, so a headset matters more than a study.

regions.name: Palm Jumeirah and Al Sufouh
regions.note: Short journeys to the Al Sufouh school strip, so students are home early and 16:00 works. This is the cluster where families most often ask for two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one, which suits timed Paper 1 practice.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai and Business Bay
regions.note: Mixed catchment with long bus routes out to Nad Al Sheba and Al Barsha. Students frequently arrive home after 16:30 and need to eat before concentrating, so a 17:30 start and a hard 18:30 finish is the realistic shape.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate and Al Quoz
regions.note: Fast-growing villa communities with a short drive to several IB and British schools. Sibling pick-ups stagger the evening, and these are the households where a fixed weekly slot that everyone plans around outperforms week-by-week negotiation.

regions.name: The Greens, The Views and Barsha Heights
regions.note: Dense, central and close to the Al Barsha school cluster. Students here often have co-curricular commitments three evenings a week, so the marked-work cycle carries more of the plan than the live session does.

regions.name: Al Qusais, Muhaisnah and Mirdif
regions.note: The eastern side of the emirate, longer commutes and a high proportion of students also doing Arabic tuition for the KHDA mandatory subjects. Later slots and a fortnightly marking rhythm work better than two live sessions a week.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: A newer catchment where students travel out to schools in Al Barsha, Emirates Hills and JVT. Journeys are the longest variable in this list, and families here are the most likely to want a single weekend session plus marked work midweek.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh, Al Barsha and the Marina corridor
schoolClusters.note: The central school strip serving Marina, JLT, Palm Jumeirah and the Greens. Group 1 provision here covers both English A courses and English B, and students from these schools are the easiest to schedule because journeys are short.

schoolClusters.city: Nad Al Sheba, Meydan and Sobha Hartland
schoolClusters.note: The newer southern cluster, drawing from Downtown, Business Bay and Dubai Hills. Several of these schools run the Diploma alongside A Levels, so Group 1 cohorts are small and a student's own teacher is often their only reader.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.modesIntro: English A moves when work is produced, marked and corrected on a cycle. The three shapes below differ in what gets marked rather than in how many hours are sold, and the right one depends on which component is closest and what the evidence says is capping the grade.

modes.title: The marked-script cycle
modes.description: The default. Your child produces one timed piece a fortnight - a Paper 1 analysis or a Paper 2 essay - and it comes back annotated with criterion letters before the next session. The live hour is then spent rewriting the weakest paragraph with the tutor rather than discovering the problem for the first time.

Criterion letters in the margin, with marks per criterion

Scores tracked per criterion so the pattern is visible

modes.title: Paper 1 procedure block
modes.description: For the commonest diagnosis: a student with good understanding and no method for an unseen non-literary text. Four to six sessions build a repeatable procedure - identify text type, reader and purpose, then argue effect - and test it against a different text type each time, from advertisement to political speech to opinion column.

modes.description: Aimed at the two components with internal deadlines. The oral is rehearsed and recorded so the student hears their own pacing across the ten minutes; the HL essay is worked on as a line of inquiry, with the tutor giving written feedback on drafts the student has written and never supplying prose.

sections.heading: What an IB DP English A Language and Literature online tutor in Dubai does in the first session
paragraphs: The first session is a reading of evidence, not a lesson. We ask for four things before it: the most recent marked Paper 1 script, a marked Paper 2 essay if one exists, the school's criterion breakdown for both, and the learner portfolio as it currently stands. Within twenty minutes a pattern is usually visible, and it is almost always narrower than the family expected. One criterion is capping the grade across every component, and the rest of the script is fine.

Four diagnoses account for most of what we see in Dubai. The first is feature-listing: the student identifies metaphor, anaphora and direct address accurately and never argues what any of them does to a reader, which caps criterion B regardless of how much they write. The second is recall, which shows only on Paper 2, where no text is in the room and a student who understood both works cannot quote precisely enough to support a comparison.

The third is structure. A script with good individual observations in no deliberate order loses on criterion C, focus and organisation, and the fix is mechanical rather than intellectual: a planning routine that takes four minutes and produces an argument rather than a sequence. The fourth is language itself, criterion D, where the ideas are present and the sentences cannot carry them. That one is slow, and it is the only diagnosis where we tell families honestly that a term will not be enough.

What the first session produces is a written finding: the criterion, the evidence it came from, and the first piece of work that will test whether it is right. Parents get that in writing. It is deliberately specific, because the alternative - your child needs to be more analytical - is the commonest comment in a Dubai mock script's margin and it has never changed anybody's grade.
bullets: Send four marked pieces before session one, not a description of the problem
Feature-listing caps criterion B; recall only shows on Paper 2
Structure is a four-minute planning routine, not a talent
Language-level problems are real and take longer than one term

sections.heading: The course on one page: three areas of exploration, seven concepts
paragraphs: Language and Literature is organised into three areas of exploration rather than into units of content, and students who cannot name them are usually the ones whose essays have no governing idea. Readers, writers and texts deals with how meaning is made and received. Time and space deals with context - the circumstances of production and of reading. Intertextuality: connecting texts deals with how texts speak to one another, which is the area Paper 2 and the oral draw on most heavily.

Running across all three are seven central concepts: identity, culture, creativity, communication, perspective, transformation and representation. They are not decoration. A strong individual oral is usually built on one of them, because they give a student a way of asking how a global issue is constructed rather than simply what it is. A student who can say that a campaign poster and a novel both work on representation has the beginning of an argument; a student who says both are about immigration does not.

The practical use of this in tutoring is as a diagnostic grid. Take a student's marked work from across the course and ask which area of exploration each piece sat in. Dubai students very often show a clean split: competent in readers, writers and texts, weak in time and space, because context has been taught as background information rather than as something that changes a reading. That produces a specific term of work rather than a general instruction to read around the texts.

The table below sets out what each area asks and where it surfaces in assessment. Treat the detail as the shape of the current course and confirm it against the subject guide your child's school is teaching, since the IB revises guides on a cycle and school text choices differ across Dubai even between schools in the same group.

sections.heading: The four components, their weightings and their limits
paragraphs: Standard Level sits two papers and submits the individual oral. Higher Level sits the same two papers, submits the same oral, and adds the HL essay, with the weightings of the shared components adjusted to make room. The table below gives the shape. Every component has a limit - a time, a word count or a running time - and in the case of the HL essay and the oral, the limit is where a great deal of the difficulty lives.

The weightings explain a strategic point families often miss. At Higher Level, Paper 1 is the single largest component at 35%, and it is the only one that is entirely unseen. Everything else is prepared: Paper 2 is on works the student has studied, the oral is rehearsed, the HL essay is written over weeks. If a family is choosing where to spend a limited number of sessions, Paper 1 is where the unprepared marks are, and it is also the component most Dubai schools practise least often under genuine timed conditions.

At Standard Level the arithmetic is different. Paper 1 and Paper 2 are 35% each and the oral is 30%, so there is no single dominant component and the oral carries more weight than families expect for something marked internally. An SL student who treats the oral as a presentation to get through rather than as nearly a third of the grade is giving away marks that are, of all the marks in the course, the easiest to prepare for.

Confirm the current weightings and limits with your child's IB coordinator before planning around them. We publish no IB examination or results dates on this page: the IB's own site does not serve its calendar to automated checks, so any date here would be second-hand, and a second-hand date in a planning document is worse than none.

sections.heading: Paper 1: the unseen text, and the three places marks go
paragraphs: Paper 1 hands a student material they have never seen and a question that guides them towards an aspect of it. At Standard Level there is one text and seventy-five minutes. At Higher Level there are two texts and two separate analyses in two hours and fifteen minutes, which is less time per text than it sounds once planning is included. The text is non-literary: a print advertisement, a speech, an opinion column, a photograph with a caption, an infographic, a public-information poster, a cartoon.

The first place marks go is the move from identification to effect. A student writes that the advertisement uses a direct second-person address and stops there. The criterion wants the consequence: who is being positioned as the addressee, what that assumes about them, and what the text gains by making the reader occupy that position. The difference between a 3 and a 5 on criterion B is frequently nothing more than the clause after the comma.

The second is text type. Each type carries conventions, and the conventions are the fastest route into a strong answer, because a text that departs from its own conventions is doing something deliberate. A student who knows what a public-information poster normally does can see immediately when one refuses to do it. Building that inventory - twelve or so text types, their conventions and their typical reader - is a term's background work and pays off on every script.

The third is time. Seventy-five minutes is enough for a planned answer and not enough for a discovered one. The students who improve fastest are the ones who adopt a four-minute routine and never deviate from it: read, name the text type and reader, choose three lines of argument, sequence them, then write. We mark timed scripts under real conditions, because a script produced over two comfortable evenings tells nobody anything about what happens in May.
bullets: Identification earns little; the clause explaining effect earns the marks

sections.heading: Paper 2 and the recall problem nobody admits to
paragraphs: Paper 2 gives four general questions, the student picks one, and answers it by comparing two of the literary works studied in the course. No copy of either text is available. For a large share of Dubai students that last fact is the whole difficulty, and it is rarely the one named in feedback. A student who discussed both novels intelligently all year produces a vague essay because they cannot summon a precise enough moment to support the point they are making.

The remedy is unglamorous and reliable. Each work needs a small bank of precisely remembered moments - perhaps fifteen - chosen because they are useful across many possible questions rather than because they are famous. A moment that bears on power, on narration, on the treatment of time and on a central relationship is worth four memorised quotations that each serve one theme. Building that bank is homework, and a tutor's job is to test it and to reject moments that only serve one question.

The second Paper 2 failure is structural. The question asks about both works, and weak essays handle them sequentially: five paragraphs on one, four on the other, a comparison in the conclusion. The criteria reward a genuinely comparative structure, where each paragraph does work on both texts. Rebuilding an essay from sequential to comparative is a single teachable operation, and students can usually do it themselves after seeing it done twice.

The third is question choice. Four general questions, and the one that looks most interesting is frequently the one the student's two works support least. Spending ninety seconds testing each question against the memorised banks before committing is worth more than any amount of writing speed. It is also the sort of discipline that only appears under timed practice, which is why the marked-script cycle is the default rhythm on this page.

sections.heading: The individual oral and the HL essay: two internal deadlines, one skill
paragraphs: The individual oral asks the student to examine how a global issue is presented in one literary work and one non-literary body of work, in ten minutes, followed by five minutes of teacher questions. It is worth 30% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher. The commonest weakness is that the student talks about the global issue rather than about how the two texts construct it. An oral about migration scores modestly; an oral about how a photo-essay and a novel each position the viewer in relation to migration scores well.

Narrowing the global issue is most of the work. It has to be specific enough to be arguable in ten minutes and broad enough to be visible in both texts, and students almost always start too wide. We rehearse the oral on recording, because pacing is the second failure: a student with four points and ten minutes typically spends six of them on the first point. Hearing their own recording changes that faster than being told.

The HL essay, 1,200 to 1,500 words and 20% of the Higher Level grade, is the same skill in written form: a narrow line of inquiry pursued through one work or body of work, developed out of the learner portfolio. Students with thin portfolios struggle here, not because they cannot write, but because they have no record of their own thinking to mine for a question worth 1,500 words.

The boundary matters on both components, and we state it before the first session. A tutor teaches the component, explains what a criterion asks, questions a line of inquiry until the student sharpens it, and gives written feedback on drafts the student has written. A tutor does not supply prose, does not rewrite paragraphs into their own voice, and does not hand over a thesis to be adopted. The submitted work is the student's own, and an academic-honesty finding falls on the student rather than on the tutor.
bullets: Analyse how the global issue is constructed, not what it is
