sections.heading: The arithmetic of catching up on nine or thirteen works
paragraphs: Literature families underestimate reading time by a consistent margin, so it is worth doing the sum in plain numbers. A substantial novel on a Diploma list runs to a few hundred pages; a play or a poetry collection is shorter but demands rereading. A student reading forty pages an evening, four evenings a week, covers a long novel in about a fortnight while also carrying five other subjects. Four unread works is therefore roughly two months of real evenings, not a weekend.

That number is why triage is sometimes the honest advice. A student in the second term of DP2 with half the list unread cannot finish it and should not try. The right move is to decide which works will carry the individual oral, which will carry the comparative essay, and which will be known adequately rather than well, then read in that order. Because no work may be used twice across components, the allocation has to be decided before the reading is sequenced, which is one hour of planning that saves a month of wasted effort.

None of that work needs a tutor beside the student while it happens, and this is the part the market obscures. The paid hours are worth spending at the start, on the plan, and at the checkpoints, where a few sharp questions reveal whether a work has been read or merely passed over. A student who cannot locate a scene, identify who speaks a line, or say what changes between two chapters has not finished the book, whatever they believe, and an hour spent discovering that is worth four spent discussing themes.

Works in translation add a specific burden that families rarely budget for. The required share of translated works means at least some of the list sits outside the student's own cultural and literary frame of reference, and the oral and comparative components both reward handling them with genuine understanding rather than respectful vagueness. Those works need more reading time, not more tutoring, and planning them early in DP1 is the difference between a translated text that carries a component and one that quietly cannot.

sections.heading: If you only buy one thing in English A Literature, buy this
paragraphs: For a student who has done the reading, the single highest-return purchase is a marked unseen passage response. Paper 1 presents poetry or prose nobody has prepared, and the only route to competence is write under time pressure, have the result scored accurately against the descriptors, correct one named fault, repeat. Four such responses across DP2 will usually do more than a term of weekly discussion, and they cost less in total at the same hourly rate.

For a student who has not done the reading, the single highest-return purchase is one hour of planning, and then nothing for a month. The plan sets the allocation of works to components, decides what will be read closely and what will be read adequately, and puts dates against each. Buying sessions before that hour is spent is buying company for a student who needs solitude and a book, which is why this page says so explicitly rather than leaving it to be discovered.

There are two decision hours worth protecting in any budget. The first is the choice of the two works for the individual oral, which has to respect the constraint that a work used in one component cannot be reused in another; a careless choice here removes the student's strongest text from the component where it would have earned most. The second, at Higher Level, is the line of inquiry for the essay, which caps the mark the moment it is set too broadly and is expensive to change once a draft exists.

What returns nothing, reliably, is paid summary. A tutor who recounts a novel the student has not read produces a session the student enjoys and an essay an examiner will see through in a paragraph. The marks in this course come from close handling of text: a quotation deployed accurately, a shift in a character's language noticed, a form used as evidence rather than mentioned. None of that survives secondhand reading, and no rate per hour changes it.

sections.heading: What the Dubai market charges, sorted by what the hour contains
paragraphs: Comparing providers by their hourly rate tells a family almost nothing, because the same number buys very different contents. The table below reorganises the published Dubai bands around what is actually delivered in the hour, which is the comparison a parent can act on. Every figure is a provider's own published rate or a band from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, read in October 2026, and none of them is our price.

Three of the six providers researched for this market publish no rate at all, and two of the three that do quote in US dollars rather than dirhams. One competitor's own frequently-asked-questions section raises the price question and declines to answer it. That absence is the reason a Dubai parent's first quote so often becomes their reference point for every subsequent judgement, and it is why these bands are set out here with their sources.

Read the rows as products rather than as tiers of quality. A reading-plan hour and a marked unseen response are both legitimate purchases, they suit different students, and a family who knows which they need can buy it at the appropriate band instead of defaulting to the most expensive option on offer. The row that deserves the most scepticism is the one in the middle: a mid-market rate with marking charged separately, which is how a budget quietly doubles.

Monthly packages circulate in this market too and should be unpacked before comparison. Figures seen include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions, while Bestimate estimates roughly AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work. Divide by the hours before you compare; the implied rate is frequently above the headline.

sections.heading: Translated works: the line nobody budgets for
paragraphs: The requirement to study works in translation is one of the defining features of Diploma Literature and one of the least discussed in this market. It puts at least some of a student's reading outside the literary tradition they have grown up with, often in a form, period or convention they have never met. For a Dubai cohort drawn from twenty nationalities that cuts in unexpected directions: the translated text is unfamiliar to almost everyone in the room, including, sometimes, the teacher who chose it.

The cost consequence is specific. A translated work usually needs more reading time than an equivalent English-language text, because the student is also acquiring context. It also needs a tutor who has taught that work, not merely a tutor who has taught Literature, and that is where the local-supply problem bites. A family in Dubai whose school has set a less commonly taught translated novel may find that nobody within driving distance has handled it, and a generalist session on it is worth very little.

This is the clearest case in the subject for widening the pool rather than widening the budget. Online delivery means a family selects on whether the tutor has taught the named work, which is a question with a factual answer, instead of selecting on who is nearby and hoping. It is also the reason this page asks families to put the set works in the first message: matching on the works takes longer than matching on the subject, and the answer is sometimes that nobody suitable is free.

When the honest answer is no match, there are two reasonable fallbacks and one bad one. The reasonable ones are to buy craft rather than content, working on comparison and close analysis using works the tutor does know and transferring the method, or to wait for a specialist and spend the interval reading. The bad one is to pay specialist rates for a tutor reading the novel alongside the student, which happens in this market and which a family can detect by asking one direct question before booking.

sections.heading: The cheapest months to book a Literature specialist in Dubai
paragraphs: Hourly rates in this market do not formally rise before the examination session, but availability collapses, and the effect on a family's bill is the same. Specialists fill their weekly slots during the first term, so a block sought in February is competing for compressed hours at unsocial times, and the choice narrows to whoever is left. The calendar below sets out what is happening in a Dubai school year and what it does to both supply and the sensible purchase.

Two features of the UAE calendar shape this more than families expect. Ramadan shortens school days and shifts household routines, which moves sessions to post-Iftar slots and compresses the week; good tutors will accommodate it, but the slots go early. And the long summer break, during which a large share of Dubai families travel for several weeks, is both the best reading window in the year and the period when a weekly in-person arrangement would collapse entirely. Online delivery survives it, which is a practical argument rather than a marketing one.

Exam-session dates themselves are worth treating carefully. This page does not publish a specific IB examination or results date, because the IB's own site cannot be verified by automated checking and an unconfirmed date on a page like this is worth less than nothing to a family planning around it. UAE IB schools sit the May session; confirm the exact windows and your school's internal deadlines with the DP coordinator, who holds the current timetable.

Cambridge and Pearson dates, by contrast, are published and sourced, and they illustrate why booking early matters in any system. Cambridge's March 2027 series has an examination period of 3 February to 4 March 2027 with final entries due 27 November 2026 — an entry deadline more than two months before the first paper. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable ending 19 November 2026. Entry and preparation deadlines sit months ahead of exams in every system, and tutor availability follows the same pattern.

sections.heading: Four things not to fund, and one claim to refuse
paragraphs: Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents, subject guides and grade-boundary tables are not a tutor's to sell. They belong to the IB, to Cambridge or to Pearson, and a legitimate provider references them and links to the official source rather than supplying copies as downloads. A bundle of copied material presented as a resource pack is somebody else's copyright exposure sold at a margin, and unreleased material carries a malpractice risk for the student too.

Nor should a family fund an accreditation claim. A provider that places the name of a regulator or an examination board next to words such as approval, accreditation or authorisation should be asked for the permit number, and a provider using the phrase loosely has told you something about their other claims. The specific permit for a training institute with premises in Dubai is an Educational Services Permit, which is not the same thing as an individual tutor's status. IB Gram holds no such permit and does not imply one.

The third thing not to fund is a statistic. Satisfaction percentages, average score claims and self-published star ratings circulate in this market without a sample size, a date or a method behind any of them; two researched competitors display conflicting review totals on the same page. A premium justified by a number that cannot be checked is a premium paid for the number. The fourth is a guarantee: nobody can promise a grade in a subject assessed externally on unseen passages, and a refund promise tied to an outcome deserves more scepticism, not less.

The claim to refuse outright is an offer to supply finished work. Providers in this market do sell completed coursework at a price that looks competitive against a term of honest sessions. Under IB academic-honesty rules the consequence of submitting work that is not the student's own falls on the student, up to the loss of the Diploma. A tutor reads, marks, questions, models and records; every word a school uploads must be the student's own. That boundary is a genuine differentiator here and it is not negotiable at any rate.

sections.heading: When nobody has taught your school's set works, and who is permitted to teach at all
paragraphs: Because Dubai schools choose their own works, matching a Literature tutor is a search for a person rather than a product, and sometimes the search fails. We say so when it does. The alternatives offered are a different time slot with a specialist who has taught the works, a craft-focused block using texts the tutor knows well with the method transferred, or a wait with a reading plan in the meantime. What we will not do is place a generalist, call them a specialist in your child's set works, and charge the specialist band.

That transparency is unusual in this market and it is the reason the delivery format matters. All Dubai sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in the UAE, because tutors travelling to a family's address is a service we offer only in India. The gain is not merely that no part of the hour is spent on Sheikh Zayed Road; it is that the question a Literature family needs to ask — have you taught this translated work? — can be answered yes by somebody, somewhere, rather than no by everybody within twenty minutes.

Before paying anyone in this market, know the permit position. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page for it lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so treat any amount quoted to you as unverified.

One final rule worth knowing before a conversation at the school gate. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a comparable restriction. Hiring your child's own Literature teacher privately is therefore an arrangement to decline rather than a shortcut to negotiate — and an external reader is more useful anyway, because they encounter the essay as an unknown examiner will rather than as the person who taught the lesson behind it.

process.title: Send the set works, not just the subject
process.description: List the works your child is studying, including the translated texts, the level, and roughly how many have been finished. That list determines both the price and whether a match exists at all, and it is the single most useful thing a Dubai Literature family can send in a first message.

process.title: Take the free diagnostic hour
process.description: One hour, online, one-to-one, no card required. A piece of existing writing is marked against the published descriptors and the reading position is tested with direct questions. You receive a written plan: works to read in what order, hours needed, and what those hours would cost at a stated rate.

process.title: Read before you buy, if that is the finding
process.description: For a student behind on the list the plan will say to spend three to eight weeks reading with checkpoints rather than booking weekly sessions. That is the honest recommendation and the cheap one. Checkpoint hours are booked individually, and nothing continues on a subscription basis.

process.title: Buy marking by the piece once the reading holds
process.description: Marked essays and unseen passage responses are bought as a defined number rather than as a standing weekly hour. Each comes back scored against every descriptor with one named fault to correct, and the dated scores accumulate into a record a parent can read without being able to mark Literature.

process.title: Protect the two decision hours, then review
process.description: One hour on the individual oral works and the allocation constraint, one on the Higher Level line of inquiry, both booked when the decision is live rather than after a draft exists. At the end of the block the record is read, and the arrangement either continues against named components or stops.

whyPoints.title: Priced from the reading list
whyPoints.description: The first question here is how much of the list is genuinely finished, because that decides the cost far more than any hourly rate. Three of the four situations it produces are cheaper than the weekly arrangement most providers propose, and one of them is free. No provider paid by the hour has any reason to tell you that.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to read instead
whyPoints.description: A student four novels behind needs evenings with the books, not sessions discussing them. The diagnostic hour says so in writing, with dates. Families who follow it spend less in total and arrive at DP2 able to quote from the works, which is what the components actually reward.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the named works
whyPoints.description: Dubai schools choose their own set works, including the translated texts, so we match on the specific titles rather than on the subject. When nobody suitable is free we say so and offer a craft block or a wait, instead of placing a generalist at the specialist band and hoping the difference goes unnoticed.

whyPoints.title: Bands published with their sources
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure names the provider and the month it was read, including the in-home bands we do not operate in. Three of the six researched competitors publish no price and two quote in dollars, so a Dubai parent is usually comparing one unexplained number against nothing.

whyPoints.title: Marking is written down and dated
whyPoints.description: Each piece returns scored against every descriptor with the specific fault named, and the scores build a record. That record is how a family judges whether the arrangement works, and it is also what makes stopping an easy decision rather than an awkward conversation.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line, stated before you pay
whyPoints.description: Finished coursework is sold in this market, and under IB rules the consequence of submitting it falls on the student. A tutor here reads, marks, questions, models and records, and nothing else. Copies of past papers, mark schemes and subject guides are referenced and linked, never supplied.

faqs.question: What should a Dubai family expect to pay for English A Literature support?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on the reading position rather than on a list price. For a student who has read the works and loses marks on analysis, four to eight marked pieces at the published IB specialist band of roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour is the purchase that pays. For a student three or four works behind, one or two planning and checkpoint hours plus several weeks of unpaid reading is both cheaper and more effective. Those bands are providers' own published figures and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, read in October 2026, not our prices.

faqs.question: My child has not finished four of the set works. What does catching up cost?
faqs.answer: Mostly time rather than money. Four substantial works is roughly two months of real evenings for a student carrying five other subjects, and no hourly rate compresses that. What is worth paying for is one planning hour that sequences the reading against the component allocation, then short checkpoint sessions that test whether each work has genuinely been read. At mid-market Dubai rates that is a small defined cost. Paying a specialist to discuss books the student has not opened is the expensive version of the same problem.

faqs.question: Is it better value to buy reading support or essay marking?
faqs.answer: Buy in that order, and only as far as you need. Reading support is cheap because most of the work is unpaid: a plan, a schedule and a few hard questions at checkpoints. Essay marking is expensive because scoring a timed response against every descriptor takes real tutor time, and it is the thing that moves marks once the reading holds. Buying marking first for a student who has not read the works produces scored essays that are thin for a reason marking cannot fix.

faqs.question: Do works in translation need extra paid hours?
faqs.answer: They need extra reading time, which is unpaid, and a tutor who has actually taught the specific text, which is a matching problem rather than a pricing one. A translated work sits outside most students' literary frame of reference and often outside the local tutor pool's experience too, so a Dubai family whose school has set a less commonly taught novel may find nobody nearby has handled it. Ask any prospective tutor directly whether they have taught that title; paying specialist rates for somebody reading it alongside your child is a poor trade.

faqs.question: Why is unseen poetry the most expensive hour in this course?
faqs.answer: Because nothing about it can be prepared and the only route to competence is repeated marked practice. Paper 1 hands a student a passage nobody has taught them, and the descriptors reward close handling of specific choices rather than general appreciation. That means the useful hour contains an accurately scored response and a named fault to correct, which takes a calibrated marker and real time. A conversation about poetry is pleasant and cheap; a scored response is neither, and it is what the grade answers to.

faqs.question: Is a cheaper tutor who has not read our school's set works any use?
faqs.answer: For craft, sometimes. For content, no. A good Group 1 tutor can teach comparison, close analysis and essay architecture using texts they know well, and the method transfers, which is a legitimate purchase at a mid-market rate. What does not work is a session on a specific novel the tutor has not read, at any price, because the detail that earns marks is exactly what they cannot supply. Decide which of the two you are buying before agreeing a rate, and ask the question plainly.

faqs.question: When in the Dubai school year is a Literature specialist easiest to book?
faqs.answer: The first term of DP1 and the long summer break. Rates do not formally rise before the May session, but specialists fill their weekly slots during the first term, so a block sought in the second term of DP2 competes for compressed and unsocial hours and the choice narrows to whoever is left. Ramadan slots and holiday intensives also go early. Booking the marking block in the first term of DP2 is both cheaper in practice and far more likely to exist when it is needed.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Literature and the Extended Essay without a second fee?
faqs.answer: Frequently yes, and it is the clearest saving available to a Group 1 family. A Literature specialist can work on the Extended Essay research question and on the Theory of Knowledge essay inside the same booked hour, because all three reward a controlled claim supported by evidence with its limits acknowledged. Confirm it before booking rather than assuming, and keep the records separate: the Extended Essay has its own supervision arrangements at the school and its own reflection requirements.

faqs.question: What is the smallest sensible purchase in English A Literature?
faqs.answer: One marked read of an existing essay, or one planning hour, depending on the reading position. Both cost a single hour at the relevant published band and both answer the question a family actually has, which is whether paid support is needed at all and what it should target. Several families buy one, act on the written output, and never book anything else. That is a good outcome and the diagnostic hour is designed to make it possible rather than to make it awkward.

faqs.question: Should we pay someone to summarise the novels?
faqs.answer: No. It is the one purchase in this course that reliably returns nothing. The marks come from close handling of text: an accurate quotation, a noticed shift in a character's language, form used as evidence rather than mentioned. A student working from a summary can produce a confident paragraph and an examiner can see through it in a sentence, because the detail is not there. Buy the book and the three weeks. Providers will sell the summary happily, which is precisely why it needs saying here.

faqs.question: Does Higher Level Literature cost more to support than Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Usually, for two structural reasons rather than because of a different rate. Higher Level requires thirteen works rather than nine, which lengthens the reading and therefore the catch-up risk, and it adds a further essay on a single studied work with its own line of inquiry to settle. In practice that is two or three more paid hours across the two years, placed at the decision points. Confirm the current requirements with your school's DP coordinator, since structural details are set by the subject guide in force for your child's session.

faqs.question: How do we check that a quoted rate includes marked written work?
faqs.answer: Ask in writing for three specifics: whether a timed response will be returned annotated, whether it will carry a score against each published descriptor, and whether the marking happens before the session or inside the paid hour. A provider who marks during the session is charging you to read your child's essay. One who charges marking as an extra should be asked for the combined figure, because a mid-market hourly rate plus a separate marking fee frequently lands above the specialist band it looked cheaper than.

faqs.question: What happens to our fee if the tutor turns out to be the wrong match?
faqs.answer: Raise it immediately rather than at the end of a block, and expect a rematch rather than an argument. A mismatch in this subject is usually specific and identifiable: the tutor has not taught the set works, or marks generously without descriptor-level reasoning, or spends the hour on texts rather than on the student's writing. Any arrangement should let a family stop after a single session, and a provider who requires a long commitment before the first marked piece comes back is asking for trust they have not yet earned.

faqs.question: Is a premium examiner-level rate worth it for one essay?
faqs.answer: It can be, for a single high-stakes component read once, and it is worth knowing what you are buying. We do not describe tutors as IB or Cambridge examiners unless current examiner status can be evidenced, and examiner experience should never be presented as access to marking, grade boundaries or paper content. What a strong single read buys is calibration: a judgement about where a piece sits against the descriptors from somebody who has applied them many times. Published premium rates in this market reach AED 650 an hour, per BartyED's own page.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram arrange a Literature tutor who comes to our villa in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram runs no home visits anywhere in the UAE; tutors travelling to a family's address is a service we offer only in India. Dubai Literature support is delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, with the student's own essay on screen while it is annotated. In this subject that widens the choice in the way that matters: a family can look for somebody who has taught their child's specific translated work rather than for somebody who can reach their community before five.

dubai/ib-dp-english-a-literature-tutor.closingBody: Before comparing quotes for English A Literature in Dubai, count how many of the set works your child can genuinely quote from. That number, more than any hourly rate, decides what this costs. Send the list of works, the level and an honest count, and take the free diagnostic hour: one piece of writing marked against the published descriptors, the reading position tested with direct questions, and a written plan giving the order to read in, the hours needed and what they would cost at a stated rate. If the plan says read for a month and book nothing, that is the plan.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach English B as a language acquisition course rather than as remedial English: receptive-skills practice at exam pace, text-type conventions, the individual oral, and at Higher Level the two literary works. Each card shows levels, Gulf Standard Time availability and current capacity.

intro.heading: Half this course is listening and reading, and almost nobody prepares for the listening
paragraphs: English B is a language acquisition course, not a watered-down English A, and the difference shows up most sharply in how the grade is built. Paper 2 is receptive skills and carries half the total: twenty-five per cent listening comprehension and twenty-five per cent reading comprehension. Paper 1 is a single piece of productive writing worth a quarter. The individual oral is the last quarter. A Dubai student who is articulate, reads comfortably and writes decent essays can still finish two grades below where their teacher expected, because they have spent two years on the half of the course that feels like work and almost no time on recordings.

The listening paper is the clearest example of a component that is under-taught for understandable reasons. It needs audio equipment, quiet, and a teacher willing to spend lesson time on something that cannot be marked collaboratively. Most Dubai cohorts meet a handful of practice recordings in two years. The paper itself presents audio at natural speed, with accents the student may not have encountered, played a limited number of times, and asks for precise answers. That is a trainable skill with a steep early curve, and it is the single most improvable thing in this course.

The second under-taught area is text-type convention on Paper 1. The writing task asks for a specific text type — a blog post, a formal letter, a speech, a proposal, a news report, a set of guidelines — addressed to a stated audience for a stated purpose. Conceptual understanding is marked explicitly, which means a student who writes excellent English in the wrong register, with the wrong layout, for the wrong reader has capped a third of the available marks before the content is even considered. Students who learned English in an essay-writing system find this counter-intuitive for months.

Dubai is where this course matters most and where it is most often misunderstood. KHDA records 387,441 students across 227 private schools teaching 17 different curricula in the emirate. A very large number of those students are working between two or three languages daily, and the placement decision between English A and English B is consequential: it affects the bilingual diploma, how a transcript reads to a university, and whether the student spends two years under-stretched or out of their depth. That decision belongs to the school's DP coordinator, and the useful contribution an outside tutor can make is marked evidence rather than an opinion.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai. Home visiting is a service we offer only in India, as every page in our UAE set states. Dubai English B students work with us one to one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. For this course the format is a genuine advantage rather than a compromise: audio can be played and replayed at exactly the exam's pace, a written task can be marked against the criteria the moment it is finished, and the oral can be rehearsed and scored with the stimulus on a shared screen.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.programmesIntro: English B sits in Group 2, language acquisition, and Dubai students reach it from several directions. The route determines which half of the course needs work first.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme English B
programmes.description: Two years built on five prescribed themes, assessed by Paper 1 productive writing, Paper 2 receptive skills in two parts (listening and reading), and an individual oral. Higher Level students additionally study two literary works, one of which supplies the extract for their oral. The course is about using the language, so marks reward message and conceptual understanding alongside linguistic control.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, English B cohorts are often large and mixed, containing students who arrived in English-medium education at eight and students who arrived at fifteen. That spread makes whole-class listening practice difficult to pitch, which is why the receptive paper is where outside help usually earns its keep.

programmes.name: MYP Language Acquisition
programmes.description: Organised in phases rather than year groups, assessed on listening, reading, speaking and writing, each on an eight-point scale. The phase system means a student's MYP record indicates their actual proficiency band, which is far more useful for the English A or English B placement decision than a year-group grade.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools running MYP into DP can look back at phase placement when deciding Group 2 entry. Students transferring into a Dubai IB sixth form at 16 have no phase record, which is why placement there is more often a judgement call that needs evidence behind it.

programmes.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
programmes.description: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language examines reading, writing, listening and speaking, which maps onto English B more closely than any other pre-16 qualification. The habits transfer well. What does not transfer is the conceptual-understanding demand: ESL rewards accuracy and task completion, while English B marks whether the student understood audience, purpose and context.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for 37% of Dubai private-school enrolment (KHDA, 2024-25), and ESL candidates from those schools make up a large share of Dubai English B entries. Their characteristic gap is register rather than grammar.

programmes.name: English A, for students deciding between courses
programmes.description: The Group 1 studies in language and literature options, where the material is literary and non-literary text analysis rather than language use. A student placed in English B who could manage English A gives up the bilingual diploma route through Group 1; a student placed in English A who cannot manage it loses marks across four components.
programmes.countryNote: This is the single most consequential decision a Dubai family faces in Group 1 or 2, and the school's DP coordinator makes it. What an outside tutor can usefully add is a marked writing sample and a timed reading response, so the conversation runs on evidence rather than on how confidently the student speaks.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: English B students in Dubai usually need support in one or two further subjects where language load is the real obstacle. These are the ones we most often run alongside it.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Productive writing, listening and reading comprehension, and an individual oral, across five prescribed themes. Marks are lost to under-practised listening and to text types written in the wrong register for the stated audience.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 alternative, with unseen non-literary text analysis in Paper 1. Relevant to any family weighing the placement decision, because the two courses demand genuinely different skills rather than different amounts of the same one.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The Group 2 Arabic acquisition course, taken by many non-Arab students in Dubai schools. The same assessment architecture as English B, which means a student can carry technique across from one to the other more easily than they expect.

subjects.name: Spanish B and French B
subjects.description: Group 2 courses sharing English B's structure: productive writing, receptive skills and an individual oral across the same five themes. Students taking two Group 2 languages benefit from learning the mark scheme once properly.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Organisational structure, marketing, operations and finance with a research project. A frequent choice for English B students and the subject where command-term precision in a second language costs the most marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Micro, macro, the global economy and a portfolio of commentaries on published articles. The commentaries demand close reading of news sources, which doubles as English B reading practice.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: An interdisciplinary course with significant extended writing and a practical investigation. Popular with Dubai students carrying a heavy language load, and the writing is where the marks go.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics-led mathematics with a graphical-calculator paper and a mathematical exploration. The exploration's written commentary is a language task as much as a mathematical one.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches with an experimental study report. The reading volume is heavy and the command terms are unforgiving, which makes it a demanding pairing with English B.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word prescribed-title essay plus an exhibition of three objects with commentaries. Students working in an additional language often have strong things to say here and need help saying them in the register the essay rewards.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities where English B demand is highest
dubai/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.regionsIntro: English B entries cluster in the parts of Dubai where families are working between languages daily, and those are not the same areas as the Group 1 Literature cohorts. These are the communities we work with most and what the local day does to a session time.

regions.name: Deira and Al Rigga
regions.note: One of the most linguistically mixed parts of the emirate, with students who speak Arabic, Urdu, Malayalam, Tagalog or Russian at home and English only at school. Listening practice matters disproportionately here, because exposure outside lessons is limited.

regions.name: Al Karama and Oud Metha
regions.note: Long-established apartment districts close to several schools, with students who can start a session at 4pm. Short, frequent listening drills work better here than long weekend blocks.

regions.name: Bur Dubai and Al Fahidi
regions.note: Dense older housing with very high language diversity. Students here frequently read well above their listening band, which is a specific and very common English B profile that needs diagnosing before anything is planned.

regions.name: Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: Close to the eastern school cluster with manageable commutes. Sessions here can reliably run timed receptive papers on a weekday evening, which makes the practice schedule easier to hold.

regions.name: International City and Warsan
regions.note: Highly mixed, largely Chinese, Russian and South Asian households with students at schools some distance away. The commute removes practice time, and an online slot immediately after school recovers most of it.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: Close to several schools and the university cluster. Students here are often targeting UAE universities, which makes the English proficiency requirements for Ministry of Education equivalency a live question rather than an abstract one.

regions.name: Discovery Gardens and Al Furjan
regions.note: Affordable apartment living with students at a wide range of schools and prior systems. Entry routes into English B vary more here than anywhere else we work, so the first session is diagnostic rather than instructional.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai IB schools with large English B cohorts
schoolClusters.note: In this group Group 2 English is a substantial class containing students at genuinely different proficiency bands. Whole-class listening practice is hard to pitch across that spread, which is the structural reason the receptive paper under-performs in otherwise strong departments.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai bilingual and multilingual IB schools
schoolClusters.note: Students here are formally educated in two languages, so the English A or English B placement decision is made deliberately rather than by default. The characteristic profile is high oral fluency with a reading band that lags, which the individual oral flatters and Paper 2 does not.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools taking students in from another language of instruction
schoolClusters.note: Students arriving at 14 or 16 from a system taught in Arabic, Russian, French, Chinese or an Indian regional language sit the widest range of English B outcomes. Their written accuracy is often good and their listening band is the limiting factor, because classroom exposure has been short.

Each session runs timed listening and reading sections at exam pace, with real recordings rather than transcripts read aloud, and then works backwards through the wrong answers to find whether the loss was vocabulary, speed, accent or question-reading. sections.heading: English A or English B: the decision that shapes two years
paragraphs: Families searching for an IB DP english B home tutor in Dubai sometimes have a prior question they have not articulated: is my child in the right course? It is a reasonable thing to ask and it is consequential, because the two routes demand different skills rather than different quantities of the same skill. English A is a literature or language-and-literature course in which the student analyses texts. English B is a language acquisition course in which the student uses the language across five themes. A strong analyst who is still building fluency belongs in one; a fluent speaker with no appetite for literary analysis may well belong in the other.

The decision sits with the school's DP coordinator and it should. What families often lack is evidence to bring to that conversation, because the signals they can observe are misleading. Oral fluency is the most visible and the least predictive: a student who speaks easily and idiomatically may still read slowly and lose marks across a receptive paper. Conversely a quiet student who reads widely may be under-placed in English B and spend two years without being stretched. Marked evidence — one timed reading section and one piece of writing against the criteria — is far more informative than either impression.

There is a further consequence worth knowing before the decision is made. The bilingual diploma can be awarded on specified combinations involving two Group 1 languages or a Group 1 language with certain other conditions, and English B is a Group 2 course, so it does not satisfy a two-Group-1 route. For some Dubai families, with university plans in mind, that matters a great deal; for others it is irrelevant. The IB's own published requirements are the thing to check with the coordinator, not any summary on a tutoring page including this one.

sections.heading: The listening paper: half of the receptive marks and the least practised component
paragraphs: Listening comprehension is twenty-five per cent of the English B grade and in most Dubai cohorts it receives a small fraction of that proportion of lesson time. The reasons are practical. It needs audio, quiet and headphones. It cannot be marked as a class discussion. And it produces uncomfortable lessons, because a student who has been told their English is good discovers they missed four answers out of ten on a recording played twice.

The losses have four distinct causes and they need separating, because the fix for each is different. Vocabulary gaps mean a known word was not recognised at speed. Processing speed means the word was recognised too late to answer. Accent unfamiliarity means a known word in an unfamiliar pronunciation was not matched to the one the student knows. And question-reading failure means the student understood the audio and answered a different question. Marking a practice section without diagnosing which of those four occurred teaches very little, which is why ordinary homework listening rarely moves the mark.

The early curve is steep, which is the good news. Students who do timed listening sections twice a week for six weeks, with the wrong answers traced back to cause, typically improve more on this component than on anything else in the course, because they are starting from very little deliberate practice. The work is unglamorous and the sessions are quiet. It is also the clearest case in this subject where a specific, measurable intervention produces a specific, measurable result, and it is the first thing we check for in a diagnostic session.

sections.heading: Paper 1: the text type decides a third of the marks
paragraphs: Paper 1 is a single piece of productive writing chosen from three tasks, each specifying a text type, an audience and a purpose, worth twenty-five per cent of the grade. Standard Level candidates write 250 to 400 words; Higher Level candidates write 450 to 600. The response is marked out of thirty, with twelve marks for language, twelve for message and six for conceptual understanding.

That six-mark criterion is where essay-trained students lose a fifth of the paper without noticing. Conceptual understanding assesses whether the student has grasped audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation — in practice, whether the piece reads like the text type it was supposed to be. A beautifully written formal essay submitted where a blog post was asked for has lost those marks and will also struggle on message, because the message criterion includes whether the task has been addressed appropriately.

The teaching here is concrete rather than abstract. A proposal needs a stated problem, options and a recommendation; a speech needs direct address and an audible structure; a set of guidelines needs imperatives and no first-person reflection; a news report puts the outcome in the first sentence and attributes claims. Each of those is a short, learnable set of conventions, and one session per text type, written to the word band and marked, covers the paper's realistic range in a few weeks. Students find this the most immediately rewarding work in the course because the mark changes quickly.

sections.heading: The individual oral: visual stimulus at SL, literary extract at HL
paragraphs: The individual oral is twenty-five per cent of the grade and the two levels start from different material, which families regularly do not realise until late. At Standard Level the student presents on a visual stimulus connected to one of the five prescribed themes and then has a conversation with the teacher. At Higher Level the starting point is an extract from one of the two literary works studied during the course, followed by the same kind of conversation extending into the themes.

The marks are split in a way that rewards something students rarely rehearse. Out of thirty, twelve go to language, and the remainder is divided between the message drawn from the stimulus or extract, the message developed in the conversation, and interactive skills — whether the student sustains a genuine exchange. That last element is why a polished two-minute monologue followed by one-word answers scores poorly. The conversation is assessed, not endured.

In practice the Standard Level failure is thin description: a student describes the image for ninety seconds, connects it loosely to a theme and runs out of material. The Higher Level failure is different — a student who knows the plot of the literary work but cannot discuss the extract in front of them, because the two literary works were covered quickly in a course whose other components take priority. We rehearse both halves, timed and marked, with the stimulus or extract on a shared screen, and the most common piece of feedback is to slow down and develop one idea rather than list four.

sections.heading: The five prescribed themes, and what gets asked about them
paragraphs: Every component of English B draws on five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation, and sharing the planet. They are not topics to be revised like content. They are the fields the writing tasks, the recordings, the reading texts and the oral stimuli are drawn from, which means the practical value of knowing them is vocabulary coverage and conceptual readiness rather than facts.

Students who prepare theme by theme do better on the receptive paper than students who prepare by grammar point, because the recordings and texts use the vocabulary of these fields. A student with solid grammar and no vocabulary for migration, urban planning, renewable energy or artificial intelligence will understand the structure of a recording and miss its content. Building theme vocabulary deliberately, with each word met in listening, reading, writing and speaking rather than only on a list, is slow and it is the thing that lifts the receptive paper at the same time as Paper 1.

There is a Dubai-specific advantage available here that very few students use. Several of these themes are visible daily in the emirate in ways that make concrete examples easy to produce: a city whose population comes from everywhere offers immediate material on identities and experiences; large-scale construction and transport infrastructure supply human ingenuity; water, energy and cooling supply sharing the planet. An oral or a written task answered with specific local examples reads as thought rather than as preparation, and examiners notice the difference.

sections.heading: Criterion marks across the components, published in full
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes the criterion breakdown for English B, and it is the fastest way for a parent to understand where their child's grade is actually going. Paper 1 is marked out of thirty: twelve for language, twelve for message, six for conceptual understanding. The individual oral is also out of thirty, with twelve for language and the rest divided between the message taken from the stimulus or extract, the message developed in conversation, and interactive skills. Paper 2's two sections are comprehension and are marked on correct answers rather than on criteria.

Reading those numbers together produces a conclusion most students resist. Language control is the largest single criterion on both productive components, at twelve marks each, which means accuracy and range genuinely matter — but it is not the majority of either paper. A student who writes flawless English that misses the task, the audience or the text type is capped. And on the receptive half, worth fifty per cent of the whole course, criteria do not apply at all: answers are either right or wrong, which is why that half responds to practice rather than to polish.

The planning conclusion follows directly. For a student whose written English is accurate, the available marks sit in the receptive paper and in conceptual understanding. For a student whose accuracy is the limiting factor, language work pays across three components at once. Diagnosing which of those two students you have takes one marked writing task and one timed listening section, and it changes the entire shape of a support plan. Confirm all weightings and mark allocations against the subject guide your school teaches, since the IB revises guides between syllabus cycles.

sections.heading: English B, MoE equivalency and the English requirement for UAE universities
paragraphs: Dubai families with UAE university plans frequently assume that a good English B grade settles the English question for admission. It does not, and the distinction is worth getting right because the requirements are published and specific. Ministry of Education equivalency for the American track requires English proficiency evidenced by an IELTS academic score of 5, a TOEFL iBT score of 61, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying.

For the British track the published requirement is different again: five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One competitor page ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the published rule is five, and inheriting that error would be worse than saying nothing.

For the International Baccalaureate there is no points threshold we can verify from the Ministry's own published material, so this page states none. Any IB equivalency figure you are shown should be checked on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority before you rely on it. Equivalency is also not something IB Gram performs, administers or guarantees — we describe it, cite the source and point you to the official channel. And nobody should suggest that tutoring is required for equivalency, admission or progression, because that is a false claim about a regulatory process.

sections.heading: The one thing a language tutor must not do
paragraphs: In a language acquisition course the honesty boundary has a particular shape, because the thing being assessed is the student's own command of the language. A tutor who tidies a student's writing into fluent English has not helped them; they have removed the evidence a teacher needs in order to teach, and if the writing is coursework they have created an authorship problem. This matters more in English B than in almost any other subject, because language control is the single largest criterion on both productive components.

Our boundary is the same across every subject and we state it plainly. A tutor teaches, explains the criteria, questions a draft and gives feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor does not produce assessed work and does not rewrite a student's sentences into their own. Feedback names the error type — tense, register, article use, collocation — and the student makes the correction. Providers in this market do sell completed coursework, one of them openly, and submitting bought work exposes a student to an IB malpractice finding that no refund covers.

There is a related point specific to this course and this moment. Generated text is fluent, and fluent text submitted by a student whose spoken English does not match it is immediately conspicuous to a teacher who knows them. We will raise it if a draft's register shifts abruptly, which is occasionally awkward and is far better handled with a tutor in February than with a coordinator in May. We also reference and link official IB subject documents rather than reproducing or supplying them, which is a copyright matter as well as an integrity one.

process.title: One timed listening section and one marked writing task
process.description: Before any plan, two pieces of evidence. A timed listening section tells us the receptive band and, more usefully, which of four causes is producing the losses. A marked writing task tells us whether language accuracy or conceptual understanding is the limiting factor. Together they take under ninety minutes.

process.title: We say which half of the course to spend on
process.description: For a student whose written English is accurate, the available marks are in the receptive paper and in conceptual understanding. For a student whose accuracy is the ceiling, language work pays across three components at once. Those are different plans and we state which one the evidence points to.

process.title: A free trial on the student's own paper
process.description: The trial runs on a marked school paper or on the diagnostic work, with the criterion wording on screen. The student should finish able to say where their marks went and why. You get our reading of the profile. No card is required and there is no obligation to continue.

process.title: Timed practice at exam conditions, twice a week where possible
process.description: Receptive practice only works under the paper's conditions: natural speed, the replay limits the paper applies, and a clock on the reading section. Wrong answers are traced to cause rather than simply corrected, because correction without diagnosis changes nothing.

process.title: Text types and oral rehearsal before the deadline run-in
process.description: One session per text type, written to the word band and marked, covers the realistic range of Paper 1 in a few weeks. Oral rehearsal is timed and scored, including the conversation that follows the presentation, because interactive skills carry their own marks.

whyPoints.title: The listening paper treated as a real component
whyPoints.description: Listening is a quarter of the grade and usually a sliver of lesson time, for practical reasons no school can easily solve. We run it with varied recordings at natural speed under the paper's replay limits, and trace every wrong answer to one of four causes, because correction without diagnosis teaches nothing.

whyPoints.title: Mark allocations published
whyPoints.description: This page sets out the mark split for Paper 1 and the individual oral and what the receptive sections are marked on. No competitor page in this market publishes it, and it is the fact that most changes how a student should spend their revision time.

whyPoints.title: Text type taught as a mark-bearing skill
whyPoints.description: Conceptual understanding is marked explicitly on Paper 1, so a proposal that does not recommend anything or a speech written in essay syntax has lost marks before content is assessed. One session per text type, written and marked, is the fastest mark movement available in this course.

whyPoints.title: Honest input on the placement question
whyPoints.description: Whether a student belongs in English A or English B is the school's decision. What we contribute is marked evidence rather than an impression, because oral fluency is the most visible signal and the least predictive one. We will say when a student looks under-placed as readily as when they look over-placed.

whyPoints.title: No rewriting into fluent English
whyPoints.description: In a course where language control is the largest criterion, a tutor who tidies a student's sentences has removed the evidence their teacher needs. Feedback names the error type and the student makes the correction. No assessed work is produced for a student at any price.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated plainly, once
whyPoints.description: All UAE tutoring on this platform is one-to-one live online, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not operate home visits in the UAE and holds no UAE office or centre. For this course the online format is an advantage, because audio can be played at exactly the exam's pace.

faqs.question: Why is my child losing marks in English B when their spoken English is good?
faqs.answer: Because half the grade is receptive — twenty-five per cent listening and twenty-five per cent reading — and oral fluency predicts neither. A student who speaks easily and idiomatically can still process a recording too slowly to answer, or read below the pace the paper demands. Spoken fluency is also the most visible signal to a family, which is why this profile so often goes undiagnosed until the mocks. One timed listening section and one timed reading section usually identify it in under ninety minutes.

faqs.question: How is the English B listening paper actually marked?
faqs.answer: On correct answers rather than against criteria, which is why it responds to practice rather than to polish. It is worth twenty-five per cent of the grade on its own, and the reading section another twenty-five. Because the answers are right or wrong, a student who recovers four marks across a paper has recovered them outright with no judgement involved. That is the most mechanical gain available in the course and it is the one most Dubai cohorts have the least deliberate practice in.

faqs.question: Why did my child get a listening answer wrong when they knew the words?
faqs.answer: One of three things, and they need separating. Processing speed: the word was recognised, but too late to produce the answer. Accent: a known word in an unfamiliar pronunciation was not matched to the one they know. Or question-reading: they understood the audio perfectly and answered a different question from the one asked. Only the first needs sustained practice; the third is the cheapest gain in the paper and is usually fixed in days by reading question stems before the audio starts.

faqs.question: How many words should the Paper 1 writing task be?
faqs.answer: Between 250 and 400 words at Standard Level and 450 to 600 at Higher Level, on one task chosen from three, each specifying a text type, an audience and a purpose. The response is marked out of thirty: twelve for language, twelve for message and six for conceptual understanding. Confirm the current bands in the subject guide your school is teaching rather than relying on a tutoring page, since the IB revises guides between syllabus cycles.

faqs.question: What does "conceptual understanding" mean on Paper 1?
faqs.answer: Whether the student has grasped audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation — in practice, whether the piece reads like the text type that was asked for. It carries six of the thirty marks and it is where essay-trained students lose a fifth of the paper without noticing. A beautifully written formal essay submitted where a blog post was requested loses those marks and then struggles on message too, because addressing the task appropriately is part of that criterion as well.

faqs.question: Which text types does my child actually need to practise?
faqs.answer: The ones the paper draws on repeatedly: proposal, speech, blog post, formal letter or email, news report, a set of guidelines or instructions, and review. Each has a short, learnable set of non-negotiable features — a proposal must recommend something, a set of guidelines uses imperatives and no personal reflection, a news report puts the outcome first and attributes claims. One session per text type, written to the word band and marked, covers the realistic range in a few weeks.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the SL and HL individual oral?
faqs.answer: The starting material. At Standard Level the student presents on a visual stimulus connected to one of the five prescribed themes. At Higher Level the starting point is an extract from one of the two literary works studied during the course. Both are followed by a conversation with the teacher, and both are marked out of thirty with twelve marks for language and the remainder across the message drawn from the material, the message developed in conversation, and interactive skills.

faqs.question: Why does a polished presentation still score badly in the oral?
faqs.answer: Because the conversation that follows is assessed, not endured, and interactive skills carry their own marks. A student who delivers a rehearsed two minutes and then gives one-word answers has performed well on a part of the component and poorly on the rest. The other common cause is listing: four ideas mentioned and none developed scores below one idea taken somewhere. Rehearsal that includes unscripted follow-up questions is what fixes both, and it has to be timed and marked to be useful.

faqs.question: What are the five prescribed themes and do they need revising like content?
faqs.answer: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation, and sharing the planet. They are not content to memorise — they are the fields the recordings, reading texts, writing tasks and oral stimuli are drawn from. What they mean practically is vocabulary coverage: a student with solid grammar and no vocabulary for migration, urban planning, renewable energy or artificial intelligence will follow a recording's structure and miss its substance. Meeting each new word in all four skills rather than on a list is what makes it stick.

faqs.question: Should my child be in English A instead of English B?
faqs.answer: That is the school's DP coordinator's decision, and what families usually lack is evidence to bring to it. The signals parents can see are misleading: oral fluency is the most visible and the least predictive, since a fluent speaker may read slowly and lose marks across a receptive paper. A quiet student who reads widely may be under-placed and go two years without being stretched. One timed reading section and one marked writing task tell the coordinator more than any impression does.

faqs.question: Does English B count towards the IB bilingual diploma?
faqs.answer: English B is a Group 2 language acquisition course, so it does not satisfy a route that requires two Group 1 languages. The bilingual diploma has published conditions and they are worth reading with your school's coordinator before Group 1 and Group 2 choices are locked in, because for some families with specific university plans the distinction matters a great deal and for others it is irrelevant. Take the requirements from the IB's own published material rather than from any tutoring page, including this one.

faqs.question: Will a good English B grade meet the English requirement for a UAE university?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Ministry of Education equivalency for the American track requires English proficiency evidenced by an IELTS academic score of 5, a TOEFL iBT score of 61, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, with SAT Math of at least 450 for mathematics. A Diploma subject grade is not any of those. For the IB there is no points threshold we can verify from the Ministry's own published material, so check moe.gov.ae or the attestation authority directly rather than relying on a figure from a tutoring site.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does the Ministry of Education actually require?
faqs.answer: Five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One page currently ranking in this market states six, which is wrong. Equivalency is not something any tutoring provider performs or guarantees, and nobody should tell you tutoring is required for it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor correct my child's English B writing for them?
faqs.answer: A tutor can name the error type — tense, register, article use, collocation, word order — and have the student make the correction. A tutor should not rewrite the sentences into fluent English. In a course where language control is the largest single criterion on both productive components, tidied writing removes the evidence the teacher needs in order to teach, and on coursework it creates an authorship problem. Fluent prose submitted by a student whose speech does not match it is conspicuous to any teacher who knows them.

faqs.question: Do you send a tutor to our home in Dubai for English B lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not operate home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visiting is a service we run only in India. Dubai students work with us one to one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. For this course the online format is a real advantage rather than a compromise: audio plays at exactly the pace and replay limit the exam applies, a written task can be marked against the criteria the moment it is finished, and the oral stimulus or extract sits on a shared screen during rehearsal.

faqs.question: How quickly can the receptive paper improve?
faqs.answer: Faster than any other part of this course, for most Dubai students, because they are starting from very little deliberate practice. Twice-weekly timed listening sections for six weeks, with every wrong answer traced back to vocabulary, processing speed, accent or question-reading, typically produces the clearest measurable movement in the subject. The early curve is steep and then flattens. Nobody can promise a particular grade from it, and the gains stop being automatic once the obvious causes have been cleared.

intro.heading: The half of English B that nobody practises
paragraphs: English B grades stall for a reason that surprises most Dubai families. The student lives in an English-speaking city, attends an English-medium school, talks to friends in English all day, and still loses marks steadily on the receptive skills paper. That paper is half the grade. Half of it is listening to recorded material once or twice under timed conditions and answering precise questions about it, and almost nobody practises that at home because it feels like something you either can do or cannot.

It is in fact the most trainable component in the course. Listening marks are lost on specific, nameable things: numbers and dates misheard, a negative construction missed so the answer reverses, a speaker's attitude inferred from vocabulary the student does not know, a question answered from general knowledge rather than from the recording. Each of those has a drill. A student who does twenty minutes of structured listening four times a week for a term moves measurably, and a student who listens to nothing and revises grammar does not. The difference between those two students is not ability or exposure to English; it is whether anybody set the practice as a weekly task with a score attached to it.

The second thing that stalls scores is the gap between fluency and accuracy under a word count. Paper 1 asks for one task from a choice of three, in a specified text type, within a word range - 250 to 400 words at Standard Level in seventy-five minutes, 450 to 600 at Higher Level in ninety minutes. A student who speaks easily can produce 600 words of pleasant, unstructured prose that misses the text type's conventions and the register its audience requires, and lose on two of the three criteria at once.

The third is conceptual understanding, which is the criterion Dubai students are least often taught explicitly. The course is built on five prescribed themes and on a set of concepts - audience, context, purpose, meaning, variation - and the criterion asks whether the student has written something appropriate for the reader and situation they were given. A technically accurate email in the wrong register scores below a slightly flawed one pitched correctly, and that is a teachable habit rather than a language level.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We hold no accreditation from the IB, KHDA or any other authority, we have no UAE office, and we do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India. Dubai families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time by a named English B specialist, with a free trial lesson first and four measures tracked from the start so you can see whether anything is changing.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-online-tutor.programmesIntro: English B sits in Group 2 of the Diploma, the language acquisition group. Dubai students reach it from three main places, and the first six weeks look different for each. The notes below cover the handover rather than the course in general, because where a student came from predicts which of the three criteria is holding the grade down.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Available at Standard and Higher Level. Both sit Paper 1, a single written task in a specified text type, and Paper 2, which combines listening and reading comprehension and carries half the grade. Both complete an individual oral assessment marked internally. Higher Level additionally requires two literary works studied in English, and its individual oral is based on an extract from one of them rather than on a visual stimulus.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools place students between English A and English B from evidence rather than preference, and families are sometimes surprised by the outcome in either direction. Group 2 cohorts in the emirate are mixed in a particular way: students who have been in English-medium education for years sit alongside recent arrivals, which widens the ability range in a single class and makes individual listening work especially useful.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition is organised into phases and assessed on listening, reading, speaking and writing criteria, so a student who came up through it has met the receptive-skills idea before. What the Diploma adds is precision under time: single or double playback, exact answers, and no credit for a generally correct impression of what the recording said.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Dubai school runs the full continuum the transition is handled internally and phase placement usually determines Diploma level. Students who finished MYP in a high phase sometimes move to English A and find the analytical demand unexpected; students who stay in English B at Higher Level meet two literary works for the first time.

programmes.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language to Diploma
programmes.description: A large share of Dubai English B students arrive from Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language, which already assesses listening formally. The main differences are the word counts, the explicit conceptual criterion, and the move from short directed writing to a single extended task in a named text type for a named audience.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for the largest share of Dubai private enrolment, so this is the commonest route into Group 2. Students arriving this way usually have functional listening technique already and lose most on conceptual understanding, because IGCSE rewards task completion while the Diploma asks whether the writing suits its reader.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: The list below is what English B actually assesses, plus the courses Dubai students most often carry alongside it. Each entry gives the format and the commonest reason marks go missing, because the three criteria fail in recognisably different ways.

subjects.name: Paper 1: productive skills, writing
subjects.description: One task chosen from three, written in a specified text type for a specified audience. 250 to 400 words in 1 hour 15 minutes at Standard Level; 450 to 600 words in 1 hour 30 minutes at Higher. Worth 25%. Marks go missing on text-type conventions and register long before they go missing on grammar.

subjects.name: Paper 2: listening comprehension
subjects.description: Recorded material with comprehension questions, 45 minutes at Standard Level and an hour at Higher, carrying 25% of the grade. The commonest losses are numbers, negatives and attitude, and all three respond to drilling. This is the part of the course almost nobody practises at home.

subjects.name: Paper 2: reading comprehension
subjects.description: Authentic written texts with comprehension questions, an hour at both levels, carrying the other 25% of Paper 2. Speed is the limiting factor for most Dubai students rather than vocabulary: the texts are longer than IGCSE equivalents and the questions follow the text closely.

subjects.name: Individual oral assessment
subjects.description: Internally assessed and worth 25%. At Standard Level the student describes and discusses a visual stimulus connected to one of the five themes; at Higher Level the stimulus is an extract from one of the two literary works studied. Both continue into a discussion with the teacher.

subjects.name: The five prescribed themes
subjects.description: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Everything in the course hangs from these, and a student who builds vocabulary by theme rather than by alphabetical list arrives at both Paper 1 and the oral with usable material.

subjects.name: Two literary works
subjects.description: Studied in English and used as the basis of the Higher Level individual oral. They are not assessed as literature in the English A sense; the point is to discuss an extract with understanding of context and message, which is a different and lighter demand than literary analysis.

subjects.name: Text types for Paper 1
subjects.description: Blogs, articles, brochures, formal and informal letters, emails, reports, proposals, reviews, speeches, interviews, sets of instructions and guidelines, diary entries. Each has conventions a marker expects to see, and the inventory is finite - which makes it learnable rather than a matter of luck.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Many Dubai English B students carry an Arabic course as well, in Group 1 or Group 2, and separately sit the KHDA mandatory Arabic lessons. A realistic weekly plan has to account for all of it rather than treating English B as the only language commitment.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Assessed in English regardless of the student's Group 2 level, which makes TOK one of the places where English B students are most exposed. Work on written structure for Paper 1 tends to help the TOK essay as a side effect.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in English B
subjects.description: Permitted in a Group 2 language, within category rules the school will explain. A tutor may discuss the research question, suggest sources and give written feedback on the student's own drafts; the essay stays the student's work and the school supervisor remains the examining relationship.
