sections.heading: What an IB DP English B online tutor in Dubai measures in week one
paragraphs: A first session on this course should produce four numbers rather than an impression. The first is a listening score on a timed, unseen recording at the right level, broken down by error type. The second is a Paper 1 piece written to the real word count under the real time limit, scored separately on language, message and conceptual understanding. The third is a reading comprehension under time, with the number of unanswered questions recorded. The fourth is a recorded three or four minute spoken response, timed.

Those four numbers do something a conversation cannot: they separate what the student can do from what the student can do quickly. A very large share of Dubai English B students are competent and slow. They answer reading questions correctly when given ninety minutes and leave four unanswered in sixty. That is a pacing problem with a pacing solution, and it is invisible to anybody who has only heard the student speak.

The error breakdown on listening is the part families find most surprising. Numbers and dates account for a steady share of losses - a price, a year, a quantity heard once and transcribed wrong. Negatives account for another, where a missed not reverses the answer entirely. Attitude questions account for a third, and those depend on vocabulary the student may simply not have. Three different problems, three different drills, and none of them is helped by more grammar revision.

What you receive after that session is the four numbers and one sentence naming the priority. If listening error types cluster on numbers, the next fortnight is number dictation and nothing else. If the Paper 1 piece scored well on language and poorly on conceptual understanding, the work is text-type conventions and register. Specific instructions can be followed; the general advice to practise more English cannot.

sections.heading: Paper 2 carries half the grade and half of it is audio
paragraphs: Paper 2 combines listening and reading comprehension and is worth 50% of the English B grade, split evenly between the two. Listening runs 45 minutes at Standard Level and an hour at Higher; reading runs an hour at both levels. The material is authentic - interviews, announcements, discussions, reports - and the questions follow it closely, which means credit comes from catching what was said rather than from reconstructing a plausible version of it.

Treating these as one paper is the first mistake. They fail differently. Reading fails on pace and on question-tracking: a student who reads the whole text thoroughly before looking at the questions runs out of time, where a student who reads the questions first and then scans has twice as long for the hard ones. Listening fails on specific comprehension events that pass in two seconds and cannot be revisited beyond the permitted playbacks.

The second mistake is leaving listening until the final term. It is the slowest-improving skill in the course and the one most dependent on accumulated hours, which makes it the worst possible candidate for a late push. Twenty minutes four times a week from the start of Year 12 is a different proposition from two hours a week in April, even though the total is similar, because the ear needs distributed exposure rather than concentrated effort.

sections.heading: An audio diet that survives a Dubai school week
paragraphs: Listening improves through distributed exposure to material slightly above the student's comfortable level, with a task attached. Without a task it is background noise; with one it is practice. The constraint in Dubai is time, so the plan has to live inside journeys and gaps rather than demand new hours, which is why the schedule below is built in twenty-minute units and assumes nothing about a quiet study.

Difficulty has to be controlled deliberately. Material that is too easy produces confidence and no learning; material far too hard produces twenty minutes of nothing. The useful band is where the student follows the gist but misses detail, and the test is simple: if they can answer three of five detail questions, the level is right. A tutor's job here is largely curation, because choosing material at the right level is the part students cannot do for themselves.

Error logging is what turns listening practice into something a session can act on. The student writes down every missed answer and tags it: number, negative, attitude, vocabulary, speed or distraction. After three weeks the log has a shape, and the shape tells you whether the next fortnight is number dictation, negative-construction drills or theme vocabulary. Without the log, every session starts with a guess.

One note for Dubai households specifically. Many families here speak two or three languages at home, and parents sometimes worry that this holds English B back. In practice multilingual students are frequently excellent at the inference questions and weak only on the detail questions, which is a technique gap rather than an exposure gap. The audio diet addresses the detail; the inference is already there.

sections.heading: Paper 1: the text types are a finite list, which makes them learnable
paragraphs: Paper 1 gives three tasks and the student picks one, writing in the text type named for the audience named. The whole difficulty of this component is that students revise their English and not the text types, when the text types are a closed list and the conventions a marker expects are specific and writable on one page. A blog opens and addresses a reader in a particular way; a formal report does not. A speech has to be audible on the page.

Marks are allocated across three criteria: language, message and conceptual understanding. The third is the one that catches fluent students, because it asks whether the piece suits its audience, context and purpose. An articulate, grammatically clean letter written in the register of a chat message loses there while scoring well on language, and students who have never had the criteria explained separately interpret the result as general disapproval of their English.

Word count is the other quiet failure. At Standard Level the range is 250 to 400 words and at Higher 450 to 600, under seventy-five and ninety minutes respectively. Writing substantially under range leaves the message undeveloped; writing well over it wastes time that was needed for checking. Students should know by the end of Year 12 what their own handwriting does - how many lines 400 words takes them - so the count never has to be estimated under pressure.

sections.heading: Vocabulary built from the five themes, not from a list
paragraphs: The course hangs from five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. They are not topics to be covered and ticked off; they are the frame from which Paper 1 tasks, reading texts, listening material and oral stimuli are drawn. A student who has built vocabulary by theme walks into any of those components with usable language, and a student who has memorised an alphabetical list walks in with words they cannot deploy.

Building it properly means collecting language in clusters that do real work: the vocabulary of obligation and permission for social organisation, the vocabulary of innovation and failure for human ingenuity, the vocabulary of belonging and exclusion for identities. Each cluster needs the noun, the verb, the adjective and the collocations students get wrong, because an English B script loses marks on collocation far more often than on tense.

The theme frame also solves the oral. At Standard Level the student describes a visual stimulus connected to a theme and then discusses it, and the predictable failure is a student who describes the picture accurately for three minutes and never reaches the theme. A student with theme vocabulary ready makes the link in the first thirty seconds and spends the rest of the time on content, which is where the marks are.

In Dubai there is a usable advantage here that most students do not exploit. All five themes are visible in the city around them. Social organisation, migration and belonging, rapid innovation, the pressure on water and energy: a student writing about something they can see is more specific than one writing about an abstraction, and specificity is what the message criterion rewards. Local examples, used honestly, are a genuine asset in this course.

sections.heading: Measuring ten weeks of English B: what moves and what does not
paragraphs: Families want to know how long it takes, and the honest answer is different for each skill. Reading pace moves fastest - two or three weeks of question-first technique usually shows. Paper 1 conceptual understanding moves in four to six weeks once text-type conventions are explicit, because it is knowledge rather than ability. Listening moves slowly and steadily over a term and keeps moving. Underlying accuracy in writing moves slowest of all, over a year, and we say so rather than implying otherwise.

That difference matters when a family has limited sessions. With ten weeks before a mock, the order that produces the most marks is reading technique first, then Paper 1 conventions, then listening drills running throughout, with oral rehearsal in the final fortnight. With two years, the order reverses: listening starts in week one and never stops, because it is the only component that cannot be rescued late.

We publish no outcome statistics on these pages and no tutor here will promise a grade. What you get instead is four measures recorded from week one and reviewed with you at week ten. The table below shows what a ten-week record typically looks like and how each item is measured, so you can judge whether the work is producing anything rather than taking that on trust.

A Dubai-specific caveat on any ten-week plan. Mock weeks, school assessments in the KHDA mandatory subjects, and Ramadan will each interrupt it. Ramadan in particular shifts the whole household day, and post-Iftar sessions are easy to arrange precisely because nobody is travelling. We put the pauses into the plan at the start, because a schedule that ignores them gets missed twice and then abandoned.

sections.heading: Permits, equivalency and the Arabic-plus-English Dubai week
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit, and the detail is worth a parent's attention. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is open to teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no fine schedule has been published, nobody should quote you a figure.

Equivalency is the other administrative thing English B families ask about, and the honest answer is narrower than the internet suggests. For the British track, the Ministry of Education requires five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count of five, plus one accredited A-Level subject at no less than E or two AS-Level subjects at the same grade. For the American track, English proficiency is evidenced by IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in SAT reading and writing, with at least 450 in SAT Math.

For the IB there is no published points threshold we are prepared to restate, because we have not read one on the Ministry's own site, and one competitor already publishes an incorrect subject count for the British track. Check the IB position directly with the Ministry of Education or the attestation authority in your emirate. Nothing about tutoring is required for equivalency, and no honest page should suggest otherwise.

Finally, the week itself. Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the international curriculum a school is licensed by KHDA to teach, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes prohibited. For an English B student frequently carrying private Arabic lessons too, that is a real constraint, and the twenty-minute listening unit exists because it is what actually fits.

faqs.question: How is the English B listening paper structured and how long does it last?
faqs.answer: Listening forms one half of Paper 2, runs 45 minutes at Standard Level and an hour at Higher Level, and carries 25% of the overall grade. The material is authentic rather than scripted for learners - interviews, announcements, discussions - and the questions follow it closely, so credit comes from catching what was actually said. Playback is limited, which is the whole difficulty: a number misheard or a negative missed cannot be revisited. Confirm the current duration and playback arrangements with your child's IB coordinator, since subject guides are revised periodically.

faqs.question: Why does my child understand English all day and still lose marks in the listening paper?
faqs.answer: Because conversational comprehension and exam listening are different tasks. Daily conversation is interactive - you can ask, infer from context and tolerate gaps. The paper asks for precise detail from a recording that does not repeat itself on request. Losses cluster on three things: numbers and dates transcribed wrong, a missed negative that reverses the answer, and attitude questions resting on vocabulary the student does not have. All three respond to drilling, which is why we log errors by type rather than recording a single score.

faqs.question: What word count does Paper 1 require at each level?
faqs.answer: Between 250 and 400 words at Standard Level in 1 hour 15 minutes, and between 450 and 600 words at Higher Level in 1 hour 30 minutes. Students should know by the end of Year 12 how many lines of their own handwriting that takes, so the count never has to be guessed under pressure. Writing well under range leaves the message undeveloped; writing well over it spends the time that was needed for checking. The task also has to be in the text type named, for the audience named, which is where more marks go than on word count.

faqs.question: Which text types can come up in English B Paper 1?
faqs.answer: The list is finite, which is the good news: blogs, articles, brochures and leaflets, formal and informal letters, emails, reports, proposals, reviews, speeches, interviews, sets of instructions and guidelines, and diary entries among them. Each carries conventions a marker expects - a report needs headings and recommendations, a speech needs direct address and signposting, a review needs a verdict rather than description. Because the list is closed, a student can build a one-page conventions sheet in Year 12 and reuse it for two years, which is more valuable than any amount of general writing practice.

faqs.question: What are the five prescribed themes and how much do they matter?
faqs.answer: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. They are the frame from which Paper 1 tasks, reading texts, listening material and oral stimuli are all drawn, so they matter a great deal more than a list of topics usually does. The practical consequence is for vocabulary: a student who collects language in clusters per theme - obligation and permission for social organisation, innovation and failure for human ingenuity - has usable material in every component. An alphabetical word list produces words a student recognises but cannot deploy.

faqs.question: How is the Standard Level oral visual stimulus chosen and used?
faqs.answer: The stimulus is a visual connected to one of the five prescribed themes, provided at the start of the preparation time, and the student describes it and then discusses it with the teacher. The predictable failure is spending three minutes describing the image accurately and never reaching the theme, which leaves the discussion to carry everything. A student with theme vocabulary ready makes the link within the first thirty seconds and spends the remaining time on content. At Higher Level the stimulus is an extract from one of the two literary works instead.

faqs.question: Can my child move between English B and English A?
faqs.answer: Schools decide Group 1 and Group 2 placement from evidence, and a change is possible but has a deadline set by the school and the IB's registration process rather than by the family. The honest test is not how fluently the student speaks but whether they can sustain written analysis of an unseen text under time, which a marked piece of work answers quickly. Moving up adds literary analysis and a heavier reading load; moving down is sometimes the right call for a student whose other five subjects are suffering. Ask the coordinator early, because the window closes.

faqs.question: How much vocabulary does an English B student actually need?
faqs.answer: Enough to handle the five themes with precision, which is a narrower target than it sounds and a different one from raw volume. What loses marks in practice is collocation rather than range: a student knows the word but pairs it with the wrong verb or preposition. Collecting language in clusters, with the noun, verb, adjective and the pairings students typically get wrong, produces usable vocabulary faster than memorising long lists. Attitude questions in the listening paper are the one place where sheer range matters, since inferring a speaker's stance depends on recognising evaluative words.

faqs.question: What does the conceptual understanding criterion mean in practice?
faqs.answer: It asks whether the piece suits its audience, context and purpose - whether it reads like the thing it was supposed to be. A technically accurate letter written in the register of a chat message loses here while scoring well on language, and students who have never had the three criteria explained separately read that result as general disapproval of their English. The fix is knowledge rather than ability: conventions written down, register practised deliberately, and the three criteria scored separately on every marked piece so the student can see which one is costing them.

faqs.question: How should my child practise listening at home in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Twenty minutes, four times a week, on material slightly above comfortable level, with a task attached and a tagged error log. The level test is simple: if three of five detail questions are answerable, the difficulty is right. The task is what distinguishes practice from background noise - transcribe every figure and date in one week, then track who argued what in the next. In Dubai the school bus is often the only reliable slot, and headphones plus a notebook there beat a desk session at nine in the evening that nobody actually does.

faqs.question: Do Dubai monthly English B packages work out cheaper than hourly sessions?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether the hours get used. Published Dubai monthly figures in October 2026 include online packages around AED 799 for eight sessions and in-home packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour sessions, while Bestimate estimates AED 240-600 a month for budget weekly tutoring, AED 600-1,200 mid-tier and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Those are other providers' published figures. A package only saves money if the sessions happen, which in a Dubai term with mocks and travel is worth being realistic about.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram offer in-home English B lessons anywhere in the UAE?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. UAE families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For this subject the format has specific advantages: the tutor controls listening playback and can stop at the exact second comprehension broke, and every oral rehearsal is recorded without anybody setting anything up, which is the fastest way to fix hesitation and repair in spoken work.

faqs.question: How do we measure progress in English B across a term?
faqs.answer: With the same four tests at the start and at week ten: a timed listening score broken down by error type, the number of reading questions left unanswered under time, a Paper 1 task scored separately on language, message and conceptual understanding, and a timed recorded spoken response. Reading pace usually moves within two or three weeks, conceptual understanding within four to six, listening steadily across the term, and underlying written accuracy over a year rather than a term. We say which is which in advance rather than afterwards.

faqs.question: Can the same tutor help with Arabic or the KHDA mandatory subjects?
faqs.answer: Rarely the same tutor, and it is better handled as a separate match. Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools whatever curriculum the school is licensed by KHDA to teach, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in those subjects, with combined classes prohibited. The subject content and the language of instruction differ accordingly. What a single plan can do is schedule around them, so English B listening tasks sit where the week actually has room.

faqs.question: Does an English B grade affect UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: For the British track the Ministry requires five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education from that count, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. For the American track, English is evidenced through IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in SAT reading and writing. For the IB we will not restate a points threshold, because we have not read one on the Ministry's own site and at least one ranking competitor publishes an incorrect figure. Verify the IB position with the Ministry or your emirate's attestation authority directly.

intro.heading: English B is an acquisition course, and it is marked like one
paragraphs: English B sits in Group 2 of the Diploma, the language-acquisition group. It is not the course for a student whose strongest language is English; that student belongs in English A: Language and Literature or English A: Literature. In Dubai the distinction matters more than almost anywhere else, because a large share of Diploma candidates arrive from Arabic-medium, French-medium, Russian-medium or Indian-curriculum primary schooling into an English-medium school at Year 7 or Year 9. By Year 12 their spoken English is fluent and their written register is not. English B is designed for that profile, and the mark scheme rewards precisely the things that profile tends to miss.

The course is built around five prescribed themes - identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet - and a set of text types the student must be able to produce on demand. Higher Level adds two literary works, read in English, which supply the extract that anchors the HL individual oral. Nothing on the course is a literature essay in the Language A sense. A student who writes a careful analysis of theme and imagery inside a Paper 1 blog post will be marked down, because the blog post was asked for and the analysis was not.

That is the commonest reason a capable Dubai student plateaus at a 4 or a 5 in English B. The English is good. The task is misread. Criterion B, message, asks whether the response does what the prompt instructed, for the audience the prompt named, in the text type the prompt specified. A tutor who marks against the published criteria rather than against general writing quality fixes this in a handful of sessions, because it is a rules problem rather than a language problem.

The second recurring problem is Paper 2. Listening carries a quarter of the final grade, and few Dubai schools timetable dedicated listening practice, because there is no obvious homework to set for it. Students hear each recording twice and lose marks on the questions that test inference rather than retrieval. Reading comprehension bleeds marks on matching and true-false items where a distractor repeats the stem's wording. Both are trainable with recorded practice and a tutor who stops the audio to ask what the speaker implied rather than what the speaker said.

Lessons are one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time so a session can start after a 15:00 or 15:30 finish and still leave the evening intact. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE - sending a tutor to an address is a service we run only in India - so the matching pool is not narrowed to the specialists who happen to live within driving distance of your community. For a subject as component-specific as English B, that widening is the whole point.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-tutor.programmesIntro: English B is a Diploma subject, but the preparation for it starts years earlier. These are the IB programmes Dubai schools run around it, and what each one contributes to a student's English before Year 12. The notes are specific to how Dubai schools sequence the programmes rather than to the IB's general description of them.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two-year Diploma takes six subjects, one from each group, with three at Higher Level. English B sits in Group 2 and may be taken at SL or HL. A candidate whose Language A is Arabic, French, Russian, Hindi or Spanish normally pairs it with English B, and that pairing is what makes a bilingual diploma possible. Group 2 cannot be dropped: every Diploma candidate studies a second language, which is why English B enrolment across Dubai schools is large and unusually mixed in ability.
programmes.countryNote: A single English B SL class at a school in Al Barsha or Emirates Hills can hold students who have spoken English since nursery alongside students who arrived from Cairo or Moscow in Year 10. Schools stream by placement test where staffing allows, and many cannot, so the published class pace sits in the middle and both ends of the class need separate work outside it.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme assesses language acquisition in phases against four criteria: comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating, and using language in spoken and written form. A student finishing MYP in Phase 4 or 5 is normally placed into English B HL, and Phase 3 points to SL. The phases are not year groups, so a student can sit in the same phase for two years without anyone raising it at a parents' evening.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run the MYP only to Year 9 and then switch to IGCSE for Years 10 and 11 before the Diploma. That break matters for English B, because IGCSE English as a Second Language rewards accuracy and fixed formats while MYP criterion C rewards risk-taking with language. Students who cross that join often need the register work rebuilt from the task instruction upwards.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme combines at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project and a personal and professional skills course. Where English B is one of the Diploma courses, the student sits the same papers as a full Diploma candidate and is marked on the same seven-point scale. What differs is the surrounding load, which carries less written coursework in other subjects and more structured reflection.
programmes.countryNote: Only a handful of Dubai schools are authorised to run the Career-related Programme, so a CP student wanting English B help is often the only one in their year on that route. School-level revision groups are built for the Diploma cohort and rarely fit the CP timetable, which is one of the clearer cases for one-to-one work rather than a class.

dubai/ib-dp-english-b-tutor.subjectsIntro: English B is one course, and a Dubai Diploma student rarely needs help with only one language component. These are the Group 1 and Group 2 courses IB Gram covers for Dubai candidates, with what each one actually assesses rather than what it sounds like it assesses.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Language acquisition for students already functional in English. Paper 1 productive writing, Paper 2 listening and reading, and an individual oral. HL adds two literary works and a longer Paper 1. Marks are lost on text type and audience far more often than on grammar.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 course for students whose strongest language is English. Paper 1 is guided textual analysis of unseen non-literary texts; Paper 2 is a comparative essay on studied literary works. HL adds a 1,200-1,500 word HL essay. A student mis-streamed here from English B usually struggles with Paper 1.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: Literary works only, across periods, places and forms. Paper 1 is guided literary analysis of an unseen extract; Paper 2 compares studied works. The individual oral examines a global issue through two works. Chosen in Dubai mainly by students heading for English, law or history degrees.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The acquisition route for students with conversational Arabic but limited Modern Standard Arabic. The same component structure as English B, with the added difficulty that classroom Arabic in Dubai is often Gulf dialect while the papers are set in Modern Standard.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 route for first-language Arabic speakers, and for many Dubai students the second half of a bilingual diploma alongside English A or English B. Papers are sat in Arabic, and the HL essay is written in Arabic on a studied work.

subjects.name: French B
subjects.description: Acquisition French for students from Francophone primary schooling or from a strong MYP French background. Structurally identical to English B, with text types that lean on formal register conventions French examiners mark strictly.

subjects.name: Spanish B
subjects.description: Often chosen in Dubai as the second language by students with no heritage connection to it, which makes the HL literary works the pressure point. Paper 2 listening is the component where ab initio habits show up most clearly.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The 1,600-word TOK essay on a prescribed title plus the TOK exhibition. English B students often find the essay harder than their grade suggests, because the marking rewards precise argumentative language rather than fluency.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in a Group 2 language
subjects.description: A 4,000-word essay in the target language, in one of three categories: language, culture and society, or literature. Supervision is about research question scope and the categories' different evidence requirements. The writing stays the student's own.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
subjects.description: The qualification many Dubai students hold on entry to English B. Its reward structure for fixed formats and formulaic phrasing is exactly what the English B criteria penalise, so the first few Diploma sessions often unpick it.

sections.heading: What an IB DP English B tutor in Dubai is actually asked to fix
paragraphs: Parents who search for an IB DP English B tutor in Dubai almost always arrive with one of four specific problems rather than a general sense that English needs work. The first is a Paper 1 grade that sits two bands below the student's class work. The second is a listening score nobody can explain. The third is an individual oral three weeks away for which the student has no structure. The fourth is a placement argument: the school has put a child in English B who the parents believe should be in English A, or the reverse.

Each of those has a different fix and a different timescale. A Paper 1 problem is usually solved by marking three or four responses against criteria A, B and C and showing the student where the message mark went. A listening problem takes six to eight weeks of twice-weekly recorded practice because it is a trained skill, not a known fact. An oral three weeks out is a structure-and-rehearsal job. A placement question is a conversation about evidence, and often ends with the school being right.

What a tutor cannot do is make the course shorter. English B is assessed on productive performance under time pressure, so the sessions that move a grade are the ones where the student writes and speaks while the tutor watches, not the ones where the tutor explains. Families who book an English B specialist expecting content delivery - vocabulary lists, grammar tables, model answers to memorise - tend to see the smallest movement, because none of those three things is what the criteria measure.

sections.heading: English A or English B? The placement decision Dubai schools make for you
paragraphs: Group 1 and Group 2 are different courses with different purposes, and the IB expects the school to place the student. In Dubai that placement is made by a Diploma coordinator in the spring of Year 11 on the basis of MYP phase scores, IGCSE results or an internal assessment, and it is reviewed rarely once made. Parents frequently disagree with it, in both directions: some want English A because it looks more rigorous on a university application, others want English B because it looks easier.

Both instincts can be wrong. A student with fluent conversational English and weak analytical writing often scores higher in English B HL than in English A SL, because the English B criteria do not require close reading of unseen literary text. A student who reads widely in English and writes well will find English B constraining and may ceiling out, because the marks available for linguistic risk are capped by the text type. The honest version of the conversation is about which set of criteria the student's existing skills already satisfy.

There is also a diploma-level consequence. A bilingual diploma can be awarded where a candidate completes two Group 1 languages, which means a student taking Arabic A and English A rather than Arabic A and English B. Some Dubai families care about that and should be told the route exists; others do not, and should not be pushed into a harder English course for a line on a certificate. sections.heading: The English B assessment structure, component by component
paragraphs: English B has three assessed components and no written coursework beyond the recorded oral. The external papers carry 75% of the grade between them and the internally assessed oral carries 25%, at both SL and HL. That split is worth saying plainly to a Dubai parent, because the school report often reflects classwork and the final grade reflects two papers sat in a hall and one recording made in a quiet room.

Paper 1 is productive writing. The student chooses one of three prompts, each tied to a prescribed theme, and writes in a specified text type for a specified audience. It is marked out of 30 across three criteria: language, message, and conceptual understanding. Paper 2 comes in two halves sat in sequence - listening first, then reading - and between them they make up half the final grade. The individual oral is recorded and assessed by the teacher, then moderated by the IB.

The difference between SL and HL is duration, depth and the oral stimulus. HL Paper 1 runs longer, HL listening runs longer, and the HL oral starts from an extract from one of the two literary works studied rather than from an image. sections.heading: Where English B marks are lost, criterion by criterion
paragraphs: English B marking is criterion-referenced, which means a student is not awarded a grade for an impression of quality but a mark for each named criterion. Paper 1 and the individual oral are each marked out of 30 across three criteria. Knowing which criterion is leaking marks changes what a session does, and it is the piece of information most students cannot get from a returned school mock, because teachers under time pressure write a total and a comment.

Criterion A, language, covers range and accuracy. It is the criterion Dubai students usually score best on and the one families assume is the problem. Criterion B, message, covers whether the ideas are relevant, developed and organised for the stated audience and purpose. It is where most marks are lost, and it is lost in the first thirty seconds of planning rather than in the writing. Criterion C, conceptual understanding, covers whether the student has registered context, purpose, audience, meaning and variation in register - the thing that distinguishes a letter to a head teacher from a post on a school forum.

The practical consequence is that the fastest grade movement in English B comes from planning discipline, not from vocabulary. A student who spends four minutes identifying the audience, the text type's conventions and the purpose before writing will pick up marks in B and C that no amount of additional lexis would have earned. That is a habit, and habits are built by repetition under supervision, which is what a one-to-one session is for.

sections.heading: The individual oral: a visual stimulus at SL, a literary extract at HL
paragraphs: The individual oral is the component Dubai students are least prepared for and the one most within reach of short-notice work. At SL the student is given a previously unseen visual stimulus linked to one of the five prescribed themes, has a short supervised preparation period, then speaks for three to four minutes before a discussion with the teacher. At HL the stimulus is an extract from one of the two literary works studied, which changes the preparation entirely: the student must know the works well enough to place the extract and argue from it.

The recurring SL failure is description. A student shown a photograph of a crowded market will describe the photograph. The marks are in using the image as a springboard to the theme - what it suggests about identity, or consumption, or urban life - and in sustaining an argument for the full time. The recurring HL failure is a reading schedule that never happened, so the student meets an extract from a work they skimmed in a week and has no textual memory to draw on.

Both are rehearsal problems. A tutor can supply unseen stimuli in the same style week after week, record the student's four minutes, play it back, and ask the discussion questions a teacher would ask. Students who have done that ten times walk into the real oral having already had the experience. Students who have not are improvising on the one occasion where improvisation is most expensive, with a recording that goes to the IB for moderation.

sections.heading: Paper 1 text types and the register trap
paragraphs: Paper 1 names the text type in the prompt, and the conventions of that text type carry marks under criteria B and C. The list a Dubai student needs to be able to produce on demand is long: blog, article, brochure, diary entry, email, essay, instructions, interview, letter, news report, proposal, review, set of guidelines, speech, and more. Each has conventions, and the conventions are not decorative. A speech that does not address an audience, a proposal with no recommendation, a review that does not evaluate - each of those loses marks that were available for free.

The register trap is specific to students in English-medium Dubai schools. They write the register they hear, which is the register of a classroom and a group chat. Asked for a formal letter to a school principal, they produce something fluent and slightly too familiar. Asked for a blog post, they produce something stiff and essay-shaped, because formal writing is the only register they have been graded on. Moving between registers on demand is a teachable skill, and it is the one that separates a 5 from a 7 on this paper.

In sessions this is drilled in pairs: the same content written twice, once as an email to a friend and once as a letter to an authority, then compared line by line. It is unglamorous and it works. The alternative - writing more full practice papers and hoping the register improves - is how students spend six months producing fifteen responses that all have the same problem, because nobody ever isolated the variable.
bullets: Text type is named in the prompt and its conventions carry criterion C marks
Fifteen-plus text types, each with a distinct opening, layout and sign-off
Register practised in pairs on identical content, not through more full papers
Audience identified in writing before the first sentence is drafted

They are the market, not an IB Gram price list: our rate for an English B specialist is quoted after the free trial lesson, when the component, level and session length are known.

What moves the number in Dubai is level, component and lead time. HL costs more than SL because the HL literary works mean preparation outside the session. The individual oral costs more per hour than Paper 1 work because rehearsal with playback is labour-intensive. And a booking made six weeks before a paper costs more per hour than the same work spread across two years, because the available tutors are the ones already carrying a full Year 13 load. Dubai school fees were held flat for 2026-27 under a KHDA decision announced in May 2026, which has not had the same effect on tutoring rates.

The one cost comparison worth making carefully is online against an in-home tutor. A Dubai in-home visit carries travel in both directions, which is why market rates for it sit above online rates even where the tutor is the same person. sections.heading: Academic honesty on a language acquisition course
paragraphs: English B carries less coursework than most Diploma subjects, which makes the academic-honesty boundary narrower but not less important. The individual oral is recorded and moderated. The Extended Essay, where a student chooses to write it in English B, is submitted work subject to the full academic-integrity framework. A tutor who crosses the line on either does not just risk their own reputation; the student faces an IB malpractice finding, and malpractice findings follow a candidate.

The boundary in practice: a tutor may teach text-type conventions, supply practice stimuli, mark the student's own responses against the criteria, explain why a mark was awarded, ask the questions an examiner would ask, and set reading. A tutor may not write any part of a submitted piece, may not dictate sentences for a student to transcribe into an Extended Essay, may not script an individual oral for memorisation, and may not supply model answers for a student to reproduce as their own. One agency in this market advertises completed Internal Assessments for sale; that is an integrity breach and we will not imitate it.

There is also a boundary around materials. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB and are licensed to schools. IB Gram links to official pages rather than redistributing files. If your child needs the current English B subject guide, their Diploma coordinator has it, and the published details in this page should be confirmed against that guide rather than treated as a substitute for it.

sections.heading: KHDA, mandatory Arabic and fitting English B into a Dubai week
paragraphs: Dubai private schools are overseen by KHDA, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. KHDA inspects annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak, and a school's band is a reasonable proxy for how much in-school support a struggling English B student will actually receive. Dubai's private sector held 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, with IB programmes accounting for roughly a fourteenth of enrolment.

The timetable constraint nobody mentions on tutoring pages is the mandatory UAE subject load. KHDA guidance requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students and specified languages of instruction. For a Diploma student that is additional timetabled periods sitting on top of six IB subjects plus the core. English B is frequently the subject that gets the least independent study time as a result, because it feels like the one the student already speaks.

That is why the session slot matters as much as the tutor. A Dubai school day that ends between 14:30 and 15:30, plus a school run, plus mandatory-subject homework, leaves a usable window from about 16:30. Sessions in Gulf Standard Time from 16:00 to 21:30, Sunday to Thursday, with weekend mornings available, is what fits. During Ramadan, families generally move sessions to after iftar, and the schedule shifts for the month rather than pausing.

process.title: Tell us the component, not just the subject
process.description: A fifteen-minute call or a short form: level, school, which of Paper 1, Paper 2 or the oral is the problem, and the most recent mark with the criterion breakdown if the school gave one. That is enough to match. Without it, the first two sessions are spent diagnosing what a mark sheet would have shown.

process.title: See two tutor profiles
process.description: You get the component history, the year groups they teach, the levels they take and the hours they hold open in Gulf Standard Time. You choose. If neither fits the slot you need, say so and we look again rather than pushing the available one.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: Forty-five minutes, one per family, no card details taken. The tutor sets a short Paper 1 task or runs a stimulus so you both see how the student performs rather than how they talk about performing. You get a written note of what the session found.

process.title: Agree the plan and the marking rhythm
process.description: How many sessions a week, which component first, how often a full task gets marked, and what you see between sessions. For English B that last point matters: ask for marks by criterion letter, because a total tells you nothing you can act on.

process.title: Review at session six
process.description: Six sessions is enough to see whether the criterion that was leaking marks has stopped. If it has not, the plan changes or the tutor does. Grade movement in English B shows up in marked task scores before it shows up on a school report, so that is what we look at.

whyPoints.description: Because delivery is online, the pool of English B specialists is not limited to those who could drive to your community by 16:30. A family in Mirdif gets a tutor who has taught the HL oral for years rather than the nearest available English teacher.

whyPoints.title: Marking against the published criteria

faqs.question: Is English B the right IB course for a child who has been in an English-medium Dubai school since Year 4?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the length of time in an English-medium school is not the deciding factor. What decides it is whether the student's analytical reading and formal written register are strong enough for Group 1 criteria. A child who has spoken English at school for eight years may still write in a classroom register and struggle with unseen non-literary analysis, which is English A Paper 1's whole business. The school makes the placement from MYP phases or IGCSE results. If you disagree, ask the Diploma coordinator which evidence they used and what a trial English A Paper 1 would show.

faqs.question: How is the English B individual oral different at HL and SL?
faqs.answer: The timings and criteria are the same; the stimulus is not. At SL the student receives a previously unseen visual stimulus linked to one of the five prescribed themes, prepares briefly, speaks for three to four minutes and then discusses it with the teacher. At HL the starting point is an extract from one of the two literary works studied during the course, so the student must know those works well enough to place the extract and argue from it. In practice that makes HL preparation a reading-schedule problem across Year 12, while SL preparation is rehearsal with unseen images.

faqs.question: What does Paper 1 in IB English B actually ask a student to write?
faqs.answer: One task, chosen from three prompts, each tied to a prescribed theme. The prompt names the text type, the audience and the purpose, and all three carry marks. A prompt might ask for a speech to a school assembly, a proposal to a local council or a blog post for a student site. It is marked out of thirty across three criteria: language, message, and conceptual understanding. Most lost marks sit in message and conceptual understanding, because students write good English that ignores the named audience or the conventions of the named text type.

faqs.question: Why does my child score well in class essays but badly in English B Paper 1?
faqs.answer: Because a class essay and a Paper 1 task are marked for different things. School essays usually reward content knowledge and clear argument. Paper 1 rewards doing what the prompt instructed, in the text type it specified, for the audience it named, and shows that in criteria B and C. A student with one good register - the formal essay - will write that register whatever the prompt asks for, and lose the conceptual-understanding marks every time. The fix is register drill on identical content across different text types, not more full practice papers.

faqs.question: How much of the English B grade comes from listening?
faqs.answer: Listening sits inside Paper 2 alongside reading, and Paper 2 is half the final grade at both SL and HL. Treating listening as a quarter of the whole course is a reasonable working assumption for planning revision, though you should confirm the current split against the English B subject guide. Few Dubai schools timetable dedicated listening practice, because there is no neat homework to set for it, so it is often the largest unworked component in a student's preparation. Twice-weekly recorded practice over six to eight weeks is what moves it.

faqs.question: Can an English B tutor help with the two HL literary works?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is where HL support earns its cost. The two works supply the extract for the HL individual oral, so a student who skimmed them in the fortnight before the recording has nothing to argue from. A tutor sets a reading schedule across Year 12, works through the sections most likely to appear as extracts, and builds a quotation and context bank the student can actually recall. The reading itself stays the student's work. The tutor's job is pacing, discussion and making sure the works are in memory before they are needed.

faqs.question: Does a bilingual IB diploma require English B or English A?
faqs.answer: A bilingual diploma is awarded on the basis of two Group 1 languages, so English B does not count towards it. A Dubai student wanting one would typically take Arabic A alongside English A rather than English B. There is a second route, through completing a Group 3 or Group 4 subject in a language other than the Language A, which some schools support and many do not. Confirm with your child's Diploma coordinator before planning around it, and weigh whether the award is worth moving a student into a harder English course.

faqs.question: How many English B sessions a week do Dubai Diploma families usually start with?
faqs.answer: One a week is the normal starting point in Year 12 and for most of Year 13, rising to two in the final term or when a specific component is close. Two a week from the start tends to produce diminishing returns in English B, because the gains come from marked written work and rehearsal, and both need time between sessions for the student to produce something. Where listening is the diagnosed problem, the pattern that works is one session plus two short recorded practice sets the student does alone.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an Extended Essay written in English B?
faqs.answer: A tutor can help with scope, research question, source quality and the differences between the language, culture-and-society and literature categories, which carry different evidence expectations. They can read a draft the student has written and ask questions about it. They cannot write any part of it, dictate sentences, or restructure paragraphs into final form. The Extended Essay is submitted work under the IB's academic-integrity framework, and a malpractice finding follows a candidate. Your child's assigned school supervisor remains the person who signs off the process.

faqs.question: Is online English B tutoring workable for a student in Mirdif with a 15:30 school finish?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the timing is the reason online works better than a visit here. A 15:30 finish plus a school run means the student is home around 16:15. An online session can start at 16:30 with no further travel for anyone. A visiting tutor crossing Dubai at that hour would arrive later, cost more because travel is priced into the rate, and be drawn from whoever covers that area. IB Gram delivers one-to-one lessons over live video and makes no home visits in the UAE, which is how the Mirdif slot stays at 16:30.

faqs.question: What does IB English B tutoring cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates in Dubai for a qualified subject tutor working online run roughly AED 150-300 an hour, with IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450 and above, on figures published by providers in this market and by Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table. In-home one-to-one sits higher, around AED 180-500, because travel is priced into the rate. Those are market figures rather than ours. IB Gram quotes after the free trial lesson, once the level, the component and the session length are known, so you are comparing a real number rather than a band.

faqs.question: Does my child need English B if their school teaches every subject in English?
faqs.answer: Every Diploma candidate takes a Group 2 language, so the question is which one rather than whether. For a student whose Language A is Arabic, French or Russian, English B is the natural pairing and the course that matches their actual profile. For a student whose strongest language is English, Group 1 English plus a different Group 2 language is usually the better fit. Being taught in English all day is not the same as being assessed against Group 1 criteria, which is the distinction Dubai placement decisions turn on.

faqs.question: How late in Year 13 is it still worth starting English B support?
faqs.answer: Components respond at different speeds, so the answer depends on which one is broken. Paper 1 register and task compliance can improve inside four to six sessions, because it is a planning habit. The individual oral responds to two or three weeks of recorded rehearsal. Listening needs six to eight weeks and does not compress well. Starting eight weeks out with a clear diagnosis is useful. Starting two weeks out is worth doing for the oral and for Paper 1 planning, and is honestly too late for listening. No tutor can promise a particular grade from any starting point.

faqs.question: Do IB English B tutors working with Dubai students need a MoHRE private tuition work permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tuition in the UAE need a private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued free of charge for two years through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those operating without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so ask any tutor you engage directly and verify on mohre.gov.ae.

faqs.question: What happens if no English B specialist is free at the time we need?
faqs.answer: You are told, rather than offered a general English teacher with the subject name attached. English B HL oral work and criterion-level Paper 1 marking are specific skills, and the pool of tutors who do them well is smaller than the pool of good English teachers. Where nobody suitable holds your requested slot, the options are a different slot with the right specialist, a tutor outside the UAE working in Gulf Standard Time, or a wait with a date attached. Delivery is online in every case, so location is never the constraint; availability is.

Lessons are one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with marked work returned by criterion letter so you can see what moved. dubai/ib-dp-environmental-systems-and-so.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Environmental Systems and Societies at Diploma level: systems diagrams, environmental value systems, the data-handling questions in Paper 1 and the extended responses in Paper 2. Each works one-to-one over live video with Dubai families, and each returns marked written work.

intro.heading: Judge an ESS tutor by what comes back marked
paragraphs: Environmental Systems and Societies is the one Diploma course that sits in two groups at once, satisfying both the individuals and societies requirement and the sciences requirement. That structure is why Dubai families choose it, and it is also why it is so often misread as the soft option. It is not soft. It asks a sixteen-year-old to hold a systems model, a set of competing value positions and a page of unfamiliar data in mind simultaneously, then write about all three in the register the examiner rewards. Students who coast on general knowledge about climate change land in the fours. Students who learn to answer the actual question land higher.

That gap is diagnosable, which is the entire argument for one-to-one support in this subject rather than a bigger class. A marked script shows exactly where a student stopped answering. A student who writes four hundred words about plastic in the ocean when the question said evaluate one management strategy has not misunderstood the topic; they have misunderstood the instruction. No amount of revision reading fixes that. Someone has to put a pen through it, show the student the sentence where the answer went sideways, and then watch them attempt the same command term again the following week.

So this page is built around evidence rather than promises. It sets out what gets marked, what you as a parent actually see between one session and the next, what the Dubai market charges for this kind of help, and where the honesty boundary sits on the individual investigation. Those four things are what a parent needs in order to decide, and they are the four things the pages currently ranking for this search leave out. Three of the six best-ranked competitor pages in this cluster publish no price at all; none of them publishes a marking cycle.

On delivery, the position is plain and it does not change. IB Gram teaches UAE students online, one-to-one, over live video with a shared screen and an annotated document the student keeps. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. That is a limit, so it is stated here rather than buried. It is also, for a subject this specialised, an advantage: the pool of people who can mark an ESS extended response properly is small, and nobody should be choosing from the subset of that pool who happen to live within a twenty-minute drive of Arabian Ranches.

What follows names the components, the places marks go missing, the draft stages of the investigation, the AED bands other providers publish, and the calendar counted backwards from the May session. Where a figure comes from somebody else, the source and the date it was read are printed next to it. Where a date belongs to the IB, this page tells you to confirm it with your school's Diploma coordinator rather than restating something that can change.

dubai/ib-dp-environmental-systems-and-so.programmesIntro: ESS sits at the end of a longer line. Most Dubai students arrive at it from the Middle Years Programme or from an IGCSE science, and most will carry it alongside the Diploma core. Each stage below changes what a session has to do.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP sciences and individuals-and-societies are assessed on criteria rather than papers, and the language is deliberately open: inquire, analyse, reflect. Students become fluent in the vocabulary of investigation without ever sitting a timed external paper. That produces a particular profile at the start of DP1 — comfortable with research, unpractised at writing a nine-mark answer in eleven minutes.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai runs a large MYP cohort because several of the emirate's IB continuum schools take students the whole way from the Primary Years Programme. The handover into ESS is usually where the pace shows: a student who has written interim reflections for five years now has to produce a definitive answer under a clock. Sessions in the first term of DP1 are mostly about that conversion.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: ESS is examined at the end of the two years through written papers plus an internally assessed individual investigation that is externally moderated. The content runs from systems and models through ecology, biodiversity, water, land, the atmosphere and climate change, to natural resources and human populations. Breadth is the problem: eight broad areas, each with its own case studies and its own vocabulary.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools timetable ESS differently from one another — some as a group 4 choice for students who want a second humanities subject, some as a group 3 choice for students who want a science they can sustain. Which slot your child's school uses changes the whole plan, because it changes what else is on the timetable and how much writing practice is already built in. Confirm the designation with the Diploma coordinator before booking any support.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS
programmes.description: The Diploma core runs in parallel with every subject. ESS students are over-represented among Extended Essay candidates in geography, biology and ESS itself, because the subject hands them researchable local questions. Theory of Knowledge sits unusually close to ESS too: both ask what counts as evidence and who gets to decide, and a student who reads one well writes the other better.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai gives ESS students a genuinely unusual set of Extended Essay sites: the Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary mangroves, the Jebel Ali Wetland Sanctuary, Al Marmoom Desert Conservation Reserve, and a city whose desalination and district-cooling load is measurable. Support here is supervision practice — narrowing a question until it can actually be answered in four thousand words, not researching it on the student's behalf.

dubai/ib-dp-environmental-systems-and-so.subjectsIntro: Families rarely need ESS alone. The subjects below are the ones that sit next to it on a Dubai Diploma timetable, and the ones where an ESS student's weaknesses usually show up twice.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: The core of this page. Systems and models, ecology, biodiversity and conservation, water, land, the atmosphere and climate change, natural resources, human populations. Marks are lost on command terms, on using a named case study when the question asked for one, and on treating a systems diagram as decoration rather than an answer.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Shares ecology and biodiversity content with ESS but assesses it far more technically. Students taking both often import ESS-style evaluation into a biology answer that wanted a mechanism, and lose marks in both directions. Sessions pull the two registers apart deliberately.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: The closest neighbour. Overlaps on water, land use, urbanisation and resource consumption, and uses the same evaluative command terms. A student strong in geography usually has the writing but not the systems vocabulary; the reverse is just as common.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Supplies the quantitative spine behind ESS topics on the atmosphere, water quality and pollution management. Biochemical oxygen demand, acid deposition and greenhouse forcing all make more sense to a student who has handled moles and equilibrium properly.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The usual maths pairing for an ESS student. Statistics, correlation and modelling are exactly the tools the individual investigation needs, so a weak AI student usually produces a weak investigation data section. The two problems are worth treating together.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Externalities, market failure and the tragedy of the commons appear in both courses under different names. Economics students write ESS evaluation well once they stop reaching for a diagram the ESS examiner did not ask for.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Shares the environmental value systems material and the whole question of competing stakeholder positions. Useful for students who find the political half of ESS more natural than the ecological half, and a good source of transferable case studies.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Sustainability reporting, stakeholder analysis and corporate social responsibility give ESS students a second vocabulary for the same arguments. Sessions are usually about keeping the two separate in an answer rather than blending them.

subjects.name: Extended Essay supervision practice
subjects.description: Not a subject, but a frequent request. Narrowing a research question, building a method that will survive a Dubai summer, and understanding what a supervisor may and may not do. The essay itself stays the student's work throughout.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Knowledge questions about modelling, uncertainty and expert disagreement map directly onto ESS content. Students who can argue about whether a climate model is knowledge tend to write stronger ESS evaluations.

dubai/ib-dp-environmental-systems-and-so.regionsIntro: Dubai is not one catchment. Where a family lives changes the schools in reach, the realistic start time for a weekday session, and — for ESS specifically — what sits close enough to be used as a local case study or an investigation site.

regions.name: Nad Al Sheba and Meydan
regions.note: Minutes from the Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary, whose mangroves and flamingo lagoon are the most used local ESS case study in the emirate. Students here can build an investigation around a site they can visit on a Saturday morning.

regions.name: The Sustainable City and Dubailand
regions.note: A purpose-built low-energy community with on-site biodomes, greywater reuse and a measurable energy balance. ESS students living here have a working model of almost every management strategy on the syllabus inside walking distance.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Coastal, with public beach access that makes intertidal and beach-profile work practical. Traffic along Al Wasl and Jumeirah Beach Road at pickup pushes realistic weekday session starts to around 17:00.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Beach Residence
regions.note: High-rise density, district cooling and a marina breakwater that visibly changes sediment movement. Apartment living means shared study space, so sessions here are usually booked for the quieter post-dinner slot.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Mushrif Park, with its ghaf woodland and recorded wildlife, sits on the doorstep. A sizeable cohort of IB students commutes from here towards Al Barsha and Umm Suqeim, which is what makes the 16:00 hour unusable.

regions.name: Jebel Ali and Dubai Investments Park
regions.note: Next to the Jebel Ali Wetland Sanctuary and the industrial and port zone, which is an unusually honest place to study trade-offs between conservation and resource extraction. Long school runs, so a later weekday start matters.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches and Dubai Hills
regions.note: Villa communities with irrigated landscaping and real water-use data available on a family bill. Students regularly build investigations around comparative irrigation or soil moisture across two community types.

regions.name: Hatta
regions.note: Dubai's mountain exclave, with wadi systems, terraced agriculture and a very different rainfall regime from the coast. The most interesting field site in the emirate for an ESS student willing to make the drive, and one almost no competitor page mentions.

schoolClusters.city: Central and coastal Dubai
schoolClusters.note: The older IB cluster, with several continuum schools that run the Primary Years Programme through to the Diploma. ESS tends to be offered here as an alternative group 4 for students whose strengths are verbal rather than mathematical, which shapes the kind of support the cohort asks for.

schoolClusters.city: Southern Dubai and the new communities

Sustainability is often part of the school's own identity here, which raises expectations on an ESS investigation rather than lowering them.

sections.heading: What you are actually buying when you search for an ESS home tutor in Dubai
paragraphs: An IB DP Environmental Systems and Societies home tutor in Dubai, in the way the phrase is normally used, means a private one-to-one teacher for a single Diploma subject. What varies between providers is whether that teacher arrives at the villa, teaches from a centre, or teaches over video — and whether they can actually mark an ESS extended response. IB Gram provides the third of those: one-to-one live video sessions, a shared screen, and the student's own written work returned annotated. There are no home visits in Dubai; that is an India-only service, and saying so plainly is better than discovering it after a deposit.

The trade is worth understanding because it is not purely a concession. An in-home tutor is drawn from whoever is available within driving distance at the hour you need. ESS is a small-entry subject; the number of people in the UAE who have taught it to examination and can mark a nine-mark evaluation against the published criteria is smaller still. Online delivery replaces a geographic shortlist with a subject-specialist shortlist. For a maths tutor at primary level, the geographic shortlist is probably fine. For ESS at Diploma level, it is the difference between a subject teacher and an enthusiastic generalist.

What is genuinely lost is the physical page. That is solvable, and the solution is the reason this page is built around evidence. Work is written in a shared document the student keeps, marked in a different colour with the criterion or command term named next to the comment, and saved with a date. Over a term this becomes the only honest answer to the question every parent asks around week five, which is whether any of this is working. A verbal assurance is not an answer. Five dated scripts with marks on them, in order, is.

Nothing on this page implies a tutor will attend a Dubai address. If the service you want is someone physically in the room, an in-home agency in the emirate is the right call and the rate table further down shows what that market charges. If what you want is the person who knows the subject best, available at eighteen hundred on a Tuesday in Gulf Standard Time, that is what is on offer here.

sections.heading: The components of ESS, and what each one punishes
paragraphs: Environmental Systems and Societies is assessed through written papers taken at the end of the Diploma plus an internally assessed individual investigation that the IB then moderates externally. The precise durations and weightings belong to the subject guide your child's school is teaching, and those guides are revised; ask the Diploma coordinator for the current version rather than trusting any figure printed on a tutoring website, including this one. What does not change between versions is the character of each component, and that is what a plan has to be built on.

One paper is built on a resource booklet — unseen material about an unfamiliar place, with questions that require the student to read data they have never seen and apply syllabus concepts to it. This is the component that rewards technique over memory, and it is where strong students who have revised content thoroughly still underperform. The failure is almost never ignorance. It is reading the question as a prompt to write about the topic rather than as an instruction to do something specific with the material on the page in front of them.

A second paper carries both short structured questions across the whole syllabus and extended responses that require a named case study, an evaluation and a judgement. Breadth bites here: eight syllabus areas, and a student who revised four of them deeply is in trouble regardless of how well they write. The extended responses also demand a particular shape — a position, evidence for it, a counter-position, and a conclusion that actually decides something — which almost no student produces naturally and almost every student can be taught in a term.

The individual investigation is the third component and it is the one that can be rescued latest, because it is coursework rather than an exam. It asks for the student's own question, their own data and their own analysis, written to published criteria. It is also where the honesty line matters, and that gets its own section below.

sections.heading: Where Dubai ESS students lose marks most predictably
paragraphs: Across the students who come to this subject needing help, the same four or five failures recur, and none of them is about intelligence. The first is the command term. ESS questions use a tightly defined vocabulary — state, outline, describe, explain, suggest, evaluate, discuss, justify — and each one sets a ceiling on how much credit an answer can earn regardless of how good the content is. A student who writes a brilliant explanation for a question that said outline has written a brilliant answer to the wrong question. This is the single cheapest fix available in the subject, and it takes about three weeks of deliberate practice.

The second is case-study poverty. Examiners want named, specific examples with real detail: a place, a scale, a date, an outcome. Students arrive with the category instead of the case — deforestation rather than a named region, overfishing rather than a named fishery. Building a personal bank of eight to ten case studies the student can actually recall under pressure is a mechanical task, and Dubai hands them several unusually good ones, from the Ras Al Khor mangroves to the emirate's desalination load to the Al Marmoom reserve.

The third is the environmental value systems material, which students either skip as woolly or over-apply everywhere. It is neither. It is the framework that lets a student explain why two well-informed people look at identical data and disagree about what should be done, and once it is understood properly it raises the quality of every evaluative answer in the course. The fourth is quantitative nerve: a page of unfamiliar figures produces freeze, so the first move in a session is often simply to read the axes, the units and the date out loud before attempting anything.

The fifth is time. Students over-write early questions worth two marks and then run out of minutes for the extended response worth many more. That is visible in a marked script and invisible in a conversation about revision, which is precisely why the marking cycle matters more than any amount of reassurance.

sections.heading: The individual investigation, draft by draft — and where the line sits
paragraphs: The individual investigation is the component where good support changes the most and where bad support ends a Diploma. IB academic-honesty rules are unambiguous: the work submitted must be the student's own. A tutor may teach, question, model technique on a different example and give feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections to a finished standard, or hand over a method and a conclusion. IB Gram does not sell finished coursework of any kind, and a provider offering to supply a completed investigation is offering a malpractice case against your child.

That boundary is easier to hold when it is operational rather than aspirational, which is what the table below is for. At each stage there is something the tutor does and something that stays the student's responsibility, and the distinction is visible in the artefacts. If the document history shows the student writing and the tutor commenting, the work is the student's. If it shows text appearing in a tutor's hand, it is not. Schools in Dubai increasingly ask for drafts and version history, so this is not a theoretical concern.

In practice the highest-value intervention happens before any data exists. Most weak investigations were doomed at the question. A question that is too broad, or whose variables cannot be measured with the equipment and access a Dubai sixteen-year-old actually has, produces thin data and then an evaluation that reads as excuse-making. Spending two sessions interrogating the question and the method — what will you measure, how many times, what would the graph look like if your hypothesis is wrong — saves the entire project.

The second highest-value intervention is reading the draft as a moderator would. Not correcting it. Asking the questions a moderator would ask in the margin: where is the uncertainty here, why this sample size, what does this graph actually show, which criterion is this paragraph trying to satisfy. The student answers those questions by revising their own work, which is both the honest route and the one that teaches something transferable to every other subject.
