sections.heading: Costing support per assessed task instead of per hour
paragraphs: An hourly rate tells a family almost nothing, because the number of hours is what determines the bill and nobody quotes it. This subject divides cleanly into four tasks with reasonably predictable hour requirements, which makes a per-task estimate possible. The textual analysis is the most tractable, because it is one extract and one piece of writing. The comparative study needs its focus tested before any recording, which is cheap, and restructuring afterwards, which is not. The portfolio needs reflections rewritten. The Higher Level report needs individual evidence organised.

The AED figures in the table are other providers' published rates, collected in October 2026, and they are included so the totals can be checked against something real rather than asserted. Read the right-hand columns rather than the rate: a comparative study whose focus was tested in DP1 costs a fraction of one rescued in DP2, and that difference is far larger than any difference between a tutor at AED 200 and one at AED 300.

One pattern recurs in this emirate and is worth pricing honestly. Families who buy support only in the final term pay the most per mark gained, because they are buying scarce hours at the point when every DP2 cohort in Dubai needs them and when several tasks are already locked. Families who buy a small block in DP1 against the textual analysis and the comparative study focus spend less in total and finish in a better place. The cheap intervention is early and unglamorous; the expensive one is late and feels urgent.

Monthly packages advertised locally at around AED 799 for eight online sessions work out well below the specialist band, and they buy general supervision. For a subject where the marks come from criterion-level feedback on four specific tasks, that is a different product. It can suit a DP1 student who needs structure, and it is the wrong purchase for a DP2 student with an unstructured comparative study four weeks from an internal deadline.

sections.heading: Why online is the cheaper unit of work for Film specifically
paragraphs: In most subjects the online argument is about travel cost. In Film it is about whether the review can happen at all. Reviewing an edit means referring to a specific frame: this cut, at this timecode, lands two frames late, and that is why the reaction reads as hesitation rather than as surprise. On a shared screen both parties see the same frame and the note can be written against the number. Two people leaning over one laptop lose that precision within a minute, and the feedback degrades into general impressions.

The second reason is pooling. Film is taught in very few Dubai schools, which means the number of people in the emirate who have marked a film portfolio against the criteria is small. A twenty-minute driving radius then reduces an already tiny pool to almost nothing, and what is available at that radius is usually a general humanities tutor or a working film-maker, neither of whom is the required hire. Online delivery removes the radius and makes the filter subject expertise rather than postcode.

The third is scheduling economics, which matter more than families expect. Published in-home rates in Dubai of AED 180 to 500 an hour have travel built into them, and a session cancelled because a shoot overran still costs a tutor their drive. Online, a session can move by thirty minutes at ten minutes' notice, which in a subject with production days, group shoots and school fixtures is the difference between twenty-eight sessions a year and twenty.

To be explicit about the trade-off: IB Gram does not run in-person lessons in Dubai and does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE, since home visiting is a service we provide only in India. What is genuinely lost is physical presence on a shoot, and no tutor should be on a student's shoot anyway, because the production decisions have to be the student's own. What is gained is frame-accurate review from someone who has marked the component.

sections.heading: How a timeline review session actually runs
paragraphs: The mechanics are worth describing because most families have never seen one and assume it involves watching a finished film and offering opinions. It does not. The student opens their editing project and shares the screen. The sequence plays once at full speed, uninterrupted, so the first impression is intact. Then it is worked through in sections, with the playhead parked and the timecode read aloud, and every note written against that number.

What gets interrogated is decisions rather than taste. Why does this scene start on the wide? What did the first version look like? What happened when the cut was two seconds earlier? The purpose is partly to improve the sequence and mostly to generate the material the student will need for the reflection, because a reflection written months later from memory is always thinner than one written from a session where the decisions were articulated out loud. Students who record their own notes after a review session arrive at the portfolio with a reflection half-written.

The practical requirements are modest. A proxy or a lower-resolution export avoids playback stutter on a domestic connection, which in Dubai apartment buildings during evening hours is a real constraint. Audio should be checked on headphones at both ends. The project file stays with the student; nobody else edits it. Notes are returned timecoded afterwards so they can be acted on alone, which is the point: the student does the work, and the record of the session is a list of their own stated decisions.

The same session format works for the comparative study, where the recorded study is itself a timeline with narration, and for the Higher Level film. For the textual analysis the format shifts to a shared document and a frame-by-frame pass through the extract, which is slower and is where the most marks per hour are usually found.

sections.heading: The Higher Level collaborative project: where group drift becomes a mark
paragraphs: Higher Level adds one component whose outcome depends on other people, and in Dubai's small cohorts that is a material risk rather than a theoretical one. A group of three where one student withdraws in January has a problem that no amount of individual talent fixes, and the component is assessed partly on each student's own documented contribution. The paperwork is therefore not administration; it is the mark.

The failures are consistent and avoidable. Roles are agreed verbally and never written down, so when two students both believe they were the editor, neither has evidence. Contribution is reconstructed after the shoot from memory, which produces reports that claim decisions the footage does not support. Schedules are planned without reference to Ramadan, half-term travel or exam leave, so principal photography lands in the one fortnight when two of the four students are abroad. And a student who did the most work often documents it the least, because they were busy doing it.

The intervention that works is unglamorous: roles declared in writing in the first week, a contribution log kept during the production rather than afterwards, and a schedule tested against the actual Dubai calendar before anybody books a location. A tutor can review all three and can tell a group that their schedule is not survivable. A tutor cannot and should not direct, shoot, edit or write any part of the film or the reports.

sections.heading: Standard Level or Higher Level, and what the choice costs
paragraphs: The level decision in Film has financial as well as academic consequences, and Dubai families rarely get the chance to think about it before the option form goes in. Standard Level is three individual tasks, all under the student's own control, with a predictable workload and a support bill that can be estimated accurately in advance. Higher Level adds a group production with a real schedule, real logistics and a dependency on other people's reliability.

For a student heading into film, media or communications study, Higher Level is the right choice and the group project is genuinely valuable experience. For a student who chose Film as a sixth subject alongside two Higher Level sciences, it is an expensive decision in hours rather than in fees: the production competes for exactly the weeks when internally assessed work across the rest of the Diploma is landing. In a Dubai school with a cohort of four, there is also no second group to move into if the first one fractures.

The honest signal to look for is whether the student initiates production work without being asked. A student who is already making things, with or without a camera, will thrive at Higher Level. A student who enjoys watching and analysing films but has never finished a project of their own will usually do better at Standard Level, where analysis carries proportionally more of the grade and nothing depends on a shoot happening.

Whichever level is chosen, the support pattern is the same in shape: test the comparative study focus early, mark the textual analysis properly, and push the reflections from narration into justification. The difference is that Higher Level adds a fourth strand of support that is largely about structure and documentation rather than about film-making at all.

sections.heading: Footage, music, locations and the rights nobody checks
paragraphs: Film is the Diploma subject most likely to produce a rights problem, because students work with other people's material by default. Clips from existing films appear in the comparative study, which is normally fine as analytical use within an assessed academic submission, and the sources have to be listed. Music is the recurring problem: a student scores their short film with a commercial track because it fits, and has no right to use it. Production music libraries with clear licensing, and music written by a classmate with permission, both solve this cheaply.

Locations are the second issue and the one specific to this emirate. Filming in managed public spaces, malls, beachfront developments and private communities generally needs permission from whoever runs that space, and policies differ between them. The right move is to ask the school first: schools usually know what has been cleared before, and a school-supported request is treated differently from a student turning up with a camera. Planning a shoot around a location nobody has asked about is how a production schedule collapses in a week.

People are the third. Anyone appearing in a student film should know what it is for and agree to it, and that applies with more care to children and to anyone filmed in a private setting. A short written consent, even an email, is the normal standard and it costs nothing. For a documentary involving a community or a workplace, consent and acknowledgement are part of doing the work properly rather than an administrative extra.

The academic boundary sits alongside all of this. A tutor teaches, questions, marks against the published criteria and explains why a passage or a sequence does not score. A tutor does not direct, shoot, edit, write or narrate any part of a submission, and the sources in a comparative study must be the student's own. Any provider offering a finished study or a written report is offering a breach that the student carries, and in this market that offer exists.

sections.heading: Seasonal pricing, availability and how the matching works
paragraphs: Specialist capacity in this subject is seasonal in a way that affects what families pay, and no competitor page says so. Demand concentrates in the weeks before school internal upload deadlines, which across the emirate fall inside the same short window because every DP2 cohort is working to the same session. In that window the few people in the market who have marked a film portfolio are fully booked, and what remains available is generalist. The price of a specialist hour does not change; the probability of getting one does.

The practical response is to buy the cheap hours early. Testing a comparative study focus in DP1 takes two or three hours and prevents the six-to-eight-hour restructure that a switched focus produces later. Marking a textual analysis draft properly before the school's own deadline is worth more than auditing it afterwards. Both of those are available in DP1 at the same hourly band and in a market with slack in it.

Where nobody suitable is free in the window you need, you will be told that, with the nearest honest alternative and the rate that would apply, rather than matched to a working film-maker or a general humanities tutor described as a Diploma specialist. Making films and marking them against criteria are different skills, and in this subject the second is the scarcer one. No ranking page in this market discloses a coverage limit, which does not mean that none of them has one.

The rest is straightforward. Sessions run one to one, online, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time, with later timing during Ramadan agreed before the month rather than during it. Anyone providing private tuition inside the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE's own e-services under 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing'. And the trial lesson is free, on your child's real cut or draft, with no card required.

A microphone, something to keep the camera still, and hours of criterion-level marking beat a camera body bought with the same money, and saying so costs us nothing and saves a family a great deal.

whyPoints.description: A useful note on an edit refers to one frame at one timecode. That precision survives on a shared screen and disappears when two people lean over one laptop, which is why online delivery is the better arrangement for this subject rather than a compromise.

faqs.question: What does online IB DP Film support cost per assessed task in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Using other providers' published hourly figures from October 2026, a textual analysis block of four to six hours at the AED 200 to 450 specialist band comes to roughly AED 800 to 2,700. Testing a comparative study focus in DP1 takes two or three hours and is the cheapest useful spend in the subject. Restructuring that study in DP2 takes six to eight. Portfolio reflections across three roles take five to seven, and the Higher Level individual report three to five. IB Gram publishes no rate card here; the trial lesson is free with no card required and the quote follows the task.

faqs.question: Do we need to buy a camera for IB DP Film?
faqs.answer: No criterion in the subject refers to image quality, sensor size or camera cost, and a recent phone exceeds every technical requirement the assessed tasks have. What genuinely helps is a cheap external microphone and something to keep the camera still, because unclear sound and unstable framing are what make student work hard to follow. Spend the rest on criterion-level marking of the written tasks, since three of the four assessed components are substantially writing and speaking. A portfolio of beautiful footage with reflections that explain nothing scores below the reverse.

faqs.question: Which editing software does my child actually need?
faqs.answer: Whatever they can run reliably. Software is never assessed, and the free or included editors on most computers handle every task in the subject, including the recorded comparative study. Paid subscriptions buy convenience and professional habits rather than marks. The only practical consideration is playback: a proxy or a lower-resolution export keeps a shared-screen review smooth on a domestic Dubai connection in the evening, when building contention makes stuttering common. Project files stay with the student in every case, because nobody else should be editing their timeline.

faqs.question: Can my child use a commercial song in their film?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and it is the most common rights problem in student productions. A commercial track used without a licence is a problem regardless of how well it fits, and it can affect how the work can be shown. The practical alternatives are cheap or free: production music libraries with clear licensing terms, or an original score written by a classmate with written permission, which also gives both students something to document. Clips from existing films inside an analytical submission sit in a different category and must be listed in the sources.

faqs.question: Can students film in public places in Dubai for a school project?
faqs.answer: It depends on the space, and the honest answer is to ask before planning a schedule around it. Managed public spaces, malls, beachfront developments and gated communities generally require permission from whoever operates them, and policies differ. Ask the school first: schools often know what has been cleared previously, and a request supported by a school is received differently from a student arriving with a camera. A production schedule built around a location nobody asked about is the most common reason a group film collapses in its first fortnight.

faqs.question: How does a tutor review an edit over a video call?
faqs.answer: The student shares their editing screen. The sequence plays once uninterrupted so the first impression stays intact, then it is worked through in sections with the playhead parked and the timecode read aloud, so every note refers to one frame. The questions are about decisions rather than taste: why start on the wide, what did the first version look like, what changed when the cut moved. Notes come back timecoded so the student can act on them alone, and those articulated decisions become the raw material for the reflection they will have to write later.

faqs.question: What is the collaborative film project and who has to do it?
faqs.answer: It is a completed short film made by a group, with each student taking a declared production role and submitting an individual report on their own contribution. Only Higher Level students do it; Standard Level is three individual tasks with nothing depending on other people. In Dubai cohorts of three or four it carries real risk, because a withdrawal in January cannot be absorbed by moving to another group. The component is assessed partly on documented individual contribution, which means the paperwork is the mark rather than administration around it.

faqs.question: Our Higher Level group has stopped working together. What happens to the marks?
faqs.answer: Each student is assessed on their own documented contribution, so the position depends almost entirely on what has been recorded and when. A student who declared a role in writing, kept a dated contribution log and can show project versions is in a defensible position even if the film suffers. A student who did a great deal of work and documented none of it is not. The first step is the school's IB coordinator, who deals with group difficulties formally. The second is to document the change at the point it happens rather than reconstructing it in March.

faqs.question: Should my child take Film at Standard or Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Standard Level is three individual tasks under the student's own control, with a predictable workload and a support bill that can be estimated accurately. Higher Level adds a group film with a schedule, logistics and a dependency on other people's reliability, which in a small Dubai cohort is a genuine risk. The useful signal is whether the student makes things without being asked. Unprompted production points to Higher Level; enjoying watching and analysing films without ever finishing a project of their own points to Standard Level, where analysis carries proportionally more weight.

faqs.question: How many hours does the textual analysis usually take to fix?
faqs.answer: Four to six hours of specialist time, provided it starts before the school's own draft deadline. The work is a frame-by-frame pass through the extract followed by marking against the criteria, which is slower than it sounds and is where the most marks per hour are usually found in this subject. Starting afterwards costs more and achieves less, because the structure is already set and the student has less room to change it. It is also the most self-contained task in the subject, which makes it the easiest thing to buy in a single defined block.

faqs.question: Is the comparative study cheaper to support early or late?
faqs.answer: Dramatically cheaper early, and this is the clearest cost decision in the subject. Testing whether two chosen films can actually be compared within a single declared focus takes two or three hours in DP1. Restructuring a study whose focus switched halfway, so that neither half is properly argued, takes six to eight in DP2 and is still a repair rather than a build. The hourly band is identical in both cases. What differs is the number of hours and whether a specialist is available at all, since DP2 demand concentrates in one fortnight across the emirate.

faqs.question: Does a Film grade help or hurt a university application?
faqs.answer: It helps for film, media, communications and some arts and humanities programmes, several of which also assess a portfolio or a showreel separately from the Diploma grade. It is neutral for most other destinations, and courses with specific science or maths prerequisites will look at those subjects rather than at Film. Read the entry requirements for the named course at the named university for the year of entry before DP1 subject selection. For UAE certificate equivalency, that is a separate Ministry of Education process and tutoring is not required for it.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Film and Visual Arts for the same student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking, because the analytical habits overlap and both subjects are assessed through submitted work rather than examinations. The limitation is practical rather than intellectual: both carry heavy documentation loads that land in the same autumn weeks of DP2, so a shared tutor can end up with a timetable problem at exactly the wrong moment. Ask any tutor claiming both which components they have actually marked, in which subject, and how recently, and treat a vague answer as an answer.

faqs.question: How late in DP2 is it still worth paying for Film support?
faqs.answer: It depends which task is still open. A textual analysis that has not been marked properly is worth addressing almost up to the school's final internal date, because it is self-contained. Portfolio reflections can be improved late if the production decisions are still remembered or documented. A comparative study whose focus is wrong is a repair rather than a rebuild once the recording exists. What cannot be fixed late is a Higher Level contribution that was never documented while the shoot happened, and no tutor should suggest otherwise.

faqs.question: Do Film tutoring rates go up before the May session in Dubai?
faqs.answer: The published hourly bands do not move much; availability does, and that is what costs families money. Film is taught in very few Dubai schools, so the number of people in the emirate who have marked a film portfolio is small, and every DP2 cohort reaches its internal upload deadlines in the same short window. In that fortnight the specialists are booked and what remains is generalist. Buying the cheap early hours in DP1, particularly the comparative study focus check, is the practical hedge against a market with no slack in it.

dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Diploma Film for Dubai students at both levels and across every task: the textual analysis of a prescribed extract, the comparative study, the film portfolio with its production role evidence, and the higher level collaborative project. Sessions work from the student's own writing and footage.

intro.heading: Diploma Film marks what a sequence does, not what a film is about
paragraphs: Film attracts Dubai Diploma students who already love cinema, and that is precisely why so many of them sit in the middle bands. Loving films produces fluent writing about stories, characters and themes. Diploma Film assesses something else: what a specific sequence does to a viewer, by what technical means, and with what evidence drawn from the frame rather than from the narrative. A candidate who writes that a scene is tense because the protagonist is in danger has described the plot. A candidate who writes that the cut rate accelerates across the sequence while the score drops out and the camera moves to a handheld low angle has analysed it.

That gap is the whole page. It is not a knowledge problem, which is why it responds quickly to one-to-one work: the student already knows a great deal about film. It is a problem of what gets written down, in what vocabulary, supported by what. We can usually diagnose it in a single paragraph of a student's own draft, because the signature is unmistakable. Plot verbs dominate, technical nouns are absent, and the paragraph could have been written by someone who had read a synopsis rather than watched a sequence.

The subject has no written examination. Everything is assessed through submitted tasks: a textual analysis of a prescribed film extract, a comparative study of films from different cultural contexts, a film portfolio documenting work in production roles, and at the higher level a collaborative film project. Each has its own criteria and its own word, time or length limits, and those limits do real work because they force selection. Confirm the current task list, limits and weightings with your school's IB coordinator before planning against them, as the guide is revised on its own cycle and no tutoring page should be the source.

The second recurring fault is scale. Film candidates consistently try to cover too much, because the subject invites breadth and the criteria reward depth. A textual analysis that moves through an entire film earns less than one that stays inside a few minutes and reads them closely. A comparative study that surveys two national cinemas earns less than one that argues a specific claim about two films. Teaching a student to narrow is often worth more marks than teaching them anything about cinema.

Delivery is online. Lessons are one-to-one over live video with screen sharing, which for a subject assessed through written analysis and edited footage is a genuinely good fit: the student's own draft, their timeline, or a frame paused for discussion is on screen for both parties and the annotated version is saved. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. Shooting and editing happen wherever the student works, and no tutor is present for that in any model.
bullets: Textual analysis: close reading of an extract in examiner vocabulary
Comparative study: a research question that forces comparison rather than inviting survey
Film portfolio: production role evidence and the reflective writing that carries the marks

dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.programmesIntro: The analytical habit Film assesses is built earlier and reused across the Diploma core. These are the three levels a Dubai family is normally dealing with when they contact us about this subject.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Arts and Language and Literature
programmes.description: Middle Years students meet moving image in both the arts and language courses, usually as a text to interpret rather than as a construction to take apart. Those that learn to ask how a shot was built, rather than what it means, arrive in the Diploma able to analyse. Those who have only been asked what a film is about arrive with a strong vocabulary for theme and none for technique, which is the exact profile that caps a Diploma Film mark.
programmes.countryNote: Few Dubai schools teach film formally before the Diploma, so most DP1 Film students begin with enthusiasm and no analytical vocabulary. That is normal and it is also the single fastest thing to fix: a term of shot-by-shot work on short extracts changes what a student notices, which changes what they can write.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Film
programmes.description: Film is assessed entirely through submitted tasks rather than examinations: a textual analysis of a prescribed film extract, a comparative study of films from different cultural contexts, a film portfolio evidencing work in production roles, and at the higher level a collaborative film project. Each carries its own criteria and its own limits on words, screens or duration. Confirm the current task list, weightings and limits with your school's IB coordinator before planning hours against them.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai provision varies sharply. A few schools run Film with a specialist and real equipment; more run it with a willing English or media teacher and whatever cameras exist; some do not offer it at all, which is why a proportion of the families who contact us are looking for teaching rather than supplementing. Ask the coordinator who teaches it and what their background is.

programmes.name: Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge
programmes.description: An Extended Essay in Film is written research rather than production, and students who choose it hoping to make something are caught out. Theory of Knowledge overlaps productively: questions about how knowledge is produced and represented sharpen a student's handling of cultural context, which is the element of the comparative study most candidates treat as background rather than as evidence.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai is a usable research location for a Film Extended Essay: the region's production and festival infrastructure, the growth of Gulf-funded cinema, and the representation of the city in international productions are all documented enough to cite. The constraint is finding scholarly writing rather than finding a topic, and that is what the first supervision session tests.

dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.subjectsIntro: Film students in Dubai usually need a neighbour or two covered as well. These are the related Diploma courses our tutors take for the same families, with the demand each one makes.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Assessed through submitted tasks with no written examination: textual analysis, comparative study, film portfolio and, at the higher level, a collaborative project. Marks turn on close analysis of technique with evidence from the frame, and on reflective writing that explains decisions. The commonest loss is plot description in place of analysis.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The closest neighbour. Its guided textual analysis trains exactly the move Film needs: attention to how a text produces an effect rather than to what it says. Students taking both usually transfer the skill once it is pointed out, and the transfer is worth more than any amount of additional film watching.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Shares the submitted-task structure and the demand for documented process. The vocabularies have to be kept distinct, because art-historical analysis and film language describe different things, but the habit of reading an image closely carries directly into shot analysis.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Overlaps on performance, staging and the documentation of a creative process. Theatre students write better on mise-en-scène and on performance in film, because they have been made to think about where a body is placed in a space and why.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Supplies the contextual discipline the comparative study assumes. Students taking both stop using cultural context as scene-setting and start using it as evidence for a claim, which is where the better contextual marks in Film actually sit.

subjects.name: Digital Society
subjects.description: Relevant to students interested in distribution, platforms, algorithmic recommendation and the economics of attention. Useful background for a comparative study that concerns how films reach audiences rather than only what is inside them.

subjects.name: Arabic A or Arabic B
subjects.description: A real advantage in this subject for a student working on Arab cinema, because it opens primary criticism, interviews and dialogue nuance that candidates working from subtitles cannot reach. Very few Diploma Film candidates anywhere have that access.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Supplies sourced material for students writing about spectatorship, attention and emotional response. The caution is to use it as evidence rather than as assertion, because a claim about how audiences feel needs support like any other claim.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Often paired with Film by students aiming at production or media management. The commercial content gives a candidate something concrete to say about financing, markets and distribution, which other candidates answer in generalities.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words of independent research, written rather than produced. Supervision is questioning and written feedback on the student's own drafts; the school's registered supervisor signs the work off and the argument remains entirely the student's.

dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.regionsIntro: Lessons run online, so a family's address does not change who can teach. It does change the school, where a student can realistically shoot, and when a session can start on a weekday.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal
regions.note: Studio, gallery and production space concentrated in one district, and the most practical area in Dubai for a student who needs an interior location or equipment hire. Screenings and talks here are also the easiest route to seeing films outside the streaming catalogue.

regions.name: Downtown, Business Bay and City Walk
regions.note: Dense, photogenic and heavily filmed, which makes it both attractive and complicated for a student production. Permission is the constraint rather than access, and shooting in managed public areas needs the operator's consent rather than a student's confidence.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Lake Towers
regions.note: Apartment living with controlled common areas, so student productions here resolve around interiors, balconies and walkways with building management agreement. Sound is the recurring technical problem, because towers are noisier than they look on camera.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Dubai Hills
regions.note: A cluster of IB and British schools within a few kilometres, a few with real media provision including edit suites. Students here are more likely to need analytical vocabulary than equipment, which is the cheaper of the two problems.

regions.name: Jumeirah, Umm Suqeim and Al Sufouh
regions.note: Beachfront and older villa streets, with usable natural light for most of the year and a long golden hour in winter. Afternoon traffic along the beach-road corridor pushes most session times past 17:00 for families in this stretch.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches, Motor City and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Space, quiet streets and controlled community access, which makes exterior shooting more straightforward than in the city centre provided community management agrees. Weekend morning sessions dominate because weekday evenings are taken.

regions.name: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: A wide catchment across several curricula where a Film candidate is often the only one in their year. With no peer group, sessions have to supply the discussion and the critical disagreement a class would otherwise provide.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: University campuses nearby with media programmes, which matters for students weighing film school applications and for seeing student work. Degree screenings are a better guide to portfolio standards than any prospectus.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai IB World Schools that run Diploma Film
schoolClusters.note: Film needs a specialist, equipment and edit facilities, so provision in Dubai follows investment and sometimes a single teacher. KHDA inspects these schools annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. Ask the coordinator whether Film will run to DP2 and what the minimum class size for it is, because small option subjects are the ones withdrawn.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools where Film students work with limited media provision
schoolClusters.note: Plenty of Dubai schools teach Film with a willing English or media teacher, a few cameras and laptops running consumer editing software. That is a workable setting, and it shifts the balance of outside help toward analytical vocabulary and task structure rather than toward production craft.
schools: Jumeirah English Speaking School, Arabian Ranches

dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.schoolDisclaimer: Named schools are listed as context for the Dubai IB ecosystem that students we support attend; no affiliation, endorsement or partnership with any school or school group is implied.
dubai/ib-dp-film-tutor.modesIntro: Film support works best bought against a task, because each one fails in a different way and each has a point past which help is worth less. These are the four blocks Dubai families book.

modes.title: Shot-analysis foundation block
modes.description: Four to six sessions, and the block that changes everything else in the subject. The work is close reading of short extracts: pause, describe what is actually in the frame, name the technique, then say what it does. Students arrive able to discuss films and leave able to analyse sequences, and every other task improves as a consequence because they are all built on the same move.
bullets: Extracts worked frame by frame, with the plot deliberately set aside
Technical vocabulary introduced as it is needed, not as a glossary to memorise
Every session ends with a written paragraph, marked before the next one
The student builds their own reference list of terms they actually use

modes.title: Textual analysis block
modes.description: Three to five sessions on the prescribed extract once the school has confirmed which text it is working from. The sessions select the minutes worth analysing, establish a structure that does not drift into narrative, and mark successive drafts against the criteria. The limit is treated as a design constraint from the first draft rather than as something to cut down to at the end.
bullets: Extract selection argued, not assumed from where the scene starts
A structure that holds analysis rather than following the story
Evidence taken from the frame and from the soundtrack, with timecodes
Word limit planned into the first draft, not imposed on the last

modes.title: Comparative study block
modes.description: Five to eight sessions, beginning with the question rather than the films. Most comparative studies fail because the question permits a survey instead of forcing a comparison, and that is decided before any research happens. Later sessions critique the argument, the use of cultural context as evidence, and the sourcing, with written feedback on the student's own drafts.
bullets: A question that cannot be answered without comparing the two films
Films chosen because they illuminate each other, not because both are liked
Cultural context used as evidence for a claim rather than as introduction
Sources cited properly, including anything in translation

modes.title: Portfolio and production block
modes.description: Recurring short sessions across the production work, aimed at the reflective writing that carries the marks rather than at the craft. The student brings a rough cut or a set of production documents and is asked what decision each one records and why. At the higher level this extends to the collaborative project, where the assessment is of the individual's own role and evidence.
bullets: Role chosen deliberately, with the evidence requirement understood first
Decisions documented as they happen rather than reconstructed later
Rough cuts reviewed with notes, never edited by the tutor
Rights and permissions checked before footage or music is committed

sections.heading: The verbs in the criteria, and the three things they ask for
paragraphs: Every mark in Diploma Film is awarded against a criterion, and every criterion contains a verb. Candidates who read those verbs and write to them outscore candidates who write what they know, and the gap is wider in this subject than in most because the natural way to write about film is the way that earns least. Describing a plot feels like engaging with a film; it satisfies no verb in any criterion.

Three demands recur across the tasks in different proportions. The first is analysis: taking a sequence apart and saying what each technical element contributes. The second is evaluation or justification: arguing a position and supporting it, whether about two films or about the student's own production decisions. The third is reflection on process, which is specific to the production tasks and is where a strong filmmaker with poor documentation habits loses most heavily.

The practical move is to read a draft paragraph and ask which of those three it performs. Most mid-band paragraphs perform none of them. They describe. Once a student can label their own paragraphs, they can rewrite them, and rewriting one paragraph properly in a session teaches more than reading a criteria grid aloud ever does.

The table below maps each assessed task to the demand it mainly makes, what counts as evidence for it, and what gets no credit however well written. Confirm the current task list, criteria and limits with your school's IB coordinator before planning around them, because the guide is revised on its own cycle.

sections.heading: Textual analysis: staying inside the sequence
paragraphs: The textual analysis is the task where the plot-summary habit does the most damage, because the whole point is to stay inside a few minutes and read them closely. A candidate who begins by explaining where the extract sits in the film, then narrates the action, then offers a paragraph about theme, has used most of the word allowance on material that satisfies no criterion.

The method we teach is mechanical and it works. Watch the extract with the sound off and describe what the image is doing: framing, camera position and movement, shot duration, cut points, staging within the frame, light and colour. Then listen with the picture off and describe the soundtrack: dialogue, effects, silence, score, whether sound is inside the scene or over it. Then put them together and ask what the combination produces at each point. A student who has done that exercise twice writes differently, permanently.

Selection is the second half of the skill. An extract chosen because it is where the DVD chapter starts is usually the wrong extract. The right one is a sequence with something to analyse: a change in pace, a shift in point of view, a moment where image and sound disagree. Arguing that selection in the opening sentences is itself a mark-earning move, because it demonstrates the analytical judgement the criteria are looking for.

The table below sets out the areas of film language an examiner expects to see handled, the vocabulary that signals a candidate knows what they are describing, and what a weak paragraph does instead. Work through it against your child's last draft, one paragraph at a time, and check the current expectations for the cohort with their teacher.

sections.heading: The comparative study: a question that forces comparison
paragraphs: The comparative study fails before any research begins, in the question. A question that can be answered by describing each film in turn will be answered that way, because that is the path of least resistance, and the result is two essays stapled together. A question that cannot be answered without putting the two films against each other produces a comparison automatically.

The difference is testable in one move. Take the draft question and ask whether a sensible answer could be written about film one alone, then about film two alone, and then joined with a concluding paragraph about similarities. If the answer is yes, the question is a survey question and needs rewriting. If an answer requires the two films to be in the same sentence repeatedly, the question is doing its job.

Cultural context is the second recurring failure, and it is a more subtle one. Candidates research context diligently and then use it as introduction: a paragraph on the country, the decade and the industry, followed by analysis that would be identical without it. Context earns marks when it is evidence for a claim about why a film makes the choices it makes, and that means it has to appear inside the analytical paragraphs rather than before them.

Scope is the third. A study comparing two national cinemas is unwritable in the length available; a study comparing how two specific films handle one specific thing is writable and scores better. Narrowing is almost always the correction a draft needs, and students resist it because a narrow question feels less impressive. It is not: it is the only kind that can be argued properly inside the limit.
bullets: Test the question: could each film be answered about separately?
Context belongs inside the analysis, not in front of it
Narrow the claim until it can actually be argued in the words available
Choose films that illuminate each other, not two the student happens to like

sections.heading: Arab and Gulf cinema: a comparative-study seam almost nobody uses
paragraphs: Most Diploma Film comparative studies worldwide compare a Hollywood film with a European or East Asian one, which means examiners read a great many studies about the same handful of pairings. A Dubai student has access to a body of work that very few candidates use, and using it well is both a genuine advantage and an exercise in doing the harder research properly.

The region's cinema offers real comparative material: the emergence of Gulf-funded feature production, Egyptian cinema's long industrial history and its position as the Arab world's dominant film culture for decades, Palestinian and Lebanese filmmaking and their relationship to documentary form, Iranian cinema's internationally recognised formal strategies, and the representation of the Gulf in productions shot here by outside studios. Any of those sets up a comparison with a non-Arab cinema that is specific rather than generic.

There are two practical cautions and both matter. The first is sourcing: scholarly writing on some of this material is thinner and more scattered than on canonical Western cinema, and a student who cannot find criticism to engage with will end up asserting rather than arguing. Check that sources exist before committing to a pairing. The second is language. A candidate working from subtitles is working at one remove, and should say so rather than make claims about dialogue nuance they cannot verify. A student who reads Arabic has an advantage here that almost no other Diploma Film candidate anywhere has.

The third point is cultural care. Writing about a cinema that is not one's own requires the same evidential discipline as any other claim, and generalisations about a region's filmmaking are as weak as generalisations about anything. The strongest studies we have read on this material are the narrowest: one formal device, two films, close reading, sourced context.
bullets: Check that citable criticism exists before committing to a regional pairing
Acknowledge working from subtitles rather than claiming dialogue nuance
Arabic reading ability is a real and rare advantage in this task
Narrow pairings on one formal device beat broad national comparisons

sections.heading: The portfolio and the production tasks: the writing carries the marks
paragraphs: Students who choose Film because they want to make films regularly discover that the making is not what is assessed. What is assessed is the evidence of their decisions: what they chose to do in their role, why, what they tried that did not work, and what they concluded. A beautifully shot sequence with no record of the reasoning behind it is thin evidence. A modest sequence with a clear record of a lighting problem identified, three solutions tried and one chosen for stated reasons is strong evidence.

The consequence is a documentation habit rather than a craft skill, and it has to start when the production does. A student who photographs a setup, saves a test clip, and writes two sentences on what the test showed has produced portfolio material in ninety seconds. A student who shoots for three months and then sits down to reflect has a reconstruction problem, and reconstructed reflection is recognisable to any experienced reader because it is tidy, confident and free of the dead ends that real production generates.

Role choice deserves more thought than it usually gets. Each production role generates different evidence, and some generate it more naturally than others. A student should choose a role where they will genuinely make decisions they can document, not the role with the most status on set. We spend a session on this before production starts, because changing role later costs weeks.

At the higher level the collaborative project adds a specific risk: the assessment is of the individual student's own contribution, and a group that drifts or divides work informally leaves individual members with nothing attributable. Agreeing roles in writing at the start, and each member keeping their own record, is the protection. A group film that turns out badly can still contain four strong individual submissions; a group film that turns out well can contain four weak ones.

sections.heading: Where Dubai Film candidates lose marks, in order of frequency
paragraphs: Across the drafts we read for Dubai students the losses fall in a consistent order, and the order tells a family what to buy first. Leading is plot description in place of analysis, which affects nearly every mid-band draft and is the fastest thing to fix. Second is breadth instead of depth: too much film covered, too little read closely. Third is a comparative study question that permits a survey. Fourth is cultural context used as introduction rather than as evidence. Fifth is reflective writing in the portfolio that records outcomes rather than decisions.

Only after those five does anything resembling a knowledge gap appear, and that ordering is the single most useful thing on this page. The instinct of a worried parent is that their child needs to watch and know more films. For most Dubai Film candidates that is the wrong diagnosis and an expensive response, because the student already watches plenty. What they need is a different thing to do with what they watch.

There is a sixth loss specific to this subject's population that deserves naming. Students who are already competent filmmakers, often with their own projects and an audience online, write about their own work with the confidence of a practitioner and the evidence of none. Examiners cannot credit an assertion that a choice was effective; they credit a decision explained and supported. Separating practitioner confidence from assessed reflection is usually a relief to these students once it is named explicitly.

A session starting from a real draft can place a student on this list in twenty minutes, which is why we ask for one before the trial lesson. Each failure has a visible signature: plot verbs and no technical nouns, a paragraph that covers ten minutes, a question that could be answered twice separately, context sitting in front of the analysis, a portfolio entry with a photograph and no reason attached.
bullets: Plot description where analysis was required
Breadth of coverage where depth was required
A comparative question that permits two separate answers
Cultural context as introduction rather than as evidence
Portfolio entries recording outcomes rather than decisions
Practitioner confidence substituted for supported reflection

sections.heading: What a session actually changes, task by task
paragraphs: Parents reasonably ask what one hour buys, and in Film the honest answer is specific. Some faults are single-session fixes because they are habits of writing. Others take weeks because they need a different question, a rebuilt structure or a documentation routine that did not exist. Knowing which is which before spending is the most useful thing a family can do.

The habits move fast. Replacing plot verbs with technical nouns, narrowing a paragraph to thirty seconds of film, quoting a timecode, naming a shot rather than describing what is visible in it: each of those can be taught, practised and visibly changed inside one session, and they appear on almost every mid-band draft. A family who buys three sessions and gets those four habits has had good value, and we would say so rather than selling a term.

The structural problems are slower and should be priced honestly. A comparative study built on a survey question needs the question rewritten and the draft rebuilt, which is several sessions. A portfolio with no contemporaneous record cannot be reconstructed, only organised, and we say that plainly even when it loses the booking. A collaborative project where the group never agreed roles may leave a student with limited attributable evidence, and the useful work then is documenting what they genuinely did rather than pretending otherwise.

The table maps what a teacher's comment usually says to what it actually means, the session's work, and the deliverable the student owes afterwards. That last column is the one that matters: every item here requires the student to write something between sessions, and a provider implying otherwise is selling attendance.

sections.heading: Rights, honesty and material that is not the student's
paragraphs: Film is built from other people's work, which makes the honesty questions in this subject both constant and practical. Clips analysed in written work are quoted for criticism and must be referenced precisely, with film, year and timecode, so a reader can check. Frame grabs used as illustration are credited in the same way. None of that is onerous and all of it is expected.

Production raises harder questions. Music is the commonest trap: a commercial track behind a student film is a licensing matter regardless of whether the film is ever published, and there is a large body of properly licensed library and creative-commons music that avoids it entirely. Archive and stock footage carries its own licence terms. Locations in Dubai need the permission of whoever controls them, which in managed communities and commercial districts means asking the operator rather than relying on nobody objecting. And anyone appearing on camera should have given consent, with additional care where they are under eighteen.

Our line on the submissions is narrow and stated before anyone pays. A tutor may ask any question about a draft, a timeline or a portfolio entry, and may not supply any sentence of a submission or touch an edit. The tutor can say that a paragraph describes rather than analyses, that a question permits two separate answers, that a portfolio entry has no reason attached, or that a cut sequence does not do what the student says it does. The tutor does not rewrite prose, does not re-cut footage, and does not produce material that appears in the work.

Generated content is the current form of the same question. Text written by a language model and lightly edited is not the student's work, and in this subject it has a recognisable profile: confident, fluent and evidence-free, with claims about effect that reference no actual shot. Generated or upscaled images and audio used in a production have to be declared in line with the school's policy. Ask the coordinator what that policy requires. We also do not reproduce or supply IB subject guides, past papers or mark schemes; those belong to the board and are the school's to distribute.

sections.heading: Permits, availability and how lessons run
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is lawful and regulated. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications run through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation service for private tutor licensing, which lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time via the ministry's app, website and e-services system. Individuals operating without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule is published, no figure appears here.

On status, a tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram holds no such permit, occupies no premises in the UAE, and claims no approval, accreditation, licensing or endorsement from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board. ADEK's professional-ethics rules in Abu Dhabi additionally bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct points the same way, which is why no family should arrange for a child to be tutored privately by their own teacher.

Availability needs saying plainly because Film is the thinnest-supply Diploma subject we handle. There are very few people regionally who can analyse a sequence to Diploma standard, mark written analysis against the criteria, and review a rough cut usefully. Where one is free for your slot we say so. Where none is, we say that and give an honest estimate rather than assigning an English teacher who likes films, which is the substitution this market makes quietly and often.

Delivery is online: one-to-one over live video with screen sharing, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time around the school week and moved post-Iftar during Ramadan as standard. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. Shooting and editing happen wherever the student works and no tutor is present for that in any delivery model. A free trial lesson comes first: a real lesson on a real draft, no card required to book it, nothing charged if you decide not to continue.

process.title: Send one paragraph of real writing
process.description: A single paragraph of your child's own film writing tells a specialist more than a conversation does, because the diagnosis is visible in the verbs and nouns used. Add the prescribed extract the school is working from and the internal deadline dates, and the first session can start on the actual fault.

process.title: We check a Film specialist is genuinely free
process.description: Film has the thinnest specialist supply of any Diploma subject we cover regionally. We check the specific slot you need in Gulf Standard Time and tell you honestly if nobody suitable is available, with an estimate, rather than substituting a teacher who is enthusiastic about cinema.

process.title: A free trial lesson on one paragraph
process.description: The trial is a working session. For most students it is spent rewriting one paragraph with the plot removed and the techniques named, which demonstrates the difference rather than describing it. No card is required and nothing is charged if you stop there.

process.title: A written plan by task with deliverables
process.description: After the trial you receive a short plan naming which block applies, how many sessions, what the student writes between them, and what should be visible to their teacher by the next draft. Habits are priced as sessions; structural rebuilds are priced as weeks.

process.title: Marked drafts accumulate in sequence
process.description: Every piece of writing comes back annotated against the criteria and the drafts stay together in order. Reading three consecutive drafts shows a parent whether the same fault keeps recurring, which is also how we decide a block has finished rather than letting it roll on.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis from a real paragraph
whyPoints.description: Nearly every mid-band Film draft fails on plot description rather than on knowledge, so recommending more films is usually the wrong and most expensive answer. We place the student on a ranked list of common losses from their own writing before proposing any hours.

whyPoints.title: Shot analysis taught as a method, not a glossary
whyPoints.description: Picture without sound, then sound without picture, then both together, with a written paragraph at the end of every session. Students who do that exercise twice write differently and permanently, and every other task in the subject improves as a result.

whyPoints.title: Regional cinema treated as a real option
whyPoints.description: Most comparative studies worldwide compare the same handful of pairings. Arab and Gulf cinema is a genuine seam for a Dubai student, and we help test whether citable criticism exists before a pairing is committed to rather than after.

whyPoints.title: Nothing of the submission is ours
whyPoints.description: A tutor may ask any question about a draft, a timeline or a portfolio entry and may not supply any sentence or touch an edit. We say that before a family pays, and we do not reproduce board materials such as guides, past papers or mark schemes.

whyPoints.title: Honest availability, not a quiet substitution
whyPoints.description: Film is the thinnest-supply subject we handle in this region. Where no specialist is free we say so and estimate when one will be, instead of assigning someone who likes cinema and letting a family find out in week three.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claims and no invented statistics
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry or examination-board approval and claims none. Figures on this page are attributed to their sources, and anything that could not be verified, including IB session dates, has been left out.

faqs.question: What does the textual analysis actually ask my child to do?
faqs.answer: Read a short sequence from a prescribed film closely and say what its film language does, with evidence from the frame and the soundtrack rather than from the story. The marks sit in named techniques tied to effects: a shot size and what it withholds, a cut rate and what it produces, a score entry and what it replaces. What earns nothing is explaining where the extract sits in the plot and narrating the action, which is where most of the word allowance goes in a mid-band draft. Confirm the current task requirements and limits with your school's IB coordinator.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter's film analysis read as a plot summary?
faqs.answer: Because that is the natural way to write about a film you love, and nobody has shown her the alternative. The signature is visible in one paragraph: plot verbs dominate, technical nouns are absent, and the paragraph could have been written from a synopsis. The fix is mechanical and fast. Watch the sequence with the sound off and describe the image, then with the picture off and describe the sound, then combine them and ask what the combination produces moment by moment. A student who has done that twice writes differently, and it usually takes two or three sessions.

faqs.question: Which film-language terms does an examiner expect to see?
faqs.answer: Enough to describe what was chosen rather than what is visible. For image: shot size, angle, lens length, depth of field, camera movement, shot duration. For editing: cut, dissolve, cut rate, continuity, eyeline match, ellipsis, montage. For staging: blocking, setting, costume, props, colour, lighting key. For sound: diegetic and non-diegetic, score, effects, silence, sound bridge, sound perspective. The useful approach is not memorising a glossary but acquiring terms as they are needed to describe a specific choice, so the student ends up with a working vocabulary they actually use.

faqs.question: How do we choose an extract that is actually analysable?
faqs.answer: Choose for analytical content rather than for convenience. A sequence that starts where a chapter starts is usually the wrong one. The right one contains something to analyse: a change of pace, a shift in point of view, a moment where image and sound disagree, a withholding of information. Arguing that choice in the opening sentences is itself a mark-earning move, because it demonstrates the judgement the criteria reward. Where the school has set the film, the selection within it is still the student's decision and worth a session on its own.

faqs.question: What makes a comparative study research question work?
faqs.answer: One test settles it. Ask whether a sensible answer could be written about film one alone, then film two alone, then joined by a paragraph about similarities. If yes, the question permits a survey and will produce two essays stapled together. If an answer requires both films in the same sentence repeatedly, the question is doing its job. Questions almost always need narrowing rather than broadening: one specific formal device across two specific films, not two national cinemas. Students resist narrowing because it feels less impressive, and it is the single most reliable correction we make.

faqs.question: Can my child compare two films from the same country?
faqs.answer: The task asks for films from different cultural contexts, so check the current requirement with your school's IB coordinator before committing, because that wording is the board's to define and not a tutoring page's. In practice the interesting question is usually not nationality but what the comparison is for: two films from the same industry in different decades can sit in genuinely different cultural contexts, while two contemporary films from different countries can sit in a very similar one. Have the coordinator confirm that a proposed pairing satisfies the requirement before research starts rather than after.

faqs.question: Where do Emirati and Arab films fit into the comparative study?
faqs.answer: They are a real and under-used seam for a Dubai student, and examiners read a great many studies on the same familiar pairings. Gulf-funded feature production, Egyptian cinema's long industrial history, Palestinian and Lebanese filmmaking and their relationship to documentary, and Iranian formal strategies all set up specific comparisons with non-Arab cinema. Two cautions: check that citable criticism exists before committing, because scholarship is thinner and more scattered on some of this work, and acknowledge working from subtitles rather than making claims about dialogue nuance. A student who reads Arabic has a rare advantage here.

faqs.question: Is the film portfolio marked on the film or on the writing?
faqs.answer: On the evidence of decisions, which reaches the examiner mainly as writing and documents. A beautifully shot sequence with no record of the reasoning is thin evidence; a modest sequence with a clear account of a problem identified, three solutions tried and one chosen for stated reasons is strong. The practical consequence is a ninety-second habit: photograph the setup, save a test clip, write two sentences on what the test showed. Students who do that during production own the component. Students who reflect afterwards produce writing that reads as reconstruction, because it is tidy and free of dead ends.

faqs.question: How is my son assessed if the group film turns out badly?
faqs.answer: On his own contribution, which is why a disappointing group film can still contain strong individual submissions and a good one can contain weak ones. The risk is not quality but attribution: a group that divides work informally leaves each member unable to evidence what they personally decided. The protection is agreeing roles in writing at the start and each member keeping their own record of their own choices throughout. If the group has already drifted, the useful work is identifying what your son genuinely decided and can evidence, rather than making claims about the project as a whole.

faqs.question: What should a first Film session cover?
faqs.answer: One paragraph of the student's own writing, rewritten. A useful first hour takes a real draft paragraph, removes the plot from it, names the techniques actually visible in the thirty seconds being discussed, and shows the mark difference. That demonstrates the subject's central move rather than describing it, and it tells the tutor immediately which of the common faults is costing most. What a first session should not be is a tour of film history or of the task list, which answers a question nobody asked and costs a family an hour of diagnosis.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether the problem is analysis or writing?
faqs.answer: Ask your child to talk you through thirty seconds of a film they like, pausing the image. If the spoken account notices framing, cuts, sound and staging, the analysis is there and the problem is getting it onto the page, which is a fast fix. If the spoken account stays with character and story, the problem is what they notice, which needs the shot-analysis foundation block and takes four to six sessions. The two need different work, and buying the wrong one is the commonest waste in this subject because both present identically on a report as needs more depth.

faqs.question: Does watching more films improve the grade?
faqs.answer: Much less than parents expect, and this is the most common misdirected spend in the subject. Dubai Film candidates generally watch plenty already; what they lack is a different thing to do with what they watch. Four extracts analysed properly, frame by frame, with a written paragraph each, will move a grade more than forty films watched attentively. Once the analytical habit exists, breadth becomes genuinely useful, because the student starts noticing comparable devices across what they see. Before it exists, more viewing mostly produces more confident plot description.

faqs.question: How late in DP2 can Film technique still be fixed?
faqs.answer: The writing habits can be changed late and that is worth knowing. Replacing plot narration with technical analysis, narrowing a paragraph to a short span of film, quoting timecodes and naming shots are all single-session fixes that appear on nearly every mid-band draft, and they work six weeks out. What cannot be fixed late is a portfolio with no contemporaneous record, which can only be organised rather than reconstructed, or a comparative study whose question needs rebuilding if the deadline is days away. Tell us which tasks are still open at the consultation and we will plan only around those.

faqs.question: Can a tutor watch my child's rough cut and give notes?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is exactly the useful form of production support: watching a cut and asking what each decision was for. A tutor can say that a sequence does not do what the student intends, that a cut point fights the sound, that the pace flattens in the middle, or that a shot is doing no work. What a tutor cannot do is touch the edit. The notes go to the student, the student makes the changes or decides not to, and the reasoning they write about it afterwards is their own. We say that before any payment.

faqs.question: Does my child need to cite the films they reference?
faqs.answer: Yes, precisely, and it is easier than students assume. A film referenced in written analysis needs its title, year and director, and any specific moment discussed needs a timecode so a reader can check the claim. Frame grabs used as illustration are credited the same way. Where secondary criticism is used, including anything read in translation, it is cited like any other source. This is not bureaucracy: precise reference is what makes an analytical claim checkable, and a claim an examiner cannot check is a claim they cannot credit.

faqs.question: Does a Film tutor working with Dubai students need a permit?
faqs.answer: An individual providing private lessons in the UAE needs the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18, and applications go through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation service for private tutor licensing. Those operating without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no fine schedule is published, no amount is quoted here. Ask any UAE-resident tutor to show their permit.

The first lesson is free, no card is needed, and lessons run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach French ab initio at Standard Level to Dubai students beginning from nothing. They teach spelling, sound and grammar as one connected problem rather than three subjects, because at beginner level in French those three are the same problem wearing different names.

intro.heading: The familiar alphabet is the problem, not the help
paragraphs: A Dubai student picking French ab initio in DP1 usually does so because the alternative Group 2 options look harder and because French uses letters they already know. The second half of that is true and it is the reason the first term goes badly if it is handled carelessly. In Arabic a beginner knows they cannot read. In French a beginner thinks they can, pronounces every letter they see, writes every sound they hear, and builds a set of habits that then have to be dismantled.

That is where the marks go, and it is specific rather than vague. A student hears a verb and writes it without its silent ending. They hear a plural and write a singular, because the ending is not pronounced. They see a word that looks English and assume it means the English thing, which is right about half the time and expensively wrong the other half. They meet a number in a listening passage, hear sixty-ten and have no idea they are being told seventy. None of this is a lack of effort. It is the predictable consequence of a familiar alphabet attached to an unfamiliar sound system.

French ab initio is Standard Level only. There is no Higher Level, which matters for the subject grid because three HLs have to come from elsewhere. The assessment is three pieces. Paper 1 asks for two short written tasks of roughly 70 to 150 words each inside an hour. Paper 2 is listening and reading together and carries half the grade. The individual oral, recorded by the school from a photograph and a conversation, carries a quarter. Twenty prescribed topics sit inside five themes.

Eligibility works the same way as for any ab initio course and is worth settling before planning. The course is for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and the school decides. A Dubai student who had French on the timetable through middle school has prior experience on record, whatever they remember, and belongs in French B. A student who arrived from a school system where French was never taught is the genuine case, and so is a student who finished MYP in French at phase 1 or very early phase 2.

What follows is organised by where the marks are lost, because at beginner level the diagnosis is almost always the same list in a different order. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, which for most Dubai households means a slot after the school run or a weekend morning. We start with a free trial lesson and no card requirement, and that trial is spent finding out which of the error classes below your child is already building.
