dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The entry route into French ab initio decides how much of the first term is unlearning rather than learning. These notes describe the three profiles Dubai schools produce and what each brings to the same Paper 1.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French ab initio satisfies the Group 2 requirement at Standard Level across roughly 150 recommended teaching hours. Five themes, twenty prescribed topics, and no literary works. Assessment is Paper 1 writing in an hour, Paper 2 listening and reading, and an internally assessed individual oral built from a visual stimulus and a conversation on the themes.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma students take French ab initio alongside demanding HL grids, often three sciences or maths plus economics. The practical effect is that French gets the leftover evening, so short frequent sessions and small daily drills beat long weekly ones. A plan that assumes two free hours a week in DP2 is a plan that collapses in October.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition runs across six phases. A student completing MYP5 in French at phase 1 or very early phase 2 is the profile ab initio was designed for. A student at phase 3 or above has genuine prior experience and belongs in French B, regardless of how insecure they feel about it.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai IB schools generally run French as the main Group 2 alternative to Arabic, so MYP French classes here are large and the phase spread inside them is wide. Asking the MYP coordinator for the actual phase before DP selection closes is the cheapest piece of planning a family can do.

programmes.name: Arriving in Dubai without French
programmes.description: A student moving from a school system with no French provision into a Dubai IB school at 15 or 16. The genuine beginner case. The work is sequencing from nothing across eighteen teaching months, with the first term spent on sound and spelling before any volume of vocabulary is useful.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai absorbs new secondary students all year, and KHDA reported 6% enrolment growth during 2025-26 with seven new private schools opening for 2026-27 adding 16,846 places. Mid-year arrivals are routine here, and ab initio is the Group 2 course that exists to take them.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: A beginners' plan in French is a list of error classes and components rather than a list of topics. These are the units of work we build sessions around, in roughly the order they start costing marks.

subjects.name: Sound to spelling mapping
subjects.description: The core of French ab initio for an English speaker. Silent final consonants, silent verb endings, nasal vowels, the difference between what is written and what is said. Taught as a two-way skill: writing what is heard correctly, and saying what is written correctly, which are separate problems.

subjects.name: Noun gender and agreement
subjects.description: Every noun carries a gender that drives articles and adjective agreement, and no reliable rule covers it. Beginners who learn nouns without the article learn them twice. We insist on le or la attached to every new noun from the first session, because retrofitting gender later is dispiriting work.

subjects.name: Verb conjugation in the present
subjects.description: Regular endings across the three groups plus etre, avoir, aller and faire, which account for a large share of everything a beginner writes. The specific trap is that several present-tense forms sound identical and are spelled differently, so listening gives the student no warning.

subjects.name: Accents that change meaning
subjects.description: The difference between a and a with a grave accent, between ou and ou with a grave accent, between la and la with a grave accent. Small marks carrying real meaning, and the ones a student who types rather than writes by hand never acquires. A proofreading pass catches most of them.

subjects.name: False friends with English
subjects.description: Words that look English and are not: a bookshop rather than a library, to attend rather than to assist, currently rather than actually, sensitive rather than sensible. Beginners from an English-medium Dubai school meet these constantly, and each one is a comprehension error rather than a vocabulary gap.

subjects.name: Numbers from seventy to ninety-nine
subjects.description: Sixty-ten for seventy, four-twenties for eighty, four-twenty-ten for ninety. A beginner who has not drilled these loses listening marks on prices, dates, ages and times, which appear in most recordings. Perhaps the highest return per minute of drilling on the whole course.

subjects.name: Negation and partitive articles
subjects.description: The two-part negation that students reduce to one part because speech often does, and the partitive articles that change form after a negative. Both are frequent enough that errors in them appear in every piece of writing, which makes them cheap to find and worth fixing early.

subjects.name: Paper 1 short written tasks
subjects.description: Two tasks of roughly 70 to 150 words each, chosen from options, each a named text type: a message, an email, a postcard, a notice, a blog entry, a short article. Writing to length and stopping is the skill. Overrunning costs accuracy and earns nothing.

subjects.name: Listening: liaison and elision
subjects.description: French in connected speech joins words together and drops vowels, so a beginner who knows every word on a transcript cannot find any of them in the audio. The drill is short spans and transcription rather than whole passages, done in small amounts frequently.

subjects.name: The individual oral from a photograph
subjects.description: Describe the image, answer follow-up questions, discuss at least one further theme. Marked on language, message and interactive skills. The decisive skill is handling a question that was not understood without the conversation breaking down, which is a drilled phrase rather than a talent.

sections.heading: What French ab initio assesses, and what each part is worth
paragraphs: Three components, fixed weightings, and a shape worth knowing before buying any support. Paper 1 is one hour and asks for two short written tasks rather than one extended piece, each roughly 70 to 150 words, each chosen from options and each a named text type. It carries 25%. Paper 2 is listening for forty-five minutes and reading for an hour, and together they carry 50%. The individual oral, recorded by the school from a photograph and a conversation, carries the remaining 25%.

The implication for a beginner is uncomfortable and worth stating early. Half the grade sits in comprehension, which is the half a student cannot practise by producing anything. Writing feels like studying because it leaves a product behind. Listening leaves nothing behind except the knowledge that you did not understand, which is why it is skipped and why it is where ab initio grades are decided. The plan has to force comprehension work into the week or it will not happen.

There are no literary works on ab initio, which removes a whole category of preparation the French B students in the same school are doing. What replaces it is coverage: twenty prescribed topics across five themes, with vocabulary at this level strictly topic-bound. A gap in topic coverage is not a thin spot spread across the subject, it is a complete blank on one specific task, which is why we keep the list in writing and mark it off as it is done.

sections.heading: Why French is not the easy option it looks like
paragraphs: The alphabet is shared, so a beginner reads French on day one and feels competent. They are reading it wrong in a particular way: pronouncing final consonants that are silent, separating words that run together in speech, and giving vowels English values. Within a fortnight that has become a habit, and habits formed in week one are what the first term is then spent correcting. A tutor who begins with vocabulary lists rather than with sound and spelling is building on that foundation.

The reverse direction causes more lost marks. A student who has learned French mostly by ear writes what they hear, and French hides a great deal in writing that it does not say out loud. Several present-tense verb forms are pronounced identically and spelled differently. Plural endings are frequently silent. Final consonants on adjectives signal agreement that the ear never registers. So a student can understand a sentence perfectly, repeat it correctly, and write it wrong three times over.

English makes one further contribution, which is false friends. A Dubai student in an English-medium school meets words that look familiar and mean something else, and each encounter produces a confident mistake rather than a known gap. The remedy is not a vocabulary list but a labelled one: the twenty or thirty high-frequency false friends written down as pairs, so the student learns the trap alongside the word rather than discovering it in a reading paper. Taught that way they stop being a hazard and start being some of the easiest vocabulary on the course to retain.

sections.heading: The eight error classes that cost ab initio marks
paragraphs: After enough marked beginner scripts the same families of error appear, and they are specific enough to be listed and tracked. Silent verb endings written as heard. Noun gender missing or guessed, which then breaks every adjective and article attached to it. Infinitives used where a conjugated form was needed. Accents omitted or wrong, including the ones that change meaning. False friends. Numbers above sixty-nine. Negation reduced to one part. Partitive articles unchanged after a negative.

That list is the whole diagnostic for most ab initio students, and the method follows from it. Rather than teaching French grammar in sequence, we build a numbered error list from the student's own marked work, usually eight to fifteen items, and the student checks their own writing against it before submitting anything. Items leave the list when they stop appearing. The list is short enough to be used under exam conditions, which is the point: a rule a student cannot apply in the last five minutes of a paper is not yet learned.

What this changes is the shape of feedback. A beginner handed a script covered in red marks learns that their French is bad. A beginner handed a script with four numbers written in the margin, each one corresponding to an item on their own list, learns which four things to check next time. The marks move because the student can act on the feedback, not because the feedback was more detailed. The table sets out each class with the fix and its honest timescale.

sections.heading: Paper 1: two short tasks, and the skill of stopping
paragraphs: An hour, two tasks, each roughly 70 to 150 words, each chosen from options and each a named text type. The shape dictates the practice. A beginner working on one longer piece every fortnight is rehearsing something the exam never asks for. Two short, complete, controlled pieces every week is the right habit, and it also produces twice as many marked data points for the error list.

Length discipline is the first thing we teach and the thing students resist. Writing past the expected length earns nothing and costs accuracy, because the tenses drift, the gender agreements go, and the text type convention is forgotten halfway down. We practise writing to the length and stopping, then spending the remaining minutes on a proofreading pass against the error list. Finishing both tasks inside the hour is its own skill, and the second task is where candidates run out of time.

Text type still carries marks at beginner level, which is good news for a student with limited French. A message, an email, a postcard, a notice and a blog entry each open and close differently and address their reader differently. That is a page of notes, learnable in two or three sessions, and the marks attached to audience, purpose and register do not depend on the sophistication of the language. For a beginner it is the most efficient revision material on the course, and unlike vocabulary it does not need maintaining once it is written down.

sections.heading: Paper 2: half the grade in the work nobody wants to do
paragraphs: Listening and reading together are 50% of French ab initio, and for an English-speaking beginner listening is the hardest thing on the course. French in connected speech joins words to each other and swallows vowels, so a student who recognises every word in a transcript can find none of them in the audio. The problem is not vocabulary and it is not attention. It is that the acoustic signal does not have gaps where the student expects them.

The drill is specific and small. Take a span of twenty to thirty seconds. Play it. Write down what was heard, including nonsense where nothing was recognised. Replay. Correct and extend. Replay once more, then read the transcript and see what was actually there. Ten to fifteen minutes four times a week, which a student does alone, with session time used for method and review rather than for playing recordings. Numbers above sixty-nine, days, months and prices are drilled separately all year, because they carry a disproportionate share of the answers.

Reading fails differently and improves faster. The beginner instinct is to read every word in order and stop at the first unknown one, rereading the same line until time runs out. The counter-habit is to locate the words that are recognised, find the question's target between them, and infer the rest. That is technique rather than language, which is why four to six sessions sorted by question type usually produce more than a term of reading whole passages. False friends need flagging here, because they generate confident wrong answers.

sections.heading: The individual oral: four moves and one real skill
paragraphs: The ab initio oral is recorded by the school and marked on language, message and interactive skills. The student describes a photograph linked to one of the five themes, answers follow-up questions on it, then talks about at least one further theme. A beginner can score respectably with modest French, provided the practice has been on photographs they have never seen rather than on one rehearsed answer delivered from memory.

We teach a fixed four-move sequence that works on any image: say what is in it, say where it is, say what the people are doing, then say something simple about the theme behind it. Four moves, learned as a routine, applied cold. It removes the panic that produces thirty seconds of silence at the start, and it gives the examiner something to ask a follow-up question about, which is how the interactive marks become available at all.

The decisive skill is not description. It is what happens when a question is not understood, which for a beginner is inevitable. A student who freezes loses the interactive marks and the rest of the conversation never recovers. A student who has drilled three phrases for asking something to be repeated, slowed down or put differently keeps the exchange going and keeps scoring. Those phrases amount to perhaps fifteen words of French and are worth more marks than any fifteen words of topic vocabulary on the course. We drill them in every oral session until a student reaches for them automatically instead of reaching for English.

sections.heading: Ab initio or French B: the twenty-topic test
paragraphs: The wrong course choice costs more marks than any teaching decision made afterwards, so it is worth settling properly. Ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience of the language and the school decides eligibility. The temptation in Dubai is to read the course as an easier option for a student who has struggled through school French. It is not a difficulty setting, and a student with several years of timetabled French has prior experience on record whatever they retained.

The test that works is neither confidence nor a grade. It is coverage and construction. Can the student conjugate four high-frequency verbs in the present without a table? Do they know the gender of twenty everyday nouns? Can they produce five connected sentences on a familiar topic without help? A student answering no to all three is a beginner in substance as well as on paper. A student answering yes is in French B territory and the work there is remedial rather than foundational.

Where the answer is genuinely borderline, the decision belongs to the Diploma coordinator and the evidence that helps them is the MYP phase or the previous school's language record rather than anyone's impression. We will give a view from a short diagnostic and we will give it even when it costs us the booking, because a beginner placed in French B spends two years scoring badly and a French B student placed in ab initio is in a course the school cannot defend entering them for.

sections.heading: What eighteen months fixes, what it does not, and what it costs
paragraphs: Honest scope first. Eighteen months of properly sequenced work will give a beginner control of the present tense and a reliable past, secure gender on everyday nouns, the eight error classes down to two or three, text type conventions, the twenty prescribed topics covered, a workable oral routine and listening that functions on familiar topics at moderate speed. It will not produce fluency, broad vocabulary, or comfortable comprehension of unfamiliar rapid speech, and a tutor implying otherwise is describing a different timescale.

On price, the Dubai market reads as follows from published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, read in October 2026: AED 45 to 150 an hour for budget or university-student tutors, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 200 to 450 and above for an IB or IGCSE specialist, and AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit where travel sits inside the billed hour. Online monthly packages around AED 799 for eight sessions appear in the same market. Those are market figures, not IB Gram prices.

The spend profile for ab initio is front-loaded, which is the opposite of how most families buy. Two short sessions a week for the first term, then one a week for topic coverage, then a component block before the oral recording. Families who fund the first term properly generally need fewer hours in DP2, because a student whose sound-and-spelling habits are right can use ordinary classroom teaching, and one whose habits are wrong is being taught over the top of them. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and lessons here are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

process.title: Settle the course question with evidence
process.description: How many years of French, in which system, and what was covered. The MYP phase or the previous school's record answers it faster than a test. Where the student can already conjugate common verbs and knows noun genders, the honest answer is French B and we will say so.

process.title: Free trial spent on a five-minute diagnostic and a first lesson
process.description: The trial runs the three-part diagnostic, then teaches one real thing: usually silent endings and a first dictation. That shows how quickly corrections stick, which is the only figure needed to plan the first term. No card is required and the diagnostic is yours regardless.

process.title: Two short sessions a week through the first term
process.description: Forty-five minutes twice weekly, live online in Gulf Standard Time. Dictation at the start, reading aloud at the end, every new noun learned with its article, and the error list opened on the first marked piece of writing.

process.title: Weekly topic coverage against a written list
process.description: Once the sound-and-spelling habits hold, one session a week works the twenty prescribed topics in a written order, each block ending in a 70 to 150 word task. The list is shared so coverage can be audited in DP2 rather than assumed.

process.title: Oral block before the school records
process.description: Five or six sessions in the three weeks before the recording window, on unseen photographs, with clarification phrases drilled. Ask the school for that date in DP1; the same block before the recording is worth several times the same block after the result.

whyPoints.title: Sound and spelling taught as one problem
whyPoints.description: The familiar alphabet is what makes French hard for an English-speaking beginner, not what makes it easy. Dictation and reading aloud in every early session attack the gap directly, rather than building vocabulary on top of habits that will need dismantling.

whyPoints.title: An error list the student can use under exam conditions
whyPoints.description: Eight to fifteen numbered items drawn from their own marked work, checked before every submission. Short enough to apply in the last five minutes of a paper, which is the test of whether a rule has actually been learned.

whyPoints.title: Numbers above sixty-nine drilled all year
whyPoints.description: Seventy, eighty and ninety are arithmetic rather than words in French, and they appear in prices, ages, dates and times across most listening passages. A weekly two-minute drill for a year is the highest return per minute available on the course.

whyPoints.title: Topic coverage you can audit
whyPoints.description: Twenty prescribed topics, a written list, marked off as sessions cover them. Beginner vocabulary is topic-bound, so an uncovered topic is a complete blank on one task rather than a general weakness. Gaps should be visible in November of DP2, not in May.

whyPoints.title: A straight answer on ab initio or French B
whyPoints.description: Three diagnostic questions settle most cases, and where the evidence says French B we say so even though it costs us the booking. The course is a starting point, not a difficulty setting, and the Diploma coordinator makes the decision.

whyPoints.title: Scope and delivery stated without decoration
whyPoints.description: Eighteen months produces control, coverage and technique; it does not produce fluency. Lessons are one-to-one and online over live video in Gulf Standard Time, no tutor is sent to a UAE address, and no approval from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE or the IB is held or claimed.

faqs.question: Is French ab initio easier than Arabic ab initio for a Dubai student?
faqs.answer: Different rather than easier, and the familiar alphabet cuts both ways. Arabic costs a beginner two months on the writing system before useful reading starts. French gives reading away on day one and then charges for it, because a student pronounces letters that are silent and writes endings they cannot hear. Arabic beginners know they cannot read; French beginners believe they can and build habits that take a term to correct. Where English is the student's main language, the French sound-to-spelling gap is usually the bigger obstacle in practice.

faqs.question: What does French ab initio Paper 1 ask for?
faqs.answer: Two short written tasks inside one hour, each roughly 70 to 150 words, each chosen from options and each a named text type such as a message, an email, a postcard, a notice, a blog entry or a short article. The practical consequence is that practice should be two short complete pieces a week rather than one longer piece a fortnight. Writing beyond the expected length earns nothing and costs accuracy, so writing to length and then spending the remaining minutes proofreading against an error list is the habit we drill.

faqs.question: Why does my child understand French in class but score badly on the listening paper?
faqs.answer: Because classroom French is spoken for a learner and exam French is not. Connected speech joins words together and drops vowels, so the acoustic signal has no gaps where a beginner expects them. A student who recognises every word in a transcript finds none of them in the audio. The drill is twenty to thirty second spans, written down including the parts not understood, replayed, corrected, then checked against the transcript. Ten to fifteen minutes four times a week, done alone, with session time used for method rather than for playing recordings.

faqs.question: Why are French numbers a problem in the listening paper?
faqs.answer: Because from seventy upwards they are arithmetic rather than single words: sixty-ten for seventy, four-twenties for eighty, four-twenty-ten for ninety. A beginner who has not drilled them hears the components and loses the number, and numbers carry prices, ages, dates, times and quantities across most recordings. A two-minute drill every week for a year costs almost nothing and is probably the highest return per minute on the whole course. Teaching them once in term one and never again is the standard mistake.

faqs.question: What are the most common mistakes in French ab initio writing?
faqs.answer: Eight classes cover almost all of them: silent verb endings written as heard, noun gender missing or guessed, infinitives left where a conjugated form was needed, accents omitted including the ones that change meaning, false friends with English, numbers above sixty-nine, the two-part negation reduced to one part, and partitive articles unchanged after a negative. All eight are listable, which is the point. We build a numbered list from the student's own marked work and they check their writing against it before submitting anything.

faqs.question: Can my child take French ab initio if they did French in middle school?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience and the school decides eligibility, so several years of timetabled French counts as prior experience whatever the student retained. The useful test is construction rather than confidence: can they conjugate four common verbs in the present without a table, do they know the gender of twenty everyday nouns, can they produce five connected sentences unaided? Yes to those points to French B, where the work is remedial. Raise it with the Diploma coordinator in DP1 while the timetable can still change.

faqs.question: Is there a Higher Level in French ab initio?
faqs.answer: No. The course exists at Standard Level only, with around 150 recommended teaching hours. That has a consequence for the subject grid that families sometimes find out too late: the Diploma requires three Higher Level subjects and none of them can be this one, so all three must come from the other groups. If the grid was built assuming Group 2 could carry an HL, it needs revisiting with the Diploma coordinator. There are also no literary works on ab initio, which is one fewer thing to prepare than French B HL.

faqs.question: How is the French ab initio individual oral marked?
faqs.answer: It is recorded by the school, internally assessed, and worth a quarter of the grade, across language, message and interactive skills. The student describes a photograph linked to one of the five themes, answers follow-up questions on it, then discusses at least one further theme. We teach a fixed four-move routine for any image: what is in it, where it is, what the people are doing, then something simple about the theme. The routine removes the opening silence and gives the examiner something to ask a follow-up about.

faqs.question: What happens in the oral if my child does not understand a question?
faqs.answer: That is the moment the marks are decided, and it is drillable. A beginner will not understand some questions; that is expected. A student who freezes loses the interactive marks and the conversation does not recover. A student who has practised three phrases for asking something to be repeated, slowed down or rephrased keeps the exchange alive and keeps scoring. Those phrases total about fifteen words of French and are worth more than any fifteen words of topic vocabulary. We drill them in every oral session until they come out without thought.

faqs.question: How many topics are on the French ab initio course?
faqs.answer: Twenty prescribed topics, four inside each of the five themes. Because it is a finite and countable syllabus, a family can reasonably ask for a coverage list and check it against the calendar, which matters more at beginner level than later. Vocabulary here is topic-bound, so a student who has covered sixteen of the twenty is not generally weaker; they are competent on sixteen tasks and completely stuck on four. We keep the list in writing and mark it off, so a gap is visible rather than discovered in an exam hall.

faqs.question: Will a French tutor come to our villa in Dubai for ab initio lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. French ab initio is taught one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, usually on a weekday evening or a weekend morning. For a beginners' course the online format carries a specific advantage: dictation, pronunciation models and short texts sit on a shared screen and can be revisited, and oral rehearsals are recorded so the student hears their own hesitations rather than being told about them.

faqs.question: How often should a complete beginner in French have lessons?
faqs.answer: Twice a week for about forty-five minutes through the first term, then once a week once sound-and-spelling habits hold. The early work is habit formation rather than content delivery, and habits form through short repeated contact rather than one long weekly sitting. Each early session should open with a five-sentence dictation and close with reading aloud. Both are mechanical and both are what make the rest of the course work. After the first term, weekly sessions tied to the prescribed topics are enough, with listening drills done alone between them.

faqs.question: What will French ab initio tutoring achieve in eighteen months?
faqs.answer: Control of the present tense and a reliable past, secure gender on everyday nouns, the eight error classes reduced to two or three, text type conventions in place, the twenty prescribed topics covered, a workable oral routine, and listening that functions on familiar topics at moderate speed. What it will not produce is fluency, broad vocabulary or comfortable comprehension of unfamiliar rapid speech, because those are functions of exposure hours that cannot be compressed. Knowing which column a goal sits in is how a family decides how much support to buy.

faqs.question: What does beginner French tutoring cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, read in October 2026, put budget or university-student tutors at AED 45-150 an hour, qualified online subject tutors at AED 150-300, IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450 and above, and in-home visits at AED 180-500 with travel inside the billed hour. Online packages around AED 799 a month for eight sessions appear in the same market. Those are market figures rather than IB Gram prices. The ab initio spend profile is front-loaded: two short sessions a week in the first term, then one.

faqs.question: My child picked French ab initio in DP1 and is already behind. What do we do first?
faqs.answer: Establish two things before buying any hours. Which of the twenty prescribed topics have actually been covered, which the school can confirm in an email. And which of the eight error classes are already present, which one marked piece of writing will show. With those, the first month has a defined job: install dictation and reading aloud, attach articles to every noun, start the error list, and drill numbers above sixty-nine. What does not help is a general French course delivered over the top of habits formed in the first weeks.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start with one marked piece of writing and the coverage list
dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tutor.closingBody: Two documents make a French ab initio plan concrete. One marked piece of your child's writing, which shows which of the eight error classes are already forming. And the school's list of prescribed topics covered so far, which shows what is missing. A free trial lesson runs the diagnostic, teaches a first dictation and tells you how quickly corrections stick, with no card required and nothing to commit to. Sessions are one-to-one, online, in Gulf Standard Time. If the evidence says your child belongs in French B rather than ab initio, that is what we will tell you.

intro.heading: The problem with a beginners' language is that nothing visible happens for months
paragraphs: A Dubai family taking on French ab initio faces a specific anxiety. The subject is new, the student has no prior French, the first grade will not arrive for a term, and in the meantime there is no way to tell whether the lessons are working. Science produces marked practicals. Mathematics produces right and wrong answers every week. A beginner language produces a vague sense of progress, and that sense is unreliable in both directions: students who feel fluent in conversation often cannot write, and students who feel lost are frequently further ahead than they think.

The answer is to make the course produce evidence from the start. Ab initio has a finite syllabus of twenty prescribed topics, four under each of the five Group 2 themes, so coverage can be recorded rather than estimated. Paper 1 asks for two written tasks of roughly 70 to 150 words inside one hour, which means a student can produce a complete, markable piece of work from early in the course. And the individual oral is a recorded performance, so improvement can be heard by comparing October with February rather than inferred from a tutor's impression.

The assessment model is straightforward and worth knowing from the first week. Paper 1, the two short written tasks, carries a quarter of the grade. Paper 2, listening followed by reading in one sitting, carries half. The internally assessed individual oral, which starts from a visual stimulus drawn from the prescribed topics, carries the final quarter. Standard Level is the only level available, there is no literary works requirement, and no component rewards breadth that the twenty topics do not already cover.

Eligibility comes first, though, and it is where Dubai families most often lose time. Ab initio is restricted to students with little or no previous experience of the language. A student who took French to IGCSE, or who studied it through the MYP in any serious way, will usually be refused by the school however rusty they feel. That decision belongs to the Diploma coordinator and it has a deadline, normally early in Year 12. Ask for the school's position in writing before building a plan around the course.

What delivering lessons online changes is the quality of the match. Teaching French to a student who already speaks some is common work. Taking a sixteen-year-old from nothing to a timed examination in two years, against a prescribed topic list, with handwriting and spelling built from scratch, is a narrower skill. The number of people in any single Dubai community who do that well and are free at five o'clock is small. Over live video the pool is defined by the skill instead of the postcode, and the lesson itself loses nothing.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-online-tuto.programmesIntro: A Dubai student arriving in the Diploma as a French beginner has usually come through one of the other IB programmes, or through none at all. The notes below set out where French sits in each and what a student brings into Year 12 as a result.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French ab initio fills a Group 2 slot at Standard Level and is examined at the end of Year 13. The two short written tasks of Paper 1 carry 25 per cent, the listening and reading of Paper 2 carry 50 per cent, and the school-assessed individual oral carries 25 per cent. The whole examinable syllabus is the twenty prescribed topics, which is what makes progress on this course measurable.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma cohorts are small beside the emirate's British-curriculum population, and ab initio classes inside them are smaller still, often four or five students. That has a direct consequence for evidence: a small class produces few assessments, so a parent relying on school reports alone will see very little until the first mock.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language acquisition in the MYP is organised in phases, with four criteria covering listening, reading, speaking and writing. A student can leave the programme in an early phase, but any serious record of MYP French is normally enough to make ab initio unavailable, because the course is reserved for beginners.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai MYP cohorts turn over heavily and students often arrive mid-programme with language records that do not transfer cleanly. A student who did two terms of French in Year 7 and nothing since sits in a grey area, and whether that counts as previous experience is a judgement the receiving Dubai school makes.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: French in the PYP is an additional language inside transdisciplinary units with no external assessment. Plenty of Dubai primaries offer a taste of it alongside KHDA's mandatory Arabic. For ab initio eligibility this rarely counts as previous experience, because very little reading or writing is assessed at that stage.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai primary timetables already carry mandatory Arabic for every pupil whatever the licensed curriculum, so a child doing French as well is managing two additional languages. Families should expect the enthusiasm for one of them to fade, and should not read that as a verdict on the child's language ability.

sections.heading: Who actually qualifies for French ab initio in a Dubai school
paragraphs: The course is designed for students with little or no previous experience of French, and Dubai schools apply that restriction fairly strictly. The reason is not bureaucratic: a student with several years of prior French in an ab initio class has an advantage the course was never built to accommodate, and the teaching has to pitch somewhere between them and a true beginner, which serves neither. The practical result is that an IGCSE French grade, or a substantial MYP French record, will usually close the door.

That produces a familiar argument in Dubai households. The student insists they remember nothing, which is often sincere. The parent sees a reasonable request to start again. The coordinator sees a record of study and says no. Persistence will not move this, but precision sometimes will: ask what evidence the school uses, how it treats a student who studied French only in primary, whether a transfer from a system with no French at all is handled differently, and what the deadline is for changing a Group 2 choice. Those four answers settle the matter in a week.

The clean cases are students arriving into Year 12 from a system where French was simply never offered. They have a real timing problem, because two years is short, and a real advantage, because they are starting with adult learning habits and a clear reason to be there. For them the question is not eligibility but sequencing: how much has to be in place by the end of Year 12 for Year 13 to be about assessment rather than about catching up. The rest of this page is mostly an answer to that question.

sections.heading: Sound before spelling: what makes French hard for a beginner
paragraphs: French is not difficult because of its grammar, at least not at this level. It is difficult at the start because the relationship between what is written and what is said is indirect in ways English learners find disorienting. Final consonants are often silent, except when the next word begins with a vowel and liaison brings them back. Several different spellings produce the same vowel sound. Nasal vowels have no English equivalent and are easy to approximate badly for months without anyone correcting them. A beginner who learns French through the page builds a private pronunciation that then fails in the listening paper.

The structural novelty is gender. Every noun carries one, almost nothing in the word reliably signals which, and gender then propagates into articles, adjectives and past participles. Teaching nouns without their article from the first lesson is the single most common avoidable mistake in beginner French, because the gender has to be relearned later alongside everything that agrees with it. Learning the article as part of the word costs nothing at the start and saves a term of correction.

The third early obstacle is verb groups. Regular present-tense patterns are learnable in a fortnight, and then the common irregular verbs, which are exactly the ones a beginner needs most, have to be acquired individually. The sequence that works is a small number of high-frequency verbs secured completely, including in the perfect tense, before any attempt at breadth. A student who can use ten verbs accurately across three tenses can say far more than one who half-knows forty, and the written tasks reward exactly that kind of controlled range.

sections.heading: What a beginner language hour costs in Dubai, by provider model
paragraphs: Dubai's tutoring market is unusually quiet about prices, and the figures below are drawn from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table rather than from any survey of our own. They are presented as market context, by model rather than by brand, because the model is what drives the number. A tuition centre carries premises. A visiting tutor carries a car. A marketplace carries neither and carries no accountability either. Those differences show up in the rate more clearly than any difference in teaching quality does.

For a beginner language specifically, the cheapest tier is the worst value. General homework help at the bottom of the market is delivered by people who can speak some French and have never sequenced a beginner course or marked against the criteria. The teaching that matters here is unglamorous and technical: sound work, article discipline, verb sequencing, timed writing at 70 to 150 words. A tutor who has not done it before will teach vocabulary, which feels productive and leaves the student unable to write a paragraph in March.

The table sets out the models with their published AED ranges and the questions that actually distinguish them. Two of those questions matter more than price. The first is whether travel is inside the rate, because an in-home hour at AED 300 containing forty minutes of driving is a different product from an online hour at AED 300. The second is what happens when a tutor does not suit the student, since on a two-year beginner course that is a real risk and a provider without a rematch policy is passing it to you.

sections.heading: Online, in-home or a group class for a genuine beginner
paragraphs: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we provide only in India. That is worth stating before any comparison, because the comparison is not a sales argument if the alternative is not on offer. What follows is an honest account of what each format does for a beginner, including where in-home genuinely wins.

In-home tuition wins on two things. It is harder for a teenager to disengage from someone sitting beside them, which matters for a student who needs supervision as much as teaching. And for families without reliable quiet space or a decent connection, a visiting tutor removes a real problem. Against that sits the cost of travel inside the rate, a tutor pool limited to people who will drive to one community at a fixed hour, and the twenty or thirty minutes a Dubai school run or a Sheikh Zayed Road delay removes from the start of the session.

Group classes are cheaper per student and suit a confident beginner who learns from hearing others try. They work badly for the specific failures that sink ab initio students, because sound correction, article discipline and handwriting are individual problems that a group hour cannot address one by one. Online one-to-one wins on pool, on cost per teaching minute, and on evidence: the written work arrives marked, the oral is recorded, and both can be looked at by a parent weeks later. sections.heading: Two tasks in sixty minutes: what Paper 1 really demands
paragraphs: Paper 1 asks for two written tasks inside one hour, each in the region of 70 to 150 words, chosen from three options, with a text type named for each. Those numbers sound generous until a beginner tries it. Planning, writing and checking two separate pieces in sixty minutes leaves roughly twenty-five minutes of writing time each, and a student who has only ever written at leisure will spend thirty on the first and abandon the second. Timing is therefore a taught skill on this course, not a test-day concern.

The text type is marked, which surprises families who assume a beginners' paper only tests language. A task naming a message wants a message: short, addressed, purposeful. A task naming a notice wants layout and imperatives. A task naming a blog post wants a voice and a reader. A student who writes the same neat paragraph for every task has capped their own score for a reason that has nothing to do with their French. Five or six forms, each practised once with a checklist, closes that gap in a term.

This is also the component that produces the evidence a parent needs. A marked task every fortnight shows three things at a glance: whether the student can produce the required length unaided, whether the form was right, and whether the errors are the same ones as last time. Those three questions answer whether the course is working far better than any conversation about confidence. We keep the scripts in order so the February one can be read beside the October one, because the change is usually obvious and occasionally it is absent, and both facts are worth knowing early.

sections.heading: Describing a photograph in a language learned last year
paragraphs: The individual oral starts from a visual stimulus drawn from the prescribed topics. The student prepares under supervision, presents on the image, answers follow-up questions, and then moves into a wider conversation. It is marked by the school and externally moderated, and it carries a quarter of the grade. For a beginner this is the component where confidence and marks diverge most sharply, because the instinct under pressure is to say less, and the criteria reward sustained interaction.

What works is a repeatable structure rather than a memorised script. A student who knows they will describe the scene, then say what is happening, then offer an opinion with a reason, has a frame that fits any photograph on any of the twenty topics. The frame is the thing to drill; the vocabulary attaches to it topic by topic. A script memorised for one image collapses when a different image appears, and it also scores badly, because the criteria notice the difference between prepared recitation and real speech.

The follow-up and conversation phases are where beginners lose most. A question answered in four words is a lost opportunity that no vocabulary work recovers. The habit worth building is one extra sentence, every single time: an example, a reason, a comparison, a mild opinion. Taught as a reflex over months it becomes automatic. Monthly recorded practice is how we check it is happening, and the recordings are kept, because a student who has moved from six-word answers to twenty-word answers can hear that themselves, which is more persuasive than being told.

sections.heading: Sequencing beginner French across a Dubai school year
paragraphs: The Dubai academic year has a shape that affects a beginner language more than it affects most subjects, because language learning depends on frequency and the Dubai calendar is full of interruptions. Term one runs from late August or early September to a winter break. Term two starts in January and includes Ramadan in the current cycle, when school hours shorten and many families prefer sessions after Iftar. Term three runs into the summer, and the long summer break is where a beginner either consolidates or forgets.

The sequencing principle is to place the hardest acquisition work in the longest uninterrupted stretch. Sound, spelling, articles and the first verbs belong in term one of Year 12, when nothing else in the Diploma is urgent yet. Topic coverage spreads across the rest of Year 12 and the start of Year 13. The oral window dominates one block of Year 13, and the final term is timed papers. The summer between the two Diploma years is the single most valuable block available, and families who book it in spring get the slots they want.

The table below sets out what should exist as evidence at each stage. It is deliberately written as checkable artefacts rather than as feelings, so a parent can ask one question at each half term and get a real answer. A course that cannot produce the artefact for its stage is not necessarily failing, but it is not demonstrating anything either, and on a two-year beginner course that distinction is worth insisting on early rather than discovering at the first mock.

sections.heading: Is a beginner language worth a Group 2 slot? The honest arithmetic
paragraphs: This question deserves a straight answer before any money changes hands. A beginner language is two years of work for a Standard Level grade in a subject the student cannot yet use, and the alternative is usually a continuation language where the student already has several years behind them. For a student whose Diploma points are tight, continuing an existing language is normally the lower-risk route, and anyone who tells a Dubai family otherwise without asking about their prior study is not advising them.

Ab initio earns its place in three situations. The first is a student with no continuation language available at all, which is common for arrivals from systems that teach no second language seriously. The second is a student with a specific destination in view, where a francophone university or a family reason gives the language a purpose beyond the grade. The third is a student who genuinely enjoys starting something new and will work at it, which sounds soft and is in fact the strongest predictor of how this course goes.

The test we suggest costs three weeks. Take beginner lessons before the Group 2 choice is finalised and see what happens to the student's appetite once the novelty wears off and the verb tables arrive. A student who finds it satisfying will be fine. One who finds it a chore has learned something cheaply and should be allowed to say so without anyone treating it as failure. We would rather tell a family that a different Group 2 subject suits better than sell two years of lessons into a course the student resents by February.

process.title: Confirm eligibility with the school first
process.description: Ask the Diploma coordinator in writing whether your child qualifies for ab initio given their French record, and when the Group 2 change deadline falls. Lessons planned around a course the school will not permit are wasted. If the answer is no, the plan becomes a French B plan, which is a different course with different components.

process.title: A free 45-minute trial that produces a document
process.description: The trial costs nothing, runs 45 minutes, and takes no card details. For a genuine beginner it covers sound, a first set of structures and a short piece of writing. You receive a written note on starting point, the realistic two-year timeline, and the first three things that need to be in place by half term, whether or not you continue.

process.title: Agree what the evidence will be
process.description: Before lessons start we agree what you will see and when: a scored written task every fortnight, a topic coverage list updated at half term, logged listening scores, and a kept oral recording each month. Agreeing this up front is what stops a beginner course running for two terms on nothing but reassurance.

process.title: Weekly sessions, work marked before it is discussed
process.description: Tasks are set between lessons and marked against the criteria before the session that covers them, so the hour starts from a diagnosis rather than from reading. The error log is cumulative across the course, and the topic list shows what is secure, so the final term can be aimed at weaknesses rather than spread evenly.

process.title: Book the summer block in spring
process.description: The summer between Year 12 and Year 13 produces more progress for a beginner than any term-time intensive, because nothing competes for attention. Slots for it fill from about March. We flag it early rather than mentioning it in July, and we are explicit that a student who loses that summer effectively loses a term.

whyPoints.title: The course produces evidence from week six
whyPoints.description: A beginner language is the easiest subject to run on reassurance, so we agree the artefacts in advance: fortnightly scored tasks, a topic coverage list, logged listening scores, monthly oral recordings kept in order. A parent can read a marked script in five minutes and know whether the two years are on track.

whyPoints.title: Sound and article discipline taught from the first lesson
whyPoints.description: Nouns are learned with their article and pronunciation is corrected from the start, because both are far cheaper to teach once than to unpick later. A student who builds a private pronunciation from the page has a listening problem that surfaces in the one component carrying half the grade.

whyPoints.title: Timing rehearsed, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Two tasks in an hour leaves about twenty-five minutes of writing each, and a beginner who has never written to a clock will not finish. Timed practice at the real word range starts in the first term, so running out of time is a problem solved in October rather than discovered in the examination.

whyPoints.title: Honest about whether the course suits
whyPoints.description: A beginner language is two years of work for one Standard Level grade, and a continuation language is usually the lower-risk route where one exists. We say so before the choice is confirmed and suggest three weeks of lessons as a cheap test, because a student who resents the subject by February costs everyone more.

whyPoints.title: A tutor chosen for beginner sequencing
whyPoints.description: Speaking French and taking a sixteen-year-old from nothing to a timed paper are different skills, and the second is uncommon. Teaching over live video means the match is made on that skill instead of on driving distance, which matters when the number of suitable people in one Dubai community is very small.

whyPoints.title: A slot that survives the Dubai calendar
whyPoints.description: Sessions are fixed for the term on Gulf Standard Time, planned around fixtures and school trips, moved to post-Iftar times during Ramadan, and extended into a summer block between the Diploma years. Frequency is what a beginner language runs on, so protecting the rhythm is the practical work.

faqs.question: How will I know whether beginner French lessons are actually working?
faqs.answer: Ask for artefacts rather than opinions. By week six there should be a short paragraph the student produced unaided. By the end of the first term there should be a scored 70-word task. By the end of Year 12 there should be a list showing which of the twenty prescribed topics are secure and a set of logged listening scores. Monthly oral recordings, kept in order, let you hear October beside February. A beginner course that cannot produce the artefact for its stage is running on reassurance.

faqs.question: Can my child take French ab initio if they did French at IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly not. Ab initio is reserved for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and an IGCSE grade is a clear record of study however much the student feels they have forgotten. The same usually applies to a substantial MYP French record. The decision belongs to the Diploma coordinator and there is a deadline for Group 2 changes, normally early in Year 12. Ask what evidence the school uses and how it treats French studied only in primary, because that is the one genuine grey area.

faqs.question: What makes French hard in the first few months for a complete beginner?
faqs.answer: Not the grammar. The gap between spelling and sound is the first obstacle: silent final consonants that reappear through liaison, several spellings for one vowel sound, and nasal vowels with no English equivalent that go uncorrected for months if nobody is listening carefully. The second is gender, which is unpredictable and then propagates into articles, adjectives and past participles, which is why nouns should be learned with their article from the first lesson. The third is irregular verbs, which are the ones a beginner needs most.

faqs.question: How long are the Paper 1 tasks in French ab initio?
faqs.answer: Each of the two tasks sits in the region of 70 to 150 words, and both must be finished inside the paper's one hour, which leaves roughly twenty-five minutes of writing time each. Each task names a text type, and the conventions of that form are assessed, so a student who writes the same neat paragraph every time has capped their score for reasons unrelated to their French. Practising to the real length against a clock from the first term is what prevents an abandoned second task in the examination.

faqs.question: What does the ab initio oral involve for a French beginner?
faqs.answer: A visual stimulus drawn from the prescribed topics, prepared under supervision, followed by a presentation on the image, follow-up questions about it, and then a wider conversation. The school marks it and it is externally moderated, carrying a quarter of the grade. The marks reward sustained interaction, which is the opposite of a nervous beginner's instinct to answer briefly. A reusable description frame beats a memorised script, because a script collapses on an unfamiliar image and the criteria notice recitation.

faqs.question: Is beginner French easier than beginner Arabic or Spanish in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Spanish is usually the gentlest start for a Latin-alphabet speaker, because its spelling maps onto sound predictably. Arabic has the steepest beginning because of the script. French sits between them: no new alphabet, but an indirect relationship between writing and pronunciation that causes months of quiet trouble if it is not addressed early. The better question is which language the student will still be using in five years, since all three take the same two years and produce the same single Standard Level grade.

faqs.question: Should my child take a beginner language at all in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: If a continuation language is available, that is normally the lower-risk route, and anyone advising otherwise without asking about prior study is not advising you. Beginner courses earn their place for students with no continuation option, students with a specific francophone destination, and students who genuinely enjoy starting something new. The cheap test is three weeks of lessons before the Group 2 choice is confirmed, once the novelty has worn off and the verb tables have arrived.

faqs.question: What do Dubai providers charge for beginner language tutoring?
faqs.answer: Published ranges run from about AED 45 to 150 an hour for generalist online tutoring, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for an independent in-home tutor with travel inside the rate, and AED 200 to 450 or more for specialist IB and IGCSE provision, with premium providers publishing up to AED 650. Those figures come from providers' own pages and Bestimate's Dubai 2026 table rather than from us. For a beginner, the cheapest tier is the poorest value, because sequencing a beginner course is a specific skill.

faqs.question: Why is an in-home hour not the same as an online hour at the same price?
faqs.answer: Because travel is inside the rate. An in-home tutor charging AED 300 is paid for the journey as well as the teaching, and in Dubai a school-run delay or a slow stretch of Sheikh Zayed Road routinely removes twenty minutes from the start of a booked hour. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE, so this is not a sales point against something we sell: in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. In-home does win on presence for a student who disengages easily.

faqs.question: Would a group class work for a beginner in French?
faqs.answer: It can, for a confident student who learns well from hearing others attempt the language, and it costs less per student. It works badly for the three failures that actually sink ab initio students, because pronunciation correction, article discipline and handwriting speed are individual problems that a group hour cannot address one learner at a time. Group provision also produces little individual evidence: class tests rather than marked scripts. As reinforcement beside one-to-one teaching it is useful; as the main provision for a beginner it usually is not.

faqs.question: How much practice should a beginner do between lessons?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to twenty minutes on six days a week beats two hours in one sitting, because vocabulary and verb forms consolidate through frequency rather than duration. The content matters as much as the time: nouns revised with their articles, verb forms said aloud rather than read, and one short piece of writing per fortnight produced without help. Students who only revise before assessments appear to progress and then cannot produce anything unaided, which the fortnightly written task exposes within a month.

faqs.question: Why does the summer between Year 12 and Year 13 matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because it is the only long stretch where nothing competes for the student's attention, and because a beginner language decays faster than any other subject over six idle weeks. Three or four sessions a week across part of the summer consolidates weak topics, builds handwriting speed and lifts listening, producing more progress than any term-time intensive. Slots fill from around March, so it is worth planning in spring. A student who loses that summer effectively starts Year 13 a term behind.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with coursework in another subject if French is the booking?
faqs.answer: A tutor supports the subject they were matched for, and on any assessed component in any subject the rule is the same: teaching, questioning, modelling and feedback on drafts the student has produced, with no text supplied for submission. IB malpractice procedures fall on the student, not the tutor, which is why the boundary is a protection. If a second subject needs support, we match a second specialist rather than stretching one tutor across work they do not teach.

faqs.question: Can we change beginner French tutors partway through the two years?
faqs.answer: Yes, and on a course this long it is better done early than endured. Tell us and we rematch at no charge. A weekly hour a student dreads will not generate the frequency a beginner language depends on, so a poor fit costs more here than it would on a six-week examination block. We would rather make the change in October than find out in March that the lessons took place and very little stuck. If no suitable beginner French specialist is free at your preferred time, we say so rather than filling the slot.

faqs.question: Does the school's report tell me enough about a beginner language?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and not through any fault of the school. Ab initio classes in Dubai Diploma schools are often four or five students, so there are few formal assessments and a termly report reasonably summarises effort and engagement rather than measurable attainment. That is exactly why a tuition plan should generate its own evidence. The two documents together are informative: the school's view of engagement in class, and a marked unaided script showing what the student can actually produce.

intro.heading: What a French ab initio tutor in Dubai costs, and what actually changes the number
paragraphs: Dubai families asking about an IB DP French ab initio tutor almost always ask the price first, and almost never get an answer. Of the agency and platform pages ranking for this kind of search, three publish no figure at all, and two quote in US dollars, a currency no family in Dubai transacts in. So start with the number. Qualified language teachers working online quote roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour in this market. IB-experienced language acquisition specialists sit at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. An in-home visit anywhere in the emirate runs AED 180 to AED 500 an hour once travel is inside the fee, and a small premium tier quotes AED 500 to AED 650. Those are market rates read in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list.

The spread is wide because an hour of French ab initio is not one thing. An hour spent building the first two hundred words of topic vocabulary is a different piece of work from an hour spent marking a written task against the message criterion, and a different piece again from an hour rehearsing a photograph description under the fifteen-minute preparation rule. Tutors price by the hardest thing they are asked to do, which is why a quote for conversation practice and a quote for criterion-referenced marking can differ by AED 150 for the same sixty minutes.

Dubai adds its own pressure on supply. The emirate ran 227 private schools in 2024-25, teaching 387,441 students across 17 different curricula, and IB programmes account for roughly seven per cent of that enrolment. The French-teaching pool is small relative to the francophone and bilingual-stream families who want it, and it empties in the weeks when individual orals are recorded, because every ab initio candidate in the city needs the same fortnight. Price follows that calendar more than it follows anything on a tutor's CV.

Geography is the other half of the bill, and it is the half families underestimate. A tutor driving from Al Barsha to Mirdif at four in the afternoon spends longer in the car than in the lesson, and that time is inside the quote whether it is itemised or not. IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. French ab initio tuition for Dubai is delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time, which means the fee buys teaching and your child's tutor can be the right French ab initio specialist rather than the nearest one.

The rest of this page is the arithmetic in detail: the market bands with their sources, the five factors that move a quote in this emirate, what the four assessment components actually demand, a twenty-four-month budget for a student starting in DP1, what the MoHRE permit costs a tutor, and where tutoring sits against Dubai school fees after KHDA confirmed no fee increase for 2026-27. Every figure carries where it came from, because an unattributed number is worth nothing to a parent deciding how to spend AED 1,200 a month.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-tutor.programmesIntro: French ab initio sits in the final two years of a longer arc. What a Dubai family pays for in DP1 depends heavily on what happened in MYP, so the programme notes below are written around the French-specific handover points rather than as a general tour.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French ab initio is one of the Group 2 language acquisition options and runs at Standard Level only. Over two years a student moves from no French to handling five prescribed themes with twenty topics between them, writing two short tasks under timed conditions, understanding recorded French at ab initio pace, and sustaining a recorded oral of roughly ten minutes built from a photograph.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the ab initio cohort is usually small, sometimes a single class across a year group, which concentrates the teaching on whoever the school can timetable. That is the gap most families are filling when they look for an IB DP French ab initio tutor in Dubai: not a weak teacher, but one teacher covering a wide spread of starting points in one room.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP language acquisition runs in phases rather than levels, and a student can finish Year 11 anywhere from Phase 1 to Phase 4 in French. The phase reached is what decides whether ab initio is the honest choice or whether French B SL is the right course, and it is recorded in the school's own reporting rather than in any external grade.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students move schools and curricula more often than most, and a transfer between a British stream and an IB continuum school mid-MYP frequently breaks the French thread entirely. A student who did two years of Phase 1 French, stopped for a year, then arrived in DP1 is the classic Dubai ab initio candidate, and the first tutoring hours go on finding out what actually survived.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The CP includes a language development requirement rather than a graded Group 2 subject, so a CP student working on French is building a documented portfolio of language development rather than preparing for Paper 1 and Paper 2. The teaching looks different and the evidence requirements are different.
programmes.countryNote: Only a handful of Dubai schools run the CP alongside the Diploma, so families often discover the language development strand late and want help structuring it. Tutoring here is about recording progress credibly for the portfolio, not about command terms, and it is usually a shorter engagement than a two-year ab initio plan.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: PYP schools introduce an additional language from the early years, and in Dubai that is commonly French or Arabic alongside the mandatory Arabic requirement. Nothing at this stage is examined, but a child who reaches Year 6 comfortable reading French aloud arrives in MYP at a phase that keeps French B open later.
programmes.countryNote: For a Dubai parent weighing whether to keep French going through primary, the financial argument is simple: the gap between arriving in DP1 as an ab initio candidate and arriving as a French B candidate is roughly two years of catch-up that nobody has to pay for if the thread is never dropped.

dubai/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-tutor.subjectsIntro: A French ab initio tutor in Dubai is rarely hired in isolation. Families usually have one language problem and one other subject in the same term, so the grid below lists the language acquisition courses we cover alongside the subjects that most often share a timetable with them.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: Five prescribed themes, twenty prescribed topics, four equally weighted components. The teaching load is front-heavy: vocabulary and the present tense in DP1, then text types and past tenses, then oral rehearsal. Marks are lost on text-type conventions far more often than on grammar.

subjects.name: French B
subjects.description: For students with three or more years of French behind them. HL adds two literary works and lengthens every written task, which is why the HL tutoring bill is consistently higher than the SL one. The individual oral is built from a literary extract at HL and a visual stimulus at SL.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: Same four-component structure as French ab initio and the same prescribed theme framework, but a different grammar sequence: Spanish verb morphology arrives earlier and the pronunciation load is lighter, so a Dubai student often reaches comparable written accuracy sooner.

subjects.name: Spanish B
subjects.description: Widely taken in Dubai's IB schools. The listening paper is where this subject bites, because recordings draw on more than one variety of Spanish and a student trained only on peninsular audio stalls on Latin American speakers.

subjects.name: German B
subjects.description: Case endings, verb-final subordinate clauses and the Perfekt-Präteritum choice account for most lost marks in written work. Diagnosing which of the four cases a student is actually guessing at is the first hour of any German B engagement.

subjects.name: Hindi B
subjects.description: Common in Dubai given the size of the Indian-curriculum community. The split is unusual: many candidates speak fluently and read Devanagari slowly, so the tutoring is script and register work rather than conversation.

subjects.name: Mandarin ab initio
subjects.description: The heaviest ab initio option for a late starter because character recognition has to be built from nothing alongside the same four components. Dubai availability is thin, and this is the language where a family most often waits for a match.

subjects.description: Group 1 rather than Group 2, but it shares the oral-assessment season with French ab initio, so the two compete for the same revision weeks in DP2. Families frequently book both and need the sessions sequenced rather than stacked.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The TOK exhibition and essay land in the same DP2 window as the language orals. A tutor here coaches the student's own thinking and gives feedback on their own drafts; the essay must be written by the student.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Dubai private schools must teach Arabic regardless of the licensed curriculum, so a French ab initio candidate is usually carrying Arabic on the same timetable. Knowing that helps when planning which evenings are realistically free.

sections.heading: What the Dubai market charges for IB DP French ab initio
paragraphs: A qualified language teacher working online one-to-one in Dubai quotes AED 150 to AED 300 an hour. An IB-experienced language acquisition specialist quotes AED 200 to AED 450 and above. An in-home visit runs AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel inside the fee. Those bands were read from published provider rate cards and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table in October 2026.

The table below is the thing almost no page in this market publishes. It compares provider models rather than brands, because the model is what determines the rate: a university student doing conversation practice and an IB-experienced teacher marking against the message criterion are selling different work, and a parent comparing them on price alone is comparing the wrong column. Read it with the right-hand column in view, because a rate with no stated source is a rate somebody invented.

Monthly packages are quoted as often as hourly rates in Dubai, and they are where the arithmetic gets slippery. Online packages around AED 799 a month for eight sessions work out near AED 100 an hour, which looks like a bargain until you check the session length and whether written tasks are marked outside the hour. In-home monthly packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions sit near AED 200 an hour with the travel absorbed. Bestimate's own monthly estimates for weekly one-hour tutoring in Dubai run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support.

IB Gram does not publish a price list on these pages, and the honest reason is that the rate depends on the match: subject, level, how far into the two years you are, and whether the tutor is teaching, marking or rehearsing an oral. What we do publish is the market, with sources, so that the quote you receive from anybody can be checked against it. The free trial lesson comes first, one per student, with no card details taken, and the rate is agreed after you have seen the teaching.

sections.heading: Five things that move a French ab initio quote in this emirate
paragraphs: The same tutor, the same hour and the same subject can be quoted AED 180 or AED 380 in Dubai depending on five variables, none of which is quality. Knowing which one is driving your quote is the difference between negotiating and guessing. The table sets out the direction and the typical swing for each.

Native-speaker scarcity is the first. Dubai's francophone teaching pool is sized for the French national curriculum community, not for IB language acquisition, and a native speaker who also knows how Paper 1 is marked is genuinely uncommon. That combination attracts a premium of roughly AED 30 to AED 80 an hour over a well-qualified non-native teacher who marks to the criteria just as accurately. For an ab initio beginner in DP1 the native-speaker premium buys very little; for oral rehearsal in DP2 it buys something real.

The oral recording window is the second and the sharpest. Individual orals are internally conducted and recorded inside a narrow window set by each school, and in Dubai those windows cluster. Every ab initio candidate in the city wants the same four weeks, specialists sell out, and quotes rise AED 20 to AED 60 an hour for late bookings. A family that books oral rehearsal in November pays the ordinary rate; the same family booking in the week the school announces its recording dates pays the scarcity rate.

The remaining three are in your control. Ninety-minute blocks cost less per hour than sixty-minute ones because setup and warm-up happen once rather than twice. Two siblings at a similar stage sharing one block cuts the per-student cost by a quarter to two-fifths, though it only works when both are genuinely at the same point. And starting late is the most expensive decision available: a student beginning in the second term of DP2 needs two or three sessions a week instead of one, at a higher rate, for a worse result than the same money spent eighteen months earlier.
