sections.heading: Paper 2: the core units, the visual stimulus and the infographic trap
paragraphs: Paper 2 covers the three core units in 75 minutes and is worth 40% at Standard Level and 25% at Higher Level. Section A asks structured questions across changing population, global climate, and global resource consumption and security. Section B works from an infographic or visual stimulus. Section C asks for one extended answer from a choice of two. For a Standard Level student this is the single largest component in the subject, which makes it the first place a tutor should look at marked work.

Section A is where easy marks leak. The questions want a definition stated correctly, a figure read accurately from a resource, and a calculation or comparison performed without arithmetic slips. Students who read widely about climate change frequently lose marks here for writing a paragraph where a definition was asked for. The repair is mechanical and quick: a glossary of the course's own terms, drilled, and timed practice at reading values off unfamiliar graphics.

Section B catches almost everyone once. An infographic contains far more information than the question needs, and the instinct is to summarise the graphic. The marks are for using the specific data the question points at, with the course concepts attached. The students who do well here treat the stimulus as a data source to be interrogated rather than a text to be described, and that habit takes two or three timed attempts to build. Section C then follows the same rules as a Paper 1 extended answer, so practice transfers directly between the two papers.
bullets: Section A: definitions and data manipulation across the three core units
Section B: use the data the question points at, do not summarise the graphic
Section C: one 10-mark extended answer, same demands as Paper 1 part B
Largest single component at Standard Level, so review marked work here first

sections.heading: Paper 3 and the Higher Level core extension
paragraphs: Higher Level students sit a third paper of one hour, worth 20%, on the core extension: power, places and networks; human development and diversity; global risks and resilience. Two extended answers are written from a choice of three, each worth 12 marks. Nothing else in Diploma Geography asks for this writing task, and it arrives at the end of DP2 in most schemes of work, which is why it is the least rehearsed component in the subject.

The demand is synthesis. A 12-mark Paper 3 answer is expected to draw on the whole course, so an answer about global risk that uses only the extension material is thin by design. Students who do well have built a small number of cross-cutting examples they can deploy in either paper, and they know the conceptual vocabulary of the extension well enough to use it rather than to define it. Twelve marks also changes the shape: there is room for a genuine counter-position, and the top descriptors expect one.

The practical plan for a Higher Level student in Dubai is to start Paper 3 answers early, even before the extension is fully taught, using course material already covered. Two answers in one hour is tight, and the second answer is routinely rushed. Timing practice therefore comes before polish. A student who can produce two structured 12-mark answers in 60 minutes by February is in a far better position than one who understands the extension deeply in April but has never written to the clock.

sections.heading: The fieldwork internal assessment, criterion by criterion
paragraphs: The fieldwork report is the component where evidence of progress is clearest, because the marks are published by criterion and a draft can be scored against each letter. The report runs to a maximum of 2,500 words and is marked out of 25. No competitor page in this search names a single criterion, let alone its allocation, which is strange given that this is 25% of a Standard Level grade and 20% at Higher Level.

Two criteria carry more than half the marks between them. Criterion C, quality and treatment of information collected, is worth 6 and rewards data that was gathered properly and presented in a form that supports analysis: appropriate graphs, maps that are actually used, data that has been processed rather than dumped. Criterion D, written analysis, is worth 8 and is where most Dubai reports stall, because students describe their results instead of explaining them against the geographic context set up in criterion A.

The small criteria are the cheapest marks in the subject and are routinely thrown away. Criterion E, the conclusion, is worth 2 and must answer the fieldwork question directly, which sounds obvious until you read a conclusion that summarises the method. Criterion F, evaluation, is worth 3 and wants specific, honest limitations with their effect on the findings named, not an apology for the weather. Scoring a draft letter by letter turns a vague instruction to improve into a list of five concrete tasks.

sections.heading: Fieldwork a student can realistically collect in Dubai
paragraphs: Criterion A fails most often because the question needs data that cannot be collected here. That is a solvable problem if it is addressed before any writing happens, and it is the single most useful hour of tutoring in the whole internal assessment. Dubai offers genuinely good primary data for several of the optional themes, and almost none for a few others, and knowing which is which saves a student weeks.

Urban environments is the strongest fit. Land-use mapping and pedestrian counts across the Deira and Al Fahidi transition, environmental quality surveys comparing a planned community with an older district, and microclimate transects along a high-rise street in Dubai Marina all produce data a student can gather in a morning with a clipboard and a phone. Oceans and coastal margins works along the Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim shoreline, where beach profiles and visitor surveys are practical. Extreme environments suits the desert margin near Al Qudra, and resource consumption pairs well with a comparison between The Sustainable City and conventional suburban development.

Three constraints are specific to this emirate and belong in criterion F rather than in a complaint. Heat makes outdoor data collection unsafe between late May and September outside early morning, which compresses the fieldwork window into the first and second terms. Permission matters: questionnaires and photography in commercial districts and private communities need asking first, and a school risk assessment usually governs where a student may go. Ramadan shifts the hours when streets and leisure sites are busy, so footfall data collected during Ramadan and footfall data collected afterwards are not comparable, which is a limitation worth naming explicitly and is exactly the sort of honest, specific evaluation criterion F rewards.

sections.heading: How the Geography grade is assembled, and what to prioritise
paragraphs: The weighting table decides the tutoring plan, and most families never see it. At Standard Level, Paper 2 is the largest component at 40%, Paper 1 is 35% and the fieldwork report is 25%. At Higher Level, Paper 1 stays at 35% while Paper 2 drops to 25%, Paper 3 arrives at 20% and the report falls to 20%. The practical consequence is that a Standard Level and a Higher Level student with the same weaknesses should be taught in a different order.

For a Standard Level student, Paper 2 comes first because it is the biggest share and because Section A marks are the quickest to recover. The fieldwork report comes second, since 25% of the grade is sitting in a document that can be improved against six published criteria at any point before the school's internal deadline. Paper 1 extended-answer technique runs alongside both, because the skill transfers to Paper 2 Section C.

For a Higher Level student the order changes. Paper 1 is the largest single component, and the third optional theme is often the least secure. Paper 3 needs starting earlier than any scheme of work suggests, because it asks for a writing task nothing else in the course rehearses. The report should be finished early rather than optimised late, because its 20% is the easiest 20% to bank. Any tutor you speak to should be able to state this order for your child's level in the first conversation.

sections.heading: Materials, honesty and the permit question in Dubai
paragraphs: Fieldwork creates an academic-honesty situation that essays do not, and it is worth being explicit about. The data must be the student's own collection, the analysis must be their own, and a report that reuses a sibling's data set from a previous cohort is a malpractice matter. Group data collection is normal and allowed where the school organises it, but the processing, analysis and conclusions have to be individual. A tutor may teach how to present and interrogate data, read one draft and score it against the criteria, and give written feedback. A tutor does not supply analysis for a student to insert.

The same line applies to materials. Published IB papers, markschemes and subject guides are cited and linked at their official source rather than reproduced, because copying them is a copyright problem and, for unreleased material, a malpractice exposure. Generative tools can help a student find reading and can check their own grammar; they cannot produce sentences that go into an assessed report. Keeping a short research log makes that defensible if anyone asks, and takes a student about two minutes a week.

On the regulatory side: anyone tutoring privately in the UAE needs the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and granted free of charge for two years. The straightforward thing to do is ask any tutor whether they hold it. Dubai's private schools sit with KHDA, which oversees the quality of private education in the emirate; Abu Dhabi and Al Ain sit with ADEK, Sharjah with SPEA, Ras Al Khaimah with its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah with the federal Ministry of Education. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or endorsement from any of them, or from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and nothing on this page should be read as claiming one.

A photograph of the school's course outline does the job. That information decides which tutors can actually teach the paper your child sits.

process.title: Send one marked piece of work
process.description: An extended answer with the teacher's mark on it, or a Paper 2 Section A set, tells a tutor more in two minutes than a report card does in a term. It shows whether the problem is precision, argument, command terms or content, and the trial lesson can then start on the real issue rather than on diagnosis.

process.title: Take the free trial and watch for marking
process.description: One full session at no cost, no card, no package. The thing to watch is whether the tutor marks your child's own writing during or after the session and names a level descriptor when doing it. A session spent explaining coastal processes is a lecture; a session spent improving a 6 out of 10 answer is teaching.

process.title: Fix the weekly slot and the marking cycle
process.description: A repeating hour in Gulf Standard Time, set around bus times, pick-ups and prayer times, with Ramadan timings shifted so the session does not sit across Iftar. One written piece goes back marked between every session, because that cycle rather than the hour itself is what moves the grade.

process.title: Read the six-week evidence pack together
process.description: Marked extended answers with descriptors, Section A accuracy, the current fieldwork score by criterion letter, and the command-term audit. If the trend is flat after six weeks of consistent work, the plan or the tutor changes. That conversation is scheduled rather than left to a parent to initiate.

None of it waits for a mock paper, which is the point: a mock in February cannot change anything a weekly marked answer could have fixed in October.

whyPoints.description: A question that needs data nobody can collect in Dubai produces a weak report however hard the student works. One session tests the question against what is genuinely gatherable here, including the heat window that closes outdoor collection from late May to September.

faqs.question: How will I know whether Geography tutoring is actually working?
faqs.answer: Ask for four things and they can all be produced within six weeks. A marked 10-mark extended answer with the level descriptor named. A Paper 2 Section A set with accuracy on definitions tracked separately from interpretation. The fieldwork report scored against criteria A to F so you can see which letters moved. And a command-term audit listing the verbs your child can and cannot structure an answer around. A tutor who cannot generate those is relying on your impression instead of evidence, and in a subject marked against published descriptors that is a choice rather than a limitation.

faqs.question: Why does my child know the content but score 6 out of 10 on extended answers?
faqs.answer: Because Diploma Geography pays for argument, not for knowledge. A 10-mark part B answer marked against level descriptors needs a sustained position answering the command term, with specific places and figures used as evidence. An answer that describes three coastal management strategies accurately cannot reach the top band when the question asked you to examine a view. The fix is a 30-second plan: a line of argument, two named places, and a decision about what the final paragraph concludes. Students resist planning because it feels like lost writing time, so it is practised against the clock until it stops feeling optional.

faqs.question: How many marks is the Geography fieldwork report worth, and how are they split?
faqs.answer: The report is out of 25 and runs to a maximum of 2,500 words, worth 25% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher Level. The marks split across six criteria: 3 for the fieldwork question and geographic context, 3 for methods, 6 for quality and treatment of information collected, 8 for written analysis, 2 for the conclusion, 3 for evaluation. Analysis and data treatment hold more than half the total between them, which is why a report with excellent data and descriptive analysis stalls in the middle. Scoring a draft letter by letter produces a short, concrete task list.

faqs.question: What fieldwork can a Dubai student realistically collect primary data for?
faqs.answer: Urban environments is the strongest fit: land-use mapping and pedestrian counts across the Deira and Al Fahidi transition, environmental quality surveys comparing a planned community with an older district, and microclimate transects along a Dubai Marina street. Oceans and coastal margins works along the Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim shoreline through beach profiles and visitor surveys. Extreme environments suits the desert margin near Al Qudra. Resource consumption pairs well with The Sustainable City against conventional suburban development. Test the question against collectable data before writing anything, because criterion A fails most often for this reason.

faqs.question: Does the Dubai heat affect when fieldwork has to be done?
faqs.answer: Significantly. Outdoor data collection between late May and September is unsafe outside the early morning, which compresses the practical fieldwork window into the first and second terms. Families who leave the internal assessment until DP2's summer discover there is no window left. Heat also belongs in criterion F rather than in a complaint: if a pedestrian count was taken at 7am because midday was unusable, say so and explain what that does to the validity of the comparison. Specific limitations with their effect on the findings named is exactly what the evaluation criterion credits.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the fieldwork report without crossing the IB's rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, inside a clear boundary. A tutor may test whether the question is answerable with collectable data, teach which sampling methods criterion B credits, show how to process and present data so criterion C is satisfied, read one draft and score it against all six criteria with reasons. A tutor may not supply analysis, provide a data set, or hand over text for the report. Collecting data with the class is normal and allowed where the school organises it; the processing, analysis and conclusions must be the student's own. Reusing a previous cohort's data is a malpractice matter.

faqs.question: Which paper should a Standard Level Geography student work on first?
faqs.answer: Paper 2. At Standard Level it is the largest component at 40%, covering the three core units in 75 minutes, and its Section A marks are the quickest in the subject to recover because they turn on definitions and accurate data reading rather than on argument. The fieldwork report comes second, since 25% of the grade sits in a document that can be improved against published criteria at any time before the school's internal deadline. Paper 1 extended-answer technique runs alongside both, because the same skill is examined in Paper 2 Section C.

faqs.question: Why is Paper 3 the component Higher Level students are least ready for?
faqs.answer: Because it comes last and asks for a writing task nothing else rehearses. Paper 3 is one hour, two answers from a choice of three, 12 marks each, on the core extension, worth 20% of the Higher Level grade. Twelve marks leaves room for a genuine counter-position and the top descriptors expect one, which is a different shape from a 10-mark Paper 1 answer. Most schemes of work teach the extension in DP2, so students meet it weeks before the session. Starting timed practice in term one, using course material already covered, is the single most effective adjustment.

faqs.question: What is the infographic question on Paper 2 and why do students lose marks on it?
faqs.answer: Section B works from an infographic or visual stimulus and contains far more information than the question needs. The instinct is to summarise the graphic, and the marks are for using the specific data the question points at with course concepts attached. Students who do well treat it as a data source to interrogate rather than a text to describe. It takes two or three timed attempts to build the habit, which is why it appears regularly in weekly practice rather than once before the mock. Accuracy in reading values off unfamiliar graphics is the underlying skill.

faqs.question: My child's Geography class in Dubai has only six students. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It cuts both ways. A small group means more teacher attention and usually better fieldwork supervision. It also removes the informal benchmarking most students rely on: with six scripts in the room, a student has no idea whether a 6 out of 10 is the class norm or the class ceiling. That is a real argument for marked work from outside the school, because it supplies a comparison against published descriptors instead of against five classmates. Small Diploma Geography groups are common in Dubai, where the IB accounts for 7 per cent of private-school enrolment.

faqs.question: Should my child choose Diploma Geography or A Level Geography?
faqs.answer: Several Dubai schools offer both, and the assessment difference should be seen before the choice is made. Diploma Geography requires a 2,500-word fieldwork report marked against six criteria, examines three core units plus optional themes, and at Higher Level adds a synthesis paper. A Levels concentrate more weight in terminal written papers. A student who writes well under time pressure and dislikes extended coursework may suit one route; a student who works steadily across two years and collects data carefully may suit the other. Ask the school for the component weightings of both.

faqs.question: How do command terms change the way an answer should be written?
faqs.answer: They change the structure, not the content. Examine wants the strengths and limitations of a view set against each other. Evaluate wants a judgement supported by criteria you have named. Discuss wants a balanced treatment that still arrives somewhere. Suggest wants plausible reasoning rather than certainty. Justify wants a choice defended against alternatives. Most mid-band answers are correct content answering the wrong verb, which is why an audit of the terms a student can and cannot handle is kept and updated. Examine and evaluate are usually the last two to come off that list.

faqs.question: Can Geography sessions work around a Dubai school bus timetable?
faqs.answer: Yes, and more easily than in-home tutoring allows because nobody is travelling. Apartment households in Dubai Marina, Business Bay and Jumeirah Lakes Towers usually settle on 7pm to 9pm once a parent is back. Villa communities such as Arabian Ranches and Dubai Hills often take a weekend morning, which suits timed paper practice far better than a weekday evening. Families in Mirdif, Al Warqa and International City gain most from online delivery, because their school runs are long and in-home rates in this market price the tutor's travel into the hour.

faqs.question: Does a Geography tutor in the UAE need a licence from a regulator?
faqs.answer: A tutor needs the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. A tutoring business with premises in Dubai is different again and needs an educational services permit from KHDA. IB Gram holds no approval or endorsement from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and no page here should suggest otherwise.

faqs.question: What if the Geography marks stay flat after six weeks of tutoring?
faqs.answer: Then something changes, and the conversation is scheduled rather than left to you to start. Flat extended-answer marks after six weeks of consistent marked work usually means one of three things: the feedback is not specific enough to act on, the student is not writing between sessions, or the match is wrong for this subject. All three are visible in the evidence pack. A different tutor is offered rather than argued about, and the fieldwork score by criterion letter usually shows which of the three it is before anyone has to guess.

The school's Diploma Geography course outline, so a tutor can be matched to the optional themes your child actually sits, and one marked extended answer, so the first session starts on the real weakness instead of a diagnosis. Say whether your child is at Standard or Higher Level, where the fieldwork report has reached, and which hours work in Gulf Standard Time. You get a proposed tutor, a rate in AED per 60 minutes with marking stated as included, and one free trial lesson with no card attached. Six weeks later you read the evidence pack and decide whether it is working.

intro.heading: Geography is the Diploma subject most Dubai students underestimate
paragraphs: Geography looks like the safe Group 3 choice. It has maps, it has case studies, and it does not demand the essay stamina of History or the abstraction of Philosophy. Then DP1 students meet the command terms. A question that says examine wants a different answer from one that says evaluate, and a student who writes a well-informed description when the paper asked for a judgement forfeits most of the marks on offer. That gap between knowing the content and answering the question is where nearly every lost mark in this subject sits.

The second surprise is the fieldwork. Geography's internal assessment is a 2,500-word report built on data the student gathered themselves, worth a quarter of the Standard Level grade and a fifth at Higher Level. It is read against six criteria, lettered A to F, and the marks are not spread evenly across them. Written analysis carries eight of the twenty-five marks on its own. A student who spends three weekends perfecting a questionnaire and then produces four thin paragraphs of analysis has optimised the wrong criterion, and no amount of neat graphing recovers it.

Dubai adds its own texture. Schools here teach different option themes depending on who is in the department, so two candidates at IB schools ten minutes apart may sit completely different Paper 1s. A family moving from a school that taught Freshwater and Urban Environments to one teaching Geophysical Hazards and Extreme Environments has a real content gap to close, not a style adjustment. Fieldwork is also harder to arrange in a city where much of the accessible landscape is engineered, which pushes students towards human geography enquiries they have not thought through.

An IB DP geography online tutor in Dubai earns their hour because this work is diagnosable. A marked Paper 2 answer shows within minutes whether the problem is content recall, data-response technique or command-term reading. A fieldwork proposal shows whether the question can be answered with the data the student can realistically collect on a Friday morning. Both are fixable in a handful of sessions, and neither needs anyone sitting in the same room as the student. What is not fixable in a handful of sessions is a fieldwork report discovered three weeks before the school's internal upload deadline, which is why the calendar matters here more than the hours.

That is why delivery here is online and one-to-one, over live video, on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. The trade is deliberate. Instead of whichever Geography teacher happens to live within a twenty-minute drive of Al Barsha, a Dubai student works with someone who has taught the specific option themes printed on their paper and has supervised fieldwork reports to a submission deadline before.

dubai/ib-dp-geography-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Geography sits at the end of a pathway, and Dubai students reach DP Geography from two very different places: MYP Individuals and Societies, or a Cambridge or Edexcel IGCSE Geography course. The two entry points leave different gaps. Here are the IB programmes Dubai schools run, and what each one means for a student heading towards Diploma Geography.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is inquiry-led rather than subject-led, but the habits that decide a Geography grade start here: reading a map, describing a place without listing it, noticing that a pattern needs an explanation. Students complete the exhibition in their final PYP year, which is the first time most of them design a question and gather evidence for it themselves.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai runs a large number of PYP primaries, several of them feeding directly into a Diploma school on the same campus. Where a family changes school at Year 7 the transition is usually smooth on content and rough on independence, because PYP students arrive used to choosing their own enquiry and MYP Individuals and Societies narrows that quickly.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Individuals and Societies in the MYP is assessed against four criteria: knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Those four are a reasonable rehearsal for Diploma Geography because they separate knowing a case study from using it. The MYP personal project in Year 11 is also the last piece of independent research a student does before the fieldwork report.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run MYP to Year 11 and then put students straight into the Diploma, skipping IGCSE entirely. Those students arrive at DP Geography with strong enquiry skills and no experience of a timed, externally marked paper. The first thing a tutor usually does with an ex-MYP student in Dubai is run a one-hour Paper 2 under exam conditions to show them what the clock does.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Geography in the Diploma is a core of three compulsory units plus a menu of seven option themes, of which Standard Level candidates study two and Higher Level three. Higher Level adds a core extension on power, places, networks, human development and global risk, examined in its own paper. Everyone writes the fieldwork report, and everyone sits the data-response and infographic questions on Paper 2.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma cohorts are unusually mobile, and Geography is the subject where mobility costs most, because option themes do not transfer. A student arriving in DP2 from a school in Singapore or London may find that two of their three taught themes are not on their new school's Paper 1 at all. That is the single most common reason a Dubai family looks for Geography support mid-course.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme pairs at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project and a personal and professional skills course. A CP student can take Geography as one of those Diploma courses, sitting the same papers and writing the same fieldwork report as a full Diploma candidate.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is thinly represented in Dubai compared with the full Diploma, so a CP student taking Geography is often the only one in their year doing it. Support for those students usually looks less like revision and more like someone to check that the fieldwork question and the reflective project are not quietly duplicating each other, which the school may not be watching for.

dubai/ib-dp-geography-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Geography is not one syllabus; it is a compulsory core plus a menu. What appears on your child's Paper 1 depends entirely on which option themes the department chose to teach. Below are the units and themes a Diploma Geography tutor works across, with what each one assesses and where its marks usually go missing.

subjects.name: Changing Population
subjects.description: Population distribution, megacity growth, the demographic dividend, ageing, forced migration and gender inequality indices. Marks are lost on scale: students describe global patterns when the question asked about one named country, or quote a dependency ratio without saying what it implies for policy.

subjects.name: Global Climate: Vulnerability and Resilience
subjects.description: The energy balance, atmospheric circulation, the causes and consequences of warming, and the civil-society and government responses to it. The technical half is where marks go. Students who cannot explain albedo or the enhanced greenhouse effect mechanically end up writing opinion where the paper wanted physics.

subjects.name: Global Resource Consumption and Security
subjects.description: Changing consumption of water, land and energy, the nexus between them, recycling, waste and resource stewardship. This unit rewards a student with two or three sharp, current examples and punishes one with a general sense that consumption is rising. Figures need a year attached to them.

subjects.name: Option A: Freshwater, Drainage Basins
subjects.description: Hydrographs, river processes and landforms, flood prediction, dams and integrated basin management. The diagrams are the marks here: a labelled storm hydrograph with lag time identified answers in thirty seconds what three paragraphs of prose does badly.

subjects.name: Option B: Oceans and Coastal Margins
subjects.description: Ocean currents and nutrient flows, coastal processes and landforms, sea-level change, fisheries, and conflict over marine territory. Coastal management questions are a reliable source of marks for a Dubai student, who can see hard engineering from almost any beach in the emirate.

subjects.name: Option C: Extreme Environments
subjects.description: Hot arid, semi-arid, periglacial and high-mountain environments, their processes, their human use and their management. Students lose marks by treating deserts as empty. The syllabus wants the opportunities and risks of extreme environments as places people live and work.

subjects.name: Option D: Geophysical Hazards
subjects.description: Plate margins, earthquakes, volcanoes, mass movement, hazard risk, vulnerability and the disaster-response cycle. The common failure is writing the event rather than the hazard: a narrative of a named earthquake earns far less than an analysis of why the same magnitude killed different numbers of people in two places.

subjects.name: Option E: Leisure, Tourism and Sport
subjects.description: Participation, sphere of influence, tourism and sport as development strategies, carrying capacity and the sustainability of mega-events. A theme where Dubai students have unusually good primary knowledge and unusually weak discipline about turning it into an evaluated argument.

subjects.name: Option F: The Geography of Food and Health
subjects.description: Food systems, the spatial pattern of calorie intake, disease diffusion, barriers to health, and the role of international agencies. Disease diffusion diagrams and the epidemiological transition model are the two things students most often cannot draw under time pressure.

subjects.name: Option G: Urban Environments
subjects.description: Urban growth, land use, social deprivation, the urban microclimate and resilience planning. The microclimate content is worth rehearsing properly because the urban heat island is one of the few topics examined with both a diagram and a mechanism.

subjects.name: HL Core Extension: Power, Places and Networks
subjects.description: Global interactions, flows of people, capital and data, multi-governmental organisations, and the measurement of globalisation. Examined on Paper 3 as an extended answer, which means structure carries as much weight as content: the question wants a position defended, not a survey.

subjects.name: HL Core Extension: Global Risks and Resilience
subjects.description: Geopolitical and economic risk, the threats from global flows, the role of civil society and the possibilities for resilience and adaptation. Students who revise this as a list of problems struggle on Paper 3, where almost every question asks them to weigh responses against each other.

subjects.name: Fieldwork and the Internal Assessment
subjects.description: A 2,500-word report on primary data the student collected, marked out of 25 against criteria A to F. The written analysis criterion alone carries eight marks. Most of the achievable gain in Geography sits in this one document, because it is the only component a student can still improve after the content is taught.

dubai/ib-dp-geography-online-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Dubai changes two practical things: when a session can start after the school run, and what primary data is within reach for the fieldwork report. Both matter more in Geography than in any other Group 3 subject. These are the parts of the emirate the question comes from most often.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: The accessible coastline for anyone attempting Option B fieldwork. Beach profiles, groyne fields and sediment accumulation are all measurable from the public beaches here with a tape and a clinometer, which makes a coastal enquiry genuinely viable rather than aspirational.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate and Al Barsha South
regions.note: New-build, planned, and therefore ideal for an Urban Environments land-use transect: a student can walk from villa plots through mid-rise to a mall catchment in under an hour. Sessions here usually start at five, after a school run that rarely exceeds twenty minutes.

regions.name: Deira and Al Ras
regions.note: The oldest continuously used urban fabric in the emirate, with souk land use, abra crossings and pedestrian densities that no planned district replicates. Dense enough for a defensible footfall count, and close enough to the Creek for a water-use or informal-economy enquiry.

regions.name: Ras Al Khor and Nad Al Sheba
regions.note: The wildlife sanctuary at Ras Al Khor is one of very few places in Dubai where a student can look at a protected wetland against an advancing urban edge. Access is restricted and must be arranged through the school, so this needs planning a term ahead, not a weekend.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Lakes Towers
regions.note: Extreme vertical density, which makes the urban heat island and street-canyon microclimate measurable with a thermometer and an anemometer at fixed points through a day. Families here often need a later slot because evening traffic on the Marina loop is unpredictable.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Established villa suburbs with long school runs towards Festival City and Nad Al Sheba. Students in this band often cannot start before half past five, which is why their Geography sessions tend to be ninety minutes once a week rather than two shorter ones.

regions.name: Hatta
regions.note: The only relief landscape inside the emirate's boundary, with wadi channel forms, scree slopes and a reservoir. Far enough from the city that it is a planned school trip rather than an afternoon, but the one place a Dubai student can collect genuine physical geography data.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Dubai Industrial City
regions.note: Industrial and warehousing land use, with labour accommodation alongside it. A difficult but high-ceiling setting for a Changing Population or resource-consumption enquiry, provided the ethics of surveying residents are handled through the school rather than independently.

schoolClusters.city: Emirates Hills, Al Barsha and Dubai Hills
schoolClusters.note: The densest band of IB Diploma provision in Dubai, and the one where Geography is most reliably offered with three option themes at Higher Level. Families in this band usually ask for support on Paper 1 depth rather than on fieldwork, because the departments here tend to run a structured fieldwork programme already.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Nad Al Sheba and the Festival City corridor
schoolClusters.note: A band where Diploma cohorts are smaller and option themes are therefore driven by whoever teaches Geography that year. Families here more often need help closing a theme gap after a transfer, and more often need a tutor who will supervise the fieldwork report from question to submission.

schoolClusters.city: Umm Suqeim, Al Jaddaf and the inland Dubailand schools
schoolClusters.note: A mixed band, with some Diploma schools running Geography only at Standard Level. That matters: a student who wants Higher Level Geography for a planning or environmental-science degree may need to take it as an external candidate or change school, and that decision is worth modelling early.

dubai/ib-dp-geography-online-tutor.modesIntro: Geography support splits cleanly into three jobs: teaching option-theme content a student has missed, supervising the fieldwork report, and converting content knowledge into marks under a clock. They need different session shapes, and mixing them in one weekly hour is why some families feel a year of tutoring changed nothing.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one across the two Diploma years
modes.description: A single ninety-minute session each week, live over video, following the school's scheme of work about a fortnight behind so the tutor is consolidating rather than pre-teaching. Content gaps get closed as they appear instead of accumulating into a DP2 crisis. This is the shape most Dubai families use when they start in DP1.
bullets: Session recorded and shared, so revision does not depend on notes taken live

modes.title: Fieldwork supervision block
modes.description: Four to six sessions concentrated around the internal assessment: narrowing the question until it can be answered, choosing methods that produce analysable data, sanity-checking the sampling, then reading the student's own draft against criteria C, D and F. The tutor comments; the student rewrites. Nobody supplies text.

modes.title: Paper-focused sprint before the May session
modes.description: Six to ten sessions in the final term, built entirely around timed answers. No new content unless a diagnostic finds a hole. The work is command-term discipline, case-study recall under pressure, and for Higher Level candidates the structure of a fifteen-mark Paper 3 answer, which is the component most students have never written to time.

modes.title: Option-theme catch-up after a school transfer
modes.description: A short, intense block for the student who has arrived in Dubai mid-Diploma and discovered that one or two of the themes on their new Paper 1 were never taught to them. Typically two sessions a week for six to eight weeks, which is roughly what one option theme takes from nothing to examinable.

sections.heading: What an IB DP Geography online tutor in Dubai actually works on
paragraphs: A Dubai family searching for an IB DP geography online tutor is almost always solving one of four problems: a theme the school never taught, a fieldwork report drifting towards a deadline, a student whose essays describe rather than judge, or a Higher Level candidate who has never written a Paper 3 answer to time. Each has a different fix, and the first session should establish which one you have rather than starting to teach.

The diagnostic is cheap and specific. Give the student one past Paper 2 data-response question and one fifteen-mark essay from a taught theme, under time, and the marking tells you nearly everything. Blank recall means content. A full answer that misses the command term means technique. Good content and a thin conclusion means structure. A student who runs out of time at question three has a planning problem, not a knowledge problem, and six months of content revision will not touch it.

After that, the work is ordinary and unglamorous. Themes taught in syllabus order with their diagrams drilled. Case studies cut down to a named place, a date, two figures and one evaluation point. Command terms practised until the student can tell you what examine obliges them to do differently from evaluate. For most Dubai candidates the whole programme is between twenty and forty hours spread across eighteen months, not a heroic sprint in April. The hours are also front-loaded in a way parents rarely expect, because the fieldwork chain begins in DP1 and the papers can wait.
bullets: A content gap shows up as blank recall, not as a weak argument
A technique gap shows up as a complete answer that scores badly
A structure gap shows up in the last paragraph of a fifteen-mark essay
A timing gap shows up as an unfinished paper, and is fixed in two sessions

sections.heading: The assessment structure, component by component
paragraphs: Geography is examined in two papers at Standard Level and three at Higher Level, plus the internally assessed fieldwork report that both levels write. The split matters when you are deciding where to spend tutoring hours. At Standard Level the core units on Paper 2 carry the largest single share of the grade, which makes the compulsory content the priority. At Higher Level the weight shifts outwards: Paper 1 and the two extra components between them account for most of the available marks.

The practical consequence is that Higher Level and Standard Level students need different tutoring plans even inside the same family. A Standard Level candidate who is strong on their two option themes and weak on climate mechanisms should be spending almost every hour on Paper 2. A Higher Level candidate in the same position has three themes to hold and a separate Paper 3 to learn to structure, and will usually need their hours split between Paper 1 breadth and Paper 3 technique.

Weightings and durations shift between syllabus revisions, and the version your child is examined on is the one their school registered them for. Ask the Geography department for the subject guide they are teaching, or ask the IB coordinator directly. A tutor working from last cycle's structure will teach competently towards the wrong paper, and that is one of the few errors that is genuinely expensive. The subject guide also lists the command terms and the assessment objectives, which is the document a tutor should be planning from rather than a textbook.

sections.heading: The six criteria on the fieldwork report, and what each one is worth
paragraphs: The Geography fieldwork report is marked out of twenty-five against six criteria, lettered A to F, and the marks are deliberately lopsided. Written analysis is worth eight on its own; the conclusion is worth two. Students almost universally invert this, pouring effort into data collection and presentation because those feel like work, and treating the analysis as a commentary on the graphs they have already drawn. That inversion is the single largest avoidable loss in the subject.

Reading the criteria as a budget changes behaviour immediately. If analysis carries eight marks, the report needs analysis that does something: links a pattern to a process, explains an anomaly, tests the result against the theory named in criterion A. If the method criterion carries three, a four-page account of how the questionnaire was designed is three marks of work occupying ten marks of space, and the word ceiling of 2,500 makes that space expensive.

Criterion letters and their mark allocations are published in the subject guide your school holds, and they do change between syllabus cycles. Use the table below as the shape of the problem and verify the exact numbers against the guide. What does not change is the ordering: the analytical criteria dominate, and a report that is beautifully presented and analytically thin will land in the middle band however much time went into it. Ask the department for the criteria sheet they mark against, and read it with your child before the question is settled rather than after the data is collected.

table.caption: GEOGRAPHY FIELDWORK REPORT - THE SHAPE OF THE MARK SCHEME AND THE USUAL FAILURE
columns: Where the mark is usually lost
rows: A - Fieldwork question and geographic context
A question narrow enough to answer, in a located real place, tied to a named theory or model
A question so broad that no data set could resolve it, and no theory named at all
B - Method(s) of investigation

Describing what was done without ever saying why that method suits this question

sections.heading: Where Dubai Geography candidates actually lose marks
paragraphs: Command terms first. The Diploma publishes a list of them and examiners apply it literally. Describe asks for a pattern. Explain asks for a mechanism. Examine asks for an argument with its assumptions exposed. Evaluate and discuss ask for a judgement, supported and weighed. A student who treats all five as invitations to write what they know will score respectably on description-led questions and badly on everything worth more than six marks, and the pattern is visible in a single marked paper.

Second, stale case studies. Geography is the Group 3 subject where currency is marked. A migration case study resting on 2011 figures, or a resource-security example that predates the last five years of water policy, reads as a student quoting their teacher's old slides. Three or four well-dated examples per theme, each with a year, a figure and a named place, outperform a dozen vague ones. This is a mechanical fix and a fast one.

Third, data response. Paper 2 opens with resources: an infographic, a map, a graph, a short text. Marks go to candidates who quote the resource precisely, use its units, and notice what it does not show. Dubai students who have been taught in discussion-heavy classrooms are often strong on interpretation and weak on this discipline of citing the figure in front of them, and that costs a handful of marks on every paper they sit. Fourth, and smallest, is diagram accuracy: an unlabelled axis or a hydrograph without lag time marked throws away marks that required no additional knowledge at all.

sections.heading: Fieldwork in a city built largely on reclaimed land
paragraphs: Dubai makes physical geography fieldwork genuinely difficult. Rivers are absent, most of the coastline is engineered, and the parts of the landscape that would support a geomorphology enquiry sit either inside protected areas or an hour away at Hatta. Students who set out to study natural coastal processes on a nourished beach usually discover halfway through that the variable they are measuring is a management decision rather than a process, and the report then has to argue that instead.

The workable enquiries here are mostly human, and the city is unusually good for them. Land-use transects work because districts change character over a few hundred metres. Urban microclimate work is rewarding because the contrast between a Marina street canyon and an open plot in Al Barsha South is large enough to measure with ordinary instruments. Footfall, sphere of influence and mall catchment studies produce clean data. Each of those maps onto a named option theme, which criterion A requires.

What a tutor adds at this stage is realism about logistics rather than geography. Surveying residents needs the school's involvement and a clear purpose, not an independent student with a clipboard. Access to Ras Al Khor is restricted. Outdoor measurement between May and September is limited by heat for most of the day, which pushes data collection into the cooler months and therefore into the same term as everything else. Planning around that is most of the difference between a report that gets written and one that gets abandoned.

sections.heading: The Diploma Geography deadline chain, counted backwards
paragraphs: Dubai schools sit the May session, and the May session is not when Geography is decided. The fieldwork report is finished and uploaded months earlier, and the single round of written feedback a student is permitted on a draft falls even earlier than that. Families who start looking for help in February are usually past the point where the largest single block of marks in the subject can still be influenced, which is a timing problem rather than a quality one.

The table below counts the chain backwards in relative windows rather than dates. That is deliberate. Exact IB session and results dates are published by the IB and revised from time to time, and the version that applies to your child is the one their coordinator holds; we do not restate them here. Cambridge and Pearson publish their own series dates directly, and those are the ones to check if your child is also sitting an international GCSE or A Level alongside the Diploma.

Read the chain against your child's own school calendar, because internal deadlines are always earlier than the IB's. A Dubai department that wants fieldwork reports submitted before the winter break has effectively moved the entire chain forward by two months, and the student who planned against the official upload date will be late. Ask for the department's internal dates in writing at the start of DP1 and work back from those. Put them in a shared calendar with the mock session marked, because the mocks and the fieldwork deadline frequently land in the same fortnight at Dubai schools.

sections.heading: Academic honesty on a report built from the student's own data
paragraphs: The fieldwork report is assessed work, and the rules around it are strict and worth knowing before a tutor is hired. A student is entitled to one round of written feedback on one draft. Comments may point at a criterion, note that an argument is unsupported, or ask why a graph was chosen. What is not allowed is anyone else supplying sentences, restructuring paragraphs on the student's behalf, or returning a marked-up version that only needs accepting.

The line is easier to hold than it sounds, because it maps onto good teaching anyway. A useful comment on a thin analysis section says that criterion D rewards explanation and this paragraph only describes. An unhelpful one rewrites the paragraph. Ask any prospective tutor directly how they handle a draft, and be wary of an answer that involves editing. Services in this market do sell completed coursework; for the student that is a malpractice finding, and the consequences fall on them, not on the seller.

The same applies to data. Numbers must come from the fieldwork the student actually did, and secondary material must be cited where it is used. A report that quietly borrows a classmate's transect data, or reuses figures from a published study as though they were collected, fails on integrity rather than on geography. A tutor's most valuable contribution here is often to say early that a data set is too thin and that another morning of collection is needed, rather than helping to dress it up later.

sections.heading: KHDA, your school's Geography department and what an inspection report tells you
paragraphs: Private schools in Dubai are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Inspection reports are published and readable, and they are more useful to a Geography parent than any league table, because they comment on teaching quality by phase and subject group rather than on headline results. A report that praises inquiry and criticises assessment literacy tells you precisely what a tutor should be doing.

What an inspection band does not tell you is whether the Geography department is strong. A school rated highly overall may have a single Geography teacher covering both Diploma years and all three option themes at Higher Level, which is a workload rather than a failing but has consequences for how much individual feedback a candidate receives. Ask the department two questions: which option themes are taught this cycle, and how many rounds of written feedback the fieldwork report gets internally.

Dubai's private school sector is also growing, which affects staffing. KHDA has reported that the 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four of them UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six schools opened in 2025-26 and enrolment rose six per cent. Rapid expansion moves experienced Diploma teachers between schools, and a change of Geography teacher between DP1 and DP2 is one of the more common reasons a family starts looking for outside support.

sections.heading: Online one-to-one against an in-home Geography tutor in Dubai
paragraphs: Families ask for a home tutor because they want someone in the room, and that instinct is reasonable for a nine-year-old who needs supervision. For a seventeen-year-old sitting Diploma Geography it matters much less than who the tutor is. The binding constraint on an in-home arrangement in Dubai is geography itself: the pool shrinks to people willing to drive to your district at the hour you want, and option-theme specialists are not evenly distributed across the emirate.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Lessons for Dubai families are delivered live, one-to-one, over video, and home visits remain a service we run only in India. Said plainly so there is no ambiguity before anyone books. What that buys is selection: the tutor is chosen because they have taught Geophysical Hazards and Urban Environments and supervised fieldwork reports, not because they live fifteen minutes from Dubai Hills.

The subject also happens to suit a screen unusually well. Geography is taught through maps, hydrographs, climate graphs, transect data and spreadsheets, and all of those are easier to work on shared than passed across a table. An annotated storm hydrograph built live on a shared screen, saved and sent, is better revision material than the same diagram drawn once in a notebook. The comparison below is the honest version, including where in-home genuinely wins. Read the last row first if your child is the sort who closes the laptop the moment an adult leaves the room, because that is a supervision problem and no delivery format solves it.

process.title: Tell us the themes, not just the subject
process.description: The first message that helps says which option themes the school teaches, whether the candidate is Higher or Standard Level, and where the fieldwork report has got to. Geography support is only as good as that information, because a tutor who has taught Freshwater and Urban Environments is the wrong match for a Paper 1 on Extreme Environments and Food and Health.

process.title: A diagnostic hour, marked honestly
process.description: The free first lesson is a diagnostic, not a sales call: one data-response question, one fifteen-mark essay from a taught theme, both under time. You get the marks and a written read on whether the problem is content, command terms, structure or timing. One free lesson per student, with no card details taken and nothing to cancel.

process.title: Agree the plan and the measure
process.description: Before any paid hour, we agree what the block is for and how you will know whether it worked: themes examinable by a date, a fieldwork report through its draft round, a Paper 3 structure that holds under time. Hours without a measure are how families end up a year in with nothing they can point at.

process.title: Weekly sessions with marked work between them
process.description: Each session ends with something to produce and the next one starts with it marked. A Geography hour spent talking about a theme is pleasant and nearly useless; an hour spent on a marked answer with the mark scheme open is where movement comes from. Recordings are shared so revision does not depend on live note-taking.

process.title: Reassess at each milestone
process.description: At the fieldwork submission, at the mock session, and six weeks before the exam window, the plan gets rebuilt from fresh marked evidence rather than from momentum. Sometimes that means stopping. A student who is reliably hitting the top band on both papers does not need the hour, and we will say so.

process.title: Change the tutor if the fit is wrong
process.description: A different tutor costs nothing and does not need a reason beyond it not working. Geography matters here more than in most subjects because the match is to specific themes and a specific fieldwork context; a tutor who is excellent on physical geography may be the wrong person for an urban enquiry, and that is a matching error rather than a quality one.

whyPoints.title: Matched to your Paper 1, not to your postcode
whyPoints.description: Option themes vary school by school in Dubai, so a Geography tutor is only useful if they have taught the themes on your child's paper. Online delivery is what makes that selection possible: the search is across people who have taught Geophysical Hazards, rather than across people who can drive to Mirdif by five.

whyPoints.title: The fieldwork report treated as the main event
whyPoints.description: A quarter of the Standard Level grade sits in one 2,500-word document, and it is the component a student can still move after the content is taught. We plan backwards from it, supervise the question before the data is collected, and read the draft against the criteria once, which is what the rules allow.

whyPoints.title: Command terms drilled, not mentioned
whyPoints.description: Most Geography marks are lost to a student answering a question the paper did not ask. That is trainable and it is trained here explicitly, with marked answers and the published command-term list open, until the difference between examine and evaluate changes what the student writes rather than what they can recite.

whyPoints.title: Case studies with a year and a figure attached
whyPoints.description: Examiners reward currency and specificity. Sessions include rebuilding the student's case-study bank as one sheet per theme, each example carrying a named place, a date and at least one number, because that is the form that survives exam pressure and the form that scores.

whyPoints.title: Honesty about what a tutor may touch
whyPoints.description: The fieldwork report must be the student's own work, and we say what that means before you book: one round of comments on one draft, pointed at criteria, with no sentences supplied and no restructuring done for them. Services in this market sell completed coursework. The risk of that lands on the student.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated plainly before you pay
whyPoints.description: Lessons for UAE families are live, one-to-one and online, on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. That is written on every page rather than discovered after a deposit, and the comparison table above sets out what the trade actually costs and buys.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP Geography tutor in Dubai do in the first session?
faqs.answer: Diagnoses, mostly. A useful first hour puts the student in front of one data-response question and one fifteen-mark essay from a theme their school has already taught, both timed, and then marks them with the criteria open. That tells you whether the problem is missing content, misread command terms, weak essay structure or simply running out of time, and those four need completely different plans. You should finish the session with marks, a written read on which of the four you have, and an estimate of hours. If the first session is mostly introductions and a description of the course, you have learned nothing you did not already know.

faqs.question: How much of the IB Geography grade comes from the fieldwork report?
faqs.answer: Roughly a quarter at Standard Level and roughly a fifth at Higher Level, which makes it the largest single block of marks a student can still influence once teaching is under way. The exact share is published in the subject guide your school holds and shifts between syllabus cycles, so confirm it with the IB coordinator. The practical point stands either way: this is one 2,500-word document, written months before the exams, marked against six criteria, and it is the component where good supervision changes the most. Families who treat it as homework and the papers as the real assessment have the priority backwards.

faqs.question: How long is the Geography internal assessment allowed to be?
faqs.answer: Two thousand five hundred words. The limit is firm and it is the reason so many reports score poorly on analysis: by the time a student has described their methods in detail and walked through each graph in turn, there is no room left for the criterion that carries the most marks. Treat the word count as a budget allocated by criterion rather than as a target to fill. Tables, labels on diagrams and the bibliography sit outside the count in most years, but check the current guide, because exactly what is excluded has changed before and schools apply it strictly.

faqs.question: My child changed school in Dubai and the Geography themes are different. Is that serious?
faqs.answer: It is the most common genuine emergency in this subject, and it is fixable. Option themes are chosen by each department, so a transfer can leave a student holding two taught themes that do not appear on their new Paper 1. Nothing about study skills closes that gap; the content has to be taught. One option theme takes roughly six to eight weeks at two sessions a week to go from nothing to examinable, including the diagrams. Audit it immediately rather than at the end of term: ask the new department which themes are examined this cycle, and compare that against what your child was actually taught.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child choose a fieldwork question?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is where an hour buys the most. Choosing a question is a teaching conversation: does it name a geographic concept, is it located in a real place, can the data needed be collected in the time and heat available, and will the results be analysable rather than obvious. A tutor who says a question is unanswerable before a weekend is spent on it has already paid for themselves. What a tutor must not do is hand over a question or write any part of the report. The question has to be the student's choice, defended by them.

faqs.question: Where can a Dubai student realistically collect primary geographical data?
faqs.answer: Human geography is the practical route. Land-use transects work well because Dubai districts change character over a few hundred metres, from villa plots to mid-rise to mall catchment. Urban microclimate work is strong here: the temperature and wind contrast between a Marina street canyon and an open plot in Al Barsha South is large enough for ordinary instruments. Footfall and sphere-of-influence studies produce clean numbers. Physical geography is harder, with the coastline largely engineered and the only real relief at Hatta. Outdoor collection between May and September is limited by heat, so plan it into the cooler months.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Geography at Higher and Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Three things. Higher Level candidates study three option themes rather than two, so Paper 1 is longer and broader. They also take a core extension on global interactions, power, networks, human development and global risk, examined in a separate paper of extended answers. And because those components take weight, the compulsory core units carry proportionally less of a Higher Level grade than a Standard Level one. Both levels write the same 2,500-word fieldwork report. In tutoring terms, Standard Level hours usually go to the core units, while Higher Level hours have to be split between option breadth and extended-answer structure.

faqs.question: What is Paper 3 in IB Geography, and who has to sit it?
faqs.answer: Higher Level candidates only. It is an hour-long paper of extended answers drawn from the Higher Level core extension, which covers global interactions, flows of people and capital, human development and diversity, and global risk and resilience. It is the component students most often arrive at having never written to time, because schools teach the content late and the answer format is unlike anything on the other papers. Each answer needs a defended position in the opening lines, not a survey of the topic. Two or three rehearsed answer plans, drilled until the structure is automatic, is usually the whole fix.

faqs.question: Why does my child know the Geography content but score badly on papers?
faqs.answer: Almost always command terms. The Diploma publishes a list of them and examiners apply it literally: describe wants a pattern, explain wants a mechanism, examine wants an argument with its assumptions exposed, evaluate wants a weighed judgement. A student who answers every question by writing what they know will do respectably on description-led questions and poorly on anything worth more than six marks. It shows up in one marked paper and it is trainable in a handful of sessions, because the fix is a habit rather than knowledge. The second likeliest cause is not quoting the Paper 2 resources precisely.

faqs.question: Can a tutor read my child's fieldwork draft before it is submitted?
faqs.answer: Within limits that are worth knowing precisely. A student is entitled to one round of written feedback on one draft. Comments may name a criterion, point out that an argument is unsupported, or ask why a particular graph was chosen. What nobody may do is supply sentences, restructure paragraphs on the student's behalf, or return a version that only needs accepting. Ask any tutor directly how they handle a draft and treat an answer involving editing as a warning. The report has to be the student's own work, and the consequences of a malpractice finding fall on the student.

faqs.question: How many sessions does the Geography fieldwork report usually need?
faqs.answer: Four to six, if they are placed correctly. One before the question is settled, to test whether it can be answered with reachable data. One on methods and sampling, before a morning of collection is wasted. One on turning raw tables into graphics that earn marks rather than default spreadsheet charts. One on reading the student's own draft against the analysis, conclusion and evaluation criteria. Sometimes one more on the evaluation, which students write generically. Six well-timed hours across DP1 is worth considerably more than twenty hours in the fortnight before the school's internal deadline.

faqs.question: Are the case studies in my child's Geography notes too old to use?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and it is worth auditing. Geography marks currency: a migration example resting on census figures from over a decade ago, or a resource-security case that predates recent water policy, reads as a student quoting old slides. The fix is mechanical. Rebuild the bank as one sheet per theme, with three or four examples each carrying a named place, a year and at least one figure. That form survives exam pressure and it scores. Students usually find they have twelve vague examples and need four sharp ones, which is a shorter job than it sounds.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring work for a subject built on maps and diagrams?
faqs.answer: It works better than paper, which surprises families. Geography is taught through hydrographs, climate graphs, transect data, annotated maps and spreadsheets, and every one of those is easier on a shared screen than passed across a table. A storm hydrograph annotated live, saved and sent, becomes revision material; the same diagram drawn once in a notebook does not. Statistical work on the fieldwork data happens in the spreadsheet the student will actually submit. Sessions are recorded, so a diagram built in October can be rewatched in April, which no in-person lesson offers.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with Dubai Geography students need a UAE permit?
faqs.answer: If they are providing private tuition in the UAE, yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. According to u.ae it is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Ask any tutor whether they hold it, and note that Abu Dhabi school staff face additional restrictions on tutoring their own students.

faqs.question: What happens if no Geography specialist is free in our time slot?
faqs.answer: You get told, rather than matched with somebody approximate. Geography is a smaller Group 3 subject than History or Economics, and Higher Level option-theme coverage is thinner still, so a specific combination at a specific hour is not always available in the UAE time zone. Where that happens the realistic options are a tutor in another time zone whose working day overlaps your evening, a different slot, or a short wait. A Geography-trained generalist who has never taught your option themes is not a substitute, and we would rather say so than fill the hour.

faqs.question: Is Geography an easier Group 3 choice than History for a Dubai student?
faqs.answer: Different, not easier. Geography asks for less sustained essay writing than History and more technical precision: diagrams drawn correctly, data quoted with units, mechanisms explained rather than narrated. It also carries a fieldwork report that has to be designed, collected and analysed, which History does not. Students who write fluently and dislike numbers often find History the softer landing; students who like structure, maps and measurable things usually do better in Geography. Choose on the basis of a term's marked work in both if the school allows it, not on the subject's reputation in the year above.

Lessons run live and one-to-one over video on Gulf Standard Time; we do not visit homes in the UAE.

dubai/ib-dp-geography-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma Geography at Standard and Higher Level, including the Higher Level core extension and the statistical and cartographic techniques the course expects. Each profile names the option themes that tutor has taught. The first lesson is free, and you can change tutor at no charge if the fit is wrong.

intro.heading: Ask what will exist in four weeks that does not exist today
paragraphs: Geography is the Diploma subject where a parent is least able to judge progress from the outside. In mathematics a wrong answer is visibly wrong. In Geography a student can write a fluent, accurate, well-organised page about water scarcity and score 6 out of 10, and the reason will not be apparent to anyone who has not read the markbands. That opacity is why this subject attracts the vaguest tutoring arrangements of any in the Diploma, and why the only sensible thing to ask before paying anybody is what will physically exist in four weeks that does not exist today.

The answer should be concrete. Marked scripts, with the band stated and three specific corrections written on each. A techniques checklist showing which graphs, maps and statistical tests the candidate can now produce without help and which they still cannot. A one-page case-study sheet per unit, built by the student. A short written note each month saying what has moved and, more usefully, what has not. If a provider cannot describe those artefacts in advance, the arrangement is a conversation about Geography rather than a plan to change a grade.

This matters because the three things that hold a Geography candidate back behave differently and need different evidence. Content gaps show up as claims without case-study support and close permanently in two to four hours per unit. Technique problems show up as a correct idea that scored half the marks, and they need repeated marking over a term rather than teaching. Data-handling problems show up only in the questions with a figure or a map attached, and they are the fastest of the three to fix once anyone notices them.

The evidence approach also makes stopping possible, which is the part most tutoring arrangements quietly avoid. If four weeks of marked scripts show the same band and the same three corrections, the diagnosis was wrong. That is useful information, not a failure, and the correct response is to change the plan or end it rather than to renew it for another term. A plan built around artefacts can be audited by a parent who has never read a markband in their life, which is the whole point of building it that way.

One practical warning before any of that. Seven option themes exist in this course and your child's school chooses two or three of them, so a tutor who has taught the other four will handle the compulsory core competently and miss half the examination. That mismatch usually surfaces only when the first past paper is attempted, by which time a term has gone. Email the department for the themes and the order they are taught before you book anybody, and treat the answer as the first piece of evidence in the file.
